name: Nevada Current
title: El Salvador temporary protected status set to end Sept. 9, thousands in NV affected
description: Thousands of people from El Salvador living in Nevada could face deportation if the Trump administration decides not to extend their protected status next week. Temporary protected status (TPS) for El Salvador is scheduled to end on Sept. 9, ending the longest-running TPS designation in U.S. history.  Nevada is home to about 6,000 TPS recipients, […]
text:
Demonstrators chant and hold signs outside U.S. Supreme Court on April 29, 2026 in Washington, DC. The court heard arguments challenging the government's termination of temporary protected status for immigrants. (Photo by Tom Brenner/Getty Images)Thousands of people from El Salvador living in Nevada could face deportation if the Trump administration decides not to extend their protected status next week.
Temporary protected status (TPS) for El Salvador is scheduled to end on Sept. 9, ending the longest-running TPS designation in U.S. history. 
Nevada is home to about 6,000 TPS recipients, the majority of whom are Salvadoran nationals who face the loss of work authorization and deportation protection.
El Salvador was first designated for TPS in 2001, when President George W. Bush extended temporary protected status to Salvadorans living in the U.S. after major earthquakes devastated parts of El Salvador. The designation has since been extended repeatedly over the years.
Salvadoran TPS holders have built careers, purchased homes, and raised children after more than two decades living in the United States. 
Jose, a bartender on the Las Vegas Strip and a member of the Culinary Union, is one of the thousands of Salvadorian nationals living in Nevada under temporary protected status. He now faces uncertainty about his status after living in the U.S. for 25 years. 
“I appreciate the opportunity this country gave me, but now that same opportunity is being taken away,” said Jose, who asked that his real name not be used out of fear of being targeted for detention or deportation. 
If he loses his work permit, Jose fears being left without a job and unable to cover his mortgage, utilities, food and other expenses. His wife works, but they both calculated that her income would not be enough to maintain their current payments, especially as the cost of living rises. 
“The United States has become my country because I’ve lived most of my life here, it’s where I raised my family, and I don’t see a future anywhere  else,” Jose said. 
In August, the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services notified Salvadorans that their temporary protected status would expire Sept. 9. But immigration experts say federal law requires the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to decide whether a country still qualifies for a TPS designation at least 60 days before it expires.
That means for the termination to take effect Sept. 9, the administration would have had to publish a notice in the Federal Register in July, which it did not. 
As of Thursday, DHS had not announced whether the designation will be extended or terminated, leaving many Salvadoran families in Nevada uncertain about what comes next. 
If no determination is made by the statutory deadline, the protections automatically extend for six months under federal law. 
Jose said there is little information about what will happen next for Salvadorians awaiting a determination, which has frustrated him as he tries to navigate his next steps.
“I got a letter from human resources asking for documentation from immigration, but I don’t have anything and I don’t even know what’s going to happen, nobody knows,” Jose said. “All I know is that I’m going to lose my job. I’m going to be unemployed.”
Automatic extensions have come late in the game in the past. In May, the Trump administration did not announce Lebanon’s automatic TPS extension in the Federal Register until two days after it was set to expire. 
However, the Trump administration has ended temporary protected status for more than a dozen countries since President Donald Trump took office in 2025. Temporary protected status was most recently terminated for Haitians, Ethiopians and Syrians in August following a Supreme Court ruling that DHS has broad authority to eliminate TPS.
Culinary Union Secretary-Treasurer Ted Pappageorge called the Trump administration’s move to remove TPS status from Salvadorians “misguided,” adding that it will have deep impacts on Nevada’s economy and members of his union. 
“We have thousands of TPS members that are Culinary union members. Many of them, like our Salvadorian brothers and sisters, have been here for decades and have children, grown kids. They have homes. They pay taxes, and they’re critical to our economy here in Las Vegas,” Pappageorge said, during a press conference Wednesday. 
The press event was held by Nevada’s U.S. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto, who urged the Trump Administration to extend TPS for Salvadorians. 
“The president can do the right thing for our country ahead of this September 9th deadline. He and his administration must extend TPS for Salvadorians,” said Cortez Masto.
“Here in Nevada, we have more than 5,800 TPS holders, most of whom are Salvadorans, and they are critical to our hospitality industry and our construction industry. Salvadorian TPS holders helped build Las Vegas as we know it, and they work in nearly every hotel on the Strip,” Cortez Masto continued. 
Last year, Cortez Masto and 28 other Democratic senators introduced the Safe Environment from Countries Under Repression and Emergency (SECURE) Act, which would provide qualified TPS recipients a path to legal permanent residency.
“I would ask for a year or two years for that extension, so that our TPS recipients can stay here, and we can help them work toward a long-term path to permanent citizenship,” Cortez Masto said.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri school leaders concerned ahead of ‘A’ through ‘F’ report card rollout
description: Missouri educators voiced concerns Thursday that the state is rushing to roll out an “A” through “F” report card system for public schools without fully considering its provisions. In the second of four feedback sessions the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education is holding to meet with stakeholders about the proposal, public school leaders peppere[...]
text:
Missouri Department of Elementary and Secondary Education's Deputy Commissioner of Learning Services Lisa Sireno explains the department's 'A' through 'F' report card framework to the State Board of Education on Aug. 18, 2026. The department is holding feedback sessions to gather educators' input on the plan (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent)Missouri educators voiced concerns Thursday that the state is rushing to roll out an “A” through “F” report card system for public schools without fully considering its provisions.
In the second of four feedback sessions the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education is holding to meet with stakeholders about the proposal, public school leaders peppered state officials with questions about the plan — particularly the prospect of publicly labeling schools as failing based on a system that is still being developed. 
“It is tough to address the (questions) that are asking for justification for what was written in the executive order,” Stuart Smith, the department’s improvement and accountability manager, told the session’s 275 attendees Thursday. “We received that as it was written, and that’s kind of been our operational approach: to address the language as it was written.”
The initiative to assign schools letter grades stems from an executive order Gov. Mike Kehoe issued in January with specific requests regarding the content and presentation of the report cards.
The department is not legally obligated to enact Kehoe’s request, though its staff and the State Board of Education appear poised to follow the executive order completely.
“We’ve got the executive order, and we’re trying to make the best of it that we can,” said Jeremy Ellis, the department’s National Assessment of Educational Progress coordinator.
The department plans to release a draft of the report cards within weeks using data from the 2024-25 school year. This first report will be simplified and lack some elements that will later impact scores, like a metric tracking students’ progress toward proficiency.
Officials told the State Board of Education in August that the draft report was intended to meet Kehoe’s call for a fall 2026 rollout, with financial and time constraints pushing full implementation to sometime next year.
Some of Thursday meeting’s participants worried that districts have not yet seen how they might score even though the grades could soon become public.
Sandy Leech, Hollister R-V School District’s assistant superintendent of teaching and learning, typed into the virtual meeting chat that she understood the department’s “challenge” but was looking for more support between the state and districts.
“Will releasing the A-F draft report card publicly, before running simulations and qualifying data (support students)?” Leech asked. “Or will an unintended consequence be that it pits districts and communities against each other due to inaccurate data and potentially low scores across the state?”
Jocelyn Strand, the department’s incoming improvement and accountability administrator, said she doesn’t “have any really specific thoughts” on circulating the draft to schools without a public release but pointed to the executive order’s call for schools to post their report on their websites “no later than Sept. 30 of each year.”
“We are going to follow the executive order’s requirements related to the release of data and anticipate that the governor’s office and others expect to see data released,” Strand said.
Earlier in the department’s development of the report cards, the state’s 12 largest school districts got a preliminary look at their performance, Ellis said.
“Our biggest concern is that you create this thing and it doesn’t actually categorize the buildings, at least in comparison to each other, correctly,” he said of the initial test. “So we are still very concerned about that. All of these chats are discussions we’ve had over the last six months internally fighting about what we should do and how to do it best.”
The department has made some tweaks to the plan in response to feedback over the past few months. Previously, it had anticipated that the testing window for teachers would be shortened by two weeks but has since backtracked at least for the current school year.
Other details have yet to be finalized, like whether schools with few students or limited grade levels receive a grade. The department is also asking the state board whether demographic information, like socioeconomic status, should be included.
A handful of attendees commented that they were concerned the scores would penalize schools with a large population of low-income students. Joplin Schools Superintendent Kerry Sachetta, pointed to Texas’s report cards, which have a section dedicated to vulnerable student groups, like those enrolled in special education or learning the English language.
“What precludes (the department) from adding the socioeconomic Status of each district on the grade card to provide context and offer a grade for each area of the grade card like Texas does?” she asked.
The State Board of Education briefly discussed the idea in August and appeared opposed to improving the scores of districts who educate a large number of low-income students.
“We should have the same expectation for all children,” said board member Kerry Casey, of Chesterfield.
The board’s vice president Jon Otto, from Kansas City, said he liked the idea of a disclosure giving context to schools’ report cards while not impacting scoring.
The department has two in-person feedback sessions scheduled for Sept. 9 in St. Louis and Sept. 10 in Columbia before presenting the A-F framework to the state board for approval Sept. 15.

text:
Former Gov. Matt Bevin was arrested in Bourbon County on an outstanding warrant on Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo courtesy Louisville Metro Detention Center)Former Gov. Matt Bevin was arrested in Bourbon County Thursday an outstanding warrant for contempt of court, police said. After his arrest by the Bourbon County Sheriff’s Office, he was booked into the Louisville Metro Detention Center on Thursday, where he was also charged with resistance to a court order. 


According to Louisville Public Media, Bevin was arrested on the set of a Christmas movie filming in Paris, where he was an extra.
Jefferson Family Court Judge Angela Johnson had issued the bench warrant earlier this year when Bevin failed to disclose financial documents or show up to hearings in a dispute over child support for one of his adopted children, Jonah Bevin.
Bevin skipped one hearing in the case the judge had asked him to attend, claiming he was tending to damage at his home in Maine from a boulder that crashed into it.
Because of Bevin’s frequent absences, the hearing over support for Jonah Bevin has stretched out over several months. In July, Glenna Bevin and Jonah Bevin testified over why the Bevins left Jonah at an abusive school in Jamaica that was eventually shut down by the state.
Jonah is seeking support and help with his education, including a valid high school diploma. His lawyers also are seeking attorneys’ fees, which they said in a court filing exceed $47,000.
This is a developing story and will be updated.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Union seeks more solitary confinement in NJ prisons as answer to assaults on guards
description: The prison guards' union wants NJ lawmakers to ease restrictions on solitary confinement, an effort to reduce assaults on officers.
text:
A tier of cells in a restricted housing unit wing at Northern State Prison in Newark. (Photo courtesy of the New Jersey Office of the Corrections Ombudsperson)The union that represents New Jersey corrections officers wants lawmakers to expand solitary confinement in state prisons, saying changes are needed to reduce inmates’ assaults on guards.
William Sullivan, who heads the officers’ union, is urging lawmakers to introduce a bill this fall that would ease restrictions mandated in a 2019 law that limits how long prisoners can be in solitary confinement. The union wants prisons to regain the ability to place certain inmates in solitary for disciplinary infractions and isolate others deemed repetitively violent for longer periods of time.
Current law now prohibits solitary confinement altogether for vulnerable people, defined as those who are young or elderly, pregnant or postpartum, LGBTQ, mentally ill, developmentally disabled, significantly visually or hearing impaired, or diagnosed with serious medical conditions. It also restricts it for everyone else to no more than 20 hours a day, 20 consecutive days, or 30 days during a 60-day period.
The proposed changes would ensure both that habitually abusive prisoners get serious sanctions for assaulting or hurling bodily waste at officers (an activity known as “splashing”) and that troublemakers don’t dodge punishment by faking a vulnerability, Sullivan said.
“The vulnerable tag means you can’t discipline the inmates, and it’s very easy to be put in the vulnerable category. All you have to do is say you’re LGBQT and you’re vulnerable. All you have to do is say you have a psych history, and they make you vulnerable. The main thing is changing it so that somebody can’t just self-identify as vulnerable to get out of sanctions for bad behavior,” Sullivan said.
Prison justice advocates fear the changes will balloon the number of people held in solitary confinement in a system that a state watchdog found has routinely flouted the 2019 law, called the Isolated Confinement Restriction Act. Corrections ombudsperson Terry Schuster reported in 2023 that about 750 people were living in isolation on any given day, with some held far longer and for flimsier reasons than the law allows.
The department’s most recent legislatively mandated report suggests the state has made progress in reducing its rate of isolated confinement since Schuster’s investigation. That data shows 87 people were being held in solitary at six of the state’s nine adult prisons on June 30. A total of 690 isolated confinement placements were made in all nine prisons between April 1 and June 30.
The Rev. J. Amos Caley, an organizer with New Jersey Prison Justice Watch and pastor at the Reformed Church of Highland Park, opposes any effort to expand solitary confinement, saying prolonged isolation does significant harm to one’s mental and physical health and does not improve prison safety.
“When you treat people like animals, you can expect that their behavior is going to be in accordance with the desperation and recklessness with which they’ve been treated,” Caley said.
A draft of the proposed legislation obtained by the New Jersey Monitor calls for the 2019 law to be amended to:

Require people who say they’re LGBTQ to be proven so by a medical or mental health examination, or a judicial determination that they’re in imminent danger of being abused or harassed because of their sexual orientation.
Allow officials to put vulnerable people in solitary if staff believes they will seriously harm an officer, other staffers, or themselves, or if the inmates want to be placed there and provide informed, voluntary, written consent.
Lower the minimum age of someone eligible for solitary from 21 to 20.
Create a new definition of “repetitively violent inmate” as someone who’s already served two or more stints in solitary or close custody or who’s believed to pose “substantial risk of serious harm” to themselves or others.
Remove restrictions on how many days repetitively violent inmates can remain in isolated confinement.
Expand how many hours anyone can be held in solitary in state prisons from 20 to 22 hours a day.

The bill draft says its intent is to reduce assaults on correctional officers. It cites data from the Department of Corrections and Sullivan’s union that shows attacks on staff rose from 200 in 2021 to 424 in 2022, with nearly half involving bodily fluids. More than 10% of the union’s 4,500 members were out on leave in 2024 due to assaults, the draft legislation notes.
Chris Greeder, a Department of Corrections spokesman, didn’t respond to a request for comment.
According to state budget documents, assaults on correctional staff soared to 964 in the 2025 fiscal year, as chronic staffing shortages strained prison operations.
Officials projected assaults would fall to about 650 in the 2026 fiscal year, which ended on June 30, as they hired more staff to shrink shortages and beefed up staff protections. That work included installing new food ports designed to foil splashings, creating incentives for good behavior, bolstering efforts to prevent and intercept illicit substances (a “frequent driver of volatile behavior”), and removing more items from restricted housing units that could be weaponized, budget documents show.
The department’s strategy in reducing assaults on staff also included cutting the population in disciplinary housing, according to budget documents, suggesting Sullivan might encounter opposition from the department in his bid to ease restrictions on isolated confinement.
“Most of these assaults are taking place in the wings where there is close custody,” Caley said. “When you’re talking about using isolated confinement to treat a problem that is happening mainly in isolated confinement spaces, you’re talking in circles.”
Schuster thinks lawmakers would do well to wait before considering any revisions to the law.
“The Department has some new initiatives in the works aimed at people who have repeatedly assaulted staff,” Schuster said. “I would want more time to track these trends and to observe the new initiatives to play out to see if the problem with assaults can be resolved without revisions to the law.”
Instead of expanding solitary confinement, Caley said state corrections officials should fix the long-simmering problems that torpedo morale and fuel disruptive behavior in prison, including crumbling building conditions, staffing shortages, and the recurring lockdowns and inadequate access to programming and treatment the shortages cause.
Ending the state’s practice of reincarcerating technical parole violators also would free up officers to focus on the most dangerous people in state custody, Caley added. Those are parolees who skip curfew, miss a check-in with their parole officer, or otherwise break the conditions of parole rather than committing new crimes. Former Gov. Phil Murphy unsuccessfully pushed for that policy change last year, and several legislators reintroduced it just before they went on summer recess.
“Until we fix the culture and the implementation problems of these facilities, then any amount of permission to brutalize people and revoke the restrictions of the Isolated Confinement Restriction Act is not even putting a Band-Aid on a bullet wound — it’s like putting a knife inside of a bullet wound,” Caley said.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah won’t enforce new VPN rules for Pornhub’s parent company as litigation continues
description: Utah won’t enforce a new law requiring pornography websites to verify users’ ages even if they hide their location. But the state says the exception is only temporary and just for Pornhub’s parent company as litigation over Utah’s restrictions on adult content websites unfolds.  Years of legislation and legal fights between Utah and Aylo Freesites, […]
text:
The Capitol in Salt Lake City is pictured on Thursday, Feb. 6, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Utah won’t enforce a new law requiring pornography websites to verify users’ ages even if they hide their location. But the state says the exception is only temporary and just for Pornhub’s parent company as litigation over Utah’s restrictions on adult content websites unfolds. 
Years of legislation and legal fights between Utah and Aylo Freesites, Pornhub’s parent company, led to the platform’s essential exit from the state’s market. However, their dispute isn’t over. The company sued the state over a 2026 law that establishes that Utah rules must be applied for all individuals accessing websites from the state, regardless of whether they use a virtual private network “or other means to disguise or misrepresent the individual’s geographic location.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“That is impermissible extraterritorial legislation: Utah is projecting its policy choices onto conduct occurring entirely outside its borders, in states and countries that have made different legislative judgments,” the complaint filed in April says. 
The state reached an agreement with Aylo Freesites in late August extending the suspension of the Utah Division of Consumer Protection’s enforcement of the law until the division’s rule takes effect, potentially in October, or when a judge issues a final ruling, whichever is sooner, the division said in a statement on Thursday.
“This agreement is strictly limited to AYLO and is contingent upon AYLO maintaining its geofencing restrictions within Utah,” the division said, adding that “nothing in this agreement precludes the Division from taking enforcement action against other age-assurance non-compliant entities.”
Currently, Aylo is able to identify users who appear to be located in Utah by referencing the IP address associated with their connection to block their access to adult content, the company said. 
Aylo Freesites’ attorneys wrote in the agreement filing that they believe the Utah rule “is fundamentally flawed,” and that the deal doesn’t eliminate their request to block the enforcement of the law. 



Let us know what you think...


 


However, “this Period of Continued Forbearance allows Plaintiffs to participate in that rulemaking process without the threat of liability in the interim,” the filing says. 
The company’s complaint describes the law as unconstitutional, since “it constitutes impermissible extraterritorial legislation, it violates the dormant Commerce Clause, and it also violates the Foreign Commerce Clause by interfering with purely international transactions involving foreign entities and foreign nationals.”
If the law were to take effect, Aylo would have to pay fines of up to $2,500 for each violation of the law, as well as other actions in court.
Utah had already established an age-verification mandate in 2023 for adult content websites, prompting Aylo to block its free websites in Utah. But, recently the company made “safe for work,” or non-explicit content, which doesn’t fall under the scope of the state’s age-verification law, available to Utah users. 
Some other Aylo sites distribute paid adult content to Utah users. However, those are permitted since customers link a form of identification when paying for their accounts. 
“There is no feasible way for a private company like Aylo to reliably verify whether any particular individual is using a virtual private network (VPN), proxy server, or other location- masking technology — and therefore no way to determine whether a user who appears to be located outside Utah is, in fact, located inside Utah,” the company’s complaint says. “This is not a temporary technological limitation awaiting a solution; it is an inherent feature of how VPNs and proxy servers work.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: An out-of-state private equity firm shouldn’t have ownership of 13 Michigan dams
description: In June, a Michigan judge overseeing deliberations regarding Consumers Energy’s proposed dam sale recommended that the Michigan Public Service Commission (MPSC) reject the proposed sale of 13 dams to an out-of-state private equity firm. Consumers’ plan would sell the aging and expensive dams to private equity-backed Confluence Hydro for just $1, while requir[...]
text:
Map of the 13 hydroelectric dams proposed for sale by Consumers Energy. (Graphic by Consumers Energy)In June, a Michigan judge overseeing deliberations regarding Consumers Energy’s proposed dam sale recommended that the Michigan Public Service Commission (MPSC) reject the proposed sale of 13 dams to an out-of-state private equity firm. Consumers’ plan would sell the aging and expensive dams to private equity-backed Confluence Hydro for just $1, while requiring ratepayers to purchase the electricity generated by the dams at an inflated price. Meanwhile, Consumers would walk away with hundreds of millions of dollars in profit.
As a Michigander who researches the impacts of private equity ownership across the country, I believe the Public Service Commission should follow this recommendation.
This proposal also comes at a time when Wall Street firms are increasingly targeting regulated utilities and other essential infrastructure. BlackRock recently acquired Minnesota Power’s parent company despite significant community opposition. Blackstone is seeking to acquire TXNM Energy in New Mexico. And shareholders recently approved the sale of utility giant AES to BlackRock. With multiple utility transitions proposed by private equity firms currently, regulators must carefully examine whether the financial incentives driving these investments are compatible with the public interest.
Michigan’s dams unquestionably require investment. But the source of that investment matters. Dams are long-lived public infrastructure that require continuous maintenance, long-term planning, and investments that may not generate immediate financial returns. That makes ownership incentives and transparency especially important. Private equity firms pursue investments with the expectation of generating strong financial returns over relatively short timelines, raising legitimate questions about whether those incentives align with assets that demand decades of stewardship to keep communities safe.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Critics of the Consumers proposal have already raised concerns about whether Confluence Hydro’s ownership model reflects the kind of long-term commitment these dams require. Since 2017, Hull Street Energy, the private equity firm behind Confluence Hydro, has sold 46 of the 47 dams it acquired. That history raises an obvious question: is this the type of ownership model Michigan should rely on for infrastructure that requires sustained investment over generations?
Michigan has already experienced the devastating consequences of deferred maintenance. The failures of the Edenville and Sanford dams in 2020 came after their private owners delayed critical safety upgrades for years. The resulting disaster displaced thousands of residents, caused hundreds of millions of dollars in damage, and left hard-working Michigan taxpayers helping shoulder the cost. We should not ignore those lessons when evaluating who should own and operate our critical infrastructure today.
When we look at private equity’s track record in utilities more broadly, Michiganders have additional reasons for caution. In 2014, the Upper Peninsula Power Company was acquired by a private equity firm. Soon afterward, the utility sought significant rate increases, including another $10 million increase just four years later. Similar concerns are emerging just across the state line. After Blackstone acquired roughly a 20% ownership stake in Indiana utility NIPSCO and secured a seat on its board, customers experienced some of the largest electric rate increases in the state, with bills rising by roughly 20% in recent years.
Michigan’s dams undoubtedly need investment should they continue to operate, but not all investment is the same. Assets that protect communities, generate electricity, and require decades of maintenance should be owned by organizations whose incentives align with long-term stewardship, not financial models built around maximizing investor returns.
The MPSC should ensure these dams remain in the hands of those committed to the long-term public interest of our state.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Wildfire risks are driving up costs for Northwest utilities
description: When power lines are blamed for starting a wildfire, costs to utilities can stretch into the billions and trickle down to consumers.  Earlier this year, PacifiCorp settled a federal lawsuit over its lines allegedly starting six fires in Oregon and California, burning nearly 300,000 acres of public land. Thousands of residents also filed claims against […]
text:
(Stock photo by Thianchai Sitthikongsak via Getty Images)When power lines are blamed for starting a wildfire, costs to utilities can stretch into the billions and trickle down to consumers. 
Earlier this year, PacifiCorp settled a federal lawsuit over its lines allegedly starting six fires in Oregon and California, burning nearly 300,000 acres of public land. Thousands of residents also filed claims against the investor-owned utility, which serves 2 million customers in the West.
The company has agreed to pay $2.2 billion to settle roughly 90% of all claims, and it’s preparing to settle more. 
PacificCorp’s woes come seven years after the country’s largest utility company, California-based Pacific Gas & Electric, filed for bankruptcy. This came as the utility faced tens of billions of dollars in potential liability related to deadly fires in 2017 and 2018 that destroyed tens of thousands of structures. 
Anxious to avoid a similar fate, utilities in the Pacific Northwest are spending millions of dollars each year on wildfire mitigation projects. With around 20,000 miles of transmission lines across the region, fire-proofing the grid is a major engineering problem that’s not cheap or easy to solve. 
“At some point, the system will break,” said Jake Gentle, a research manager at the Idaho National Laboratory who tests wildfire technology for grid infrastructure. “And unfortunately, the corporations are the ones that have to pay, which then bill the customers.”
Consumer advocates worry that unchecked wildfire spending will drive up electricity rates. The state’s Utilities and Transportation Commission will soon begin reviewing utilities’ wildfire projects, but there’s concern that it isn’t well equipped to do so. Meanwhile, one state lawmaker is looking at how to safeguard both utilities and residents from the costs of wildfire damages.  
“We’re putting a lot of our wildfire mitigation efforts in Washington state on the backs of utility customers,” said Emily Moore, senior director of climate and energy at Sightline, a sustainability think tank. 
“I think there’s a risk that they are overspending,” Moore said, noting that investor-owned utilities earn a profit after investing in grid infrastructure. 
Utility spending and rate hikes
Washington is unique in that most of its power is supplied by not-for-profit publicly owned utilities and cooperatives, with rates set by city councils or member boards.
The three investor-owned utilities operating in the state — Puget Sound Energy, Avista and Pacific Power, a division of PacifiCorp — serve roughly 1.5 million electricity customers.
When these utilities spend on capital costs to upgrade the grid, including wildfire mitigation measures, they can point to that spending to justify higher electricity rates and earn a return on their investment. The state’s Utilities and Transportation Commission regulates and approves rate increases. The utilities’ profits depend on these hikes. 
Puget Sound Energy, the largest of the three, has spent more than $200 million on wildfire mitigation efforts since 2024, according to a company spokesperson. That funding covers equipment upgrades, smoke-detecting cameras, vegetation management and more.
For wildfire mitigation projects, the utility is spending 10 times more on capital than on operating costs, according to company documents submitted to the commission. 
When utilities spend more on capital projects, it’s “a challenge for affordability, obviously,” Moore said. Higher electricity rates also disincentivize people to switch from natural gas or other fossil fuels to clean energy, she added. 
To ensure cost-effective wildfire spending and avoid excessive rate increases, regulators should scrutinize wildfire mitigation plans, Moore said. But she fears that regulators don’t have enough resources to do so adequately. 
Puget Sound Energy raised its rates by almost 19% for residential customers in January and it’s preparing to increase them again, according to Gerald Tracy, a Puget Sound Energy spokesperson. The utility is spending heavily to meet rising electricity demand and to comply with Washington’s clean energy requirements.
Its new proposal, to be submitted this month, would increase rates over three years with a steep 16.75% hike starting in January 2027, pending the commission’s approval.
“Capitalizing costs enables us to spread the rate impact over several years instead of hitting customers all at once,” Tracy said. 
What if they’re not spending enough?
Powering homes across Washington, Oregon, Idaho and Alaska are 19,000 miles of Avista’s distribution lines. Of those, 36% are in areas with a high risk of wildfire, according to the company’s wildfire mitigation plan. 
“Our power lines go to where our customers are,” said Josh DiLuciano, vice president of energy delivery at Avista. “The nature of our geography is more arid, more dry, more fire-prone.”
The Washington State Department of Natural Resources determined that, in 2019, Avista’s infrastructure sparked the Babb Road Fire in the town of Malden, population less than 250, after a branch struck a power line.
Though the company maintains it was not negligent, total liability costs for the Malden fire were $27 million, according to an Avista filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. Avista reported the fire costs had “no impact” on the utility’s net income. It’s possible insurance covered the expense.
Avista is now spending around $65 million a year on wildfire projects, which is less than 10% of its overall investments, DiLuciano said. 
Those projects include burying wires underground, cutting back vegetation, and wrapping poles in fire-resistant material. DiLuciano added that information recorded by the utility’s wildfire cameras is shared with local first responders. 
Gentle, the research manager at the Idaho National Laboratory, thinks utilities are having to “do more with less” as they prepare grids for worsening wildfire conditions. 
Utilities can monitor equipment and model risk, Gentle said, but they cannot predict with certainty which pole or power line will fail. Every risk-reducing option comes with a cost, and in recent years, it’s become more expensive. 
Gentle and his colleagues at the federal research lab have been testing grid technologies under simulated wildfire conditions. The idea is to help utilities decide which to invest in. 
“We got to spend a little bit of money to harden our electric grid so that these massive catastrophic events don’t continue to make the electric bill even higher,” Gentle said.
“Anybody who wants to accuse any type of utility of spending too much money,” Gentle added, “I don’t think they’re spending enough.” 
State regulators
Washington is in the early phase of trying to limit rate hikes caused by a utility’s spending on wildfire projects. A law that took effect in 2025 requires utilities to submit plans that outline such projects to the Utilities and Transportation Commission.
Though the commission received plans from the three investor-owned utilities in 2024, it did not have the authority to approve or reject them. The commission’s first review will occur next year. Three to seven commission employees will review the plans, according to a spokesperson. 
Utilities are required to submit a plan at least once every three years, but there is no standard format. In the 2024 plans, Puget Sound Energy and Avista did not disclose how much they spent on wildfire mitigation projects, but Pacific Power forecasted investing over $10 million.
At the state Legislature, Rep. Kristine Reeves, D-Federal Way, proposed a bill this year that would have created a wildfire liability fund for utilities to tap into to settle wildfire claims. It would have also created a council to oversee the fund. 
“Think of it as like a state version of wildfire insurance,” said Reeves. Utilities could “default to the state” for costs beyond what their insurance covers. She’s worried what will happen if the damage to homes from a fire sparked by power lines is more extreme than what utilities can pay.
The bill didn’t pass because of concerns it would raise utility rates. Reeves plans to bring back a similar bill next year. This time, she’s looking at requiring utilities to carry a certain level of liability insurance. 
“They need to have a level of insurance that’s going to help their community recover,” Reeves said.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Boston is arguing about crime statistics. The real test is the walk home.
description: The test is simple: Are people safe, and do they feel safe, walking through downtown’s streets, stations, and parks? Judge our progress by that standard.
text:
IN THE SPAN of a few weeks this summer, violence unfolded across some of Boston’s busiest public spaces. On a Monday night, three people were shot steps from Boston Common. On a Wednesday, a man was fatally beaten at the edge of the Common as the sun rose. Days later, a Friday afternoon altercation ended in a stabbing on the Common. A few weeks later, a man was fatally stabbed inside South Station during the evening rush hour. The next morning, a domestic violence stabbing occurred near North Station.  
The circumstances were different, and not every incident was random. That distinction matters. But so does what thousands of people encountered: blood, police tape, emergency vehicles, and violence in places they use every day. 
Yet Boston’s public safety debate has increasingly become an argument about statistics. 
One side points out, correctly, that homicides and some serious crimes are down citywide. Others point to the recent violence and say the numbers obscure what is happening on the ground. Both risk talking past the people who live, work, study, visit, and move through the neighborhood. 
The data matters. Through the end of July, Boston had recorded fewer homicides than at the same point last year. But in the downtown core, per Analyze Boston data, assaults rose from 124 to 157, or nearly 27 percent, over the same period. Residents do not experience a citywide annual average. They experience a particular block, subway entrance, park path, or walk after dark. Those experiences accumulate. 
We should not have to choose between acknowledging Boston’s real progress and demanding more when conditions deteriorate. Both can be true. An “isolated incident” is not the same as an inconsequential one. And a city can be comparatively safe while still having places and moments that demand urgent attention. 
That is the gap Boston should focus on: the distance between what aggregate data tells us and what people are experiencing on the ground. A parent dropping off a child, a nurse leaving a late shift, a hospitality worker commuting before dawn, a resident walking her dog after dark, or a student crossing the Common does not experience public safety as a citywide trend line. 
When statistics are cited to counter those experiences, trust erodes. And trust is itself a public safety asset. People who trust institutions report problems, cooperate with police, use public spaces, and remain invested in their neighborhoods. 
The encouraging part is that we know how to meet this moment. In 2023 and 2024, downtown Boston faced many of the same concerns. In early 2025, government, law enforcement, businesses, institutional partners, nonprofits, service providers, and residents coordinated around specific hotspots and interventions. Conditions improved. That is not nostalgia. It is proof of concept. 
For much of early summer, downtown also showed what is possible. Boston welcomed enormous crowds for major events while our parks, streets, and commercial corridors felt energetic, safe, and well-managed. As residents, we should not accept a lower standard once the banners come down. 
The answer is not in slogans or spreadsheets. It is doing two things at once: visible police presence and consistent enforcement of laws and ordinances, alongside greater outreach capacity and behavioral health and addiction services. Treating compassion and safety as competing values is how we fail at both. 
Residents cannot legislate or enforce laws. But we can organize, identify problems, offer solutions, and insist on urgency and accountability. That is the compact: residents do our part, and we expect our partners in government to do theirs. 
In August, I helped convene 77 people representing 48 organizations and agencies for a downtown public safety working session. We reviewed downtown and Boston Common block by block. The point was not to organize another meeting. It was to turn shared concern and frustration into coordinated action. 
Some of that action is already visible: increased police presence in key locations, renewed attention to problem areas, private-sector investments, and changes to public spaces. But public safety is not a destination; it must be earned every day. 
Boston Common is our nation’s oldest public park. Downtown Boston is a regional gateway, a neighborhood, and an economic and transit hub. Its future depends not on winning an argument over whether crime is “up” or “down,” or whether incidents are “isolated” or “unrelated,” but on whether people can move through these places safely and with confidence. 
Residents have high expectations for safety and quality of life. We all should. 
The test is simple: Are people safe, and do they feel safe, walking through downtown’s streets, stations, and parks? Judge our progress by that standard. 
Rishi Shukla is co-founder of the Downtown Boston Neighborhood Association, co-chair of the One Downtown public safety task force, and a downtown Boston resident.

name: WyoFile
title: Bison become cinematographers in new documentary
description:
Film shown at Smithsonian offers viewers a first-of-its kind look into the lives of bison.
The post Bison become cinematographers in new documentary appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
A bison’s shaggy beard hangs in the top of the frame as a calf sleeps in the sun. The camera lilts slightly from one side to another as the scraggly fur moves up and down, up and down, attached to a mouth that’s chewing lunch perhaps, or dinner, or a snack. Another shot shows bison standing belly deep in a river. In another they’re racing through a snow-covered field. 
The vantage point for all of these isn’t some far away hillside, it’s right there, among the largest land mammals in North America. 
A new film from the Wyoming Migration Initiative feels intimate and rare because the footage is closer to than any human dare to be from a 2,000-pound animal. The cinematographers? A handful of bison who wore cameras around their necks for nearly a year, offering science and the public a first-of-its-kind look into their lives.
“We got to see something no one has ever seen. You can get pretty close to bison when you film them by your vehicle, but it’s not like you can go up and follow a bison all day and live in their world,” said Pat Rodgers, the film’s producer and co-director. “It was cool to get into their world in an intimate way. To get to see what bison see.”
A cow bison returns to the herd wearing a GPS tracking collar with a built-in HD camera affixed by National Park service biologists. (Screenshot from video by Patrick Rodgers, Wyoming Migration Initiative at the University of Wyoming)
And soon anyone visiting Washington D.C. will be able to watch “What Bison See: Restoring Yellowstone’s Lost Migrations” in the Smithsonian’s Museum of Natural History, the country’s premier nature and science museum. The film shows how bison learned to migrate after near extermination and how the landscape depends on these movements. It will play in the museum for three years as part of its Bison: Standing Strong exhibit as well as in two Yellowstone National Park visitors centers. 
A 2,000-pound comeback
By now, almost everyone knows the story of the buffalo, how 200 years ago 30 million to 60 million of them roamed great swaths of North America; how European settlers killed them by the thousands and then millions; and how only a few hundred remained in isolated pockets. 
What fewer people know is how they returned in places like Yellowstone National Park, where at one point only 23 buffalo clung to life. Year by year, those buffalo reproduced, then their offspring reproduced, and then their offspring reproduced. They largely stuck to the Lamar Valley portion of Yellowstone until the brutal winter of 1942, when about 130 of them mobilized and headed northwest to less snowy pastures. Each decade after, Yellowstone buffalo continued to expand their movements, walking through valleys, trudging through snow and fording rivers following the green wave of nutrition. 
Bison graze in the upper Lamar Valley near Soda Butte Creek. (Screenshot from video by Patrick Rodgers, Wyoming Migration Initiative at the University of Wyoming)
Fast forward to today, and Yellowstone’s more than 5,000 bison make a dizzying array of migrations through the park, some up to 70 miles long. Yet researchers still didn’t know how bison knew to make the various migrations, to find better food or escape deep snow. 
So University of Wyoming researcher and the film’s co-director Janey Fugate combed through historical records looking for any mention of bison that would indicate a possible migration. Her work built on decades of data compiled by the park’s first female biologist, Mary Meagher. Fugate realized that bison repeated, over and over, the same approach they took in the 1942 winter. They tended to stay in an area until their numbers were large enough and the snow piled deep enough that it pushed them to search for food elsewhere.
Then they established that path as an annual migration option for when conditions merited movement, passing that knowledge to the next generation.
“Bison are very dynamic in their groups and spend lots of time with each other in the park as their individual knowledge gets passed rapidly back and forth,” said Chris Geremia, a biologist and Yellowstone National Park’s bison manager. 
In their wake, they left “interstates,” he added, pathways sometimes 20-animals-wide and visible from space. 
Biologists with the National Park Service bison team outfit a female bison with a GPS tracking collar. The built in HD camera allowed the research and film production teams to peer into the bison’s world from a unique perspective. (Screenshot from video by Patrick Rodgers, Wyoming Migration Initiative at the University of Wyoming)
But their impact on the landscape wasn’t just in highways. Years ago, Geremia noticed a kind of perpetual spring in areas where bison grazed. The grass kept growing back over and over late into the season. So he and University of Wyoming researcher Jared Merkel, along with Washington and Lee University researcher Bill Hamilton, studied the soil and grass in areas heavily grazed by bison, and discovered that bison feces acted as a natural fertilizer, stabilizing the soil’s carbon and speeding up its nitrogen cycling. 
The buffalo, Geremia realized, were farming portions of Yellowstone, creating more nutritious grass, not just for themselves, but all the other herbivores in the system. And because buffalo moved around so frequently, those farming techniques spread far and wide.
Neither the film nor the bison story stops there, though. 
Room to roam
Plenty of habitat still exists in Yellowstone for more migrations, Geremia said. But states like Montana, where bison migrate out of the park, have minimal tolerance for the large-bodied species with little respect for fences. Bison can also carry brucellosis, a disease that causes cattle to abort their fetuses. Brucellosis rates in wild Yellowstone-region bison run around 60%, but there’s never been a confirmed case of wild bison transmitting the disease to cattle.
“Bison tend to travel together in large groups,” Geremia said. “If you map the best bison habitat out there it will overlap exactly with private lands outside our protected areas.”
And Montana doesn’t want them. The state went so far as to sue Yellowstone, demanding the Park Service cut bison numbers and prevent the creatures from leaving the park. 
Meanwhile, many tribes do want Yellowstone’s bison. The Wind River Reservation, for example, has welcomed quarantined Yellowstone buffalo with open arms. 
A bull bison bellows and chases off challengers during the summer rut as seen from the camera worn by a nearby bison. (Screenshot from video by the National Park Service and the Wyoming Migration Initiative at the University of Wyoming)
There, the buffalo are still raised more like livestock than wildlife, said Jason Baldes, Wind River Tribal Buffalo coordinator. But he has hope that one day the creatures will be allowed larger spaces to migrate. 
“In order to meaningfully restore this keystone species we have to think bigger,” Baldes said. “And that means that they need to be able to move. They need to be able to cover ground.”
It will require compromise and understanding from both sides, he said, those who want to see buffalo fully restored and those who fear the consequences of an animal that size migrating once again in large numbers. 
That’s where the film comes in, Geremia said. The hope is if people can see how bison live, how they raise their calves, the conditions they endure to move to greener pastures and the way they farm their landscape, then maybe minds and hearts can begin to change. 
If nothing else, viewed on the big screen, the film gives an intimate look into an animal that is otherwise best viewed from a distance.

title: 80 trail miles, 700 downed trees: Wyoming Forest Corps brings muscle to maintenance backlog
description:
Crew spawned from 2025 effort to bolster understaffed Forest Service districts after DOGE cuts is still going strong, clearing the way for summer recreation.
The post 80 trail miles, 700 downed trees: Wyoming Forest Corps brings muscle to maintenance backlog appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
When trails snaking through Wyoming’s 9 million acres of national forests go unmaintained or unused, nature can begin to reclaim them with remarkable speed. 
Look no further than sections of the Wyoming National Recreation Trail in the Bridger-Teton National Forest’s Big Piney District, where the path had become barely discernable under a mat of scrubby grasses. 
“It’s just been overgrown for years,” said former U.S. Forest Service employee Monica Elliott.
It was there that Wyoming’s newest trails crew, the Forest Corps — which Elliott manages — landed in July for a work hitch to assist the district recreation staff. After eight days of digging, clearing and delineating, voilá. The trail boasted the shiny new-dirt look of a just-constructed path. 
It was among the 2026 projects undertaken by the Forest Corps. The nonprofit Friends of the Bridger-Teton created the Forest Corps in 2025 after seeing U.S. Forest Service district offices hollowed out by DOGE cuts and facing mounting maintenance backlogs. 
The Corps was designed explicitly to help the agency on summer-season field projects in the Bridger-Teton National Forest, one of eight national forests within Wyoming’s borders. Friends of the Bridger-Teton hired former U.S. Forest Service staff, including Elliott, who had lost her job in the cuts, for the Corps. 
In its inaugural season, the team communicated with each of the Bridger-Teton forest’s six districts to identify a high-impact project to assist on. The Corps painted picnic tables, installed a puncheon trail over marshy terrain and cleared trails in wildfire burn areas. 
Once the demand for such an auxiliary crew became clear to the Friends nonprofit, which works to assist its namesake national forest in managing visitor impacts, the organization decided to make the initiative permanent. 
Even with the Forest Service rehiring many of its seasonal recreation workers in 2026, Elliott said, “there is so much need” when it comes to maintaining the inventory of trails and infrastructure on the 3.4-million-acre Bridger-Teton National Forest. 
This summer, the crew has worked six hitches lasting eight days and a couple lasting four. Along with projects like the Big Piney region trail, Elliott and the four-person team have cleared 700 downed trees from 80 miles of trail across the forest, including the Pack Creek Fire burn area.
The season’s not over yet; the Forest Corps still has two hitches to go.

title: Some places in Wyoming are too important to gamble with
description:
The Seminoe Pumped Storage Project is a bad project in a bad location and a bad deal for our state, writes guest columnist Bralli Clifford.
The post Some places in Wyoming are too important to gamble with appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The first hike my husband and I took after he nearly lost his life was in the Bennett Mountains.

Opinion

We chose that place intentionally. From the ridges, you can look out over our ranch. In many ways, it is our backyard. This country has shaped our lives, and over the years we have built countless memories among its mountains, wildlife and open spaces.
As on many past hikes, we were fortunate to see Ferris-Seminoe bighorn sheep that day. Their presence was a reminder that some things endure, even after life has been turned upside down.
After the uncertainty, fear and emotional toll of a sudden, life-threatening illness and a prolonged hospital stay, returning to this landscape was healing. Being surrounded by familiar country, by the wildlife that has always shared this habitat with us and by memories of healthier days gave us the opportunity to reset, reflect and find hope again.
To many, the Bennett and Ferris mountains may appear to be little more than rugged hills above Seminoe Reservoir. But to those of us who know it, this place is so much more.
It is home to the Ferris-Seminoe bighorn sheep herd, one of Wyoming’s great wildlife success stories and the state’s healthiest bighorn herd. For those of us who care about wild sheep, this herd is irreplaceable. It is the only viable source population for future bighorn sheep restoration across Wyoming, which means what happens here matters far beyond the Bennett and Ferris mountains.
This is not just a local herd. It is the foundation for restoring wild sheep in other places across our state.
That is why the proposed Seminoe Pumped Storage Project is so troubling.
Put simply, this is a bad project, in a bad place, and a bad deal for Wyoming.
The project would put the Miracle Mile, Seminoe State Park, local recreation, North Platte communities and the Ferris-Seminoe bighorn sheep herd at risk. For me, the clearest warning sign is what it could do to this herd.
The Ferris-Seminoe bighorn sheep herd pictured in December 2025. (Carl Myers)
The project would be built directly in crucial winter range and lambing habitat, with years of construction disturbance. For bighorn sheep, those are not minor impacts. Stress, displacement, lambing disruption, disease risk and lost access to seasonal habitat can have consequences that last long after construction equipment leaves.
Recent reporting raised another basic concern: water. Seminoe Reservoir was reported at roughly 30% capacity in early August, raising serious questions about whether this pumped storage project would have enough water to operate as designed without adding risk to the Miracle Mile trout fishery and downstream users. In a state where water defines what is possible, approving a massive water-dependent project on uncertain assumptions should give every decision-maker pause.
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s final environmental impact statement acknowledges that pumped storage projects are net energy consumers. In plain English, this project would use more energy pumping water uphill than it generates when water flows back down. Wyoming would carry the impacts to fish, wildlife, water, recreation and local communities while the benefits flow into broader electricity markets.
Even worse, this project appears to depend on federal tax subsidies from the Inflation Reduction Act and a five-to-seven-year waiver of seasonal wildlife protections in the Bureau of Land Management’s Rawlins Resource Management Plan to be financially feasible. Those protections exist for a reason. They are meant to safeguard bighorn sheep winter range, lambing habitat, sage-grouse habitat, raptor nesting areas and other wildlife values that matter to Wyoming.
If a venture only works by waiving protections for Wyoming’s most important bighorn sheep herd, the problem is the project, not the protections.
Wyoming supports responsible energy development. But responsible energy development should be sited well, protect fish and wildlife, respect local communities and deliver real benefits here at home. This project fails that test.
Some places cannot be replaced once they are changed. The Bennett and Ferris mountains and Seminoe Reservoir are among those places.
I’m grateful Sen. John Barrasso has already raised Wyoming’s concerns about the project’s wildlife impacts, including bighorn sheep, directly with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. That kind of leadership matters, and I hope Wyoming’s full congressional delegation will continue pressing federal agencies to take the state’s concerns seriously before this project moves any further.
Please join me and hundreds of hardworking Wyomingites in respectfully asking Wyoming’s congressional delegation to stand with Wyoming’s hunters, anglers, local communities and wildlife by opposing the Seminoe Pumped Storage Project.
You can contact the delegation here.

title: Immigrant advocates highlight Tennessee role in Trump administration’s mass deportation plans
description: During the early hours of Sunday morning, legal advocates with the Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition awakened to buzzing cellphones. More than 120 men and women had been rounded up by immigration agents inside the Memphis nightclub, El Corralón. Their families and friends needed help. “Parents didn’t come home. Roommates and friends stopped answ[...]
text:
Members of the Tennessee National Guard on Nov. 21, 2025, patrol Memphis as part of the Memphis Safe Task Force. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)During the early hours of Sunday morning, legal advocates with the Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition awakened to buzzing cellphones.
More than 120 men and women had been rounded up by immigration agents inside the Memphis nightclub, El Corralón. Their families and friends needed help.
“Parents didn’t come home. Roommates and friends stopped answering the phone. Workers and business owners didn’t show up on Monday morning and cars were left in the parking lot of the nightclub,” said Lisa Sherman Luna, the coalition’s executive director. 
The raid, executed through at least two search warrants obtained by the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation in Shelby County Criminal Court, and reviewed by the Tennessee Lookout, was among the largest immigrant roundups in recent Tennessee history. 
The incident occurred amid an escalation in immigrant arrests nationwide that began at the start of summer, following a temporary decline in activity after the January shooting deaths by ICE agents of two Minneapolis residents.
Homeland Security confirms 121 immigrant arrests in Memphis nightclub raid

Trump administration officials have touted the immigration crackdowns, in Memphis and elsewhere, as both part of a broader public safety push and a fulfillment of the president’s campaign promises to stem illegal immigration. 
“Thanks to President Trump’s leadership, crime in the city of Memphis has plummeted,” a statement from Department of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said this week. 
“A big part of that success comes from arresting and deporting illegal aliens in the city,” the statement said.
On Thursday, Sherman Luna joined national immigration advocates during a press conference to discuss the Memphis raid and other recent events in Tennessee that, they said, highlight the state’s increasingly pivotal role in the Trump administration immigration enforcement and deportation agenda.
The Memphis nightclub raid is among a recent string of events in Tennessee tied to the Trump administration’s immigration policies.
In May and June, four Black men were fatally shot in separate incidents by members of the Memphis Safe Task Force, a concentrated crime fighting effort that has brought multiple federal and state agencies, and the Tennessee National Guard, to Memphis. The task force includes Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Homeland Security Investigations, which both enforce immigration law. A Homeland Security Investigations officer fired her weapon during one of the four fatal encounters, according to the TBI.  No charges have been brought against officers in any of the fatal shootings.
Late last month, the Lookout first reported the federal government’s $63 million contract with the Alaska-based Koniag corporation to establish a 24-7 ICE call center in Tennessee to more closely coordinate with local law enforcement across the country to locate and detain immigrants, including children. 
ICE changes location of Tennessee call center site from Adams to Nashville

(Contract documents initially placed the ICE coordination center in Adams, Tenn. before being updated to reflect Nashville is its planned location). A spokesperson for Koniag this week did not respond to a request for more information. A spokesperson for ICE declined to discuss details of the planned coordination center.
The federal activities, paired with a slew of state-level legislation introducing immigration status verification into routine interactions with state and local government, “are turning Tennessee into a national hub for the mass deportation machine,” Sherman Luna said. 
Hadi Sedigh, senior strategist with the National Immigration Law Center called Tennessee a “testing ground” for the Trump administration as it puts into place similar task force collaborations between federal and local law enforcement elsewhere. Sedigh also highlighted a key priority of the Trump administration to expand so-called 287(g) agreements that delegate immigration arrest powers to local police and sheriffs. 
The administration’s goal has been codified into law in Tennessee, with legislation enacted this year requiring all sheriffs and police departments to enter the agreements by 2027. Tennessee was among the first states to implement the requirement as part of a package of legislation targeting immigrants that grew out of meetings between Tennessee House Speaker Cameron Sexton and White House advisor Stephen Miller. 
“The mechanisms that helped make the midnight raid in Memphis possible, namely the 287(g) agreements and the joint federal task force model are, in effect, rapidly increasing in a number of jurisdictions throughout the country,” he said.

title: Jones outraises Tuberville in August; Tuberville retains large funding edge
description: Democrats and Republicans running for Alabama statewide offices largely kept pace with each other in August, the last month before the kickoff of the fall campaign season. According to campaign finance reports filed this week, Democratic and Republican candidates for governor, lieutenant governor secretary of state and commissioner of agriculture and industr[...]
text:
Former U.S. Sen. Doug Jones (left), the Democratic nominee for Alabama governor, outraised Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville in the month of August, the last before the fall campaign takes off. (Photos by Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Democrats and Republicans running for Alabama statewide offices largely kept pace with each other in August, the last month before the kickoff of the fall campaign season.
According to campaign finance reports filed this week, Democratic and Republican candidates for governor, lieutenant governor secretary of state and commissioner of agriculture and industries are mostly evenly matched with the attorney general race being the only outlier.
Governor
Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones outraised Republican nominee Sen. Tommy Tuberville in August, according to campaign finance reports. Jones raised $1.1 million while Tuberville raised $848,500 last month.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Jones also outraised Tuberville in July, receiving $622,000 in donations in July to Tuberville’s $290,000. However, Tuberville retains a substantial fundraising edge, finishing the month with $9.5 million on hand to Jones’ $2.5 million. Tuberville also spent more than Jones in August spending $573,200 while Jones spent $252,900.
Messages seeking comment were left with Tuberville and Jones Thursday.
Both candidates received major campaign contributions in August with Tuberville receiving a total of $315,000 and Jones receiving $20,000.
Tuberville did not receive any money from political action committees (PAC) last month but did receive $25,000 from Applied Digital Corporation, a Dallas-based data center development company, and a $100,000 donation from VGW Luckyland, a sweepstakes company from Colorado. Jones received $21,200 in PAC donations including $1,000 from the Blount County Democratic Club and $5,000 from the United Steel Workers.
Attorney General
Republican nominee Katherine Robertson has consistently outperformed her Democratic opponent Jeff McLaughlin in campaign donations, raising $180,300 last month.
A message seeking comment was left with Robertson Thursday. 
McLaughlin, who has been running a low-profile campaign, saw a significant increase in his campaign donations going from $100 raised in July to nearly $14,000 in August. A message seeking comment was left with McLaughlin Thursday.
Robertson received a $25,000 major campaign contribution in August and a total of $136,000 in PAC money including $10,000 from the Alabama Power Co. Employees State PAC; $50,000 from the Alabama Realtors PAC and $2,500 from the Boeing Company PAC. McLaughlin has not received any PAC contributions; he has traditionally refused to accept campaign contributions. 
McLaughlin did not spend any money last month. Robertson spent $15,800 last month leaving her with $197,000 on hand.
Lieutenant Governor
Republican nominee John Wahl raised $140,200 last month while Democratic nominee Phillip Ensler raised $41,500. Wahl also maintains the lead with cash on hand with $214,200 to Ensler’s $96,000.
Messages seeking comment were left with Wahl and Ensler Thursday.
In August, both candidates received PAC money. Wahl received $47,700 from PACs including $2,500 from the Alabama Federation of Republican Women PAC Account; $25,000 from Progress PAC and $10,000 from the ABC Merit PAC.
Ensler received less in PAC donations, including $1,000 from the Alabama AFL-CIO PAC; $1,000 from the Alabama CPA PAC and $2,750 from the Persistence PAC.
Last week, Ensler criticized Wahl’s campaign for receiving PAC donations saying his July fundraising “made some special interests nervous” in a fundraising email.
In July, Ensler raised $27,800 to Wahl’s $52,100, with $25,000 of Wahl’s money coming from a major campaign contribution.
Wahl also spent more than Ensler last month. Campaign finances show he spent $70,400 while Ensler spent $43,600.
Commissioner of Agriculture and Industries
Ron Sparks, the Democratic nominee for commissioner of Agriculture and Industries, out-raised his Republican opponent Corey Hill.
According to campaign finance records, Sparks, a former Democratic gubernatorial nominee who served as agriculture commissioner from 2003 to 2011, raised $29,500 to Hill’s $23,250 in August.
While Hill outpaced Sparks in fundraising in July raising $11,700 to Sparks’ $9,000, both candidates raised over $11,000 in June.
Sparks said in an interview Thursday evening the money he raised came from working hard to spread his campaign message.
“It just goes to show that the the people of Alabama have an interest in this race, and and I think they look at the job that we did, and we’re working hard and trying to raise as much as we can to get our message out,” Sparks said.
A message seeking comment was left with Hill Thursday.
Hill received $10,900 in PAC donations last month including $2,000 from the Alabama Beef PAC and $2,500 from the Alabama Federation of Republican Women PAC. Sparks received $15,000 in PAC contributions, including $10,000 from the Alabama AFL-CIO PAC and $5,000 from the IBEW PAC Voluntary Fund.
Hill spent significantly less money than Sparks did last month, with only $8,100 compared to Sparks’ $33,500.
Secretary of State
Democratic Secretary of State nominee Wayne Rogers also outraised his opponent Caroleen Dobson last month with $6,200 to Dobson’s $5,600. However, Dobson maintains a large cash on hand edge, with over $470,000 to Rogers’ $18,200. Dobson also spent more than Rogers spending $47,100 while Rogers spent $1,300. 
A message was left with Dobson Thursday afternoon. Rogers said in an interview Thursday that he was “pleased” with the money he raised.
“We have not done a whole lot of fundraisers or anything lately. Just have a lot of folks that are really good people that want to see us do well, and and I appreciate all the help that we got (last) month,” Rogers said.
Both candidates got donations from PACs.  Dobson received $3,500 in PAC contributions including $1,000 from the Alabama CPA PAC and $2,500 from the Alabama Credit Union Legislative Action Council while Rogers received $2,7500 from the Persistence PAC.

title: Republican Victor Marx faces fine over ‘unprecedented’ campaign finance violations
description: Victor Marx, the Republican nominee for Colorado governor, is starting to feel the heat from state elections officials over a litany of alleged violations of campaign finance laws. Regulators in the Elections Division of the Colorado secretary of state’s office are seeking a $51,427 fine against Marx’s campaign for accepting contributions over the legal limi[...]
text:
Victor Marx, the Republican nominee for Colorado governor, speaks at the 2026 summer conference of the Colorado Water Congress in Steamboat Springs on Aug. 19, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Victor Marx, the Republican nominee for Colorado governor, is starting to feel the heat from state elections officials over a litany of alleged violations of campaign finance laws.
Regulators in the Elections Division of the Colorado secretary of state’s office are seeking a $51,427 fine against Marx’s campaign for accepting contributions over the legal limit. A hearing in the case is scheduled for Sept. 10 — and it’s only the first of several potential proceedings against the first-time candidate, which also include complaints alleging Marx is illegally collecting unlimited campaign contributions through his online merchandise store.
“Respondents’ noncompliance with applicable contribution limits was unprecedented,” the Elections Division’s wrote in an Aug. 31 filing in the case. “Respondents accepted and had the benefit of the prohibited contributions throughout Respondent Marx’s gubernatorial campaign and a competitive Republican primary election.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Colorado’s campaign finance laws limit individual donors to a maximum of $1,450 in contributions to a candidate for governor. The Elections Division investigated complaints filed against Marx in May and June by Darcy Schoening, a former state GOP official, who pointed to disclosure reports that showed contributions received in excess of the $1,450 limit.
The division’s filing lists a total of $83,560 in excess contributions from over 100 individual donors since Marx launched his campaign last year, with overages ranging from 27 cents to multiple thousands of dollars.
Marx had previously called the complaints a “nothingburger,” and said the “secretary of state has been great” in working with the campaign as it refunded excess contributions to cure the alleged violations. But regulators and the campaign are now at odds over whether all the issues have been resolved.
“Respondents have not, in fact, cured all their campaign finance violations,” wrote the division, which says only $61,029 in prohibited donations appear to have been refunded.
Marx’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment.
Part of the dispute stems from the Marx campaign’s claims that it has “reattributed” some excess contributions to spouses or other family members who are joint account holders with the contributors in question. In its own filing, the campaign says it contacted those individuals and “spoke with the joint account holders in order to determine whether any apparent overage could be reattributed to the other joint account holder.”
But elections officials say the campaign hasn’t properly reported those reattributions.
“Respondents have provided no credible evidence that the reattributed contributions were made from joint accounts and did not specify the contributors,” the division’s filing states. “Nor have Respondents provided credible evidence that they notified all joint account holders of the apportionment of the contribution.”
Additional complaints pending
Marx, who narrowly won the GOP nomination in June, is considered a heavy underdog in the race against the Democratic nominee for governor, Attorney General Phil Weiser. Colorado has elected only one Republican governor in the last 56 years, and Democrats are widely expected to gain ground in a favorable midterm election year.
Both of Marx’s GOP primary opponents said they would not support him in the general election, calling him a “grifter” and a “con man.” A ministry leader in Colorado Springs, he has struggled to answer questions about his sensational claims about his own life, including the practice of exorcisms and work overseas as a self-described “high-risk missionary.”
He faces additional campaign finance complaints, also filed by Schoening, in relation to his solicitation of unlimited donations through an online merchandise store, a scheme that one campaign finance attorney described as “patently illegal.” Those complaints underwent an initial review by the Elections Division and are still pending.
A third round of proceedings against Marx could follow Schoening’s latest complaint, filed on Aug. 27. Citing reporting last month by 9News, the new complaint concerns a new disclaimer linking Marx’s merchandise store to a Wyoming-registered business, “Not Shook LLC.” A campaign disclosure filed in July identified Marx as the company’s owner, which he subsequently called a “silly mistake.” An initial review of the latest complaint is due by Sept. 11.
