title: Voters will see statement on WA income tax measure’s budget effects
description: A last-ditch legal effort nearly succeeded Thursday to knock a statement off ballots that characterizes how repealing Washington’s new income tax on high earners would affect the state budget. The state Supreme Court deadlocked 4-4 on Arthur West’s motion for an emergency injunction to prevent the secretary of state’s office from including the “public invest[...]
text:
The Washington state Supreme Court building in Olympia. (Photo by Jacquelyn Jimenez Romero/Washington State Standard)A last-ditch legal effort nearly succeeded Thursday to knock a statement off ballots that characterizes how repealing Washington’s new income tax on high earners would affect the state budget.
The state Supreme Court deadlocked 4-4 on Arthur West’s motion for an emergency injunction to prevent the secretary of state’s office from including the “public investment impact disclosure” for Initiative 645. Voters will consider the tax repeal measure in the Nov. 3 election.
Absent a majority, the motion was denied, ensuring voters will see the one-sentence disclosure — that West argues is government-crafted propaganda — on their general election ballots. 
West said late Thursday he was “disappointed but hopeful” that the law requiring the disclosure statement will eventually be declared unconstitutional.
Justices Charles Johnson, Sheryl Gordon McCloud, G. Helen Whitener, and Theo Angelis voted to grant his motion, with Chief Justice Debra Stephens and Justices Steven González, Sal Mungia, and Colleen Melody voting to deny it. 
Justice Raquel Montoya-Lewis was ill, and the court proceeded because of the time-sensitive nature of West’s request, a Supreme Court spokesperson said.
West is fighting to overturn the 2022 law requiring the disclosure statements to appear on ballots. He argues it is unconstitutional because it allows the executive and legislative branches to improperly intrude on the citizen’s power to make laws via initiative. 
Statements are required for ballot measures that repeal, levy or modify a tax or fee, and if it would cause a net change in state revenue. State attorneys are required to write the sentence using “neutral, nonprejudicial” language.
West directed his attention to Initiative 645. It seeks to repeal the 9.9% tax on individual and household wage income above $1 million a year that Gov. Bob Ferguson signed into law in late March. The tax takes effect Jan. 1, 2028 and is projected to bring in roughly $3.1 billion in 2029, the first year of collections.
The statement for I-645 crafted by state lawyers reads: “This measure would decrease funding for public K-12 education, higher education (including universities and community colleges), and human services (primarily healthcare).”
West has argued that language is not neutral and it will cause voters to reject the measure.
Thursday’s decision means the focus will shift back to the broader issue of the law’s legality. West said he is waiting to see if the Supreme Court will retain the case or require it to be considered by a lower appeals court.
West initially sought an injunction in Thurston County Superior Court to block the disclosure statement for I-645. On Aug. 7, Judge Chris Lanese upheld the statute, concluding that the state-authored statement “ensures voters are aware of trade-offs. There’s nothing unconstitutional about giving voters more information.”
West appealed directly to the Supreme Court. Last month, Court Commissioner Michael Johnston also turned West down, setting the stage for Thursday’s decision.
“The fact that four of the justices were in favor of granting a preliminary injunction augurs very well for the ultimate constitutional challenge because that is decided on a lesser standard than an emergency injunction,” West said.

title: Defense contractor to lay off 127 workers in Hardeman County
description: A defense contractor will lay off 127 workers at its Hardeman County manufacturing plant by the end of October, according to a notice filed with Tennessee’s department of labor Wednesday. Kilgore Flares Company manufactures infrared decoy flares — a defense countermeasure used to deflect heat-seeking missiles from targets — at its facility in Toone, an […]
text:
Kilgore Flares Company filed a notice informing the Tennessee Department of Labor and Workforce Development that the company intends to lay off 127 employees by October 31, 2026. (Photo: Cassandra Stephenson/Tennessee Lookout)A defense contractor will lay off 127 workers at its Hardeman County manufacturing plant by the end of October, according to a notice filed with Tennessee’s department of labor Wednesday.
Kilgore Flares Company manufactures infrared decoy flares — a defense countermeasure used to deflect heat-seeking missiles from targets — at its facility in Toone, an unincorporated Southwest Tennessee town home to less than 300 people.
The facility’s employees are not represented by a collective bargaining agreement, and the Southwest Local Workforce Development Area rapid response team will coordinate services for affected employees, according to the notice.
The company employed 308 people at the plant as of February 2021, according to a report submitted to the state.
Hardeman County Mayor Todd Pulse stated Thursday that he has been in “constant contact” with state and local representatives along with Kilgore Flares Company’s human relations department.
“The layoff notice was given because of contracts,” Pulse wrote in a social media post, clarifying that the plant is not closing. 
“This is an extremely difficult time for our employees and their families, our community and the county,” Pulse wrote. “I ask that we pray for them during this time and come together for support.”
Kilgore Flares Co. is part of British defense technology company Chemring Group. The company is one of three major industrial plants in Hardeman County, a rural county with a population of around 25,500 according to the 2020 U.S. Census.
Kilgore Flares Co. invested $40 million to expand the facility in 2018, receiving a $2 million grant from the Tennessee Department of Economic and Community Development to create 97 jobs.
Kilgore Flares Co. has operated in Hardeman County since 1960.

title: Alaska legislator asks state to prosecute candidate for Lt. Gov. and former attorney general
description: Anchorage Democrat Rep. Andrew Gray has asked acting attorney general Cori Mills to prosecute former attorney general Treg Taylor and his wife, Republican lieutenant governor candidate Jodi Taylor, for allegedly failing to file required financial reports. Gray, chair of the House Judiciary Committee, made the request in a letter sent Tuesday and shared with[...]
text:
Rep. Andrew Gray, D-Anchorage, speaks in favor of House Bill 62 on Friday, May 16, 2025. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)Anchorage Democrat Rep. Andrew Gray has asked acting attorney general Cori Mills to prosecute former attorney general Treg Taylor and his wife, Republican lieutenant governor candidate Jodi Taylor, for allegedly failing to file required financial reports.
Gray, chair of the House Judiciary Committee, made the request in a letter sent Tuesday and shared with reporters.
In the letter and speaking by phone, Gray said he was inspired to write the letter because the Alaska Department of Law is criminally prosecuting 11 Whittier residents from American Samoa for allegedly voting illegally.
Gray said those defendants were misinformed about the law, and it makes no sense to prosecute them while not prosecuting an attorney general who knowingly violated an election law.
“I just feel like it’s a no-brainer,” he said.
Treg Taylor had been a Republican candidate for governor until last week, when Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom ruled him ineligible because he failed to follow a state law mandating the disclosure of his personal financial information. 
The Alaska Public Offices Commission, which regulates candidates’ campaigns, had recommended that he be disqualified for failing to disclose the full names of people renting apartments that he owns.
Taylor’s lieutenant governor candidate, Candi English, took his spot as a governor candidate, and Jodi Taylor filed to run as English’s lieutenant governor candidate.
Together, the two make up one of four governor-lieutenant governor tickets in Alaska’s November general election.
Jodi Taylor’s financial disclosure form, filed last week, contains a partial list of renters that is similar to the one flagged as problematic by the commission.
Under state law, Jodi Taylor has 30 days to amend that disclosure. If she does not, she could be ruled ineligible, just as Treg Taylor was.
But federal law requires the state to mail ballots to military and overseas voters no later than 45 days before Election Day. 
To meet that deadline, the Alaska Division of Elections is planning to send out ballots starting Sept. 18, a week and a half before the deadline for changes to Taylor’s financial disclosure form.
If Dahlstrom rules Jodi Taylor ineligible as a candidate after that, Alaskans would end up using ballots containing an ineligible candidate.
For the moment, that remains a hypothetical scenario that depends on how Jodi Taylor, APOC and Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom may act. 
Treg Taylor’s previous campaign spokesperson no longer works for the English-Taylor campaign, and the Taylors’ daughter Quincy Azimi-Tabrizi — who spoke for the campaign last week — did not return phone calls seeking comment on Thursday.
A spokesman for the Alaska Department of Law also did not return phone calls or emails asking whether the attorney general had received the letter and if so, whether she had a response. 
Gray said on Thursday that he has not received any response either but is preparing a public letter about the issue.
He said he has been particularly taken aback by the idea that Treg Taylor, as attorney general, directed the criminal prosecution of voters in Whittier for allegedly breaking state elections law but isn’t being held to the same standard.
“It makes my head explode,” Gray said.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Amid fractured GOP field, a Democrat could be headed for the Alaska governor’s mansion
description: This story was originally published by the Anchorage Press.  The improbable rise of a long-shot Democratic candidate now has the party positioned to capture the Alaska governor’s mansion for the first time in more than two decades, veteran political observers from across the ideological spectrum said this week. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a 37-year-old former s[...]
text:
Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a Democratic former state House member, won the state's gubernatorial primary last month. (Nathaniel Herz/Anchorage Press)This story was originally published by the Anchorage Press. 
The improbable rise of a long-shot Democratic candidate now has the party positioned to capture the Alaska governor’s mansion for the first time in more than two decades, veteran political observers from across the ideological spectrum said this week.
Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a 37-year-old former state House member from Sitka who’s never run for statewide office, won Alaska’s open primary with 22.5% of votes, according to official results released Monday.
The second-place finisher and the only other Democrat in the field, former state Sen. Tom Begich, dropped out of the race last week — leaving Kreiss-Tomkins, known as JKT, with what insiders say is a clear path to victory amid a splintered Republican field and voter disaffection with incumbent GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy, who’s term-limited and can’t run again.
Last month, Begich’s campaign had touted analysis by political and polling forecaster Nate Silver that gave his campaign a 71% chance of winning the primary — and Kreiss-Tomkins a 0.0% chance. Prediction markets similarly gave Kreiss-Tomkins long odds.
Now, after a primary campaign that blanketed voters with text messages and sent him to far corners of the state, Kreiss-Tomkins’ political stock is booming and those markets show him as the favorite.
A chart on Polymarket, the prediction market site, showing Alaska Democratic gubernatorial candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins’ odds over time. (Polymarket)
“Jonathan carved 20 points out of thin f—n’ air,” said Joelle Hall, president of the Alaska AFL-CIO, the state’s largest organized labor group, which has endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins. “Everyone else is stuck in another century. JKT is the only one running communications and a campaign that exists in 2026. Everyone else is running a 1990s playbook, and it’s not working.”
Lest you think that’s an opinion held only by his allies, even some of Kreiss-Tomkins’ political adversaries agree.
“He is running a campaign unlike any that has ever been seen in Alaska history,” said Suzanne Downing, the prominent conservative blogger and former spokesperson for the Alaska Republican Party. “He’s running circles around people, because they don’t even know the questions to ask.”
With the Democratic field clear, Kreiss-Tomkins is now poised to also draw support from national groups. The chair of the Democratic Governors Association, which boosts the party’s candidates across the country, issued a statement Tuesday saying the organization “looks forward to working alongside Jonathan to deliver the change Alaskans deserve.”
The Republican Governors Association, meanwhile, has not issued a statement on the Alaska gubernatorial race since primary voting took place last month. Officials there did not respond to a request for comment this week.
Will Republicans ‘rank the red’?
Alaska’s last Democratic governor was Tony Knowles, who left office in 2002. The state has twice as many Republicans as Democrats — some 24% of registered voters to 12% — but nearly 65% of voters are independent, meaning that Democrats can occasionally make competitive runs for statewide office.
Of 17 primary election candidates in the governor’s race, 12 were Republicans, who collectively won some 49.5% of the vote — more than the combined total of 43.3% for Kreiss-Tomkins and Begich.
But many observers say they expect the conservative vote to be split between the three Republicans who advanced to the general election.
Those Republicans include conservative activist Bernadette Wilson, who won 10% of votes in the primary; former Anchorage mayor Dave Bronson, who won 8%; and businesswoman Candi English, who was on the ballot as the running mate to a former Alaska attorney general, Treg Taylor, who was ultimately disqualified from the general election due to violation of the state’s financial disclosure law.
Bernadette Wilson was the top-ranked GOP gubernatorial candidate after last month’s primary. (Nathaniel Herz/Anchorage Press)
Alaska has a ranked choice voting system that theoretically should allow the top GOP candidate to consolidate the second- and third-choiced votes from supporters of the two lower-finishing Republicans. Supporters of the system say it works best when party candidates cooperate.
But political insiders say that they expect infighting among the Republican campaigns to cause a significant fraction of conservative voters to rank only their favorite candidate and not the others — meaning that some of the votes for the lower-placed Republicans may not help the top GOP candidate in a final tally against Kreiss-Tomkins.
Downing, who’s a friend and supporter of Wilson, is one example. She described Bronson as “pugnacious” and “pigheaded” and said his campaign has been attacking Wilson for weeks through third-party surrogates.
“There’s nothing you could do today to get me to rank Dave Bronson,” Downing said in a phone interview.
Downing and other Republicans noted that if Kreiss-Tomkins is elected, he’s likely to get legislative cooperation from the same type of ruling coalitions that have led the state House and Senate for the past two years — which have tilted Democratic. Primary results suggest those coalitions are likely to persist into next year.
One veteran GOP operative, who spoke anonymously to share frank opinions about the party’s odds in November, also said he was deeply pessimistic about the chances that conservative voters will rank more than one Republican gubernatorial candidate.
He cited the 2022 U.S. House race, in which Republicans Sarah Palin and Nick Begich III traded attacks on each other leading up to the general election. The pair together won more than 50% in the early ranked choice vote count — but ultimately lost to a Democrat in part because nearly 14,000 people who ranked Begich declined to rank Palin, meaning their ballots were “exhausted.”
“I don’t think there’s any way conservatives rank the red,” the operative said. “Dave and Bernadette are going to be Sarah and Nick all over again.”
A spokesperson for Bronson’s campaign, Jesse McCarty, said Bronson was unavailable for an interview but added that “we have made it very clear that we will not speak poorly of Republican candidates publicly.”
“Dave and this campaign will be asking the voters to rank the conservatives,” McCarty said in a text message.
The Alaska Republican Party’s chair, Carmela Warfield, did not respond to requests for comment Tuesday. Wilson did not respond to requests for comment, and a spokesperson for English declined to make her available for an interview.
Kreiss-Tomkins targets moderate voters
Kreiss-Tomkins, meanwhile, was busy campaigning Tuesday. He said he started the morning with an 8 a.m. coffee with a state legislator after working until 2:30 a.m. the night before, then spent the rest of the day on calls and meetings with other donors, business and labor leaders and campaign staff.
“We’re just going to be super heads-down, a heat-seeking missile toward Nov. 3,” Kreiss-Tomkins said in an interview, referring to the general election date. “We just want to focus on the fundamentals and outwork every other campaign, out-raise every other campaign, out-travel every other campaign.”
Kreiss-Tomkins’ primary campaign took him far across the state, from boating down the Yukon River to driving a snowmachine in Alaska’s Northwest Arctic. He also raised more money than any other candidate — though not without drawing criticism for taking hundreds of thousands of dollars from California-based employees of an AI company, Anthropic.
He has been using a texting service that’s allowed him to directly exchange messages with hundreds of voters, he said in an interview last month.     
Screenshots of text messages sent by Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins’ campaign.

Now that the primary election is over, Kreiss-Tomkins said, he’s planning more outreach to moderate Republicans who are “disillusioned with the Dunleavy era and want change.”
Kreiss-Tomkins has hired national campaign consultants who have supported strident progressives like former U.S. Senate candidate Graham Platner in Maine and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. But he noted that one of those consultants has also worked with centrist candidates like independent Nebraska U.S. Senate candidate Dan Osborn, who’s volunteered to help Trump build a border wall.
“I’m not an ideological zealot — I never have been,” Kreiss-Tomkins said.
Underscoring Kreiss-Tomkins’ bid to consolidate support among moderates, he spent part of last week in conversations about taking on a new running mate: Click Bishop, a moderate Republican former state senator who also ran in the gubernatorial primary but finished outside the top four.
Kreiss-Tomkins declined to comment directly on those discussions, but a spokesperson for Bishop, Shannon Mason, confirmed that they took place.
Hall, the labor leader, said she expects Kreiss-Tomkins to make inroads with conservative leaning voters who assume the candidate is more liberal than he actually is because of his relative youth.
“Just because he’s young, they believe that he is less moderate than Tom Begich,” Hall said. “He’s 100% a negotiator. He’s the kind of guy who’s going to bring everybody in a room.”
Downing, the blogger and Wilson supporter, said she hasn’t totally given up hope that her preferred candidate could still come out of the race as the winner.
She’s hoping Bronson can still be convinced to suspend his campaign and consolidate support for Wilson. And she said she also thinks that English, the third GOP candidate, may have to drop out: Her current running mate is Jodi Taylor, the wife of the former attorney general who was disqualified for financial disclosure violations. Jodi Taylor made the same omissions on her financial disclosure — some of the details of her sources of income — that her husband did.
“I see a path,” Downing said. “But it’s a narrower path with Bronson in.”
Disclosure: Kreiss-Tomkins facilitated some early-stage meetings around the revitalization of the Anchorage Press. He has no involvement with the organization today.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Concerns swirl over a developer’s push for a Tooele Valley data center, but plans are on pause
description: Tooele County residents concerned about a developer’s proposal to build a large-scale data center near the southern shore of the Great Salt Lake turned their frustrations and demands to put a stop to the proposal on the Utah Inland Port Authority Board on Thursday.  The group TooeleCARES delivered a letter signed by more than 1,100 […]
text:
The Utah Inland Port Authority's Tooele Valley Project Area is pictured with a view of a new road and rail line leading into Grantsville in September 2025. (Photo courtesy of the Utah Inland Port Authority)Tooele County residents concerned about a developer’s proposal to build a large-scale data center near the southern shore of the Great Salt Lake turned their frustrations and demands to put a stop to the proposal on the Utah Inland Port Authority Board on Thursday. 
The group TooeleCARES delivered a letter signed by more than 1,100 Utahns from in and outside of Tooele calling on the Utah Inland Port Authority to “decline to authorize any bonds or public financing” for the Interstate Technology Park Public Infrastructure District, an entity the port authority board created earlier this year meant to finance infrastructure within the port authority’s 585-acre Tooele Valley project area located near Burmester Road and I-80. 
That project area plan lists “data centers” as one potential industry (along with light industrial, manufacturing and distribution) that could be favored for incentives, but it also says that “no businesses are guaranteed an incentive and the UIPA board may decline an application for any reason.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“None of this has been presented to the public,” Amy Lawson, a Tooele resident, told the board Thursday. “We already carry more than our share of the state’s industrial burden. We are asking you not to help finance more of it sight unseen. We all live by the same dying (Great Salt) Lake, and our wells are already struggling.” 
A developer, Chuck Akerlow, has been pushing county officials behind-the-scenes to allow building a data center on the south end of that project area. That’s according to emails obtained by members of TooeleCARES through a public records request, which were shared with Utah News Dispatch this week. 
Ben Hart, executive director of the Utah Inland Port Authority, addressed Tooele County residents at the beginning of Thursday’s board meeting, telling them the port authority is taking their concerns “seriously.” 
“There’s one thing we always promise, which is we’re not going to try and slam anything through,” Hart said. “We try and be very thoughtful and take a balanced approach with public comment before we ever act.” 
However, Hart also said the port authority didn’t have anything on its agenda Thursday that had “anything to do with supporting a data center in Tooele Valley.” 
“On the contrary,” he added, “not only do we not have anything on this agenda, but it’s possible and even likely that we will never have anything on our agenda to consider for that project area.”
Tooele County and Utah Inland Port Authority officials told Utah News Dispatch on Thursday that plans to build a data center in Tooele Valley aren’t currently moving forward — and it remains to be seen whether it will go anywhere at all. 
Asked if that means the project is dead, Hart told Utah News Dispatch on Thursday that “dead is a very strong word” but “I don’t consider it alive right now, that’s for sure.” 
Concern about data center impacts on Great Salt Lake grows, now for Tooele project’s wastewater

A data center ordinance is in the works
Tooele County leaders have pushed pause on considering any data center applications until after the county’s planning commission and the Tooele County Council consider an ordinance regulating data center development. That ordinance isn’t expected to come before the planning commission until October and the County Council in November. 
Tooele County leaders maintain land use authority in the port authority’s Tooele Valley project area — so development there hinges on what the Tooele County Council allows, Hart told Utah News Dispatch in an interview. 
“So we know nothing can move forward right now,” Hart said. He added that it remains to be seen what the county will or won’t allow, “so it’s really hard to say that something is active or moving forward when there’s not even a pathway to move forward right now.” 
While addressing Tooele County residents during Thursday morning’s board meeting, Hart referenced a part of their letter that asks the board to “formally condition any future consideration of financing” for the Tooele Valley project area on the County Council first adopting a data center ordinance. 
“You have our 100% commitment,” Hart said. “We’re not bringing anything to our board until we get a very clear green light from any community that we’re working with.”
Hart added that the port authority will “never bring anything to our board unless we know that the community is OK with it.” 
“Very clearly,” he said, “Tooele Valley (and) Tooele County are signaling they are not OK with it. And thus, we are not OK with it. So we are not going to be moving anything forward until we know that a local community is OK with it.” 
Cox orders ‘higher bar’ for data centers, says public input ‘absolutely matters’ 

Earlier this year — as concern over data centers spread across the country — the Utah Inland Port Authority issued a statement explaining its position on data centers and answering frequently asked questions. That statement said the port authority is taking a “measured and transparent approach” and that “any conversation about future development must reflect Utah’s priorities: economic competitiveness, responsible growth, community health and protection of the state’s natural resources.”
“UIPA’s purpose is to strengthen Utah’s transportation network and regional economies by supporting logistics, infrastructure and manufacturing growth while protecting sensitive lands and the Great Salt Lake,” the statement says. “UIPA will not risk those resources, or the integrity of the organization, by fast-tracking data center development.”
Hart also noted that Utah lawmakers earlier this year passed a law, HB507, which bans cities and counties from providing incentives to a “large load” data center unless it’s located within a “regionally significant development zone.” That would be a separate process overseen by the Governor’s Office of Economic Development, and any tax incentives would require approval from a different board created to consider the application.
That provision of HB507 doesn’t take effect until May 2027, but Hart told Utah News Dispatch the port authority board “has already determined they want these types of projects … going through the regionally significant development zone process.”
“So regardless of what the county does, we will probably push this through the new regionally significant development zone process for any tax increment involvement,” Hart said, “which means it’s not our board that makes the final say. It would be the board that is put together under the new RSDZ law.” 



A developer’s push for a Tooele Valley data center
Akerlow, principal owner of Zenith Development, is a member of the Interstate Technology Park Public Infrastructure District that could approve infrastructure financing for the project. So is one of his Zenith Development partners, Matt Smock. 
In an email obtained by TooeleCARES that was sent a year ago, on Sept. 3, 2025, Akerlow told Rachelle Custer, Tooele County’s community development director, that “we have committed to bring a 24 (inch) high pressure natural gas line to our property and have the funding to do it.” 
“This gas line, at present, can produce 140 MegaWatts which is sufficient to launch that area as a high-tech center for more than just data storage,” Akerlow wrote. “We are under Non-Disclosure Agreements so we cannot tell you with whom we are currently dealing, but they are companies you will recognize as being prominent in the high-tech world.” 
He also wrote in that email that “additional sources of power are likely to be nuclear, and we have a Letter of Intent with a public nuclear power well funded company that would build it, operate it, own it and buy the land from us.” 
However, Akerlow also told The Salt Lake Tribune earlier this year that his project wouldn’t be possible without the incentives and financing that would be provided by the port authority. 
Emails also show Akerlow has been running into some permitting obstacles, including frustrations over a version of the data center ordinance that county officials considered but did not approve in July. 


Let us know what you think...


 

“We can live with the difficult application process prescribed in this very long ordinance. But to protect the County you ought to have the same process for every new tenant in every building in the Park,” Akerlow wrote in a July 21 email to Tooele County officials. “And your Ordinances cannot discriminate against technology companies while happily approving manufacturers of all varieties.”
Some of Akerlow’s emails also contain an undertone that appears to threaten potential litigation against Tooele County, in some cases warning against measures county officials were considering in their data center ordinance that Akerlow said could be violations of developers’ rights to equal protection under the law. At the same time, however, Akerlow also committed to working together on the ordinance and cooperating “with you to the fullest extent.” 
In other emails, Akerlow also floated the idea of annexing into Grantsville to deal with that city’s regulations rather than Tooele County’s. Those emails caught at least one Grantsville City Council member, Derek Dalton, off guard. Dalton wrote in a social media post that he learned about the data center proposal and the developer’s interest in annexation through a public records request. 
Akerlow didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on Thursday or answer questions about the current status of the proposed data center project and if he’s still pursuing it. 
Asked if Tooele County faces any threats of a lawsuit over the project, Assistant County Manager Brittany Lopez told Utah News Dispatch on Thursday, “We have not, and that’s not something that we’re concerned about because we’re just following the process the way it needs to be.” 
“We don’t go off of pressures,” she said. “Things take time. We’ve met with the developer. We meet with the inland port. And we walk them through the timing of the process. … We need to make sure that we have a proper land use code in place so that we are having the right guardrails if a development like this were to come in.” 
Opponents outnumbered supporters of a proposed shipping, manufacturing and data center hub near the Great Salt Lake’s southern shore during a public hearing held on Monday, July 27 by the Utah Division of Water Quality. (Courtesy of Dave Noriega/Utah Department of Environmental Quality)
Frustrations over transparency
A major driver of Tooele County residents’ frustrations stem from many of them finding out about the data center proposal from emails obtained through a public records request rather than a public process.
The TooeleCARES letter called on county and state officials to discuss the potential data center project in public, “not just behind closed doors.” The letter also called on the port authority to “suspend all informal briefings, site tours, and private coordination between UIPA staff or board members and the developer or his representatives until a public process, with real notice to Tooele Valley residents, is in place.” 
When asked about those transparency concerns, Lopez noted that Tooele County officials have “never received an application, and as far as we know, we don’t know of any developer in the county that has signed a commitment with a data center.” 
Those emails showed preliminary discussions rather than a firm proposal, Lopez said. The developer reached out to county officials with a proposal to build a data center, not the other way around. 
“These are concepts and ideas,” Lopez said. “Companies are interested in coming to communities all the time. Sometimes they come and talk to you first and they kind of tell you what they’re thinking, but that doesn’t mean that that’s what happens. It’s part of the economic development process. … There’s just not a way that you could tell the public every time.” 
However, Lopez said she and other Tooele County officials welcome any concerned residents to reach out to them and ask questions. She also said concerns raised in recent meetings with Tooele County residents have been taken into consideration while county leaders work to draft their data center ordinance. 
“We just encourage them to come in and talk to us, and we’ll be willing to set up meetings to answer any questions,” Lopez said. “I think there’s a lot of misinformation out there, and we’d just love to take the time to talk to them and really work through their concerns and hear their concerns.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ panels OK rate hike for public worker health plans, deadlock on increase for teachers
description: A state panel approved double-digit hikes Thursday for state and local government workers' health plans, but a separate panel deadlocked on increases for school workers.
text:
A state panel approved double-digit hikes Thursday for state and local government workers' health plans, but a separate panel deadlocked on increases for school workers. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)A New Jersey commission approved double-digit premium increases for state and local government workers’ health premiums in divided votes Thursday, but a separate panel that oversees the state-run health plan for school workers again deadlocked on a vote to raise rates.
The State Health Benefit Commission’s votes will increase local government workers’ health premiums by 17.3% on average, but state workers will be spared the brunt of the increases under a deal announced Wednesday with Gov. Mikie Sherrill’s administration.
Billy Gallagher, a spokesman for Communications Workers of America, said in a statement that reforming the State Health Benefits Plan to avoid big cost increases in the future must be a top priority in the coming months.
“There is still an enormous amount of work to do for local government workers, who are being crushed under sky-high premiums that eat up 15-20% of their paychecks — an unsustainable and unacceptable burden that has been allowed to fester for far too long,” Gallagher said.
The latest movement comes amid steep rises to the cost of public and private health plans nationwide, but the impact has been particularly keen for New Jersey’s plans for local government and school workers.
These plans have faced mounting pressures as cost increases push units with younger, healthier workforces to cheaper options in the private market, raising rates for those who remain and prompting more departures that only lead to more increases.
This year, state actuaries said premiums for school workers’ plans would need to rise by 34.4% on average to fund claims, rebuild a month of surplus, and repay $90 million in loans the plan is expected to owe to the state next year.
Those increases have created a split between the panel’s four union members and four others who represent the state or school boards. But the panel has deadlocked only because one of its nine seats is vacant and has been since at least 2024. Typically, union members hold a minority of the commission’s seats.
It’s not clear when the School Employees Health Benefit Commission will reconvene for another vote, and some members repeated warnings that delaying rate approvals could create problems when open enrollment begins in October. Rates in some past years have been approved later in September.
“Unfortunately, this is not an optional thing. We need, as a commission, to address the rates. It’s not optional. It is our statutory duty, and it’s time sensitive. Open enrollment will begin as scheduled,” said Sergio Arvizu, the panel’s representative for the state Treasury.
Hundreds of public workers rally outside the Statehouse in Trenton on June 18, 2026, to demand lawmakers rein in rising healthcare costs. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
At past meetings, some commissioners have said delaying rates could force members to choose their health plans without knowing their costs, prompting appeals that state officials would be forced to deny. Unions have disputed a delay would have such effects.
Other members of the panel warned that approving another year of steep increases could conscribe districts to financial doom if their workforces are too small or sick for private-market alternatives.
“These rates are going to bankrupt districts,” said Commissioner Michael Salerno.
Salerno added that large increases for the public plan could prompt insurers in the private market to make their own large increases.
“If we approve a 34% rate, they can come back with a 30% increase and be heroes. The idea of what this will do to education in New Jersey is, to me, a catastrophe,” he said.
Late Wednesday afternoon, Sherrill announced New Jersey would forgo increasing state workers’ share of health premiums while the administration pursues compromises with the 17 unions that represent state workers here to provide time for officials to seek comprehensive reforms.
“The severe financial challenges facing the State Health Benefits Program did not emerge in one year or from one decision, and there is no single fix — this is complicated,” Sherrill said in a statement. “This agreement brings key stakeholders to the table to take on this challenge together, to address rising costs, while preserving high-quality benefits and putting the program on a more sustainable path for the future. “
It’s unclear how much deferring those increases will cost New Jersey. The state’s actuaries in a rate renewal report said state workers’ plan would need to collect $397.2 million more in premiums for 2027 than it did in 2026, but that amount includes premium increases that would have been paid by the state and its workers.
Commissioners from both sides of the issue saw that agreement and its promise to gather state and union officials, along with other stakeholders, in a working group by October as a chance at meaningful reform.
“I do hope that the framework established for state employees … is something that results in greater cost controls and transparency among the plans and what we are actually paying for, both as public employees and public servants and taxpayers,” said Jennifer Higgins, a State Health Benefit Commission commissioner who represents state workers.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri voters will decide limits on lawmakers rewriting ballot measures
description: An effort to restrict the legislature’s ability to rewrite laws and constitutional amendments approved by voters through the initiative process will be on the Nov. 3 ballot, the Missouri Supreme Court ruled Thursday. In a unanimous decision overturning Cole County Circuit Judge Daniel Green, the court ruled Secretary of State Denny Hoskins improperly declare[...]
text:
Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins listens to three cases during Missouri Supreme Court arguments Wednesday (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).An effort to restrict the legislature’s ability to rewrite laws and constitutional amendments approved by voters through the initiative process will be on the Nov. 3 ballot, the Missouri Supreme Court ruled Thursday.
In a unanimous decision overturning Cole County Circuit Judge Daniel Green, the court ruled Secretary of State Denny Hoskins improperly declared the proposed Amendment 6 insufficient. The judges also rejected the constitutional objections Hoskins relied on to keep it off the ballot. .
Hoskins on Aug. 4 issued a “certificate of insufficiency” and based it on constitutional violations identified in an opinion letter from Attorney General Catherine Hanaway. Attaching that letter and adopting its findings as his own by reference was not the way it should have been done, Judge Ginger Gooch wrote for the court.
“Because his certificate fails to identify any reason the petition is insufficient under the
Missouri Constitution, it does not comply with (Missouri statutes) and preserves nothing for this
court’s review,” Gooch wrote. “Even if the secretary had preserved his claims, nearly all assert constitutional violations that may or will occur if the petition is approved. These hypothetical claims are not ripe for review. The two pre-election claims-violation of the single-article and single-subject requirements…lack merit.”
A political action committee called Respect MO Voters circulated petitions and obtained more than 350,000 signatures to put Amendment 6 on the ballot. It comes on the heels of voter rejection in the primary of Amendment 4, which would have made it more difficult to amend the Missouri Constitution by initiative petition.
Immediately after the ruling, Respect MO Voters announced it would immediately begin its advertising campaign to pass it.
“For more than 118 years, Missourians have had the power to put issues directly before the voters,” said Eric Bronner, co-founder of Veterans for All Voters, a supporter of Amendment 6, in a news release. “Amendment 6 is about protecting that right and making sure that when Missourians vote for something, politicians can’t simply undo their decision after the election.”
Amendment 6, if passed, would put heavy restrictions on the ability of lawmakers to alter state laws and constitutional amendments proposed by initiative and approved by voters. Any changes would have to receive 80% support in the General Assembly and be ratified in a statewide vote.
Currently, there are no restrictions on lawmakers altering or repealing laws passed by initiative. That happened in 2025, when Republicans forced through a bill that repealed paid sick leave for Missouri workers and inflation adjustments to the minimum wage.
A majority of lawmakers in both chambers can propose changes in constitutional amendments but those changes must also pass statewide. 
That happened in 2020, when voters approved changes to the terms of a legislative redistricting proposal passed by initiative in 2018. Amendment 3 on the Nov. 3 ballot seeks to overturn the abortion rights measure approved in 2024.
The proposal would apply not only to measures approved in the future but also to laws and constitutional amendments previously enacted through the initiative process. 
For example, lawmakers left the $15 per hour minimum wage approved in 2024 in place when they passed the bill repealing sick leave. If Amendment 6 is ultimately approved by voters, any attempt in the General Assembly to change that minimum wage would require an 80% vote from lawmakers and statewide voter approval.
To achieve that majority, a bill would have to have broad bipartisan support. Republicans won 111 of 163 seats in the Missouri House in 2024 and hold 24 of 34 seats in the state Senate. An 80% majority would require 131 votes in the Missouri House and 28 in the state Senate.
This article will be updated.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: ACLU of Idaho calls on Gov. Brad Little to pull back Idaho National Guard from DC
description: The ACLU of Idaho has joined the national American Civil Liberties Union in calling on leaders to pull back National Guard members from Washington, D.C. Idaho leaders indicated the deployment in D.C. will continue.  Members of the Idaho National Guard have been deployed to the nation’s capital since February, although state officials did not publicly […]
text:
U.S. Army Col. Stephen Arnett speaks with members of the Idaho National Guard, assigned to the Joint Task Force-District of Columbia in support of the "D.C. Safe and Beautiful mission," at the Ulysses S. Grant Memorial in Washington, D.C., on June 16, 2026. (Photo by Spc. Keyra Moolenaar/U.S. Army National Guard)The ACLU of Idaho has joined the national American Civil Liberties Union in calling on leaders to pull back National Guard members from Washington, D.C. Idaho leaders indicated the deployment in D.C. will continue. 
Members of the Idaho National Guard have been deployed to the nation’s capital since February, although state officials did not publicly announce the deployment at the time, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. 
The soldiers are there with guardsmen from other states as part of a Joint Task Force-DC Mission in response to President Donald Trump’s executive order titled Making the District of Columbia Safe and Beautiful.
U.S. Sen. Jim Risch, left, and Idaho Gov. Brad Little, right, attend a lying in state service for former Idaho Gov. Dirk Kempthorne on May 15, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)
“Governor Little is proud of Idaho’s citizen-soldiers and the professionalism, dedication, and service they bring to every mission, including Operation Safe and Beautiful,” Emily Callihan, Gov. Brad Little’s communication director, said in an emailed statement. 
Attorneys with the ACLU-D.C. in July filed a $3 million legal claim against the Idaho National guard on behalf of a D.C. resident who says she was injured by Idaho guardsmen outside her home in May. 
“The ACLU of Idaho is demanding that Governor Little immediately remove all Idaho National Guard troops from D.C.,” ACLU of Idaho Executive Director Leo Morales said Thursday in a press release. “There is no real emergency justifying the need to send troops to the other side of the country. This deployment of National Guard members in D.C. for many months has pulled taxpayer-funded resources away from true, critical emergencies here in Idaho, including wildfires. Additionally, the lack of transparency around this deployment and the recent incident involving a D.C. veteran and Idaho National Guard members should concern all Idahoans. Governor Little has the power to put this to an end.”
As of Sept. 1, there are 24 members of the Idaho National Guard in Washington, D.C., among a total of 3,780 Guard personnel from around the country and Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands. 
Woman files $3 million claim against Idaho National Guard for detaining her in D.C.

In late July, Idaho had 99 guardsmen in D.C. 
“Idaho National Guard personnel continue to support the Joint Task Force–District of Columbia mission in Washington, D.C., while maintaining the readiness to respond to emergencies and other missions in Idaho,” said Lt. Col. Chris Borders, spokesperson for the Idaho National Guard. 
“We remain focused on accomplishing the mission while maintaining our readiness to respond to the needs of Idaho when called upon. Any future participation in JTF-DC will be based on mission requirements and direction from the appropriate authorities.” 
 The cost of Idaho’s deployment is unknown, officials say 

The Idaho National Guard’s deployment is federally funded, according to multiple officials. 
A spokesperson for the Joint Task Force told the Sun that questions about the mission’s costs should be directed to the Office of the Secretary of Defense. That office directed the Sun back to the Joint Task Force for questions related to costs. 
Asked again, a spokesperson from the Office of the Secretary of Defense said, “we will not know the cost until the mission is completed.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Bellows says election will proceed as usual, despite legal battle over Trump’s mail-in voting order
description: Despite the ongoing legal battle over President Donald Trump’s efforts to restrict voting by mail, Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows reiterated Thursday that for voters in Maine and across the country, nothing has changed. Bellows and other election officials are arguing that Trump’s executive order placing new restrictions on mail-in voting would pres[...]
text:
Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows speaks at the No Kings rally in Saco, Maine. Oct. 18, 2025. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)Despite the ongoing legal battle over President Donald Trump’s efforts to restrict voting by mail, Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows reiterated Thursday that for voters in Maine and across the country, nothing has changed.
Bellows and other election officials are arguing that Trump’s executive order placing new restrictions on mail-in voting would present massive — if not impossible — challenges to reach compliance in time for the Nov. 3 election. 
On Thursday, the Trump administration appealed directly to the U.S. Supreme Court to overturn a lower court and allow the order, which directed the U.S. Postal Service to strictly regulate the envelope design of mail-in ballots and to collect voter data from each state through an online portal, among other things. The agency has argued that its rule is not an election regulation, but is within its purview as a standard for a specific type of mail.
Why the rushed Postal Service plan for mail-in voting has states in a panic

“To be clear, we do not believe that the Constitution or federal law give the Postal Service or the Trump administration the right to restrict who votes by mail,” Bellows told Maine Morning Star. Maine is among more than 20 Democratic-led states suing to block the order. 
“We see what the Postal Service is trying to do as direct interference in the 2026 election,” Bellows added.
Still, the secretary said the state is not changing its approach. “We are not obeying in advance,” she said. “We are following the law and the Constitution, and that means proceeding with our plans for a safe and secure election.” 
With designs finalized, Maine ballots will soon be printed and distributed to towns. 
Roughly 200,000 Maine voters typically cast their ballot by mail, many of whom are older Mainers and Mainers with disabilities. Bellows said her office is “going to do everything in our power to make sure that they are able to vote just like they always have.” 
The secretary said her biggest concern for the upcoming election is that “heated rhetoric or bullying from the Trump administration” will scare people away from voting.
“Trump seems determined to try to lower voter turnout,” she said. 
Bellows is advocating Maine voters, particularly those who are concerned about mail delays or who do not want to vote in-person on Election Day, should make a plan that works for them. 
Beginning Oct. 4, voters can go to their local clerk’s office and cast a no-excuse absentee ballot. 
Ahead of that deadline, clerks will begin mailing ballots to those who have submitted a request or who are an ongoing absentee voter. Bellows noted that anyone who receives their ballot early can also return them via a ballot drop box.

name: WyoFile
title: U.S. Fish and Wildlife staff tumbles by a quarter in Director Brian Nesvik’s home state of Wyoming
description:
Nationwide, agency staffing has dropped by 36% since 2024 and wildlife refuges, already debilitated by a lack of resources, continue to lose employees.
The post U.S. Fish and Wildlife staff tumbles by a quarter in Director Brian Nesvik’s home state of Wyoming appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
In 2024, the National Elk Refuge had 11 full-time employees helping to feed elk and bison, greet 300,000-plus tourists at its visitor center and steward 24,700 scenic acres just north of Jackson. 
During the tumultuous two Trump administration-led years that followed for federal workers, six of those 11 staffers have departed. Three refuge employees described as rangers left their jobs, and so did a maintenance worker, heavy equipment operator and administrative assistant. 
Meanwhile, no employees were added, at least through late June 2026. That leaves five full-time staff — just 45% of the prior workforce — remaining to care for a wildlife refuge that was created by Congress 114 years ago in response to bad winters when elk starved to death. 
Although the National Elk Refuge’s staff has been hit particularly hard, the hollowing out of its workforce is a microcosm of how the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has fared overall. The federal agency charged with overseeing wildlife habitat and imperiled species for the United States has lost 36% of its staff, dropping from 9,957 to 6,333 total workers between 2024 and 2026. That is according to employment data acquired by the Center for Biological Diversity using the Freedom of Information Act. 
“These staff cuts are a cruel disaster for America’s endangered species and wildlife refuges,” Noah Greenwald, the organization’s endangered species co-director, said in a statement. 
Young bighorn sheep gather as a fresh dusting of snow coats the hillsides April 30, 2019, on the National Elk Refuge north of Jackson. (Ryan Dorgan)
Overall, the Fish and Wildlife Service lost 1,900 scientists, including fish and wildlife biologists, foresters and fire managers, Greenwald calculated.
“This brain drain will be hard to undo now that the Fish and Wildlife Service has lost so many expert scientists who helped save endangered animals and plants,” he said.
The data used in this story come from the Center for Biological Diversity’s information request. The agency‘s workforce in Wyoming, the home state of Director Brian Nesvik, fell by 25%, holding up better than most states. There were 64 Fish and Wildlife employees stationed in the Equality State in 2024. Since then, 20 of those employees have left, while four have been added. That leaves 48 employees in Wyoming, which is home to eight wildlife refuges and two federal hatcheries that are spread across more than 100,000 acres. 
WyoFile’s inquiry to the Fish and Wildlife Service’s regional press contact received no response before this story was published. Nesvik, who leads the agency, could not be reached for comment. 
Fish and Wildlife Service workforces in neighboring states have been hit even harder. 
Montana-based staff fell by 40% to 116 full-time employees, and Utah’s workforce slumped by 32% to 50 staffers. The Fish and Wildlife workforce in Colorado fell 41% to 272, and Idaho’s dropped by 35% to 112 employees. 
The Green River flows through Seedskadee National Wildlife Refuge. (Tom Koerner/U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)
The modern era has been tough for the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service well before cuts were imposed by the Trump administration. An audit of the service’s 573 national wildlife refuges conducted in the spring of 2025 found that not a single refuge had ideal staffing and resources.
“Capacity right now is at a tipping point that puts both the economic and the conservation vitality of the National Wildlife Refuge System at risk,” National Wildlife Refuge System Chief Cynthia Martinez told refuge advocates in April 2025. 
Nearly a year and a half later, conditions have worsened, said Desiree Sorenson Groves, president of the National Wildlife Refuge Association.
“That hasn’t improved. How could it, if you lose 35% of your staff nationwide?” Sorenson Groves told WyoFile. “There’s no refuge that all of a sudden was made whole, that I know of. If there is, that’s a unicorn that I haven’t heard about.” 
Sorenson Groves emphasized that the depletion of the workforce at the National Wildlife Refuge System has been ongoing for two decades. 
“It goes back to the Obama administration, and it is just a straight downward dive,” she said. “It’s a free fall.” 
The annual visits to national wildlife refuges per full-time employee in the nationwide system nearly doubled between 2010 and 2023, and the ratio continues to increase. (National Wildlife Refuge Association)
The total National Wildlife Refuge System staff topped 3,200 as recently as 2012, but fell to fewer than 2,200 by fiscal year 2025, according to data Sorenson Groves provided. Meanwhile, public interest in visiting the refuges has surged. 
“People want to go to public lands — that’s growing, while you have staffing going down,” Sorenson Groves said. “They’re going in completely different directions. The amount of visitors per [full-time employee] has increased by 94%.” 
Sorenson Groves did have some cause for optimism. An audit of the National Wildlife Refuge System led by Wyoming resident Josh Coursey, she said, is a “good thing.” 
“I think it’s long, long overdue, to be perfectly honest,” she said. “Brian [Nesvik] was asked at the North American Wildlife Conference if he was doing this so that he could divest refuges. He was unequivocal and said, ‘No, absolutely not.’” 
The refuge system’s been through rough stretches before, Sorenson Groves pointed out. There was a point during the mid-1990s, she said, where there was low staffing, “not a clear mission” and some “inappropriate things” happening on refuges around the country. 
A broad coalition that united parties like Defenders of Wildlife with the National Rifle Association pushed for reform, and they got it. Congress passed the Refuge Improvement Act in 1997, and conditions improved, she said. 
“Things were pretty bad then,” Sorenson Groves said. “Right now, the reason it’s not as bad is because we still have the law to guide us.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: SEC sues LSU as athletes plead in court to regain eligibility with college sports season underway
description: FILE - Alabama offensive lineman Jaeden Roberts (77) blocks Missouri defensive tackle Sterling Webb (10) during the first half of an NCAA college football game, Saturday, Oct. 26, 2024, in Tuscaloosa, Ala. (AP Photo/Vasha Hunt, File)
text:
Athlete after athlete took the stand in a state courtroom near LSU on Thursday to explain why they should be allowed to return to play college sports after turning pro while the commissioner of the powerful Southeastern Conference argued against them and the league doubled down by filing a lawsuit against the school in federal court.
The extraordinary confrontation came just two days before the 11th-ranked Tigers open the football season at home against Clemson a few miles from the courthouse. East Baton Rouge Parish Judge William Jorden scheduled the hearing over his temporary injunction preventing the NCAA from barring former pros or fifth-year college athletes, a stance also taken by the SEC and other Power Four conferences with rules adopted last week.
Former New Orleans Saints defensive lineman Zxavian Harris and former Cleveland Browns tight end Dae’Quan Wright, two players who hope to suit up for LSU, sat next to each other in the gallery as the hearing began and both took the stand.
Wright testified that he would not have tried to turn pro had he known about the possibility of getting another year in college. He said he was paid a $25,000 signing bonus by Philadelphia and would gladly pay that back for the chance to play for LSU, adding that he made around $1 million during four years in college.
Two LSU soccer players, Jazmin Ferguson and Jocelyn Ollivierre, won court earlier court orders and have already played this season. Ferguson testified that she was paid $4,500 by a USL team, but ended her contract and paid the money back in hopes of clearing the way to play for the Tigers again.
FILE – Greg Sankey, commissioner of the Southeastern Conference, speaks during NCAA college basketball women’s SEC Media Day, Oct. 16, 2024, in Birmingham, Ala. (AP Photo/Mike Stewart, File) Credit: AP Photo/Mike Stewart
The athletes testified after SEC Commissioner Greg Sankey was on the stand for more than two hours, defending the league’s authority to enforce its week-old rules barring former pros from returning to play at its 16 member schools. He said school presidents and chancellors felt that they needed to establish a line between professional and college sports and that there needed to be ways to hold schools accountable.
“The line between professional sports and college sports needs to be maintained,” Sankey testified, adding that the league was concerned about incoming athletes being displaced from limited roster spots.
As he spoke, the SEC filed the federal lawsuit against LSU and its leadership in Alabama, alleging the school had “waged a deliberate and coordinated campaign to recruit professional athletes” in defiance of league rules. The court filing against one of the league’s founding members in 1933 seeks an injunction barring LSU from violating the SEC’s First Amendment rights by forcing it to “associate with conduct that is contrary to the conference’s purpose and mission.”
Legal experts said the filing was a backup in case the the SEC loses in state court. Outside the courthouse in Baton Rouge, plaintiffs’ attorney Tony Clayton said: “I got a problem with that. I mean, you go around, you can file this suit in any state. You’re suing LSU. Sue them in Louisiana. You go to our nemesis: Alabama. Really? So, so that lets you know what the commissioner is all about.”
Questioning of Sankey turns sharp
In questioning Sankey, attorneys for the athletes cited numerous examples of when SEC eligibility rules align with NCAA rules, suggesting the potential of collusion. They questioned why league members met last week to adopt stiff penalties for the very actions addressed in the Louisiana state court’s temporary injunction against the NCAA.
The attorneys also asked why the SEC singled out players who signed contracts with specific U.S.-based leagues — the NFL, NBA and WNBA — but not overseas pro leagues or women’s pro soccer leagues. When Sankey tried to qualify an answer about whether the SEC had previously punished a school for adding a player with previous pro experience, Clayton said, “I didn’t ask how to build a clock. I’m just asking what time it is.”
Sankey acknowledged that there had previously been no such punishment, but that it had been considered against Alabama last basketball season when the Crimson Tide briefly added a former G-League player.
There was no indication when Jorden might rule but the football season is already underway and most teams playing this weekend. The SEC requires its schools to submit final 2026 rosters for the season by Friday.
Players going to court has become common
The players in question also include former Denver Broncos defensive back Blake Cotton, who like Harris and Wright is hoping to join LSU and new coach Lane Kiffin.
Wright, who played for Kiffin last season at Mississippi, started practicing at LSU this week, too late to be eligible for Saturday’s home opener against Clemson under the NCAA’s required seven days of practice. Harris, who also played at Ole Miss last season, has committed to LSU, while Cotton, who played at Utah last fall, has been recruited by Kiffin.
All three are among a host of athletes who’ve argued in lawsuits around the country that they are unfairly being denied an opportunity to spend a fifth year in college under newly adopted NCAA rules allowing for five full years of competition. In all, the NCAA says there are approximately 450 athlete plaintiffs seeking additional eligibility through litigation, with some 300 of them winning the ability to play at least for now.
The athletes in the case who signed pro contracts have argued they did so only because current rules that would have allowed them another college season weren’t adopted until after their decisions to leave for the chance to make an NFL roster.
The SEC contends the question before the judge should be a narrow one regarding whether the conference “can enforce and require its member institutions to comply with SEC rules.” The SEC’s proposed punishments include significant fines, up to half-season suspensions for coaches and member universities’ loss of voting privileges on league business matters.
Sankey provided an affidavit stating that SEC university presidents had voted 15-0 in favor of the new rules, with LSU’s Wade Rousse abstaining.
The fight over eligibility between schools and their own conferences and the NCAA has simmered for months and spilled into politics.
Georgia Attorney General Chris Carr reportedly sent a letter of support to Sankey, encouraging him to take “all measures available” to punish LSU if it added former NFL players. Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill, who attended the hearing and chatted with plaintiffs’ attorneys before the proceeding, countered in a brief that the NCAA had subjected athletes in the case to a “classic bait-and-switch.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Pillen, Evnen, county election officials call for changes to Nebraska petition circulator laws
description: LINCOLN — Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, Secretary of State Bob Evnen and multiple county election officials are calling for changes to petitioning in the state amid multiple investigations of possibly fraudulent signatures statewide. Evnen said petitioners submitted about 767,000 signatures for review across 17 separate petitions this year. That includes 85,000[...]
text:
Lancaster County Election Commissioner Todd Wiltgen speaks at a news conference alongside Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen, Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen and Hall County Election Commissioner Tracy Overstreet, from left, at a news conference in the Nebraska State Capitol on Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, Secretary of State Bob Evnen and multiple county election officials are calling for changes to petitioning in the state amid multiple investigations of possibly fraudulent signatures statewide.
Evnen said petitioners submitted about 767,000 signatures for review across 17 separate petitions this year. That includes 85,000 petition pages, each one of which can have no more than 20 signatures. The petitions included statewide ballot measures, Lincoln City Charter amendments and nonpartisan or partisan candidates for the Nov. 3 ballot.
Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen. Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Of the petitions, election officials in at least Lancaster County and Hall County caught and forwarded thousands of signatures suspected to be fraudulent to authorities. As of Aug. 19, six out-of-state circulators had been arrested, and law enforcement was searching for a seventh.
County law enforcement officers are actively reviewing signatures across at least eight 2026 petitions. 
Evnen couldn’t confirm whether more petitions or campaigns are under investigation because of the ongoing criminal investigation. He described attempted fraud as a “despicable act.”
“We caught the signature fraud. This is not an accident,” Evnen said. “This is the result of the hard work and dedication of our county election officials and the hard work and dedication of the people in the Elections Division of the Secretary of State’s Office.”
‘Open to suggestions’
Hall County Election Commissioner Tracy Overstreet hearkened back to 2024, when her office also flagged wrong dates of birth, wrong addresses, misspelled names and bad signatures on two medical cannabis petitions. Some purported signers, law enforcement said at the time, were deceased.
A Grand Island circulator pleaded guilty to having used an old phone book to add names. A jury this spring convicted a York notary for improper notarizations on the circulator’s petition pages. The notary is appealing his convictions.
Hall County Election Commissioner Tracy Overstreet. Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
This election cycle, Overstreet said, her office again flagged possibly fraudulent signatures.
“The bottom line here is that Nebraska’s system works,” Overstreet said. “It was, and it is, successful in identifying fraudulent signatures, which are then not counted toward the thresholds that need to be met to put measures on the ballot.”
Overstreet cautioned that while the process works, it comes at a cost to taxpayers, as county officials put in extra hours while petition supporters want a quick answer. 
Overstreet and Lancaster County Election Commissioner Todd Wiltgen are co-chairs of an Election Law Committee for a statewide association of all 93 county clerks, registers of deeds and election commissioners. Overstreet said the association is discussing possible improvements to signature gathering.
“Our association is pledging to work closely with the Governor’s Office, the Secretary of State’s Office, the Legislature’s Government, Military and Veterans Affairs Committee and the full Unicameral in making our gold standard election system even better,” Overstreet said.
Overstreet said whether to reform the notary process, to combat situations like that in 2024, has not come up in conversation, though a possible registry of petition circulators, similar to one for notary publics, has come up. Evnen said the role of sponsors in oversight will be part of discussions.
“We’re open to suggestions for all improvements,” Overstreet said.
‘Essential firewall’
Election officials in other states might verify a small sample of signatures, Evnen said, but in the Cornhusker State, signatures are reviewed line by line, by hand, until enough are verified according to state law.
The process includes verifying a signer’s name, date of birth and address with their information on file. If that information checks out, the voter’s signature is also cross-referenced.
Lancaster County Election Commissioner Todd Wiltgen. Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Wiltgen and his office flagged more than 13,300 signatures as possibly fraudulent on three petitions seeking to amend the Lincoln City Charter this year. The Good Government Lincoln campaign has said it supports Wiltgen’s work and his referral to law enforcement. The group restarted its efforts and submitted more signatures.
Wiltgen said all presumption is given toward a signature being valid, Wiltgen said, but there are multiple steps in checking, including for signature characteristics alone.
Pillen described the county process as an “essential firewall” achieved through a “robust, multilayered verification framework that we all need to be proud of.” At the “heart,” he said, are local officials.
Ending ‘bounty signatures’
Pillen and Evnen repeated their call Thursday to prohibit paying circulators per signature. Such a ban existed between July 2008 and August 2015. A bipartisan group of lawmakers approved that law, overriding a veto from former Gov. Dave Heineman, but seven years later, a different group of lawmakers reversed it, with no opposition, under then-Gov. Pete Ricketts.
Petition pages reviewed by local county election officials and returned to the Nebraska Secretary of State’s Office sit in the office for public inspection at the office’s Elections Division in downtown Lincoln on Aug. 24, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Former state Sen. DiAnna Schimek of Lincoln, a longtime, powerful Democrat in the Legislature who also chaired the Legislature’s Government, Military and Veterans Affairs Committee, ushered in the 2008 ban. Pillen said she “got it right.”
“The process of bounty signature gathering is sabotaging legitimate petition initiative efforts. It’s as simple as that,” Pillen said. “It’s not the Nebraska way.”
Pillen joked that the “only place” Nebraskans should be hearing the word “bounties” is on the radio and TV Western drama “Gunsmoke.”
The first petition campaigns that could again pay per signature, and which later went to voters, were those seeking to opt Nebraska into Medicaid expansion statewide and locally amend the Lincoln City Charter to place term limits on the Lincoln mayor, each in 2018. Both passed.
Other suggested reforms
Evnen said he is also working on legislation that would restrict circulators to U.S. citizens and nonfelons and require that prospective circulators complete training detailing their job and responsibilities. Circulators would also need to affirmatively consent to the laws of Nebraska.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, at podium, and Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen, center left, join Election Commissioners Danielle Jensen (Douglas County), Todd Wiltgen (Lancaster County), Tracy Overstreet (Hall County) and David Jones (Sarpy County) for a news conference regarding thousands of signatures suspected to be fraudulent on 2026 petitions in the Nebraska State Capitol on Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
In addition to legislation, Pillen said there needs to be a cultural shift where petitioners “prioritize genuine voter engagement over raw volume” of signatures.
“I’m a believer that the people speak as the second house in Nebraska,” Pillen said. “I believe the people speak when we come together without being coerced by money.”
Evnen’s office has in the past also suggested moving up the petition deadline and expanding the time for officials to review signatures. But he said he hasn’t given further thought to that idea and expects technology will become more accurate and more cost effective in the future, too.
For now, Evnen said, “we’ll stick with what we have” with physical verification.
“Nebraskans once again owe a debt of gratitude to our counties because they do this heavy lifting, and they do it very, very well,” Evnen said. “They’re dedicated, responsible people who are highly competent in their work, and they’re the ones who give Nebraskans the elections that they can be proud of.”
‘Few bad apples’
Former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha, who is challenging Pillen’s reelection under the America First Party ballot line, told the Nebraska Examiner that the reforms Evnen outlined “seem prudent.” His early nonpartisan bid for governor this summer went down in smoke, in part due to overlapping petition circulators who law enforcement say submitted fraudulent signatures.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen of Columbus, a Republican, bottom left, is running for reelection against former Democratic state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, bottom right, Rick Beard of Omaha, the nominee for the Legal Marijuana NOW party, top left, and former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha, the nominee for the America First party, top right. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Lindstrom was one of the 42 of 49 lawmakers who reversed the pay-per-signature ban in 2015. He said he learned firsthand how that could backfire.
“The vast majority of people I don’t think are out there trying to scam,” Lindstrom said. “But a few bad apples ruin the bunch, and you had this ripe for fraud.”
Lindstrom reiterated that he will be pursuing legal action because of how his nonpartisan bid ended.
Former state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, Pillen’s Democratic challenger, said in a statement that the suspected fraud this year is a “historic attack” on Nebraskans’ right to govern themselves. She said that can’t go unanswered and is calling on Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers to appoint a special prosecutor.
“Governor Pillen has spent two years trying to block and override what Nebraska voters have already decided, and now he wants to use this fraud as cover to make the citizen ballot initiative process harder to use,” Walz said. “The people in Nebraska expect answers.”
‘False implications and phony innuendos’
While not giving specifics, Evnen used his time Thursday to push back on what he described as people “running around our state doing everything they can to make Nebraskans feel worried and unsure and uncertain about our elections.”
“They don’t have facts or evidence, so they’re peddling false implications and phony innuendos. It’s shameful what they’re doing,” Evnen said. “No state runs better elections than Nebraska. No state runs elections that are more secure and accurate than we do.”
A woman signs a Support Our Schools petition in Omaha. July 8, 2024. (Aaron Sanderford/Nebraska Examiner)
Asked to clarify what he meant, Evnen said a “litany of things” regarding elections are being repeated statewide, including those he said his office has examined and found no validity. He did not give examples.
“We’re not vulnerable to these things, and yet they continue to get repeated,” Evnen said.
Evnen had been running for a third four-year term until May, when he lost the Republican primary to Scott Petersen of Omaha, who specifically criticized Evnen and has called for more significant changes to the administration of Nebraska elections.
Also running for Evnen’s seat are Democrat Sarah Slattery of Plattsmouth, Paul Rumbaugh of Omaha for the Nebraska Working People Party and former state Sen. Bob Krist of Omaha for the America First Party. Evnen has not endorsed anyone in the race.
Pillen repeated that election integrity is “about Nebraska” and that every Nebraskan should know that when they get out to vote, their voice will be heard with confidence in the outcome.
“We will continue to ensure that our ballots remain secure, transparent and driven strictly by Nebraskans,” Pillen said.
The general election is Nov. 3.
