text:
People walk through Salt Lake City International Airport in Salt Lake City on Wednesday, April 3, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Salt Lake City International Airport is one of 14 airports that will allow approved visitors to send off or greet travelers at airport gates rather than waiting outside security checkpoints.
Gateside passes are available to those approved for by the Transportation Security Administration for TSA PreCheck, according to a TSA webpage about the program. 
The passes are free and require an application one to three days before the visit using a known traveler number, according to the website, and visitors can enter the airport through TSA PreCheck lanes. Children can also be included on the pass.
“As an exclusive benefit for our most trusted travelers, this new program makes it easier to return to the gate for welcomes and send-offs, meet friends during a layover, and enjoy dining and shopping along the way, bringing back the moments that once defined air travel,” the website states. 
Accommodations for non-travelers accompanying a child or elderly passenger or a passenger with accessibility needs to airport gates currently exist through individual airlines, according to the airport.
Salt Lake City’s airport is known for large, emotional gatherings as family and friends greet missionaries from the Utah-based Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints when they return home after up to two years of service. The airport’s remodel even includes a greeting room just outside the security exit intended to move large greeting parties out of the walkway, with mixed success.
The Salt Lake airport is the 24th busiest in the U.S. and the 98th busiest in the world, according to its website, with more than 330 departures daily with 100 nonstop travel destinations.
The 14 airports participating in the gateside program are:

Arizona: Mesa Gateway Airport
Arkansas: Bill and Hillary Clinton National Airport
California: Los Angeles International Airport
California: San Diego International Airport
Indiana: Indianapolis International Airport
Kansas: Wichita Dwight D. Eisenhower National Airport
Michigan: Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport
Nebraska: Eppley Airfield
Nevada: Harry Reid International Airport
Ohio: John Glenn Columbus International Airport
Oklahoma: Will Rogers International Airport
Texas: Dallas Fort Worth International Airport
Utah: Salt Lake City International Airport

A Delta Airlines jet takes off at Salt Lake City International Airport in Salt Lake City on Wednesday, April 3, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Some university leaders not happy with Legislature’s enrollment oversight
description: Some members of the Florida Board of Governors and other university leaders hope the Florida Legislature will backtrack on a last-minute policy that ties their budgets to a limit on out-of-state enrollment.  Put simply, the BOG, which supervises the State University System, can deny a university’s attempt to increase out-of-state tuition fees if the school [[...]
text:
The University of Florida football stadium in Gainesville. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Some members of the Florida Board of Governors and other university leaders hope the Florida Legislature will backtrack on a last-minute policy that ties their budgets to a limit on out-of-state enrollment. 
Put simply, the BOG, which supervises the State University System, can deny a university’s attempt to increase out-of-state tuition fees if the school enrolls more than the system-wide cap of non-Floridian students — now a max of 10% of the student body systemwide.
That language was in HB 5601E, primarily known for transferring the University of South Florida Sarasota-Manatee campus to New College of Florida, and won approval during the Legislature’s special session to pass the state budget in May.
Board of Governors members voted without controversy Thursday to go along, following the direction of the Legislature, but held a lengthy conversation following the vote.
Board of Governors Chair Alan Levine said he hopes the panel will reach an official position on the matter during its meeting later this month.
For now, some university leaders made their position clear, citing fear of diluting academic standards of Florida universities.
“I think the question you have to ask yourselves is, how good do you want us to be? And if you don’t want us to be great, yeah, we can start admitting a lot more students that don’t meet the criteria. But I don’t think that that should be the goal,” Florida State University Board of Trustees Chair Peter Collins said.
UF Board of Trustees Chair Mori Hosseini (Photo via UF)
Instead of admitting students otherwise denied for not meeting academic standards, Collins suggested an alternative.
“The Legislature, or the BOG, instead of doing this, maybe we consider creating a new university. Maybe we just don’t have enough universities,” Collins said. 
University of Florida Board of Trustees Chair Mori Hosseini said, “I believe it is a travesty for legislators to, first of all, do the job of Board of Governors, and, secondly, in the middle of the night, pass something that would really harm the universities.” 
Hosseini said, for his part, that he will talk with legislators about addressing the policy during the next legislative session. 
To achieve higher national rankings, a university may be incentivized to enroll fewer students to avoid disrupting its average academic performance, Hosseini said.
In pursuit of earning a top-five ranking, Hosseini said, “what is going to happen is this: If we can’t get the students out of state that are high GPA and high SAT/ACT, then what we are going to do is bring the number of students down so the percentages don’t affect us.”
Florida Atlantic University President and former Florida House member Adam Hasner concurred, adding that universities cannot control how many students accept or decline admissions offers, making balancing in-state versus out-of-state admissions difficult.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Under the new state law, if a university under-projects its percentage of out-of-state students, it is required to take corrective action such as an enrollment reduction plan.
Collins suggested that if decision-makers want to slow down the number of out-of-state students admitted, it’d be wise to continue to raise tuition for out-of-state students. According to a 2025 Board of Governors report, Florida had the third-lowest out-of-state tuition in the nation, although Florida’s schools have increased out-of-state tuition in the past two years. 
The legislation also deleted language that would have capped a single-year raise in out-of-state tuition fees at 15%. 
According to the state’s 2026 accountability plan, in 2025, a majority of the state universities had greater than 10% of students from out of state, with the systemwide average at 10%.
A screenshot of the 2026 SUS Accountability Plan.
Inside the Capitol
Early in the legislative session, the House pushed to cap out-of-state enrollment for incoming freshman classes at 5%, cutting the existing regulation of 10% in half. That language did not make it through.
Lawmakers echoed concerns from constituents, claiming valedictorians of some high schools in the state were unable to attain admission to UF. Rep. Jennifer Kincart Jonsson, a Republican from Lakeland, spearheaded the effort, saying, “We need to open up as many seats for our students as possible. Again, Florida students first.”
According to UF data, the university admitted students from 58 of Florida’s 67 counties for the current academic year.
Collins suggested this provision was the next-best-thing in the eyes of lawmakers who initially pushed for that cap.
“This is like a ham-fisted solution to an issue that wasn’t going to pass the Legislature, and they’re fearful that we’re just going to start admitting a ton of out-of-state students,” Collins said. “It’s awkward, it’s ham-fisted, and it’s a solution to a problem that I’m not sure we want to solve.” 
The FSU chair advocated for a student body with zip codes beyond the Sunshine State. “What are we learning if we’re just going to school with our neighbors?” Collins asked.
“Personally, I think that all of us in this room that went to a university benefitted from meeting people outside of the state of Florida,” he observed. “We enrolled people from every state and many different countries in our upcoming fall class. The idea that we should get down to 5% out-of-state students, in my mind, is ridiculous.”
Former state Sen. Doug Broxson. (Photo via Florida Senate)
Board of Governors member Doug Broxson, a former legislator, encouraged caution in bucking the Legislature. 
“The people of the state gave $8 billion to higher education last year. With that, comes the responsibility to those citizens who paid that money,” Broxson said. “This is something we need to be extremely careful that we do not offend our provider in saying that we are resisting what they are hearing from their constituents.”
Levine acknowledged the frustration, but added, “If UF is trying to cement its place as a top tier university … well, the reality is that’s not by accident, that was a lot of hard work and by design. … If we don’t have the policy levers to use to make decisions for each of our institutions based on what we’re trying to accomplish for that institution, that’s a disservice.”
“There are times where the Board of Governors needs to assert our policy independence as it comes to our ability to govern these institutions,” Levine said.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Gold argues for more state money for university, despite Nebraska’s financial woes
description: LINCOLN — University of Nebraska President Jeffrey Gold sought Thursday to make the case for NU’s request for more money in the state budget as the Nebraska Legislature braces to address the state’s financial woes in the upcoming legislative session.  In his State of the University speech, Gold gave a laundry list of how the […]
text:
University of Nebraska President Jeffrey Gold gives his State of the University speech in the Capitol Rotunday on Sept. 3, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — University of Nebraska President Jeffrey Gold sought Thursday to make the case for NU’s request for more money in the state budget as the Nebraska Legislature braces to address the state’s financial woes in the upcoming legislative session. 
In his State of the University speech, Gold gave a laundry list of how the university brings “more than $10 for every dollar of state investment.” He pointed to the university’s involvement in responding to a hantavirus outbreak earlier this year, including the quarantine of 18 Americans at the National Quarantine Unit in Omaha, and he noted that Nebraska Extension was “central” to the state’s response to the wildfires this spring and summer. 
He told the crowd at the State Capitol Rotunda that the university has “long been a careful steward of the resources entrusted” to it.
“But after years of reductions, we have reached a point where continued cuts will unfortunately increasingly mean doing less for the people who depend on us,” Gold said. “We have lost talented people and valuable programs that make a difference for our students, our communities and our state.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The university is seeking $166 million more from the state’s next biennium budget. That sets up a likely clash with Gov. Jim Pillen, who is asking NU and other state agencies to cut spending by 5% — though Pillen’s memo raised questions from others about whether the governor has the power to impose such a cut without legislative approval.
Nebraska is facing a nearly $850 million deficit by mid-2029 that state lawmakers will have to figure out. In 2024, NU requested a 3.5% increase for each year of the 2025-27 budget cycle; Pillen suggested a 2% cut in the first fiscal year in January 2025. 
Ultimately, lawmakers increased NU’s budget by about 0.6% each year of those two years. Gold told the press after his address that NU has “tried to do more with less. In the last couple of years, we tried to do the same with less.”
“Last year we had to make some very hard decisions,” Gold said. 
The University of Nebraska-Lincoln saw four programs eliminated as part of $27.5 million in budget reductions, including $6.5 million in proactive cuts. The NU system cut $40 million across all its campuses.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Two former top Jackson State University administrators settle sex discrimination lawsuits
description: The H. P. Jacobs Administration Tower on the Jackson State University campus in Jackson, Wednesday, Aug. 13, 2025.
text:
Jackson State University and the state college board have settled two sex discrimination lawsuits that were filed during Marcus Thompson’s brief tenure as the university’s president. 
On Aug. 25, the Mississippi Institutions of Higher Learning Board resolved a sex discrimination lawsuit filed in federal court by Debra Mays-Jackson, former JSU vice president and chief of staff. The details of the settlement are not publicly available, though Mississippi Today has filed a public records request for the settlement agreement from the state’s college board.
Marcus Thompson addressed reporters in his first press conference as Jackson State University’s 13th president on Nov. 30, 2023. Credit: Molly Minta/Mississippi Today
In 2023, Mays-Jackson sued the IHL board of trustees the same day it tapped Marcus Thompson to be president of Jackson State. Mays-Jackson contended that she was passed over for JSU’s presidency in favor of Thompson, a less experienced man. 
In her lawsuit, Mays-Jackson alleged she applied for the top job but was denied an interview. She said she wasn’t given the opportunity to be considered for the role because the state’s college board used a policy that allowed trustees to suspend the president search and hire anyone known to the board, regardless whether that person applied for the role.  
Trustees claimed qualified immunity, a legal protection from liability for government officials, in an effort to have the case dismissed. A district court judge ruled the trustees could not claim qualified immunity, but trustees appealed that decision.
In December, a federal appeals court sided with the lower court’s ruling and the case moved forward. Trustees and Mays-Jackson reached a settlement Aug. 25 and the case was dismissed, bringing closure to the three-year legal battle. Thompson resigned as president in May 2025 after a little more than a year of becoming leader of the institution. 
Attorneys for both Mays-Jackson and Thompson declined to comment when reached by Mississippi Today.
In June, Jackson State University reached a $150,000 settlement with Linda Rush, the former interim vice president of enrollment management at JSU. Rush alleged in a federal lawsuit that Thompson passed her over for a promotion and that she was subsequently fired because of her age and sex. A federal judge dismissed several of Rush’s claims last year but allowed one sex discrimination claim against Thompson to proceed.
Rush, who was 61 when she was fired, worked at Jackson State for nearly 25 years before her termination, according to her lawsuit. 
Thompson became JSU president in November 2023 and selected Kylon Alford-Windfield to lead the enrollment management division in January 2024. 
In her lawsuit, Rush accuses Thompson of favoring Alford-Windfield, a younger male colleague, for the permanent role. Thompson and Alford-Windfield were classmates in Jackson State’s executive doctoral program in urban higher education and fraternity brothers in Kappa Alpha Psi, according to the lawsuit. 
Rush alleges that after Alford-Windfield took over the division, she continued performing duties associated with his job, including preparing his cabinet reports and speaking notes. Sixty days later, Alford-Windfield fired Rush without reason, offered to write her a letter of recommendation and had her escorted from campus, according to the lawsuit. 
As part of the settlement, Rush also agreed not to apply to work at Jackson State or other public universities IHL oversees. If she does apply, the agreement says the university is not obligated to consider her application. Jackson State and Thompson did not admit wrongdoing as part of the settlement.
Ross, who also represents Rush, declined to comment, as did attorneys for Alford-Winfield, Thompson and the university. Attorneys for the state’s college board did not respond to a request for comment.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Fazio opposed to data-center tax break, not data centers
description: Fazio sidestepped the broader data center controversy by focusing on an economic development measure signed into law five years ago.
text:
Republican gubernatorial candidate Ryan Fazio nibbled Thursday at the edges of a national controversy over data centers that grew hotter Monday with President Donald Trump mocking opponents, even those who are in his own party and on the ballot this year.
“The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” Trump posted on his Truth Social site. “If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign. The good news is that there are plenty of other places that want them.”
Fazio sidestepped the broader controversy — or any conflict with the president — by focusing his opposition to a bipartisan economic development measure that Gov. Ned Lamont signed into law five years ago with hopes of drawing NASDAQ, the tech-heavy stock index, to Connecticut.
The law offered a sales tax rebate that has been used by just one company: Cigna saved an estimated $17 million of the $21 million in sales taxes on $386 million in improvements to its data center in Windsor through July 1, 2025, according to the Department of Economic and Community Development’s annual report.
“We now have a very clear example of unfairness and unaffordability in the case of the Windsor data center — $17 million in a special tax subsidy for a data center in Windsor paid for by you, the taxpayer,” Fazio said in a press conference in Windsor.
Fazio, the ranking Republican on the legislature Energy and Technology Committee, said he was not calling for a blanket ban or moratorium on data centers, which are major consumers of electricity that are blamed for increasing rates by driving up demand.
“We’re calling to end this special tax benefit for data centers, to put guardrails on the industry, and to require that they bring their own power if they are to plug into the grid,” Fazio said. “These are common-sense reforms that will protect taxpayers, will protect ratepayers, make Connecticut more affordable.”
Public and private polling indicates that the rapid growth of artificial intelligence and the data centers necessary for A.I. are a potent issue.
The National Republican Senatorial Committee warned in a recent memo reported by the New York Times and others that former U.S. Sen. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat seeking a comeback in Ohio for the seat once held by Vice President JD Vance, is using data centers to generate opposition to U.S. Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio.
“Ohio is one of the leaders in building these AI factories. Brown has made his opposition to them the centerpiece of his campaign against Husted. Brown is using it because it works. More than any other thing in this race, data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck,” the NRSC wrote in an Aug. 18 memo.
Fazio said he was unaware of Trump’s widely reported social media mockery of opponents to data centers.
The bill passed five years ago preceded the A.I. revolution — and the growing hostility to data centers. 
“This was not about hyperscale data centers and what we’re all thinking of now. This was for data centers that could be used for biotech companies,” said Sen. James Maroney, D-Milford, the legislature’s expert on A.I. “It was about insurance companies being able to better provide the services and keep their data centers and invest in an existing data center.”
Legislative leaders fast-tracked the bill with an emergency certification that bypassed the normal process of review by legislative committees or a public hearing. It passed on votes of 29-5 in the Senate and 133-13 in the House and was signed by the governor on March 4, 2021.
Only one Republican in the Senate was opposed. Fazio won his Senate seat in a special election five months later.
Maroney was dispatched by the governor’s campaign to offer a rapid rebuttal to Fazio.
“We passed this back at a time before hyperscale data centers were envisioned, and many other states did the same thing,” Maroney said. 
The majority of states waive at least some of the sales taxes on computer hardware equipment for data centers, he said, citing a survey by the National Conference of State Legislatures.
“And some even give incentives reducing the cost of electricity for data centers, which we do not do,” Maroney said.
The 2021 law authorizes DECD to reach tax incentive agreements with “qualified data centers” for 20- or 30-year terms, depending on the size and location of the investment. To be eligible, a data center must agree to make a “qualified investment” of at least $50 million if located in an enterprise zone or a federal opportunity zone or $200 million if located elsewhere.
The law also exempts the improvements from the property tax, while allowing host communities to negotiate offsetting fees.
The program is one of many offering tax incentives for capital investments and job creation and retention. Their efficacy is a frequent source of legislative debate.
Fazio counted himself among the doubters.
“I think that everybody needs tax relief in this state, and when you give one dollar to a large corporation, that tax relief is coming at the expense of everybody else,” Fazio said. “Why isn’t this small business that we’re in today getting a special tax benefit? They create jobs. They create more jobs than the data center, and yet they don’t have access to a special tax benefit.”
The press conference was in the bar of a downtown restaurant in a converted firehouse.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota lawmakers call Military Gallery a ‘black eye,’ but will move forward
description: The North Dakota Senate passed a $20 million construction loan to restart work on the stalled Military Gallery, though several are disappointed no one is being held accountable for the project’s failures.  Members approved Senate Bill 2407 by a vote of 39-8 on Thursday during a special session called to address the lack of kratom […]
text:
Bill Peterson, director of the State Historical Society of North Dakota, gives a tour of the unfinished Military Gallery to state lawmakers on Sept. 2, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)The North Dakota Senate passed a $20 million construction loan to restart work on the stalled Military Gallery, though several are disappointed no one is being held accountable for the project’s failures. 
Members approved Senate Bill 2407 by a vote of 39-8 on Thursday during a special session called to address the lack of kratom regulation in the state. 
Sen. Dale Patten, R-Watford City, said the Legislature should focus on finding solutions to an unfinished building project on the Capitol grounds. 
“That black eye stays on the Capitol grounds until we do find a solution. Every morning when we get up and we haven’t solved it is like getting punched in the eye again,” Patten said.

More special session coverage

The amended bill will be considered by the House on Friday. It unlocks $15 million of funding that had already been earmarked for the project and authorizes a $20 million line of credit to keep construction going while fundraisers renew efforts to seek private donors. 
“I think we need to honor the military,” said Sen. Randy Burckhard, R-Minot. “And it’s too late to go back.”
Sen. Brad Bekkedahl, R-Williston, said he has confidence donations will be able to repay the $20 million line of credit in full. The line of credit is officially due to be repaid by March 31, 2029, but future lawmakers will have the option to extend the deadline. 
Sen. Ron Sorvaag, R-Fargo, said the fundraising firm for the project “failed at their job” so far. But he said he still supported the bill as the best option.
“Could the state get stuck paying for that? Absolutely,” Sorvaag said. “They fundraised but they didn’t collect any money. Why would they now? I don’t think there’s any guarantees, except for the fact that it’s in the spotlight now.”
Sen. Brad Bekkedahl, R-Williston, speaks on the Senate floor during a special session of the Legislature on Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Sen. Jose Castaneda, R-Minot, said it is his intention that future lawmakers will extend the deadline for as long as it takes for private donations to repay the loan from the Bank of North Dakota. The only additional cost on taxpayers should be potentially paying the interest that accrues over time, he said. 
New $20M loan recommended for Military Gallery to restart construction

The $78 million project’s funding will remain evenly split between the state and private donors, so long as the $20 million construction loan is repaid. But that balance would be disrupted if private fundraising doesn’t pick up. 
“The state will have an exposure of $59 million,” said Sen. David Clemens, R-West Fargo. 
Insufficient oversight
Legislative leaders emphasized the special session was not the appropriate venue to hold officials accountable for past mistakes on the project. Bekkedahl said this week it is a time for “resolution, not recrimination.”
But that can’t be a permanent attitude, multiple lawmakers said. 
“We have to look back to have accountability,” Castaneda said. “Something needs to be done because this was atrocious and unacceptable.”
Sen. Jose Castaneda, R-Minot, speaks on the Senate floor during a special session of the Legislature on Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
While Castaneda supported the bill, other lawmakers said they opposed it because it didn’t hold officials accountable for the project’s failures and did not create enough new oversight.
“We’re doing an incredible disservice to our constituents,” said Sen. Sean Cleary, R-Bismarck. “This is just kind of a lose-lose situation at this point.”
Clemens, a veteran, said many members of his family have served in the country’s wars going back nearly a century. He said he is grateful for the state’s veterans, but wouldn’t support the bill out of respect to taxpayers. 
“As we move forward, I believe we owe the taxpayers of North Dakota an apology for not being better watchmen. I apologize, and to the best of my ability, will work to see that it never happens again,” Clemens said. 
The bill places oversight of the project in the hands of the Capitol Grounds Planning Commission, which includes four lawmakers. The State Historical Society will also be required to report quarterly to the Legislature’s Budget Section on the status of construction and fundraising progress.
Sen. David Clemens, R-West Fargo, speaks on the Senate floor during a special session of the Legislature on Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Sen. Jonathan Sickler, R-Grand Forks, said he understands the project is at a standstill and a solution needs to be found. But he said in an interview he wants to see accountability from those involved in the project’s key decisions in the wake of the July 3 pause of construction. 
“That’s a clear sign something has gone wrong,” Sickler said. 
Sickler said he is particularly concerned about what he has heard about apparent disagreements among project leaders as to whether construction should have begun when it did in the summer of 2025. 
“Particularly as we look at agency budgets, I suspect there will be a strong amount of attention paid to how agencies performed during this process, and there will be additional due diligence done as part of that,” Sickler said. 
Military Gallery construction project stalls with fundraising lagging in North Dakota

House to vote Friday
The bill appears to have support among the Republican majority in the House, according to representatives’ comments during a caucus meeting Thursday. 
“I think we’ve landed in a good spot. We’re being good stewards. We’re not spending more money than we appropriated this session, and we’re giving our contractors the ability to move forward,” said Rep. Glenn Bosch, R-Bismarck, one of the key lawmakers involved in drafting the amended bill. 
Rep. Don Vigesaa, R-Cooperstown, said the pause in construction was costing the state $157,000 per month, and something has to be done to get the project moving again. He added that he is optimistic about the update provided Wednesday. 
“There’s a lot of potential fundraising that’s going to be coming in, and I love the fact that this construction loan doesn’t have an end date. So they can keep paying on it as long as it takes,” Vigesaa said. 
Graphic rendering of the courtyard and amphitheater area outside of the North Dakota Military History Museum. (Contributed/State Historical Society of North Dakota)
Rep. Brandy Pyle, R-Casselton, said the bill shows their commitment to North Dakotans, that lawmakers believe in the military and that the state of North Dakota has confidence the fundraisers will get the job done.
“It’s not the fundraisers’ fault that the shovel went in early. But they’re kind of getting blamed for it, and I don’t think that’s fair,” Pyle said.

title: Wildfire SNAP benefits extended to Sept. 7
description: Northern Nevada residents who lost food purchased with Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits due to the Bug, Fred, Stallion or Hawk fires or related power outages can request replacement benefits through September 7, 2026. Four major fires in the last month have burned through more than 100,000 acres in Northern Nevada, prompting the evac[...]
text:
(Stock photo by hapabapa/Getty Images)Northern Nevada residents who lost food purchased with Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits due to the Bug, Fred, Stallion or Hawk fires or related power outages can request replacement benefits through September 7, 2026.
Four major fires in the last month have burned through more than 100,000 acres in Northern Nevada, prompting the evacuation of thousands of residents and the breakdown of major infrastructure. 
The U.S. The Department of Agriculture’s Food and Nutrition Service approved an extension to allow those affected by the fires to report their losses and receive replacement SNAP benefits beyond the standard 10 days.
Each request will be reviewed to determine eligibility and, if eligible, the amount of replacement benefits that may be provided, according to the Nevada Division of Social Services. 
SNAP recipients affected by the fires or related power outages can report their food loss by visiting a local DSS office or calling (775) 684-7200.
The Nevada Division of Social Services said they are also pursuing options to support households affected by the Oxley-McConnell fires as they await federal approval for a SNAP extension.
“DSS understands the profound impact these fires have had on individuals, families, and communities across Nevada. We recognize that losing food and other essential resources can add to the stress and uncertainty families are already experiencing. DSS is committed to standing with affected households and helping them access available resources and assistance as they recover and move forward,” said Kristle Muessle, a public information officer with DSS.
The White House issued a presidential emergency declaration for Nevada following the Hawk Fire impacting northwest Reno on Wednesday.
The emergency declaration seeks immediate federal assistance to protect public health and safety, as well as to maintain essential services and support communities still recovering from the Hawk Fire.
The Federal Emergency Management Agency approved federal disaster assistance for Washoe County in Nevada following the Hawk Fire. 
The emergency declaration authorizes immediate federal assistance to protect public health and safety, as well as to maintain essential services and support communities still recovering from the Hawk Fire.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kobach urged Congress to legislate birth tourism hours before judge blocked Trump’s order
description: TOPEKA — Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach slammed the U.S. Supreme Court majority that blocked President Donald Trump’s effort to unravel birthright citizenship, suggesting its decision “may not stand the test of time.” Testifying before a U.S. House subcommittee Wednesday, Kobach encouraged Congress to pass a law that would cement Trump’s Aug. 6 executiv[...]
text:
Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach appears on Capitol Hill on Sep. 2, 2026, testifying before a U.S. House Judiciary subcommittee about birthright citizenship. His daughter appears behind him. (U.S. House Judiciary Committee)TOPEKA — Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach slammed the U.S. Supreme Court majority that blocked President Donald Trump’s effort to unravel birthright citizenship, suggesting its decision “may not stand the test of time.”
Testifying before a U.S. House subcommittee Wednesday, Kobach encouraged Congress to pass a law that would cement Trump’s Aug. 6 executive order that targeted “birth tourism.” He made the urging hours before the executive order was blocked Wednesday by a federal judge.
Kobach was one of at least 25 state attorneys general who supported the government’s position in the U.S. Supreme Court case Trump vs. Barbara that upheld birthright citizenship, the constitutional guarantee that people born in the United States are United States citizens regardless of the parents’ citizenship. 
He called the court’s June decision “weakly reasoned.”
But Kobach praised Justice Clarence Thomas’ 91-page dissent and said it was “truly bizarre” that the majority opinion rested “on this futile notion that you are attached to the lord of the soil.”
“I suggest that this decision may not stand the test of time,” Kobach said.
He added: “This one, because it is so weakly reasoned, is particularly vulnerable.”
Democrats on the U.S. House Judiciary’s subcommittee on the Constitution and Limited Government expressed frustration and confusion as to the purpose of the hearing, since the Supreme Court decision precludes Congress from altering birthright citizenship in the way Trump envisioned.
But Kobach encouraged Congress to consider narrowly tailoring a federal law to address “birth tourism,” or the act of entering a country while pregnant to secure U.S. citizenship for one’s child once born. Mimicking Trump’s Aug. 6 executive order in statute could pass muster, he said.
Then, a federal judge Wednesday blocked the Trump administration from enforcing the order that attempted to redefine birthright citizenship. U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman referred to the Supreme Court’s June decision in her own decision, calling Trump’s order “almost certainly unconstitutional.”
Kobach appeared alongside Ken Cuccinelli, former acting deputy secretary of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and former Virginia attorney general; Rosemary Jenks, policy director at the Immigration Accountability Project; and Jonathan Weinberg, Wayne State University law professor.
Kobach, Cuccinelli and Jenks shared the sentiment that the Supreme Court got its decision wrong.
Weinberg said it would be “chaos” to implement Trump’s vision for eradicating birthright citizenship. Applying it prospectively, as the president intended, would be chaotic on its own, Weinberg said, and he theorized Trumps theory would render every current U.S. citizen’s status questionable.
“We’d all have to look around and find out whether we’re citizens or not, trace our lineage back and see if our parents or our grandparents could pass the test set by President Trump’s executive order,” Weinberg said.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico land commissioner shoots down Canadian data center company’s pitch at Spaceport America
description: New Mexico Commissioner of Public Lands Stephanie Garcia Richard on Thursday shot down a Canadian company’s pitch to build a solar-powered data center at Spaceport America. A number of New Mexico county commissions — including the one in Sierra County, where Spaceport is located — have approved data center moratoria this year.
text:
The Gateway to Space building at Spaceport America, pictured on June 8, 2024. (Danielle Prokop/Source NM)New Mexico Commissioner of Public Lands Stephanie Garcia Richard on Thursday shot down a Canadian company’s pitch to build a solar-powered data center at Spaceport America.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Green Data CEO Jason Bak has been in talks with Spaceport officials for years about building a data center on the property, which is on leased state trust land. Bak has engaged in those talks on behalf of another one of his companies, Aetherion.
Earlier this year, Bak unsuccessfully pursued a partnership with New Mexico Tech in Socorro to build a solar-powered data center on 10,000 acres of land. The university in June backed out of the deal, in large part because it lacked enough contiguous land to make it work.
Bak, who has a background in renewable energy infrastructure, has pitched rural New Mexico communities on an eco-friendly vision. He often speaks of employing technology known as “atmospheric water generation” to harvest moisture from the air and turn it into usable water for cooling the data center. At public meetings, he has previously said that he believes such a model could generate a surplus of water for the excessively parched region.
However, neither Bak nor his company has successfully built a data center.
A Canadian developer’s New Mexico data center pitch may be dying. It wouldn’t be the first time

A number of New Mexico county commissions — including the one in Sierra County, where Spaceport is located — have approved data center moratoria this year. In her Thursday letter, Garcia Richard said that applies to the land on which Spaceport sits, too.
“Simply put, I will not be approving any data centers, including the proposed Aetherion sublease at Spaceport America,” she wrote. “It is NMSLO’s position that the County’s moratorium is applicable to proposed activities at Spaceport America.”
Bak did not respond to a request for comment.
Scott McLaughlin, Spaceport’s executive director, told Source NM that he will abide by Garcia Richard’s letter, but left the door open to collaborating with Bak in the future once any applicable moratoria expire.
“We consider the State Land Office and the county to be partners and we want to work together to do what’s best for the county and the state and, of course, for our customers to the extent that we can,” he said, adding that future discussions regarding a potential data center “will be up to Aetherion and Jason Bak.”
A grassroots group of local residents, who have dubbed themselves Project Consequences, on Thursday lauded Garcia Richard’s decision.
“This letter closes the loophole that some apparently hoped existed at Spaceport America,” Monticello resident Sulome Anderson said in a statement. “A developer cannot evade the community simply by putting its project on state land. The State Land Office has now made clear that the county’s moratorium matters, the contractual requirements matter and — most importantly — the will of the impacted community matters.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: In Danbury, Sen. Blumenthal hears ‘emotional’ accounts of ICE operation
description: Richard Blumenthal hosted a town hall with local officials, attorneys and organizers about last week's ICE raid—among largest in CT history.
text:
U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal hosted a town hall in Danbury on Thursday to hear accounts from local elected officials, attorneys and organizers about last week’s immigration enforcement operation — among the largest in the state’s history.
Nearly 100 people across Connecticut were detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers, including more than 60 in Danbury, according to CT Students for a Dream, which tracks arrests based on video footage submitted by rapid response teams.
On Thursday, community organizers described instances of excessive force used by ICE officers during stops. Attorneys said in some cases they’d been prevented from visiting with the detainees who were being held in Hartford. 
“Cruelty is the point. Fear and terror are the goal,” Blumenthal said. “I don’t recognize America in what I saw in Danbury last week.
Blumenthal said the purpose of the town hall event was to “bear witness” and establish a record of what happened in an effort to hold immigration enforcement authorities accountable. House Resolution 1 — often referred to as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” — provided roughly $170 billion for immigration enforcement and border security, Blumenthal said.
A spokesperson for ICE did not respond to a request for comment in time for publication.
Glenn Formica, an attorney with The American Immigrant Legal Clinic, TAILC, recounted being refused access to detainees he believed were being held in Hartford. When Formica asked to meet with them, he was told on several occasions that they were being held in a different location, he said during an interview after the town hall.
“I could have gotten people released potentially from Connecticut, and now I’ve got to travel to Colorado,” said Formica, who is representing roughly 14 Connecticut residents currently being detained there, including four people who he said have “serious medical conditions.”
Formica said Connecticut residents detained last week are now mostly at detention facilities in Massachusetts, Colorado and Rhode Island.
Celina Beatriz Curillo, also an attorney with TAILC, described seeing detainees in Hartford “being brought out in chains — in a chain gang.” Curillo also cautioned people seeking legal representation to be on the lookout for scammers posing as immigration attorneys.
“Please, if you’re hiring a lawyer, always make sure they are a lawyer,” she said in Spanish.
Organizers described seeing and following ICE agents around the city last week. 
Volunteers with Danbury Unites For Immigrants strategize as suspected Immigration and Customs Enforcement vehicles are spotted on Fourth Street in Danbury on Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026.  Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Scott Kemp, a member of the rapid response team with Danbury Unites for Immigrants, described a scene where someone was detained by ICE in front of a Danbury daycare center. When Kemp arrived at the scene, he saw the detainee’s car had a broken window. An agent immediately told him to back up, and motioned toward his handcuffs and pepper spray, Kemp said.
Prior to the town hall, Blumenthal met with families of people who had been detained, who he said preferred not to speak publicly for fear of repercussions for their loved ones. He called their accounts “heartbreaking” and “powerfully emotional,” but declined to provide further details.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Andrew Young visits Mississippi for Medgar Evers lecture
description: Andrew Young shared memories from the civil rights era as he toured the Mississippi Civil Rights Museum, Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026, in Jackson.
text:
Andrew Young wheeled through the Mississippi Civil Rights Museum on Thursday, soaking in the history that he helped make.
The former pastor and civil rights leader, who worked closely with Martin Luther King Jr. at the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, was there during the 1966 March Against Fear in Mississippi. He was there when Grenada public schools began to integrate. Two years later, he was there when King was assassinated at the Lorraine Motel in Memphis. 
When the bullet struck King, it severed his spinal cord, Young said. “He couldn’t feel anything or hear anything.”
The first thing Young thought of as he witnessed the assassination was the Bible story of the prophet Elijah.
Young looked out over the Mississippi River as the sun was sinking in the sky. “It was a beautiful set of clouds,” he said. “It was about 6 o’clock in the evening. I said, ‘Damn, Martin’s going to heaven in a flaming chariot.’”
The former U.S. ambassador to the United Nations is slated to speak at 6 p.m. Thursday in the Medgar Wiley Evers Lecture at the museum. Ebony Lumumba, who chairs the Department of English at Jackson State University, will interview him for the event, sponsored by the Mississippi Department of Archives and History, W.K. Kellogg Foundation and the Medgar & Myrlie Evers Institute.
Inside the museum Thursday, Young saw the pictures of the fight for civil rights and voting rights. He played a role in pushing the 1964 Civil Rights Act and the 1965 Voting Rights Act through Congress.
Two Mississippi Museums Director Michael Morris, left, and civil rights icon Andrew Young talk about the young man between them in the photograph during a tour at the Mississippi Civil Rights Museum, Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
He glimpsed photographs of himself, King and James Meredith making their March Against Fear in Mississippi in June 1966. That march included a terrifying encounter in Philadelphia, where a white mob, including Klansmen, hurled eggs, rocks and racist slurs at the marchers.
In September 1966, when the first Black students tried to attend what had been an all-white public school in Grenada, a white mob attacked them with chains, pipes and clubs.
The mob broke plate glass windows where the students were, Young said. Days later, on Sept. 20, 1966, he, King and folk singer Joan Baez safely escorted the students to school. Young is expected to reunite with some of those former students Thursday.
Young recalled, too, the 1968 Poor People’s March on Washington that started in Marks and ended at the nation’s capital a month later.
In 1972, Young became the first Black member elected to Congress from Georgia since Reconstruction. He served as mayor of Atlanta during the time the city hosted the 1996 Olympic Games and served as co-chair.
Rob Carpenter, left, drove from his Baton Rouge home in order to donate Charles Evers campaign posters to the museum. Carpenter met Reena Evers-Everette, daughter of Medgar Evers, and civil rights icon Andrew Young, Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
The 94-year-old native of New Orleans continues to chair GoodWorks International, an organization that pushes for economic development in the Caribbean and Africa. His memoirs include “A Way Out of No Way” and “An Easy Burden.”
When he saw a photograph of Fannie Lou Hamer, he talked about hearing that she had been beaten in the Winona jail in 1963. Those from the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee who tried to free her were arrested, too.
Young said SCLC intervened to help free Hamer and the others. When Hamer and the others emerged, they heard the awful news that NAACP leader Medgar Evers had been assassinated.
“Medgar Evers has been a hero in my head and my heart,” Young said. “In every picture I see, I see his strong character, and his faith in his people.”
In 1977, the White House provided a plane for Young to travel to Mississippi for Hamer’s funeral, he said. “To have a presidential delegation attend her funeral showed how much progress had been made.”
After finishing his tour Thursday, Young said it’s easy to think the museum deals only with the past.
“We’re not looking back on it, we’re in the middle of it. We would normally look at this exhibit as the old days,” he said. “The only thing we can do is realize this is not history. We’re still in a struggle to save Black men’s bodies and white men’s souls.”
This story will be updated.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Trump administration notches another victory in case on slavery exhibits at Philly President’s House
description: Third Circuit Court of Appeals Judge Thomas Hardiman denied a request from the city of Philadelphia’s lawyers to rehear arguments in its case against the U.S. Department of the Interior and the National Park Service.
text:
An exhibit at the President's House site in Philadelphia featuring the story of Ona Judge before they were replaced. (Photo by Ian Karbal/Capital-Star)Third Circuit Court of Appeals Judge Thomas Hardiman denied a request from the city of Philadelphia’s lawyers to rehear arguments in its case against the U.S. Department of the Interior and the National Park Service.
The city sued after National Park Service workers quietly removed exhibits on slavery from the President’s House historical site in Philadelphia in January.
The signs were reinstalled following a ruling from District Court Judge Cynthia Rufe in February, who issued an injunction ordering the Trump administration not to tamper with them. 
But a panel of judges at the Third Circuit Court of Appeals reversed the injunction, unanimously siding with the federal government and finding the city had no standing to block the move. New exhibits were installed weeks ahead of the July 4 holiday and America250 celebrations.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
While the request for what’s called an en banc review of that decision — essentially a request for a do-over before the full court — was denied Thursday, the case can continue in District Court. The city could also appeal to the conservative-majority U.S. Supreme Court.
“The Department is pleased the Courts have sided with the Trump administration on restoring truth and sanity to our country in our nation’s 250th,” a spokesperson for the U.S. Department of the Interior said in a statement, “These new panels are full of historical context and highlight the momentous events that took place in the President’s House and the other sites at Independence National Historical Park. They acknowledge the evils of slavery, including its injustices and hypocrisies.”
A spokesperson for the city of Philadelphia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The exhibits the Trump administration replaced focused on the lives of nine slaves who served George Washington at the presidential residence in Philadelphia. They were intended to highlight the paradox of freedom and slavery at the founding of America.
Experts have warned that the new exhibits downplay Washington’s role in perpetuating the institution of slavery.

The founder of the Black Journey Philly walking tour on the loss of history at the President’s House


It’s a pattern, historians say, in how the Trump administration has sought to retell American history.
While the Third Circuit Court’s June decision allowing the federal government to replace the exhibits focused on the city of Philadelphia’s lack of legal standing, other plaintiffs in the case can make arguments about harm done to them.
The city is joined by The Black Journey Philadelphia, a company that provides walking tours focused on Black history, and the Avenging the Ancestors Coalition, a Philadelphia-based organization focused on preserving Black history and remembering the legacy of slavery.
The signs were initially removed following an executive order signed by President Donald Trump entitled “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History.”
The order called for a review of material in federally-run museums and national parks that cast “our Nation’s unparalleled legacy of advancing liberty, individual rights, and human happiness is reconstructed as inherently racist, sexist, oppressive, or otherwise irredeemably flawed.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Jobless Iowans accused of workplace misconduct seek unemployment benefits
description: A mental health worker who was fired after being criminally charged with sexual enticement of a minor is entitled to collect unemployment benefits, a judge has ruled. State records indicate Gabriel Kelley, 23, of Cedar Rapids, began working as a full-time, community-based lead worker for the Abbe Center for Community Mental Health in July 2025. […]
text:
Iowa Workforce Development manages unemployment claims filed on behalf of Iowans. (Photo by Getty Images, logo courtesy the State of Iowa)A mental health worker who was fired after being criminally charged with sexual enticement of a minor is entitled to collect unemployment benefits, a judge has ruled.
State records indicate Gabriel Kelley, 23, of Cedar Rapids, began working as a full-time, community-based lead worker for the Abbe Center for Community Mental Health in July 2025. As part of his duties, Kelley was responsible for overseeing two residential facilities, supervising a staff of direct-support professionals and training new employees.
According to state records, Kelley was fired on June 5, 2026, after being charged with two felonies: sexually enticing a minor under the age of 16 and grooming. He later applied for unemployment benefits, which led to a hearing before Administrative Law Judge Patrick Thomas.
Noting that the charged offenses were for alleged conduct that took place outside of work and did not involve any coworkers or individuals associated with the Abbe Center, Thomas ruled recently that Kelley was not discharged for conduct that disqualifies him from collecting jobless benefits.
Thomas noted Kelley has not been found guilty of any criminal offenses and that he maintains his innocence. Unproven and unsubstantiated allegations do not constitute disqualifying, job-related misconduct, Thomas concluded.
Court records indicate Cedar Rapids police created a Reddit profile portraying themselves as a 13-year-old female named Bella. Officer then posted a Reddit thread with “Bella” saying she was bored and looking for fun.
That post allegedly led to Kelley contacting “Bella,” and during the ensuing exchange “Bella” indicated she was 13 years old. According to police, the discussions then became sexual in nature, and Kelley eventually messaged “Bella” to say he was on his way to meet her at her purported home.
At the house, police confronted Kelley, seized his phone, and placed him under arrest. Kelley later entered a plea of not guilty to the charges of sexually enticing a minor under the age of 16 and grooming.
Court records indicate prosecutors offered Kelley a plea deal of some kind on Aug. 27, 2026. A plea hearing is now scheduled for Oct. 1, 2026.
Other Iowans whose unemployment cases were recently decided include:
Heather Dohrmann, who worked for the City of Davenport as a code enforcement officer from June 2024 until she resigned in the spring of 2026. State records indicate Dohrmann was sent to a house on Feb. 11, 2026, to look into a report of vehicles being parked in the yard. During the visit, the homeowner was hostile, began swearing at Dohrmann, and police were summoned. The police arrested the homeowner, and Dohrmann obtained a no-contact against the individual, according to state records.
Sometime later, Dohrmann was asked to go back to the house for a compliance check. She explained to her supervisor she couldn’t go due to the no-contact order, but the supervisor allegedly continued to insist on the compliance check. Without informing the human resources department or upper management of her concerns about intolerable working conditions, Dohrmann quit, according to state records.
Administrative Law Judge Stephanie Adkisson recently ruled Dohrmann was ineligible for jobless benefits, finding that the city had no way of knowing Dohrmann was considering resigning and had no chance to remediate any issues.
Madison Oswalt, who worked for the Animal Rescue League of Iowa as a full-time animal services officer from May 2019 until she was fired on July 15. 2026. As an animal services officer, Oswalt was responsible for responding to calls from citizens and police.
On the night of July 13, 2026, Oswalt was assigned to be the on-call officer tasked with responding to any police calls for assistance with animals. At around 11 p.m., a Des Moines police dispatcher tried calling Oswalt to respond to an incident involving two large, aggressive dogs that were not contained, according to state records. When Oswalt didn’t answer, the dispatcher immediately called Oswalt’s supervisor, who unsuccessfully tried reaching Oswalt several times.
At around 11:30 a.m., Oswalt called the dispatcher and apologized for having missed the earlier call. When informed of the need for assistance, Oswalt appeared to question the nature of the request, then asked the dispatcher for the names of the officers at the scene, according to state records. The call allegedly ended without Oswalt agreeing to respond to the request for assistance.
After speaking to her supervisor, who instructed Oswalt to respond to the call, Oswalt arrived at the home where the dogs were located at about 12:30 a.m. At the time, the ARL later alleged, Oswalt was not wearing the required uniform, protective body armor or body camera. She allegedly spoke so aggressively to the homeowner that the police officers intervened and separated the two, according to state records. A few days later, the ARL fired Oswalt for unprofessional conduct and insubordination, after which Oswalt filed for unemployment.
Recently, Administrative Law Judge Patrick Thomas ruled Oswalt, “through her aggressive and unprofessional conduct,” had committed job-related misconduct that disqualified her from collecting unemployment benefits. Oswalt is now obligated to repay $1,028 in unemployment benefits already collected, Thomas ruled.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Data center nondisclosure bill dies in North Dakota Senate vote
description: North Dakota legislators on Thursday rejected a push to ban the use of nondisclosure agreements between government entities and developers of data centers and other industrial projects. Bill sponsor Sen. Tim Mathern, D-Fargo, tried to persuade lawmakers that the bill was needed to preserve trust in government in the face of multi-billion dollar data center [[...]
text:
Sen. Tim Mathern, D-Fargo, speaks on the Senate floor during a special session of the Legislature on Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota legislators on Thursday rejected a push to ban the use of nondisclosure agreements between government entities and developers of data centers and other industrial projects.
Bill sponsor Sen. Tim Mathern, D-Fargo, tried to persuade lawmakers that the bill was needed to preserve trust in government in the face of multi-billion dollar data center development projects that are popping up around the state. 
“Secrets destroy trust in government,” Mathern said.
Senators voted 32-15 to reject Senate Bill 2406, which included penalties for companies that enter a nondisclosure agreement, also known as an NDA, with a government agency or official. 
A committee on Wednesday recommended rejecting the bill and Republican Gov. Kelly Armstrong on Tuesday testified that the state’s transparency laws were already sufficient, though he said enforcement could be debated. 
Sen. Jerry Klein, R-Fessenden, speaks on the Senate floor during a special session of the Legislature on Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Sen. Jerry Klein, R-Fessenden, on Thursday said the three-day special session was not enough time to deal with all the questions about the bill language that came up in committee, which he chaired. 
“This bill needs full hearings. It needs votes in both chambers. It needs public testimony, and a lot more discussion,” Klein said. 
That discussion could continue in a legislative committee developed to address data center and artificial intelligence issues and in the regular legislative session that begins in January. 
Sen. Janne Myrdal, R-Edinburg, who also is a member of that committee, said the bill was an overreaction, with evidence of only one NDA related to a data center in North Dakota
“Let’s not live in fear,” she said. 
Sen. Dale Patten, R-Watford City, added that local governments in North Dakota are free to pass their own restrictions on nondisclosure agreements. 
The North Dakota League of Cities did not take a position on the NDA bill, said Matt Gardner, executive director for the organization.
“They are not widely used,” Gardner said. “Open records is open records, and cities comply with that all the time.”
He said League of Cities provides training on the state’s open records and meetings laws to its members. 
Rep. Jonathan Warrey, R-Casselton, chair of a legislative committee studying data centers, said he believes a similar bill will be brought forward during the 2027 session. He added the bill shined a light on the issue and put public officials on notice for what specific information can be withheld through the state’s open records laws, such as proprietary, financial, trade secret and health information.
“I don’t want people to be left in the dark,” Warrey said. “The law is already clear on what we can or can’t keep from the public.”
Reporter Michael Achterling contributed to this article. 
Reach North Dakota Monitor deputy editor Jeff Beach at jbeach@northdakotamonitor.com

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Final Journey: Carlisle begins its ninth repatriation of students who never made it home
description: This story was originally published by ICT. WARNING: This story contains disturbing details about boarding schools. If you are feeling triggered, here is a resource list from the National Native American Boarding School Healing Coalition. CARLISLE, Pennsylvania — The Carlisle Barracks Post Cemetery is once again solemnly shrouded with black privacy fencing a[...]
text:
Black privacy fencing shrouds the Carlisle Barracks Post Cemetery on Monday, Aug. 31, 2026, as officials prepare for the disinterment and repatriation of the remains of 12 students who died while attending the notorious Carlisle Indian Industrial School more than 100 years ago. The repatriations are scheduled to run from Sept. 1 to Oct. 12, 2026. (Photo by Charles Fox/Special to ICT)This story was originally published by ICT.
WARNING: This story contains disturbing details about boarding schools. If you are feeling triggered, here is a resource list from the National Native American Boarding School Healing Coalition.
CARLISLE, Pennsylvania — The Carlisle Barracks Post Cemetery is once again solemnly shrouded with black privacy fencing as families and tribal leaders gather to reunite with ancestors who died while attending the Carlisle Indian Industrial School.
Disinterments are set to begin Tuesday, Sept. 1, of the first of 12 students who will be returned to their homelands over the next six weeks as part of the Office of Army Cemetery’s annual repatriation of remains of children who died at the school.
Among the first to go home will be three students from the Fort Peck Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes, who arrived at Carlisle together on April 15, 1890. They all died of tuberculosis over the the next few years.
Descendents and tribal leaders gathered at Carlisle on Monday, Aug. 31, to help them begin their journey home. A celebration is planned for their arrival in Montana.
“The community becomes the family,” Dyan Youpee, the tribe’s cultural preservation director, told the Fort Peck Journal, referring to a phrase that is at the heart of the planned celebration welcoming the children home.     
Christine Redstone was one of three students from the Fort Peck Assiniboine and Sioux Tribe who died while attending the notorious Carlisle Indian Industrial School in Pennsylvania. The remains of Redstone and two other students, Peter Howe and Richard Morgan, were set to be disinterred beginning on Sept. 1, 2026, and repatriated to their homelands in eastern Montana. (Photo by Charles Fox/Special to ICT)
 
Youpee told ICT the event is designed to “shed positive, healing light on the repatriation efforts, journey and reburial.”
The repatriation experience can be a wrenching emotional journey for descendants and tribal leaders, as they retrace the footsteps of ancestors who never have made it back to their families, paired with the triumph of finally bringing them home.
For the Office of Army Cemeteries, which oversees the Carlisle cemetery along with other Army facilities, this will be the ninth round of disinterments, with forensic archaeological and anthropological experts from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers.
Since the repatriations began in 2017, the remains of 58 students have been returned home, leaving numerous gaps among the headstones in the cemetery. Of the 138 graves that remain, the burial sites of 22 children are designated as unknown, with the identities lost to human error when the cemetery moved in 1927.
“The Office of Army Cemeteries team is inspired by the strength and courage from the Native American and Alaska Native Tribes as they make this journey to bring their children home,” Renea Yates, director of the Office of Army Cemeteries, stated in a press release.
“Navigating the disinterment and return process requires the highest level of professional care and compassion and we are committed to providing the expert assistance needed to return their loved ones to their families and communities,” Yates said.
The Army reimburses families for their travel to participate in the disinterment process, the transfer ceremony that follows, and the cost of transport and reburial of the children. After the transfer of custody, families and tribes are free to rebury these children to a location of their choice.
 Government assimilation
The students, who ranged in age from 11 to 18, also include four Alaskan Native students, and a student each from the Comanche Nation, Absentee Shawnee Tribe, Shoshone Paiute Tribes, Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians and the Keweenaw Bay Indian Community.
Most of them died from tuberculosis, although the cause of death was not listed for several of the students in school records.
The barracks housed the Carlisle school from 1879-1918, where nearly 8,000 students from more than 140 tribes attended as part of a government assimilation program that separated them from their families, language and culture. It was the first federally funded, off-reservation Indian boarding school in the U.S., and it served as a model for boarding schools across the U.S. and Canada.
Alaskan Native students Lucy Spaulding (shown as Spalding on the gravestone) and Mabel Stack (shown as Stock) died while attending the Carlisle Indian Industrial School in Pennsylvania more than 100 years ago. Their remains are set to be repatriated back to southeastern Alaska in September 2026. ( Photo by Charles Fox/Special to ICT)
The research of the Alaska Native Heritage Center, known as ANHC, has been instrumental in bringing home the four Alaskan Native students scheduled for disinterment.
“When we do research aimed at bringing home our children, we hope to bring healing to our communities affected by the era of assimilation and its continuing effects,” Benjamin Jacuk, director of Indigenous Research and Healing at ANHC, recently told ICT. “Our work is to bring home the children above all else… Because at the end of the day these children are worth that hard work and that trust.”

The Carlisle Barracks Post Cemetery has been closed to visitors since Aug. 14, and access to the cemetery, enclosed in privacy fencing, will be restricted to federal staff along with tribal members and their families until the completion of the scheduled disinterments, tentatively set for Oct. 12.
 Homecoming preparations
At Fort Peck in eastern Montana, organizers are optimistic the event will bring out a large welcoming crowd.
On July 31, Youpee and others did a non-stop 89-mile Awareness Walk from one end of the reservation to the other to make sure everyone was aware of the upcoming event. Organizers have encouraged people to arrive wearing orange shirts to acknowledge boarding school survivors or traditional regalia, and to create an escort of horseback riders and a caravan of cars to welcome the children home as they reach the reservation border.
More than 135 years after the children left their homelands, the homecoming is an attempt to show love and recognition to the three students.
Organizers want to ensure they are not forgotten or reduced to names on school records, in hopes the community comes together to make sure that no child comes home alone.
 COMING HOME
The remains of 12 students who died at the Carlisle Indian Industrial School are set to be disinterred starting Sept. 1 through Oct. 12. The students include four Alaskan Natives, three from the Fort Peck Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes, and students from five other tribes across the U.S.
Alaskan Natives
*Mabel Stack arrived on Oct. 24, 1903, at age 11, and died Aug. 14, 1904, of tuberculosis. Her last name is listed as Stock on the gravestone and Stack in the Carlisle records, but Booth is believed to be her correct last name.
*Edward Angalook, who is listed as Angelook on his gravestone, arrived Nov. 23, 1903, at age 18, and died Sept. 24, 1905 of tuberculosis.
*Lucy Spaulding arrived Oct. 24, 1903, at age 14, and died March 25, 1905, of tuberculosis. She is listed as Spalding on her gravestone, although her correct last name is believed to be Guthrie.
*Tummassak arrived on Nov. 14, 1897, at age 12, and died on April 8, 1900, of tuberculosis. She is listed as Tomicock on her gravestone and also as Tomiclock in Carlisle archives.
Fort Peck Assiniboine and Sioux Tribe
*Peter Howe arrived at the school on April 15, 1890, at age 16, and died six years later on June 5, 1896, of tuberculosis.
*Richard Morgan arrived  April 15, 1890, at age 17, and died March 25, 1891, of tuberculosis.
*Christine Redstone arrived April 15, 1890, at age 15, and died July 19, 1899, of tuberculosis.
Comanche Nation
*Frances Bones arrived on Nov. 8, 1894, at age 14, and died on May 7, 1895. Her cause of death was not listed in Carlisle records.
Absentee Shawnee Tribe
*Fannie Gibson arrived on Dec. 24, 1899, at age 17, and died on Dec. 6, 1900, of tuberculosis.
Shoshone Paiute Tribes
*Della Atkins arrived on Dec. 13, 1900, at age 17, and died 12 days later on Dec. 25, 1900. Her death was attributed to a brain tumor.
Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians
*Susie King arrived at the school on Oct. 25, 1890, at age 16, and died Oct. 21, 1891. Her cause of death was not listed.
Keweenaw Bay Indian Community
*Margaret Davis arrived at the school on Sept. 15, 1889, at age 14, and died Dec. 21, 1892, of tuberculosis.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: SJC sides with Nahant’s choice to eminent domain Northeastern land
description: “In short, the town's stated purpose for the taking is a proper public purpose” that aligned with past actions by the town indicating interest in preserving the area, and not a bad faith ploy, wrote Justice Elizabeth Dewar for a unanimous court.
text:
THE TOWN OF Nahant had the right to seize property owned by Northeastern University, blocking a planned university science center expansion, to preserve the parcel for open space, the Supreme Judicial Court ruled on Thursday.  
The ruling settled eight years of debate and litigation over a 28.7-acre parcel known as East Point at the edge of the tiny peninsula community. 
Town Meeting voters in 2021 decided to use eminent domain powers to claim about 12 of 21 acres and access rights to land owned by Northeastern University since the 1960s to preserve it for conservation.  
University officials argued successfully before a lower court that this was simply a pretext to stand in the way of a planned 55,000-square-foot development, and that it was effectively letting the town sidestep limits on local zoning powers. 
But the state’s highest court disagreed. 
“In short, the town’s stated purpose for the taking is a proper public purpose” that aligned with past actions by the town indicating interest in preserving the area, and not a bad faith ploy, wrote Justice Elizabeth Dewar for a unanimous court. The court, she wrote in a 43-page opinion, was also “unpersuaded” by the university’s other arguments against the taking. 
The court reversed the Superior Court’s summary judgment in favor of Northeastern and sent the case back for an order establishing the town’s right to take the property. 
The town is “pleased” by the SJC’s reversal of the Superior Court ruling, Town Administrator Alison Nieto said in a statement, and “looks forward to moving forward with this process.” 
Northeastern did not immediately respond to a request for comment. 
Both Northeastern and the tiny North Shore community own part of East Point, which includes the university’s Marine Science Center and a coastal open area overlooking the Atlantic Ocean, with beaches, a meadow, woodlands, cliffs, and other shoreline. 
Northeastern’s land has long housed a 31,083-square-foot research facility, repurposed from three former military bunkers, as well as other smaller structures and parking lots. The rest of the land to the east was largely kept as open space, with uplands, wetlands, and a beach. Alongside that land, the town’s 8 acres on East Point operate as a public park. 
That open space and Northeastern’s land were designated as a “Natural Resource Zoning District” in 1991. In the years since, the SJC noted, public planning and public surveys demonstrated an interest from Nahant and its residents in protecting East Point’s open space, conserve natural areas, and provide access to the coastline. 
In 2018, the university announced plans to expand its presence with a new Coastal Sustainability Institute, anchored by a 55,000-square-foot building. All three members of Nahant’s Board of Selectmen announced their opposition to the project, the high court noted. 
Years of public back-and-forth followed, with locals decrying possible infrastructure strains, disruption to the habitat, and the impact on the beauty of East Point. 
A supermajority of Nahant Town Meeting voters in 2021 authorized the Board of Selectmen to create easements on Northeastern land “for open space, recreation, conservation and/or historic preservation purposes.” The move would block development on a portion of the site and allow public access. 
The town filed a petition in the Superior Court requesting authorization to take the property and create the easements. Northeastern opposed the petition, arguing that despite Nahant’s claims that the taking was to preserve open space and for related purposes, the action was actually for the sole purpose of stopping Northeastern’s project.  
The SJC took up the case, with justices seemingly troubled about whether they should parse the motivations of the town’s voters. 
“To be sure,” Dewar wrote, “it is undisputed that the town pursued the taking in response to Northeastern’s announcement of the project, that there was vehement opposition to the project on the part of town officials and residents, and that the taking would in effect block the project.” 
But that is the nature of reserving land for conservation, she noted. 
“It is axiomatic that taking a conservation easement will have the effect of preventing development; preventing development is the very purpose of imposing such an easement on land valued as an open space resource,” she wrote. 
Justices dislike second-guessing the intentions of a Town Meeting or other local legislative body. The court’s posture in cases like this is to presume that the reasons given for using town powers are valid, unless the property owner can prove otherwise. 
The long history of the town acting to try to use East Point for conversation and recreation cuts against Northeastern’s claim that the motive was “solely” to block the project, the court concluded. 
As to the public policy implications, Northeastern argued that Nahant was pulling a fast one to get around the state Dover Amendment, which bars municipalities from imposing zoning ordinances or bylaws that regulate or restrict the use of land or structures for educational purposes on land owned or leased by a nonprofit educational corporation. 
“The Town is using the threat of eminent domain as a cudgel to force Northeastern to submit to regulation that the Town is powerless to effect through its zoning powers,” the university wrote in its brief. 
But the high court rejected the claim. As the Legislature has limited the way cities and towns can use their zoning powers on educational parcels, Dewar wrote, it could have done so with eminent domain powers if it wanted. So as long as the taking was for a constitutional public purpose, like conservation, this was a perfectly legitimate use of eminent domain powers.
