text:
The University of Nebraska Board of Regents held a special meeting Tuesday to approve sharing governance of the Nebraska Medicine healthcare system with the Omaha Community Foundation.  (Fred Knapp/Nebraska Public Media News)The University of Nebraska Board of Regents gave the final go-ahead Tuesday to share governance of the Nebraska Medicine healthcare system with Omaha philanthropists and bring in money to expand facilities.
The new board governing Nebraska Medicine will include four regents and four members from the  Omaha Community Foundation, which will contribute an initial $300 million, said Regent Chairman Paul Kenney. Neither the regents nor the foundation representatives have yet been named publicly.
The money will go toward a more than $2 billion development in Omaha called  Project Health, which will replace the 70-year old Clarkson Hospital with a new, 14-story, 1.5 million-square-foot teaching hospital.
Until this year, Nebraska Medicine had been jointly owned by the University of Nebraska Medical Center and Clarkson Regional Health Services.
When Clarkson left the partnership, the university assumed a debt of $600 million for its share of the land and buildings it acquired. That caused some members of the Nebraska Legislature heartburn, said Speaker John Arch, who said it was a “no-brainer” to seek help from the Omaha philanthropic community.
Arch, along with Gov. Jim Pillen and UNL Athletic Director Troy Dannen were on hand to endorse the deal at Tuesday’s meeting.
NU President Jeffrey Gold said the project will be historic. He said it would be “the largest public-private partnership ever contemplated in the state of Nebraska” and “the largest economic development project, which will bring over 8,000 new high-paying jobs to the state,” while improving health care.
UNMC Chancellor H. Dele Davis said the state has so far provided $300 million, the university and UNMC about $250 million, and Nebraska Medicine more than $500 million toward Project Health.
The regents voted unanimously to authorize Kenney to negotiate final arrangements with the Omaha Community Foundation, to be approved at a future meeting.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Pappas is making campaign finance part of his US Senate bid. His opponents cry hypocrisy.
description: In his effort to convince voters to send him to the U.S. Senate, Chris Pappas, who currently represents the eastern half of New Hampshire in the U.S. House of Representatives, has begun touting an agenda to keep big money out of politics. “One of the major issues that we’re hearing about everywhere across New Hampshire […]
text:
U.S. Senate candidates (clockwise from left) Chris Pappas, Karishma Manzur, John Sununu, and Scott Brown. (Pappas photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin; Manzur photo courtesy; Sununu photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin; Brown photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin)In his effort to convince voters to send him to the U.S. Senate, Chris Pappas, who currently represents the eastern half of New Hampshire in the U.S. House of Representatives, has begun touting an agenda to keep big money out of politics.
“One of the major issues that we’re hearing about everywhere across New Hampshire is how we confront the culture of corruption in Washington, how we address the influence of big money in our political system, which is so corrosive to our democracy,” Pappas said at an event in Manchester last week. “And we’ve got to clean house in order for us to be able to make progress on the things that people are counting on.”
As a solution, Pappas is promoting the DISCLOSE Act, which aims to stem “dark money” — campaign donations delivered in a way that obscures their source, typically by routing it through an intermediate organization. The DISCLOSE ACT would require groups like super PACs, 501(c)(4)s, and other organizations to disclose any political donors who give more than $10,000. It would also attempt to shut down money transfers between organizations, which are meant to hide the identity of the original contributor; expand disclosure requirements for the funders of political ads; and close loopholes in bans on foreign money being donated to campaigns. Pappas was the lead sponsor for the House version of the legislation this year.
“This is something that cuts across party lines,” Pappas said. “This is not a Democratic talking point. This is for the good of the country and American democracy. Two hundred and fifty years after our independence, the power should be in the hands of the people, not monied corporate special interests. And Republican voters believe that just as much as Democratic voters do.”
No money from corporate PACs but lots of money from pro-Israel PACs
Pappas also boasts that he does not accept any money from corporate PACs that disburse money to campaigns on behalf of their supporters. 
“I don’t take corporate PAC money in my campaigns,” Pappas said. “And I’m proud in our Senate race that we have over 120,000 donors who have given, on average, about 30 bucks online, contributing and chipping in to our effort.”
However, while none of his campaign war chest comes from corporate PACs, the congressman has long been supported by pro-Israel PACs. That includes over $600,000 in direct and earmarked contributions from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC, over the course of his career, as well as more money from other pro-Israel sources.
AIPAC seeks to promote support for U.S. military aid to Israel. And the group has become a flashpoint in Democratic politics as public opinion sours on Israel amid its multi-front wars and as more and more independent experts conclude the country is committing genocide against the Palestinian people.
Pappas has supported U.S. aid to Israel throughout his time in Congress. In February, at AIPAC’s 2026 Congressional Summit, he called himself “a strong supporter of the bipartisan U.S.-Israel relationship, which is a cornerstone of our national security policy.” However, he has moderated his stance on the issue in recent months. In July, he voted “present” — neither in favor nor against — on an amendment that would’ve restricted arm sales to Israel. He called that a “tough vote” when asked about it at the Manchester event, adding “what (Israeli President Benjamin) Netanyahu has done over the last few years is indefensible and unsupportable, and I think this is an important moment for a reset with respect to the U.S. policy toward Israel.”
Asked if he views pro-Israel PACs differently than corporate PACs, Pappas said: “I support individual citizens being able to participate in the democratic process, but I’m taking on every source of effort in our political system to skew things in favor of special interests. I don’t care what PAC it happens to be.”
His progressive challenger
In Tuesday’s Democratic primary election, Pappas will face Karishma Manzur, an activist who has never before held public office.
“Chris Pappas had eight years to not take money and to actually bring honor back to public service,” Manzur said in an interview. “So for eight years, he’s been part of the problem.”
“As people are turning towards me, Chris Pappas has decided that he has to step in and actually put forth the legislation,” Manzur said. “Why in 2026? Why not for the last eight years? And that is the question that all of us in New Hampshire should ask.”
However, Pappas first co-sponsored the DISCLOSE Act in 2019, his first year in Congress.
“Did it ever get passed,” Manzur said when presented with that fact, “or was it just a show?”
Manzur has made Pappas’ donations from pro-Israel groups a centerpiece of her campaign. She’s tried to contrast that with her own campaign funding.
“I’m not taking a single cent from corporate PACs, super PACs, AIPAC, foreign-aligned lobbies,” she said. “Nothing. I’m only taking money from regular folks here in New Hampshire and across the country.”
She said “every piece of legislation that I will advance, every vote, people in New Hampshire can be 100% assured that it will be in their best interest.”
An August poll from St. Anselm College shows Pappas beating Manzur 59% to 28%, with 13% of respondents unsure. The most recent UNH Granite State poll, also from August, points to a tighter race: a 47%-34% advantage for Pappas, with 18% undecided.
Asked what he’d say to voters considering supporting Manzur, Pappas deflected, saying: “I’m proud of the support I have, which comes from organized labor across the board in New Hampshire, which comes from small dollar donors. … But again, this is a campaign of ideas that’s really focused on how we beat John Sununu and MAGA Republicans, and flip the majority in the U.S. Senate.”
Looking ahead to the general
Throughout the primary, Pappas has continually tried to focus on his potential general election opponent, John Sununu.
“The big money campaign is the campaign behind John Sununu,” Pappas said. “The fact is, we’re outraising his campaign based on the individual support we’re drumming up, but he’s got a huge head of steam based on super PACs and special interests that are outspending us 3-to-1 on TV because they know he’s going to be a reliable vote for them.”
Sununu and Scott Brown, both former U.S. senators trying to return to Washington, D.C., lead the Republican primary.
Sununu did not respond to the Bulletin’s request for an interview. He was first elected to the U.S. Senate in 2002 but lost his 2008 reelection bid to current U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. Now that Shaheen is retiring, he’s asking Granite Staters to give him back the seat.
Brown served in the U.S. Senate from 2010 to 2013, representing Massachusetts after winning a special election. After losing reelection, he moved to New Hampshire and has sought to win election here in multiple races.
Like Manzur, Brown also accused Pappas of hypocrisy.
“Chris’ efforts are too little, too late,” Brown said. “He’s been there for seven years and has not made it any part of his campaign.”
Brown pointed to his own work on financial ethics in 2012, when he introduced the STOCK Act, which required members of Congress to disclose stock transactions and sought to ban insider trading. In an interview, he recalled his plea to President Barack Obama after the bill got stuck in the Senate.
“During the State of the Union, the president was walking up the dais,” Brown recounted. “And I said, ‘Sir, my insider trading bill is stuck, and it needs your help.’”
Obama signed the bill into law in April 2012.
“It was great,” Brown said. “It was bipartisan. It really did make a real difference. … But when I left, they weakened it, and I think it’s disingenuous for Chris now that he’s running to all of a sudden take on these great, amazing causes.”
Asked if he would try to reverse the rollbacks of the STOCK Act should he be reelected, Brown said, “I’d like to look at what they’re proposing now and see if it’s something that could certainly help.”
Brown also took aim at Sununu’s campaign.
“If you look at John Sununu, he’s got the Senate Leadership Fund, NRSC paying for all his ads, Americans for Prosperity paying for all his ads,” Brown said. “He approves them, but they’re paying for it — millions and millions of dollars. So while they’re not writing checks, they’re doing all of his commercials, and he has all those special interests: big oil, big pharma, big tech, big banks.”
Sununu holds a commanding 54%-24% lead over Brown in the St. Anselm Poll, and a 60%-20% advantage in the UNH poll.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Hunger crisis widens in North Carolina as food banks face more demand, federal cuts
description: On a steamy September morning, all of North Carolina’s agricultural bounty is on display at the State Farmers Market in Raleigh. The boxes and crates of neatly stacked fruits and vegetables stand in stark contrast to new data that reveals a worsening hunger crisis in North Carolina. According to Feeding America’s annual Map the Meal […]
text:
New data shows a growing number of families are struggling to afford fresh fruits and vegetable, like those available at the State Farmers Market in Raleigh, North Carolina.  (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)On a steamy September morning, all of North Carolina’s agricultural bounty is on display at the State Farmers Market in Raleigh. The boxes and crates of neatly stacked fruits and vegetables stand in stark contrast to new data that reveals a worsening hunger crisis in North Carolina.
According to Feeding America’s annual Map the Meal Gap analysis, 1 in 7 North Carolinians are unsure where their next meal will come from. That compares to 1 in 9 individuals in 2021.
“There are now close to 630,000 people in the 34 counties our food bank serves who are food insecure, meaning they don’t have the resources to consistently keep food on the table,” said Amy Beros, president of the Food Bank of Central and Easten North Carolina.
Food Bank President Amy Beros discusses hunger with Attorney General Jeff Jackson during a August 18, 2026 visit to their Raleigh warehouse. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)
Beros told reporters this week that nearly 180,000 more people are facing food hardship than at the height of the COVID pandemic in 2021. She said they are calling attention to the increase during September, which is Hunger Action Month.
Farmers, community allies, and supporters have all been working to increase the supply of food at local pantries, but Beros said federal funding cuts and eligibility changes are taking their toll.
Rising food prices have also forced consumers to stretch their budgets or make do with less. According to the USDA, grocery prices have gone up 2.7% on average in the past year, with some items like ground beef up 10% to 18%.
“Across the more than 700 local pantries, meal and food distribution sites, many partners have been reporting to us increases in visits ranging from 20% to 60%,” said Beros.
Demand is breaking records across the state. Community of Hope Ministries in Garner recently served 597 households in a single month. At the coast, Martha’s Mission served 4,400 families in Morehead City over the past year. At Feed Your Neighbor in Greenville, more than 700 households now rely on the community pantry to put food on the table.
Beros highlighted the local organizations this week as she warned that the demands on the largely volunteer pantries are not sustainable.
More hungry children, fewer choices for families
Children are disproportionately likely to be hungry. Statewide, 21.5% of North Carolina’s children face food insecurity, meaning that more than one in five kids and teens are worried about their next meal. Experts estimate 57,000 more children are facing hunger than in 2021.
And that hunger is not experienced equally.
Nearly one in three Black households and nearly one in four Latino households face food insecurity. That’s two to three times the rate of white households, where hunger touches one in nine households.
Families on a tight budget rely on cheaper, more processed foods, which are higher in fat, sodium and sugar.
“It is not because they do not want to eat healthy. It is because oftentimes that food is just not accessible to them because it is the most expensive food out there,” said Beros.
A big part of the organization’s 2030 strategic plan is to increase access to fresh produce and protein. But the Trump administration has cut funding for a program that buys fresh foods from local farmers to donate to food banks.
Trump Canceled 94 Million Pounds of Food Aid. Here’s What Never Arrived.

New SNAP restrictions
Beros said the Food Bank is grateful that the new state budget includes $9 million for food purchases, but the state investments will not erase larger federal losses or cuts that are coming.
Statewide more than 1.2 million North Carolinians rely on SNAP, commonly called food stamps, to purchase groceries. But strict work and reporting requirements have led to a decline of more than 100,000 in enrollment in just the last year.
Beginning October 1st, the federal government will shift an additional quarter of SNAP administrative costs to the state and counties. While the state’s portion is covered in the recent budget, the county portion is not, adding to the workload and paperwork of county social service offices.  That loss of support will send more people to their local pantries.
Next October, states will be required to pay a portion of the SNAP benefit costs based on their payment error rate. The Stein administration estimates that North Carolina may be responsible for paying $140 million or more each year because of the federal changes.
Beros said there is no way North Carolina’s large hunger relief network can make up what is being cut at the federal level.
For every one meal that the Food Bank of Central and Eastern North Carolina provides, SNAP provides nine.
Beyond donations, food bank leaders are urging North Carolinians to contact elected officials and ask them to protect SNAP and restore strong federal food purchase programs.
“What we are trying to make sure is that the humanity remains at the center of how we talk about this crisis. These are not just numbers. These are our neighbors,” said Beros.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV Justice Wooten treated for dehydration, released after medical incident Wednesday
description: West Virginia Supreme Court Justice Bill Wooten was treated for dehydration and released from Charleston Area Medical Center Wednesday evening, hours after he had a “medical incident” while on the bench, a spokesman for the court said Thursday.
text:
The West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals. (Photo by West Virginia Legislative Photography)West Virginia Supreme Court Justice Bill Wooten was treated for dehydration and released from Charleston Area Medical Center Wednesday evening, hours after he had a “medical incident” while on the bench, a spokesman for the court said Thursday. 
Justice William R. Wooton
Oral arguments before the court were canceled Wednesday, the first day of the court’s fall term, after Wooten, 81, had the medical incident. Wooten is feeling better and went back to work Thursday, Jared Hunt, communications director for the Supreme Court, said in an email. 
“I want to thank everyone for their prayers and best wishes for my complete recovery. I was feeling a bit under the weather yesterday and had apparently become quite dehydrated, which triggered my sudden illness during Wednesday’s oral arguments,” Wooten said in a statement.
Wooten added that he’s grateful for the quick action of his colleagues, court security and first responders for coming to his aid. 
“After an evaluation at the hospital and influx of fluids, I’m happy to report that I am feeling much better today and have returned to work at the Court,” Wooten said in the statement. “Again, I want to thank everyone for their concerns and well wishes and am grateful to be able to get back to work for the people of West Virginia.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Rob Sand says Iowa needs to ‘reduce red tape’ to meet housing needs
description: Rob Sand, current state auditor and Democratic candidate for governor, said simplifying inspections and cutting red tape that stands in the way of building new housing will help improve affordability.  Sand spoke Thursday morning at the Frank W. Smith Retirement Center, a recently renovated affordable housing building for seniors in Des Moines, after touring[...]
text:
Democratic candidate for governor Rob Sand speaks with Carolyn Scott, a resident at Frank W. Smith Retirement Center in Des Moines on Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Rob Sand, current state auditor and Democratic candidate for governor, said simplifying inspections and cutting red tape that stands in the way of building new housing will help improve affordability. 
Sand spoke Thursday morning at the Frank W. Smith Retirement Center, a recently renovated affordable housing building for seniors in Des Moines, after touring a unit and speaking with a resident. 
Lowering housing costs is one of the points in Sand’s recently released “Affordability for All” plan that also looks at potential policies to reduce the cost of healthcare, education and energy in the state.
“We have people who want to be in Iowa, and they’re struggling to pay the bills, and one of the biggest issues that they’re oftentimes facing is housing,” Sand said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The retirement center was initiated by the nearby First Church of the Open Bible in Beaverdale during the 1990s, but Sam Erickson, the CEO of the nonprofit affordable housing developer Community Housing Initiatives, said it had fallen into disrepair. Community Housing Initiatives was asked to step in and help renovate the facility. Erickson said a subsidy helps to ensure the cost to live at the retirement center is capped at 30% of a resident’s income. 
“This property actually exemplifies the importance of affordable housing,” Erickson said. “All of us coming together, collaborating to meet the needs of seniors, particularly for people that are on very low incomes.” 
Sand said nonprofit models like Community Housing Initiatives and land trusts can be “incredibly effective” at making housing costs affordable. 
“To me, the bottom line is that I think we need to have state government be refocused on the issues that are impacting 100% of Iowans: costs, corruption, cancer – and housing is a huge piece of the affordability question for most Iowans,” Sand said. 
Sand’s policy proposal includes steps to “cut the bureaucratic red tape” that makes it more difficult, cost more and take longer to build more homes and other housing types like duplexes or accessory dwelling units. 
For example, Sand said Thursday, inspectors should have the authority to approve things required by municipal and state inspections so that developers aren’t waiting so long on inspections.
In 2025 the Legislature passed a law to make it easier for Iowans to add accessory dwelling units to their properties. Sand said there’s still work to be done to ensure the “spirit” of this law is followed, that local regulations don’t overcomplicate these types of buildings to the point where they do not actually get built. 
While “cutting red tape” has been a common theme among Republican policies in Iowa and federally, Sand said there’s always room to “take it another step, two more steps, continue moving in that direction.” 
His housing proposals also include protecting Iowans against price “gouging” from artificial intelligence models and creating interest-free down payment assistance programs for first-time homebuyers. 
Sand’s opponent, Zach Lahn, has also proposed tax rebates that would help with a down payment on a home for young Iowans who stay in the state.
The “Affordability for All” plan from Sand includes efforts to reduce energy costs, including a cap on service or meter fees for utilities, a call to expand electric grid capacity, ratemaking transparency and a push for more affordable renewable energy. 
The plan also includes a renewed call to end the privatization of Medicaid in Iowa. Sand said Thursday he thinks “nonprofit-based managed care” would be a better solution to provide Iowans with healthcare coverage. Sand said he would also like to “cap” insulin costs for Iowans and expand laws that protect against “surprise” medical bills. 
The final pillar of Sand’s affordability plan includes providing universal free school meals – which he said could be paid for with federal funds – and providing universal, free all-day pre-kindergarten for Iowans. The latter, he said, could be paid for by putting income limits back on the state’s private school voucher system which Sand has criticized while serving as auditor.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Darline Graham’s inherited Senate seat revives the ‘widow’s mandate’ with a sibling twist
description: South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster’s July 2026 appointment of Darline Graham to fill the remainder of her late brother Lindsey Graham’s Senate term — and her subsequent decision to run for the seat — may seem unusual. After all, Darline Graham has no experience in elected office and was virtually unknown outside of the small […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Darline Graham speaks to supporters during her election night watch party Aug. 25, 2026, in Columbia, South Carolina, after being declared the winner of the GOP nomination for the next six-year Senate term. Behind her are Gov. Henry McMaster and first lady Peggy McMaster. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)
South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster’s July 2026 appointment of Darline Graham to fill the remainder of her late brother Lindsey Graham’s Senate term — and her subsequent decision to run for the seat — may seem unusual.
After all, Darline Graham has no experience in elected office and was virtually unknown outside of the small circle of people who knew her from her time heading the South Carolina Commission for the Blind, or the slightly larger group of people who knew her as Lindsey Graham’s sister.
Nevertheless, she’s made history as the first woman to represent South Carolina in the U.S. Senate.
Graham has since demonstrated how quickly a family connection can translate into electoral support. On Aug. 11, she finished first in a 10-candidate Republican primary with nearly 33% of the vote. In the runoff two weeks later, she won the GOP nomination by defeating U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman with a 5-percentage-point lead.

U.S. Sen. Darline Graham walks into a room filled with supporters in Columbia, South Carolina, after she’s declared the GOP nominee on Aug. 25, 2026, in Columbia, South Carolina, for the next six-year Senate term. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)

Her appointment belongs to a long American tradition of family succession in politics.
For much of the 20th century, political parties, particularly in the American South, routinely turned to relatives — particularly widows — to fill congressional vacancies.
The practice persisted because it provided continuity during moments of uncertainty, preserved party control of valuable seats, avoided divisive nomination fights and capitalized on the electoral value of a familiar name.
Although family succession might seem at odds with democratic ideals of open competition, it also created one of the first pathways for women to enter Congress.
As scholars of elections and Southern politics, we see the Graham appointment as a reminder that political inheritance has never been fully absent from American democracy. What has changed is the form it takes and the role it plays in the recruitment of political leaders.
Why widows become the preferred successors
Beginning in the 1920s, congressional widows frequently became the preferred choice to fill legislative vacancies.
According to the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University, 48 women have been elected or appointed to fill congressional vacancies created by the deaths of their husbands – 40 in the House and eight in the Senate.
The route into office differed by chamber.
In the case of Senate vacancies, states may allow governors to temporarily fill those spots, whereas House vacancies can be filled only by election.
Congressional widows, therefore, reached Washington through both gubernatorial appointments and special elections. But in the one-party South, where Democrats held virtually every elected office from roughly 1900 to 1960, receiving the dominant party’s nomination was effectively a guarantee of a general election victory.
Supporters often argued that these women could provide continuity because many had served as trusted advisers, campaign surrogates and informal political partners to their husbands. They knew the district, understood constituent concerns and were familiar with ongoing legislative priorities. Much like Darline Graham, they also carried a last name that voters already associated with a familiar brand.

A woman holds a sign at the Myrtle Beach Convention Center on Friday, Aug. 21, 2026, ahead of President Donald Trump taking the stage at a rally supporting U.S. Sen. Darline Graham. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)

Political considerations also mattered. Party leaders often viewed a widow as a politically safe choice who could preserve a seat while avoiding a potentially damaging intraparty battle.
Voters, for their part, were presented with a familiar and trusted name at a time when replacement elections were often held quickly.
This was essentially the logic behind the appointment of Hattie Caraway, who was appointed to the U.S. Senate in 1931 by Arkansas Gov. Harvey Parnell after her husband, Thaddeus Caraway, died. Caraway was subsequently elected with only token opposition to complete the remainder of her husband’s term, becoming the first woman elected to the U.S. Senate.
This “widow’s mandate” was particularly prevalent in the South, although scholars have found that Southern widows served shorter terms than their counterparts elsewhere in the country, perhaps owing to the South’s embrace of more traditional gender norms.
Some women who entered Congress under these circumstances went on to build significant political careers of their own, though.
Perhaps the best-known example is Margaret Chase Smith of Maine.
After her husband’s death in 1940, she won a special election to succeed him in the House. She later won election to the Senate and became one of the most influential women in 20th-century American politics. Her famous “Declaration of Conscience” speech challenged the tactics of Sen. Joseph McCarthy at the height of the Red Scare.

U.S. Sen. Darline Graham speaks to reporters Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026, in Columbia, South Carolina, after leading a 10-candidate field in the special GOP primary and advancing to the runoff against U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)

Why the Graham case is different
The appointment of Darline Graham highlights an aspect of family succession that was often less visible in traditional cases of widow succession.
Historically, widows were frequently defended as logical successors because they had participated in campaigns, advised their spouses and possessed extensive knowledge of district politics. Whether those claims were always accurate is debatable, but they provided a justification rooted in continuity and experience.
Darline Graham was not entirely absent from her brother’s political career. She supported his campaigns and appeared in his ads. Their personal relationship was also unusually close because Lindsey Graham helped raise his sister after their parents died.
Unlike some congressional widows, however, Darline Graham was not her predecessor’s longtime governing partner.
Her appointment rests less on the notion of a political partnership and more directly on the value of a well-known political name and identity. Lindsey Graham served in Congress for more than three decades, first in the House and then in the Senate. His name recognition, political network and long-standing visibility in South Carolina politics created advantages that extended beyond the officeholder himself.

U.S. Sen. Darline Graham, her husband Larry Nordone, and their daughters Nicole Nordone and Emilie Roberts watch the funeral procession for her brother, U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham, outside First Baptist Church of Columbia in Columbia, S.C., on Wednesday, July 29, 2026. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)

The Graham appointment therefore makes visible one of the central forces that has sustained family succession throughout American history: the enduring electoral value of political brands.
The political benefits of continuity
Widow succession still happens, but it is less common than it once was.
This decline largely reflects the rise of women’s independent political careers. As women increasingly won local, state and federal offices on their own in the late 20th century, family connections became less necessary as a pathway into Congress.
Yet family succession has never completely disappeared. Darline Graham’s appointment and strong showing in the Republican primary demonstrate that the political benefits of continuity, name recognition and established networks remain powerful.
The old “widow’s mandate” may have faded, but the broader dynamics that sustained it continue to shape American politics.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Va. House speaker details ‘concerns’ about NextEra-Dominion merger in letter to state regulators
description: In an official filing in the State Corporation Commission’s review of the proposed $67 billion NextEra-Dominion Energy merger, Speaker of the Virginia House of Delegates Don Scott, D-Portsmouth, on Wednesday aired his concerns and advice about the deal in a letter to SCC Chair Kelsey Bagot. “If this merger is not built around affordability for […]
text:
Virginia House Speaker Don Scott, D-Portsmouth, seen here Nov. 6, 2024, sent a letter to state regulators about key considerations in the proposed NextEra-Dominion Energy merger. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)In an official filing in the State Corporation Commission’s review of the proposed $67 billion NextEra-Dominion Energy merger, Speaker of the Virginia House of Delegates Don Scott, D-Portsmouth, on Wednesday aired his concerns and advice about the deal in a letter to SCC Chair Kelsey Bagot.
“If this merger is not built around affordability for Virginians then it should not go through. That is my starting point, and it should frame every question this Commission asks over the coming months,” Scott wrote in the Sept. 2 missive. The House leader has received nearly $4 million in campaign donations from Dominion over the years. 
Scott included a list of eight key points of consideration that he said commissioners should keep top of mind, including ensuring that the combined company adheres to Virginia Clean Economy Act environmental and clean energy standards, and that Virginians don’t “see a single dollar of rate increase as a result of this merger.”
Data centers should “cover the full cost of the generation, transmission, and distribution infrastructure required to serve them,” Scott wrote. He also emphasized that Virginia jobs must be protected, and suggested the planned energy titan host its co-headquarters in Richmond.  
“Virginia has the chance to get this right and to show the rest of the country how it is done. But that outcome depends on this Commission demanding more than assurances,” Scott wrote. “It depends on enforceable conditions, on real accountability, and on affordability being the organizing principle of the entire review.”
SCC commissioner, former NextEra attorney declines to recuse herself from merger case

Days before Scott’s letter to Bagot, a former NextEra attorney who has declined to recuse herself from reviewing the merger case, 14 state lawmakers signed onto a letter to Gov. Abigail Spanberger, urging her to call a special session to facilitate an extension of the SCC’s review period for the merger. 
Under current law, the SCC must approve or reject the merger proposal within 180 days of its official application, which was filed July 15. 
The all-stock trade deal between Virginia’s largest utility and the Florida-based NextEra has raised concerns for a growing cadre of lawmakers who say review period is too short for such a major decision that could have major implications for ratepayers.
“Ratepayers, local governments, businesses, and consumer advocates need a real opportunity to examine the filings, participate in hearings, and submit comments — not a compressed window that forecloses genuine scrutiny,” the lawmakers’ Aug. 31 letter stated.
The democratic legislators’ letter echoes similar concerns of two Republican lawmakers, who called for a special session earlier this summer.
Lawmakers call for special session to debate Dominion-NextEra merger

In order for legislation passed in a special session to go into effect, the session has to be officially adjourned sine die, and then the legislation is enacted 90 days later. This leaves a narrow window for the legislature to meet and pass a bill allowing for an extension before the SCC’s Jan. 11 deadline, the lawmakers’ letter said. 
Currently, the General Assembly is in an active special session. Because that session was recessed, not adjourned, theoretically they could call themselves back in to do the work. It’s not yet clear if lawmakers will use this option.
Spanberger has not confirmed whether she will fulfill the request to convene a special session.  She made the unprecedented move to file as an official intervenor to the case last month. 
As an intervenor, her administration will be allowed to directly question the companies, review confidential documents and argue for conditions in the agreement. 
A few localities and advocacy group Clean Virginia have also filed motions to intervene in the case.
Lt. Gov. Ghazala Hashmi has been traveling the state this summer on a listening tour, asking residents to discuss their concerns of the merger and learn how they submit official testimony in the case. The latest stop was in Loudoun on Wednesday. 
Utility regulation experts have also warned lawmakers about potentially concerning impacts to ratepayers should the merger succeed. 
The public testimony portion of the case is set to begin on Nov. 5. A full schedule of hearings can be found on the SCC website.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Legislators to subpoena Secretary of State on voter roll question
description: Members of a legislative oversight committee voted 10-1 this week to subpoena Secretary of State Christi Jacobsen for the type of information her office turned over to the U.S. Department of Justice. Sen. Mike Cuffe, a Eureka Republican, cast the only opposing vote. Cuffe said some of the discussion in recent months had been partisan, […]
text:
The Secretary of State’s office in the Montana State Capitol in Helena on Wednesday, April 26, 2023.  (Photo by Mike Clark for the Daily Montanan)Members of a legislative oversight committee voted 10-1 this week to subpoena Secretary of State Christi Jacobsen for the type of information her office turned over to the U.S. Department of Justice.
Sen. Mike Cuffe, a Eureka Republican, cast the only opposing vote. Cuffe said some of the discussion in recent months had been partisan, and he believes Jacobsen was trying to follow the rule of law.
For months, lawmakers have tried to learn what voter information Jacobsen’s office provided to the Department of Justice in response to its demands that states turn over voter rolls so it can confirm ineligible voters aren’t on the lists.
Jacobsen, a Republican, has been largely unresponsive to legislators. She did not appear at the State Administration and Veterans’ Affairs Interim Committee meeting Wednesday or send a representative from her office.
Secretary of State spokesperson Richie Melby said Jacobsen was not invited to that portion of the meeting and was occupied with a security test in preparation for the general election in November.
“The Secretary of State’s Office and its partners are focused on protecting Montana’s elections from bad actors in China, Iran and Russia,” Melby said in an email. “I think you would agree that ensuring the physical and cyber security of Montana’s midterm federal general election is pretty significant.”
Melby did not address a question about how Jacobsen would respond to the subpoena.
Committee chairwoman Theresa Manzella, a Hamilton Republican, defended Jacobsen’s response to the federal government, saying the Secretary of State was obligated to work with “federal partners in verifying citizenship and purifying the voter rolls.”
But Manzella ultimately said the committee made a limited request, and she expected the Secretary of State to respect its position. Six Republicans and all four Democrats on the committee voted to approve the subpoena.
In a statement after the vote, Sen. Jacinda Morigeau, an Arlee Democrat, said election administrators across the state maintain accurate voter rolls.
“Montana’s Secretary of State should not be in the business of second-guessing them and sending private voter information to the federal government,” Morigeau said. “The federal government overstepped its authority, but this boils down to a simple question: What did the Secretary of State share?”
Morigeau and other committee members said the subpoena was the only way to answer the question. Members of the public, including with the League of Women Voters and a grassroots group called Project Paperclip, spoke in favor of the subpoena.
The language in the subpoena demands a copy of the Montana Voter List the Secretary of State’s Office provided to the Department of Justice “containing only the column headings or labels” to indicate categories of information provided but to omit confidential information.
It said the information will be used to educate the committee as it formulates policy in advance of the 2027 Montana Legislature as part of its responsibility to monitor executive branch agencies.
“The committee will also consider whether to introduce legislation regarding the definitions and disclosure of confidential information of its citizens under Article II, Section 10, of the Montana Constitution,” the right to privacy, says the draft subpoena.
The SAVA committee oversees the Secretary of State’s Office and for months has been asking Jacobsen to disclose the categories of data her office provided to the federal government. Members of the public also have raised concerns about privacy rights.
Rep. Peter Strand, a Bozeman Democrat, said people across the political spectrum have reached out to him with concerns Jacobsen shared their private information with the federal government.
“In fact, it’s the most unifying topic I’ve experienced with my constituents,” Strand said.
Some members of the public filed records requests directly with the Secretary of State, and at the meeting, lawmakers reviewed the response from the secretary’s chief legal counsel and a corresponding memo from legislative staff.
A May 28 letter from chief legal counsel Austin James to a law firm in response to a records request said the file requested “is no longer available,” but it shared specific information “about your clients” (the publicly available copy in the committee packet redacted the clients’ details).
In the letter, James said the records request was based on misinformation the Secretary of State’s Office was forced to correct in a media report. He said the office hopes “to avoid further dissemination of knowingly false statements,” and public servants “should not be subjected to harassment.”
In response to a question from Kalispell Republican Rep. Lukas Schubert, legislative research analyst Rebecca Power said it did not appear the Secretary of State provided driver’s license numbers or the last four digits of Social Security numbers based on the letter from the chief legal counsel.
But Power also said the office shared information that couldn’t be clearly identified, and Manzella said the Secretary of State did share the last four digits of Social Security numbers, as those are issued by the federal government.
Morigeau said legislative staff and members of the public shouldn’t have to “infer an answer,” so the committee should exercise its authority to get an answer “to this very simple question.”
In a letter to the DOJ late last year, Jacobsen said she provided the information the federal agency requested, but she also has said she did not provide everything the feds wanted and has protected voter privacy.
In a meeting in April, James told members of a different legislative committee that the DOJ had sued states for voter information, and Montana wanted to avoid a lawsuit so he wasn’t talking about its position with specificity.
At the meeting Wednesday, Rep. Marc Lee, a Butte Democrat and vice chairman of the committee, said the question wasn’t about the authority of the federal government or the ability of the Secretary of State.
Rather, he said, the question was simply what information the Secretary of State had shared with the federal government, and it was within the committee’s jurisdiction to pose the question.
“That was a very easy, basic question that was asked of the Secretary of State’s Office multiple times that (it) was unable to answer,” Lee said.
In response to a question from Sen. Wendy McKamey, a Great Falls Republican, and Morigeau, Power said the Trump administration had filed lawsuits against 30 states and the District of Columbia to enforce its requests for voter rolls.
Citing a recent media report, Power said the administration had lost 23 cases as of a couple of weeks ago, and the others appear to be pending.
Andria Hardin, legislative legal staff, said the secretary of state may comply with the subpoena, or her office may try to quash it in court, which would result in litigation over whether the office is required to turn over the information.

title: Sens. Rochefort and Prentiss named to new Developmental Services Oversight Commission
description: New Hampshire Senate President Sharon Carson appointed Sens. David Rochefort and Suzanne Prentiss to the newly created Developmental Services Oversight Commission. They’re the first two appointees to the commission, which was established in the wake of a Bulletin investigation on rampant abuse and neglect in New Hampshire’s intellectual and developmental dis[...]
text:
New Hampshire Sens. Suzanne Prentiss (left) and David Rochefort have been named to the Developmental Services Oversight Commission. (Courtesy photos)New Hampshire Senate President Sharon Carson appointed Sens. David Rochefort and Suzanne Prentiss to the newly created Developmental Services Oversight Commission.
They’re the first two appointees to the commission, which was established in the wake of a Bulletin investigation on rampant abuse and neglect in New Hampshire’s intellectual and developmental disability care system.
The taxpayer-funded and state-regulated system provides care services to Granite Staters with disabilities like autism or cerebral palsy. In November, the Bulletin uncovered evidence of hundreds of people with disabilities being abused, neglected, and exploited within this system. In response to that reporting, the Legislature enacted Senate Bill 670, which established the commission, among other things.
Rochefort and Prentiss serve as the Senate’s representatives on the commission. Caleb Labbe, communications director for the House of Representatives, said in an email that House Speaker Sherman Packard, who is responsible for selecting two House members to serve on the commission, has identified one of those appointees, a Republican, and is coordinating with Democratic leadership to identify a Democratic appointee. He said the process should be completed soon.
In addition to legislators, the commission will include state officials from the Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the system; representatives of the private care agencies that contract with the state; a representative of the Disability Rights Center-New Hampshire; and people with disabilities receiving services and their families.
The DRC said it’ll be appointing Executive Director Stephanie Patrick and Senior Staff Attorney Francesca Broderick to the commission.
“However, we have not yet determined who will serve as our representative and who will serve as our alternate,” Déodonné Bhattarai, communications director for the DRC, wrote in an email. “We are awaiting notice of the first meeting.”
Gov. Kelly Ayotte is responsible for appointing the people and families receiving services as well as representatives of the private care agencies. The Bulletin has reached out to her office via email asking for an update on her appointment process.
“We are looking forward to hearing who the Governor will be appointing to serve in the seats for people with disabilities and family members as there has been great interest in these positions,” Bhattarai said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Major protest held in Danbury to denounce ICE arrests
description: Last week, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement has made more than 100 arrests across CT, more than half of them in Danbury.
text:
More than a thousand people took to the streets in Danbury on Wednesday night to protest recent immigration arrests that have stunned the community.
Over the last week and a half, Immigration and Customs Enforcement has made more than 100 arrests across Connecticut, with more than half of them being in Danbury. The bulk of the arrests were made between Aug. 24 and 28.
Officials say ICE officers have made arrests at local businesses, on the streets, and even at school bus stops.
One of the people arrested at the grocery store CTown was Luis. He was shopping with his young son when he was apprehended by immigration officers.
A fellow rally-goer translated his story for him.
“When ICE came to him and took him, they took him while he was shopping,” she said. “He told them that he was in the car with his wife and his kid, and they told him that it was okay just to step out of the car. They didn’t give him any explanations. They did not ask any questions.”
Luis said he has no criminal record. He was brought to Hartford, then Massachusetts, and finally Colorado, before his lawyer threatened to sue the federal government. He was held for a week before being released.
Luis said he knew his story — which ends with him being brought back to his family in Connecticut — was rare.
Luis waves to a crowd as Danbury Mayor Roberto Alves stands behind him. Credit: Molly Ingram / WSHU
‘I don’t know when ICE is coming’
Danbury Mayor Roberto Alves, who was undocumented until his 20s, said the fear he felt as a child is different from what his community is dealing with now.
“We feared deportation, but we didn’t fear brutality,” Alves said. “We feared the unknown of coming home one day; maybe somebody wasn’t going to be there, but I didn’t fear that my father was going to get tased on the ground in front of a daycare.”
Alves said his community has been terrified — not just by the immigration arrests, but by the uncertainty.
“I don’t know when ICE is coming. I don’t know when ICE is leaving. I don’t know who ICE arrested. I don’t know what ICE is doing because ICE doesn’t tell us what they are doing,” Alves said. “They don’t want to tell us; they want to scare us. But here’s what I know. I know we’re stronger together.”
Wednesday night’s rally was held to culminate “A Day Without an Immigrant,” during which more than 60 businesses in the city closed their doors in support of the city’s immigrant community.
Officials say ICE officers have made arrests at local businesses and on the street. Reports of arrests being made at school bus stops, as children watched from the windows, have been especially concerning to advocates.
White House Border Czar Tom Homan told CNN’s Dana Bash he wasn’t aware of the school bus stop arrests, but didn’t denounce them.
“Did somebody arrest somebody at a bus stop? I’m not aware of that,” Homan said on Sunday. “But ICE is out there to enforce the law against those who have been ordered removed by a federal judge. And especially if they’re a criminal or if they’re a national security threat, there’s no safe harbor for them in this country. We’ll go where we need to go.”
Advocates and officials, like U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy, called the alleged school bus stop arrests an “insidious tactic.”
Homan said he would check with the Department of Homeland Security to see whether they happened. ICE is allowed to make arrests there; however, they are not allowed to make arrests in homes or private offices without a judicial warrant.
“When you are pulling parents away from school bus stops, when you are intentionally traumatizing kids, when you are targeting immigrants who are here legally, you aren’t here to support Danbury,” Murphy said. “You aren’t here to protect Danbury. You are here to traumatize Danbury, and we aren’t going to let them get away with that.”
U.S. Senator Chris Murphy speaks at a rally in Danbury on September 2, 2026. Credit: Molly Ingram / WSHU
Action vs. outrage
State and city officials have faced scrutiny from advocates over what they should — and can — do.
Connecticut’s Trust Act, which was updated during the past legislative session, limits local police cooperation with ICE. Another state law bans ICE agents from wearing masks; however, local officials, including Mayor Alves, have said it has “no teeth.”
Last week, Governor Ned Lamont left the podium mid-sentence after being repeatedly interrupted by advocates calling on him to do more to stop ICE activity in Danbury.
Wednesday night’s event did not have any crowd interruptions.
Juan Fonseca Tapia, co-founder of Danbury Unites for Immigrants, wants a fund to support the families of the people who have been arrested. He also wants Connecticut cities to end contracts with Flock, and for Attorney General William Tong to “hold accountable the kidnappers that are terrorizing our families.”
Lamont, Alves, and Murphy all said electing Democrats during the November midterms should be a priority to stop ICE. Alves is also the state Democratic Party chairman.
On Thursday, U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal was scheduled to receive public testimony from Danbury officials and advocates about the ICE operation. Blumenthal is the Ranking Member of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations and has held several similar forums.
Dozens of police officers were stationed at the perimeters of the rally in Danbury in Sept. 2, 2026. Credit: Molly Ingram / WSHU
This story was first published Sept. 3, 2026 by WSHU.

name: Michigan Advance
title: After Whitmer call, Trump administration lifts halt on invasive carp project
description: More than a month after the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers halted work on a critical project aimed at keeping invasive carp out of the Great Lakes, the stop-work order barring the effort from progressing has been lifted. In a text message to Michigan Advance Thursday Morning, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s Communications Director Robert Leddy confirmed […]
text:
An aerial view of the Brandon Road lock and dam near Joliet, Illinois. Photo courtesy of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. More than a month after the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers halted work on a critical project aimed at keeping invasive carp out of the Great Lakes, the stop-work order barring the effort from progressing has been lifted.
In a text message to Michigan Advance Thursday Morning, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s Communications Director Robert Leddy confirmed that the stop-work order on the Brandon Road Interbasin Project in Illinois had been lifted. 
Whitmer spoke with President Donald Trump on Wednesday and asked him to direct the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to lift its July order, raising concerns that invasive carp were recently found 80 miles from Lake Michigan in the Illinois River.
Cosponsored by Michigan, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and the State of Illinois, the Brandon Road Interbasin Project targets a critical pinch point at the Brandon Road Lock and Dam in Joliet, Ill. By making changes to the lock and layering several types of technology to deter fish from moving upstream, the project is intended to prevent invasive carp and other nuisance species from entering the Great Lakes.
The Great Lakes Fishery Commission has identified four species of invasive carp as threats to the Great Lakes: bighead carp, silver carp, black carp, and grass carp. The commission warns that these species could outcompete native fish and that preventing their introduction to the Great Lakes is the only effective approach to sustaining the aquatic ecosystem.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
While speaking with the president, Whitmer noted that the Brandon Road Interbasin Project is the strongest available defense against this threat to both the Great Lakes and the $8 trillion economy they support.
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, a vocal Trump critic, also reached out to the president on Wednesday, demanding both an end to the stop-work order, and an explanation as to why the project was halted to begin with. 
“Invasive carp continue to present a clear and immediate threat to the Great Lakes ecosystem and the many communities, businesses, and economies that depend on it,” Pritzker said in his letter. “Yet, your administration ordered work stopped on the project at the end of July. Over a month later, the State of Illinois has not received a meaningful explanation for why.”
The Alliance for the Great Lakes, a nonprofit focused on protecting and conserving the Great Lakes, also criticized the work stoppage in a statement on Thursday, with its President and CEO Joel Brammeier underscoring the importance of the effort to both the ecosystem and the economy of the Great Lakes.
“Now that construction can resume, we will continue to make sure that it stays on track – at the construction site and in Washington, DC,” Brammeier said. “For the sake of the ecosystem and economy that our region depends on, we simply cannot afford any further disruption.”

title: Report: Feds charge ICE agent Christian Castro in connection with Minneapolis shooting
description: Federal prosecutors have charged U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent Christian Castro with making false statements about the shooting of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in Minneapolis Jan. 14, the New York Times reported Thursday, citing an unnamed person familiar with the case. The Times reported that the indictment will be unsealed after Castro is taken[...]
text:
Residents confront federal agents following a shooting incident on Jan. 14, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images)Federal prosecutors have charged U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent Christian Castro with making false statements about the shooting of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in Minneapolis Jan. 14, the New York Times reported Thursday, citing an unnamed person familiar with the case.
The Times reported that the indictment will be unsealed after Castro is taken into custody. 
The federal charge against an ICE agent is a rare move for the administration of President Donald Trump, which still has not charged any of the agents involved in the January killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti. 
The single charge against Castro is far less than the civil rights violations originally sought by local federal prosecutors. But officials at the Department of Justice in Washington D.C. insisted the charges be significantly downgraded, according to reporting from ProPublica.
Castro is also charged in Minnesota with four counts of second-degree assault and one count of falsely reporting a crime. He is accused of firing his gun through the closed front door of a north Minneapolis home, hitting Cesar-Solis in the leg and endangering other people in the home.
Castro accused Sosa-Celis and another Venezuelan immigrant of assaulting him with a broom and a snow shovel before Castro opened fire, leading to assault charges against the two men that were dropped after surveillance footage proved Castro’s statements false.
In an email obtained by ProPublica, Matthew Evans, the assistant U.S. attorney in Minnesota in charge of the case, told attorneys for Sosa-Celis and other victims that he “objected in the strongest possible terms” to his bosses’ decision not to pursue civil rights charges. 
Castro was released from a Texas county jail on Aug. 27, 90 days after his arrest by Texas Rangers, a state law enforcement agency, pursuant to the warrant related to his Minnesota charges. 
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott blocked Castro’s extradition to Minnesota, prompting a lawsuit from Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison. A federal judge in that case declined to force the extradition, paving the way for Castro’s release. 
Minnesota authorities told the federal court that Castro was in a romantic relationship with a woman in Mexico and owned property there, making him a flight risk.

name: VTDigger
title: From shut out to starting over
description:
After eight years out of the workforce, Violetta feared she had become unhireable. She returned to school, earned two nursing degrees with support from The Curtis Fund, and built a new career. Now her daughter is a Curtis Fund scholar, too.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  From shut out to starting over.
text:
Violetta Ayrapetova works on the locked unit at a residential facility in Chittenden County. She is a board-certified psychiatric mental health nurse. She plans to pursue wound care certification because many patients in psychiatric and substance use settings have untreated physical wounds. She does not want to be the provider who ignores them.
Her path began well before nursing school.
Her family came to Vermont as refugees in the early 1990s. They were Armenian minorities forced out of Azerbaijan during ethnic violence. Both parents held college degrees. Her father arrived with about $42. In Vermont, her mother cleaned houses, and her father worked as a prep cook. They bought a home and saved what they could. There was no financial cushion, no family money to fall back on, no inheritance.
Years later, Violetta was back at the starting line. She had spent nearly a decade raising her children and was out of the workforce. When she tried to return, employers saw the gap and did not hire her. Her ex-husband had kept working and advancing. She had not. She called it the gender tax.
School was the way through. She took classes at a community college, then applied to the nursing program at Vermont Technical College. Thirty spots. Three hundred applicants. She was waitlisted, waited, and finally got the call that a spot had opened. She took it.
Nursing school in your forties, as a single parent with a mortgage, is as much a financial challenge as an academic one. The Curtis Fund scholarship covered a large share of her costs for both her associate’s and bachelor’s degrees at what is now Vermont State University. She graduated with honors in 2020 and went straight into the bachelor’s program, finishing cum laude. The scholarship did not erase her debt, but it kept it manageable and kept her enrolled when quitting would have been easier.
She now holds a board certification in psychiatric mental health nursing and is pursuing wound care next. The patients she encounters in psychiatric and substance use settings often have skin wounds that go unaddressed because of the stigma attached to how they got there. Violetta doesn’t want to be a provider who looks away. “There’s such a great need for psychiatric nurse practitioners,” she says, “and so few go into that field because it’s hard and it feels overwhelming. But that’s what I want to tackle.”
After her wound care, she is considering pursuing a doctorate and possibly opening her own practice. Her mother cleaned houses. Her father prepped food. Now her daughter has received the same Curtis Fund scholarship and is heading to McGill.
“Education really touches an entire community,” Violetta says. “Not just me.” 
The Curtis Fund has always been about more than paying tuition. It is about opening doors that can change the course of a life—and sometimes a family. Violetta’s story is a powerful reminder that when we invest in one Vermonter’s education, the impact can reach far beyond a single scholarship.

To read more stories about Curtis Fund scholars, visit: https://www.thecurtisfund.org/meet-the-scholars 
Learn more about how to support Vermont students like Violetta: https://www.thecurtisfund.org/donate#give-now

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Reduced credit hour bachelor degrees approved at 3 Oklahoma colleges
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Three Oklahoma universities were given the greenlight to offer the state’s first reduced credit hour bachelor degree programs.  The Oklahoma State Regents for Higher Education on Thursday unanimously approved requests to create accelerated degree programs at University of Oklahoma, Oklahoma State University and Rogers State University that wo[...]
text:
Members of the Oklahoma State Regents for Higher Education listen to a speaker during a meeting on May 29, 2026 in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Three Oklahoma universities were given the greenlight to offer the state’s first reduced credit hour bachelor degree programs. 
The Oklahoma State Regents for Higher Education on Thursday unanimously approved requests to create accelerated degree programs at University of Oklahoma, Oklahoma State University and Rogers State University that would allow students to earn a college degree in as little as three years instead of the traditional four. 
The regents approved OU’s request to create a 90-credit hour degree in applied social work. They also signed off on OSU’s plan to offer two shortened degree pathways —  a 92-credit hour bachelor of applied science in artificial intelligence and a 90-hour bachelor of applied science in business essentials and applications. Rogers State received approval for a 99 to 103 credit hour bachelor of applied science in workforce development. 
The programs still need to go through a months-long accreditation process, but the four accelerated degrees could be offered to students as early as next fall.
The Oklahoma State Regents for Higher Education in May revised their policies to allow colleges and universities to propose bachelor degree paths in as few as 90 credit hours. This came after both Gov. Kevin Stitt and the Legislature charged the State Regents with studying the feasibility of 90-credit hour degrees in an effort to make higher education more affordable and address workforce shortages. 
Reduced credit hour degrees are an option at at least 60 schools across the country. Five other states are working to test and develop these programs, according to a report from Georgetown University. 
Courtney Warmington, chair of the State Regents, said higher education officials have been “deliberate” and “thoughtful” when designing reduced credit hour programs to ensure academic quality and rigor is not lost. 
“The traditional 120-hour bachelor’s degree has served higher education for a really long time, but innovation requires us to be willing to ask whether every degree in every field must always be structured in exactly the same way across the country,” she said. 
OU President Joseph Harroz Jr. said Thursday that while the state doesn’t know if these degrees will be perfect, he’s glad Oklahoma is “not leading recklessly, but thoughtfully.” He said reduced credit hour degrees will help to meet the needs of the workforce in Oklahoma. 
“This proposal … is a critical moment because we have to understand what the market needs and the impact that has on the wealth and health of our state,” Harroz said. 
Chris Francisco, senior vice provost for academic affairs at OSU, said the university wants to streamline pathways into in-demand industries, like artificial intelligence. 
“While we think that the traditional, four-year bachelor’s degree has served students very well and continues to serve students well, we want to develop as many flexible pathways as we possibly can to try to serve the needs of the state when that arises,” he said.

title: Federal government seeks summary judgment against Alabama Department of Corrections
description: Federal prosecutors Wednesday filed a heavily redacted motion for summary judgment ahead of a scheduled November trial over whether violence in Alabama’s prisons violate inmates’ Eighth Amendment protections against cruel and unusual punishment. The 260-page motion from the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District, which includes evidence and testimo[...]
text:
Barbed wire seen behind a fence at an Alabama prison. The federal government filed a motion on Wednesday seeking summary judgment in its lawsuit against the state of Alabama alleging that the violence in men's prisons violates inmates' Eighth Amendment protections against cruel and unusual punishment.  (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Federal prosecutors Wednesday filed a heavily redacted motion for summary judgment ahead of a scheduled November trial over whether violence in Alabama’s prisons violate inmates’ Eighth Amendment protections against cruel and unusual punishment.
The 260-page motion from the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District, which includes evidence and testimony from the incarcerated and current and former Alabama Department of Corrections officials, asks U.S. District Judge Harold D Mooty, III to rule in the government’s favor on charges ADOC failed to protect people in prison from physical violence, sexual violence and the use of excessive force by correctional staff, as well as failing to provide safe conditions for people while incarcerated.
“Alabama’s prisons are pervasively violent. Homicides, stabbings, beatings, and sexual assaults occur routinely,” the motion said. “Officers use excessive force.  Alabama does not maintain the physical condition of the prisons, putting prisoners’ health and safety at risk.  Alabama’s own conduct has created these conditions, and Alabama has failed to respond reasonably.”

A message was sent to the Alabama Department of Corrections on Thursday seeking comment. Carla Crowder, the executive director of Alabama Appleseed, a nonprofit focused on criminal justice reform, said in a statement that the motion “spells out a level of systemic incompetence and mismanagement that has not previously been spelled out so clearly.”
“What’s new is the thorough and unmitigated complacency and disregard for human life on the part of highly paid and experienced ADOC officials to address a crisis they’ve known about for nearly a decade,” the statement said.
Cindy Hamilton, whose son is currently incarcerated, expressed concerns with the amount of redactions in the motion.
Legislators look to upcoming audit as frustrations with Alabama prisons mount

“The public should know everything,” she said in an interview Thursday. “The really sad thing is nothing has changed. Nothing. The same thing is still happening every single day in every single one of these facilities.”
The November trial would come nearly six years after the U.S. Department of Justice sued the state in December 2020 over conditions in men’s prisons in the state. The charges followed the release of reports in 2019 and 2020 detailing the use of excessive force by corrections officers against inmates and physical and sexual assault of incarcerated men in the state’s prisons.
A similar DOJ investigation of sexual abuse and harassment inmates in the Julia Tutwiler Prison for Women in Wetumpka led in 2015 led to a nearly-decade long consent decree between the state and the DOC. The decree led to improvements in safety and staffing at the facility.
However, Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall in 2020 rejected a consent decree over the violence in men’s prisons, leading to the lawsuit.

‘There’s no safety, man’

The motion filed Wednesday alleges that there is a “substantial risk of violence and sexual violence” in Alabama’s correctional facilities and that the state’s conduct and failure to act “puts prisoners at risk.”
The motion also alleges that the leadership within the ADOC “does not supervise what occurs in the prisons” and that the agency fails to “effectively investigate or exercise oversight regarding uses of force.”
More than half of the 260-page motion consists of testimony from incarcerated people and current and former leadership; documents highlighting violence and extortion within state prisons and statistics on overcrowding and staff shortages.
Formerly incarcerated people, family members describe Alabama prison violence

One page recorded almost 10 “died by homicide” episodes that happened in 2019 alone.
“A prisoner testified, ‘There’s no safety man. You don’t feel safe. Anything liable to happen,’” the motion states.
Testimony from ADOC staff indicated the violence is underreported.
“ADOC staff testified: ‘Some days they just — and then if you’ve got a facility with 12 – 2,000 inmates and 15 officers, you’ve got one officer trying to cover three dorms, well, it’s very, very possible that nobody sees that. They get into fights every day. It’s a lot of them that we don’t see,’” the motion states.
The motion also provided messages sent by people incarcerated within ADOC who extorted the families or other people who are incarcerated with threats against their loved ones.
“I need at least 100 of my money tonight or I’m going to start stabbing your son point blank period … So I need to be hearing SOMETHING ABOUT MY MONEY!!!!” one message said.
The motion also said incarcerated individuals use sexual favors for protection, illicit drugs and to repay debts.
“There is also unreported sexual violence in ADOC, hidden behind sheets draped from top bunks to conceal what is happening on lower bunks, all occurring in the absence of staff,” the motion states.
The motion also accuses ADOC staff and leadership of being responsible for the violence and the influx of contraband into prison facilities, including illicit drugs.
The motion states that staff “repeatedly introduced contraband to prisoners in ADOC” and that “Alabama leadership does not supervise what occurs in the prisons.”
For example, the motion said former ADOC Commissioner John Hamm told people who took his statement that wardens must ensure the presence of adequate security staff, and that important posts are staffed appropriately because the agency uses overtime.
It also quotes Hamm saying he did not monitor information about sexual assaults or receive reports on overdose deaths in prison, though he asked about overdose deaths “periodically.”
The motion also quotes current ADOC Commissioner Greg Lovelace, who was the chief deputy commissioner at the time, as saying in a statement to the government that he spent most of his time on the construction of a new 4,000-bed men’s prison in Elmore County, “and has not seen any reports regarding the extent of violence, contraband, or sexual assaults in the system.”

title: NC announces $20 million to expand childcare in storm recovery areas
description: North Carolina is making $20 million available to expand childcare on community college and university campuses in counties affected by Hurricane Helene and Tropical Storm Debby, Gov. Josh Stein announced. The funding is part of a $75 million federal grant awarded to the state for childcare recovery in disaster-affected areas. Applications for the $20 millio[...]
text:
Children play at childcare center. (Photo: Courtesy of Stephanie Smith)North Carolina is making $20 million available to expand childcare on community college and university campuses in counties affected by Hurricane Helene and Tropical Storm Debby, Gov. Josh Stein announced.
The funding is part of a $75 million federal grant awarded to the state for childcare recovery in disaster-affected areas. Applications for the $20 million program will open Sept. 14 and close Nov. 2.
“Today marks a step forward in creating opportunity for children and restoring stability for families in areas hit the hardest by these devastating storms,” Stein said. 
More than 230 childcare centers were affected by Helene, and more than 100 in central and eastern parts of the state were affected by Tropical Storm Debby in 2024, according to state officials.  
The money can be used to build new centers and renovate older centers. The North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services says projects must address community needs. State leaders see North Carolina’s higher education campuses as ideal locations to expand childcare options on public land. 
State officials from NCDHHS say only 16 of North Carolina’s 58 community colleges currently have childcare on campus. About 10 of the 17 UNC System campuses have some form of on-site childcare. 
“This investment to expand on-site child care to college campuses will reduce barriers for students, faculty, and the surrounding communities, allowing them to learn and work knowing their children are safe and receiving high-quality education and care,” said NCDHHS Secretary Dev Sangvai.   
NC budget offers rural childcare businesses financial help they’ve sought for years

Last year, NCDHHS said that as many as 55 childcare centers in western North Carolina damaged by Helene were expected to remain closed for the foreseeable future. By March 2025, at least 10 remained closed or were operating from temporary locations. 
The remaining $55 million in federal funding is expected to support recovery payments to eligible providers, salary supplements for early-childhood educators, disaster preparedness efforts and mental health resources. 
“Childcare is essential economic infrastructure,” said Matt Calabria, director of the Governor’s Recovery Office for Western North Carolina. “When a center closes, parents can’t get back to work, employers can’t staff up, and a community’s recovery slows.”
