name: Nevada Current
title: Without posing a single question, Stadium Authority approves another $75 million in public funding
description: Allegiant Stadium, Southern Nevada’s $2 billion partially taxpayer-funded football arena, opened just six years ago but is already poised for a facelift, courtesy of taxpayers.   The Las Vegas Stadium Authority Board, without a comment or question from a single member, except Chairman Steve Hill who presented the item, voted unanimously Wednesday to allocate[...]
text:
Las Vegas Stadium Authority Chair Steve Hill, who is also president of the Las Vegas Convention and Visitors Authority, sits alone at the dais at the Stadium Authority meeting Sept. 2, 2026, while other authority members joined the meeting via Zoom. (Photo: Dana Gentry/Nevada Current)Allegiant Stadium, Southern Nevada’s $2 billion partially taxpayer-funded football arena, opened just six years ago but is already poised for a facelift, courtesy of taxpayers.  
The Las Vegas Stadium Authority Board, without a comment or question from a single member, except Chairman Steve Hill who presented the item, voted unanimously Wednesday to allocate up to $75 million to fund about half of a $158 million expansion of Allegiant Stadium. The Las Vegas Raiders are paying for the balance. 
“We need to keep driving all those great results that Jeremy (Aguero) presented,” Hill said in reference to a report from the Authority’s economic analyst in May that the stadium generated an estimated $2.6 billion in economic impact in 2025 from 30 events and 1.5 million visitors – exceeding the original projection of $890 million, adjusted for inflation. 
“It was a great investment in Allegiant Stadium to invest seven-eighths of a percent of room tax to build that stadium” and generate twice the projected revenue, Hill, who is also president of the Las Vegas Convention and Visitors Authority, said of the increase in the room tax approved in 2016 to fund the $750 million public payout. 
“We also think this is an appropriate level of cost-sharing with the Raiders,” Hill said of the plan to pay for half of the expansion. 
The Raiders and the Stadium Authority are not reading the room, say critics who contend that with Nevadans struggling to pay their bills, now is no time to sink more public money into what some contend is a vanity project. 
Richard Krebs, a retired Las Vegan, asked during public comment why the “billionaire owners” of the Raiders are seeking public money rather than self-funding the stadium expansion. 
“They came to the desert, a land of milk and money, a land of milk and government subsidizing,” Krebs said, adding the franchise was worth about $3 billion at the time and “has increased in value to about $10 billion.” 
Asked by the Current after the meeting why the Raiders aren’t footing the bill for the entire expansion, Raiders’ President Sandra Douglass Morgan said the 2016 legislation approving the stadium funding was “actually created to have continued investment in the stadium.” 
Forbes valued the team  at $7.7 billion in August 2025
Dayvid Figler, a Las Vegas attorney and former podcast host, says he blames state lawmakers who approved the public financing of the stadium for failing to put parameters on the public funds and for “almost creating a rubber stamp.” 
He says he doesn’t  “begrudge the Raiders for asking for the money, but I do begrudge the stewards of public funds for not asking one simple question: Is this the best use?” 
Hill, Figler noted, said the project is a “good use” but noted he didn’t assert it was the best use for the money.
Douglass Morgan says it’s been “well documented” that Allegiant Stadium increases sports tourism “and actually bringing people there, so that we can continue to have people be employed at the stadium, and those tax dollars then go back into the community.”
Aguero reported to the board in May that the Stadium generated $10.6 billion in economic impact from its opening in 2020 through the present and $487.3 million in tax revenue.  It supported 62,215 person-years of employment in that time, which is in line with Aguero’s 2016 projection of 6,000 permanent jobs a year, 
Aguero, however, grossly overstated the number of construction jobs projected for building the stadium at 11,000.  In May, he acknowledged Allegiant’s construction generated 7 million work hours, the full-time equivalent of 3,365 jobs.
A rendering of the proposed portico at Allegiant Stadium shown as part of a presentation at the Las Vegas Stadium Authority meeting Sept. 2, 2026. (Photo: Dana Gentry/Nevada Current)
The expansion approved Wednesday creates a new second story entrance and outdoor event space on the north side of the building. It also includes a covered area to house ride sharing services, and likely down the road, a station to accommodate Elon Musk’s Vegas Loop. 
Hill said reducing the increase in the room tax would not be meaningful for tourists, and he noted the bonds can’t be refinanced until 2028 — ten years after they are issued. 
The “waterfall” of payment obligations in the 2016 legislation applies room tax revenue first to bond payments, Stadium Authority administrative costs, and a debt reserve that has been fully funded and no longer requires annual contributions. 
Remaining funds are used to pay the University of Nevada Las Vegas up to $3.5 million to offset revenue lost to the closing of Sam Boyd Stadium and for statutory contributions to the Stadium Authority Capital Funds. 
That leaves about $13 million a year for the waterfall residual fund, which is estimated to reach $80 million by the end of fiscal year 2027, and would be used to fund the expansion. 
Figler acknowledges that Hill made a cogent argument, accompanied by reports from economists, that the expansion “is a good investment. But none of that’s definitive,” he said, adding a “more creative, thoughtful, and intelligent,” approach would  “employ economists and analysts who aren’t on the payroll of the applicants.” 
Figler, during public comment, suggested the Stadium Authority consider improving transit or housing for Southern Nevadans. Or invest in equipment for a live stream of their public meetings. 
“They’re the only public entity that spends as much money as they do without a live stream,” Figler observed after the meeting. “They’re hiding from the public by not doing what every other public agency does.”

name: Nevada Current
title: Lawmakers propose oversight for state, local agencies using AI
description: Concerned that Nevada agencies have relied on artificial intelligence without much oversight, state lawmakers are proposing legislation to establish basic standards on how the technology is used by state and local government entities.  Proposed legislation that would require transparency around AI and prevent bias in automated decision making was among the n[...]
text:
A smartphone displays the ChatGPT app. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)Concerned that Nevada agencies have relied on artificial intelligence without much oversight, state lawmakers are proposing legislation to establish basic standards on how the technology is used by state and local government entities. 
Proposed legislation that would require transparency around AI and prevent bias in automated decision making was among the nine bill draft requests approved at the Aug. 27 the interim Government Affairs Committee meeting. 
Democratic state Sen. Dina Neal, who recommended the committee pursue the AI legislation, said a variety of government departments integrated AI systems into their agencies “without statutory action.”
“I think that it’s high time that although folks see that there is a benefit to make work more efficient, there is also some risk that I think we need to evaluate,” Neal said. 
The proposal will be taken up in the 2027 Legislative Session, which begins Feb. 1. 
Agencies, including the Nevada Department of Employment, Training, and Rehabilitation and the Department of Motor Vehicles, have implemented AI to aid with the work flow. DETR began using the technology to help with the appeals process for unemployment benefits.
There are questions around its use, said Democratic state Sen. Edgar Flores, who chairs the committee.
“We want to make sure that there is a human that ultimately is making these decisions,” Flores said. He added that lawmakers have heard of situations where people were denied benefits, sought to speak to an actual person during the appeals process, but couldn’t. 
“It shuts you down,” he said. 
There hasn’t been a review of instances where the system has failed or automation bias may have occurred, and the state needs to determine “how many errors occurred where there was a need for a human response, but the human response did not occur,” Neal said. 
Lawmakers anticipate a robust response from state and local agencies when the bill comes up for the discussion. 
“When they say ‘everything’s fine,’ then I’m going to say there needs to be an audit to make sure that what you said is fine,” Neal said. 
In 2025, 38 states adopted some type of artificial intelligence related policy, according to a National Conference of State Legislatures database.
Neal introduced legislation in 2025 that sought to establish broad guardrails around artificial intelligence companies that sought to set up shop in Nevada as well as the use of the technology in various sectors. 
Senate Bill 199 sought to prohibit law enforcement from using AI to generate police reports and teachers from using software to create lesson plans. 
It received a wide range of opposition from business industry, law enforcement, and school district employees. The bill didn’t make it out of committee. 
President Donald Trump has sought to limit states from regulating AI. 
The massive tax and spending legislation passed in July 2025, called the “One Big Beautiful Bill” originally included a provision preventing states from pursuing AI regulations for a decade.
The provision was stripped out of the legislation before its final passage.  
Trump signed an executive order in December 2025 seeking, again, to limit states from taking regulatory actions. 
Republican Assemblymember Lisa Cole was worried about the state running afoul of Trump’s order.
“I’m just a little concerned that inside of the recommendations language, we’ve got protections against bias in automated decision making,” she said. 
However, Neal said she has already looked into “how far the state needed to usurp its own position under 10th Amendment,” which protects states from federal overreach. 
“An executive order, although it may state its suggestions, might not necessarily tie the hands specifically of a state,” Neal said.

title: New ‘Energy Corridor’ opens with smoother roads and, hopefully, fewer wildlife crashes
description: Bumpy roads in a 53-mile stretch of rural San Juan County are smoother now that the Utah Department of Transportation has finished its “Energy Corridor” project. Also, motorists’ possibilities of hitting a horse or cattle during their commute are lower. The updated road now features a new roundabout, new pavement, wider shoulders and a replaced […]
text:
The Utah Department of Transportation completed construction of updates along the Energy Corridor along State Route 162 and State Route 262 in San Juan County. (Photo Courtesy of Utah Department of Transportation)Bumpy roads in a 53-mile stretch of rural San Juan County are smoother now that the Utah Department of Transportation has finished its “Energy Corridor” project. Also, motorists’ possibilities of hitting a horse or cattle during their commute are lower.
The updated road now features a new roundabout, new pavement, wider shoulders and a replaced bridge over McElmo Creek, aiming to serve and improve safety for residents and visitors in the Four Corners area, as well as workers from the petroleum industry who frequent the stretch.

“A lot of times these projects are based on how many people they serve, and unfortunately a lot of these places don’t grow, so if that’s the formula, they don’t get served as often,” Dustin Jansen, director of the Utah Division of Indian Affairs, said during an inauguration ceremony for the road on Wednesday. “But these roads are just as critical. And the safety of Utah citizens, no matter where they live, should be important for everyone.”
Jansen said that he, as a parent, is grateful for projects like these providing sidewalks and safer infrastructure for everyone.
An ‘Energy Corridor’ project seeks to create safer roads in southeastern Utah by 2026

“If you’re a parent that lives out here, you’re probably 30, 40 miles away at work, and so you’re not around and close by your kids when they’re going to school,” he said. “So it’s wonderful to know that at least in getting to school and making it there, they can do it in a safe way.”
Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson shared that sentiment, saying that roads in remote areas of the state that aren’t that densely populated may be overlooked. But, they are still integral for people living in rural Utah.
“Sometimes it’s easy for policymakers to just look at numbers and to say ‘there are more people in this area, therefore we just need to spend more money in this area.’ Sometimes you have to step back and look at overall impact and choose to spend money where it maybe doesn’t make sense on paper,” Henderson said. 
It is expensive to build and maintain roads in remote areas, she said. Working on infrastructure in sovereign nations is also a challenge. But, everything came together for this project after years of planning.
The state had worked with the Navajo Nation for years to plan the corridor located along state Route 162 and state Route 262 in southeastern Utah, ultimately starting construction in 2024 with a $152 budget of federal and state funds. 
The Utah Department of Transportation completed construction of updates along the Energy Corridor along State Route 162 and State Route 262 in San Juan County. (Photo Courtesy of Utah Department of Transportation)
The project included more than six miles of guardrail, new fencing, over 50 cattle guards and two livestock crossings under SR-162, according to a news release from the Utah Department of Transportation. 
“That is all intended to keep the horses and livestock, whatever else, off of the road, so the drivers can be safe. They don’t have to worry about hitting a horse, which, you know, is something in the city you don’t really think about, but it’s an everyday thing down here,” said Dustin Squire, a UDOT project manager overseeing the project.
Slopes were flattened and signs and lane markings were updated. Crews also built a new roundabout at the SR-162 and SR-262 intersection in Montezuma Creek.
More than eight miles of SR-162 between Montezuma Creek and Aneth were also rebuilt as part of the project, shifting the highway away from the river and closer to the mountainside, the department said. 
“We made the road a lot safer out here, and I think that that’s probably the most important thing that we did. If people made a mistake before, they had the potential of falling off the side of the road and into a riverbed,” Squire said. “And now, if you make a mistake on the road, it’s recoverable, and you can get back on the road safely.”

title: Penalty for ethics violations rises to $52K for WA state Rep. Tarra Simmons
description: A state ethics panel has ordered Democratic state Rep. Tarra Simmons to pay roughly $52,000 in penalties and fees for multiple violations of Washington ethics laws. Three weeks ago, the Legislative Ethics Board ruled the Bremerton lawmaker committed three violations of conflict of interest and special privilege laws. The board levied the maximum $5,000 penal[...]
text:
Washington state Rep. Tarra Simmons discusses documents with her attorney, Doug McKinley, before testifying at a hearing in June 2026 on allegations she violated state ethics laws. (Photo by Jerry Cornfield/Washington State Standard)A state ethics panel has ordered Democratic state Rep. Tarra Simmons to pay roughly $52,000 in penalties and fees for multiple violations of Washington ethics laws.
Three weeks ago, the Legislative Ethics Board ruled the Bremerton lawmaker committed three violations of conflict of interest and special privilege laws. The board levied the maximum $5,000 penalty for each. 
Its final order, dated Aug. 28 and released Wednesday, tacked on $37,457.98 to cover costs of staff, including state attorneys, in the case. Simmons has 90 days to pay the full amount.
Simmons has said she plans to appeal. She has 30 days from when she is served with the final order to seek review by a court. 
This case stems from a complaint filed in February 2025. After a monthslong investigation, the board, last October, found reasonable cause to believe Simmons violated the Ethics in Public Service Act. Simmons denied the allegations and rejected offers to settle.
In June, the board conducted a two-day trial-like proceeding in which Simmons faced her accusers and defended her actions under oath.
The board concluded that she improperly used her position to steer public funds to a nonprofit where she worked, and tried to retaliate against the person who initiated the investigation against her.
It dismissed three other allegations concerning Simmons’ efforts to help a friend get a job, her offer to donate unspent campaign funds to the nonprofit to pay for the friend’s position, and her employment with an organization that received state funding.
Simmons, who maintains she did nothing wrong, has called the fine unfair since she had to pursue the two-day public hearing to disprove some of the original allegations. “People shouldn’t be excessively punished when they actually prevail,” she said.
The Legislative Ethics Board has nine members, including four lawmakers, one each from the Democratic and Republican caucuses in the state House and Senate.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: GOP Senate candidate Michele Tafoya reports assets totaling $10.7M to $37.9M
description: When Michele Tafoya said Americans could handle higher gas prices caused by the war in Iran with a “stiff upper lip” and “one less trip to Starbucks,” she likely wasn’t talking about herself. The retired sportscaster and Republican candidate for U.S. Senate has assets worth between $10.7 million and $37.9 million, according to her financial […]
text:
Michele Tafoya speaks during the candidate forum for U.S. Senate at Farmfest in Morgan, Minn., on Aug. 5, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)When Michele Tafoya said Americans could handle higher gas prices caused by the war in Iran with a “stiff upper lip” and “one less trip to Starbucks,” she likely wasn’t talking about herself.
The retired sportscaster and Republican candidate for U.S. Senate has assets worth between $10.7 million and $37.9 million, according to her financial disclosure, putting her near or in the top 1% of wealthiest Americans.
Conventional wisdom says an electorate deeply concerned about the cost of living doesn’t want to be told by a multimillionaire to buck up and buy fewer lattes — especially after years of inflation going back to the pandemic and now exacerbated by President Trump’s tariffs, war in Iran and cuts to safety net programs.
“If (candidates) can’t understand and show some connection with voter worries, they’re not going to get very far,” said David Sturrock, a political science professor at Southwest Minnesota State University who has been active in Republican politics.
But Sturrock also said he doesn’t think voters are casting ballots based on a close review of financial disclosures. They’re persuaded by “fleeting impressions” of candidates and their platform.
Congress is full of millionaires from both parties, though Tafoya, 61, is rich even by their standards. The median net worth in the U.S. Senate is about $4.4 million — or more than 70 times the Census-reported median U.S. household net worth — according to a NOTUS analysis of financial disclosures.
DFL candidate Peggy Flanagan, 46, may also be a millionaire, albeit with a far smaller nest egg than Tafoya’s from a career in advocacy and politics. Flanagan has between $990,000 and $2.7 million in assets, according to her financial disclosure, putting her near or in the top 10% of American households.
Flanagan frequently points to her childhood scraping by to connect with voters’ economic concerns. She was raised by a single, working mother in subsidized housing and recalls carrying commodity cheese like a football under her arm.
Seeing how government assistance uplifted her family shaped her economic populist platform: Medicare for all, universal childcare, raising the federal minimum wage and undoing Trump’s cuts to health care and food assistance.
“I know who I’m fighting for,” she said at a rally with Sen. Bernie Sanders. “I’m fighting for the mom standing at the checkout counter trying to stretch 20 bucks through the end of the month.”
Tafoya did not grow up wealthy, either. Her father was an aerospace engineer and her mother was a teacher, according to their obituaries. She told the Star Tribune in 2017 her parents had a “depression-era mind-set where you save everything,” though they weren’t destitute.
She did not respond to requests for comment.
Tafoya and her husband, Mark Vandersall, appear to have amassed their fortune through lucrative careers.
Most of her investments are spread across retirement accounts from her decades working in sports reporting for major networks including ABC, NBC and ESPN and his in private wealth management.
Financial disclosures offer only a fuzzy picture of politicians’ wealth. Federal office holders and candidates don’t report the exact value of each of their investments but rather a broad range. For instance, Tafoya owns somewhere between $1 million and $5 million of a Vanguard index fund in one of her retirement accounts.
Candidates also don’t need to report the value of their primary residence or what they owe on the mortgage, so Tafoya’s disclosure does not include her 5-bedroom, 6-bath home in Edina that she bought with her husband, Mark Vandersall, for $2.2 million in 2008, according to county property records.
Politicians also don’t report the value of personal property like vehicles; federal pensions are exempt; and the accuracy of the reports isn’t strictly policed.
Tafoya reported no income last year, but hosted a political podcast until January on the Salem Podcast Network, which includes shows by other conservative hosts like Sebastian Gorka, Lara Trump and the late Charlie Kirk.
Flanagan reported making $129,000 from the state of Minnesota last year as lieutenant governor. Flanagan and her husband, Tom Weber, bought a home in St. Louis Park for $447,500 in 2023, according to county property records.
Tafoya’s focus on fighting fraud to save taxpayers money could prove to be a potent affordability message, even if the seat she’s running for offers arguably little power over the administration of Minnesota’s safety net programs. She also calls for more cuts to taxes and regulations.
She has so far stood by her March call for Starbucks rationing, however. In an interview last month on KSTP, saying paying higher prices is part of supporting American troops.
“I do think we need to be patriotic about this,” Tafoya said.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: New ID requirement to message NJ inmates leads to data privacy fears
description: New Jersey prisons now require people to upload a passport or driver's license to message incarcerated loved ones. That's a barrier and data privacy risk, critics charge.
text:
New Jersey prisons now require people to upload a passport or driver's license to message incarcerated loved ones. That's a barrier and data privacy risk, critics charge. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey corrections officials have long surveilled prisoners’ calls, messages, and other communications to ensure they don’t plot something sinister during those interactions.
Now, the state is expanding its scrutiny to people outside prisons, requiring friends, relatives, and anyone else who tries to message those behind bars to verify their identity by uploading their driver’s license or passport to an online portal.
Chris Greeder, a Department of Corrections spokesman, described the new identification requirement as “an important public safety measure designed to protect victims, the public, and incarcerated individuals from fraud, extortion, harassment, and criminal coordination.” He did not offer any cases or data on such offenses but pointed to the State Commission of Investigation’s public hearing on organized crime in May.
“Law enforcement testimony detailed how organized crime syndicates and street gangs have increasingly adapted to modern technology, using electronic messaging and correctional devices to orchestrate illicit activity, intimidate witnesses, and direct criminal enterprises from inside correctional facilities,” Greeder said.
But critics warn the new identification requirement creates a barrier for people who don’t have passports or driver’s licenses to prove their identity, as well as anyone concerned about digital privacy risks.
“Anything that complicates or creates heightened requirements for people trying to be in communication with their loved ones is wrong, especially in the era of unclear boundaries between what is accessible and even mined by companies that are already working in collaboration with other sorts of surveillance,” said the Rev. J. Amos Caley, an organizer with New Jersey Prison Justice Watch and pastor at the Reformed Church of Highland Park. “We should be making access easier, not harder, for folks.”
The debate comes as the department wraps up a monthslong, systemwide transition to ViaPath from JPay, which had provided those services in New Jersey prisons since 2014 and did not require such identification verification. The for-profit companies, the two largest prison communications providers nationally, supply the technology and infrastructure needed for incarcerated people to make phone calls and video visits, send electronic messages, and otherwise communicate behind bars.
Greeder said the new requirement only applies to people who want to communicate with incarcerated loved ones through electronic messaging. Outsiders can still receive phone calls from inmates without showing photo identification, he added.
“NJDOC works with its vendors to ensure personal data collected for verification is handled securely and maintained strictly for authorized security and communication purposes,” he said.
ViaPath, though, has a history of data security problems.
The Federal Trade Commission found in 2023 that ViaPath failed to secure the sensitive data of hundreds of thousands of users that was stored in a cloud, failed to notify everyone impacted of the breach, and misrepresented their data security measures. The commission ordered the company in 2024 to reduce its data retention time, follow strict notification timelines, and take other remedial actions.
ViaPath spokespeople did not respond to the New Jersey Monitor’s request for comment.
East Jersey State Prison in Rahway, Friday April 10, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
William Sullivan, a correctional officer at East Jersey State Prison who heads the officers’ union, said the new identification verification requirement is worth the data privacy risks.
“You got to know who’s communicating,” Sullivan said. “People still run their gangs from inside the prisons. ViaPath is a tool that they use to communicate. Not everybody, but there’s people that’ll use it to communicate and run their nefarious activities from within the jail cells.”
Caley and other critics countered that most of those trying to communicate with people in prison are not criminals but instead family and friends, some of whom will not be able to meet the new requirement.
More than half of Americans don’t have passports, while about 30% of New Jersey adults don’t have driver’s licenses, federal and state data shows. Those more likely to lack such documents (or have outdated names or addresses that won’t pass verification tests) are already marginalized groups, such as low-income people, homeless people, those fresh out of prison, immigrants, and transgender people and others who changed their names.
“When people are inside, that lifeline, that connection to the outside, is what’s getting them through,” said Racquel Romans-Henry, director of policy and advocacy at Salvation and Social Justice. “Creating any kind of barrier that makes it hard for incarcerated people to access their support system is cruel and unusual.”
Identity verification, though, is becoming a common requirement by states and prison communications providers, along with other restrictions that have the effect of reducing prisoners’ interactions with the outside world, said Wanda Bertram of the Prison Policy Initiative.
She pointed to the federal Bureau of Prisons, which now prohibits outside communications beyond those an incarcerated person initiates, and other states that cap how many outsiders an inmate can correspond with. Besides families, such restrictions also impact prison-justice advocates and journalists who try to connect with folks inside prisons, she added.
“Prisons are increasingly demonizing people on the outside who want to communicate with incarcerated folks and instituting surveillance practices that impact everyone, which they justify by saying, ‘there are bad actors,’” Bertram said.
Prison staff often are implicated in leading or facilitating crime behind bars, Bertram added. Correctional officers in New Jersey have been disciplined and charged for crimes ranging from contraband smuggling and money laundering to accepting bribes.
Identification verification is just one of multiple “transformative technology” tools ViaPath has deployed in prisons in New Jersey and elsewhere.
The company also collects biometric data and uses artificial intelligence to analyze every call and communication, sharing its findings with law enforcement. Its contract with New Jersey includes six “investigative solutions” that can detect calls between incarcerated people, flag problematic keywords in calls and messaging, and identify the type of phone called, among other things.
The cost of such tech tools is listed as “included” in New Jersey’s contract with ViaPath, and Greeder told the New Jersey Monitor last spring that the contract didn’t cost state or taxpayers anything. Instead, incarcerated people and their loved ones pay for it, in the form of fees charged per service. They spent between $1.5 million and $3.2 million a year on calls, messaging, video visits, and other communications and recreational services since 2015.
As the surveillance and data-collection done during those interactions expand beyond prison walls, that means “families are now effectively paying for their own monitoring,” Bertram said.
“Incarcerated people are the most surveilled population in this country, and the communication technologies that allow them to talk to their loved ones on the outside also extend that surveillance to the people on the outside,” she said.
Families who object to New Jersey’s new identification verification requirement, or any other contract terms they deem exploitative or unfair, should push for change, she added.
“This is not some implacable, divine law. This is a line in a contract, and contracts are amended all the time,” Bertram said. “This is a misguided focus on incarcerated people and their families as being a threat or a safety risk when the vast majority of them are just trying to keep in touch with their loved ones. That’s good for everyone, including the public, when those family connections are fostered.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: OPINION: In tackling the childcare challenge, Nebraska’s advantage is working together
description: When a community is facing a challenge as complicated as early childhood, it is easy to ask who is responsible for solving it. Do we look to government? Nonprofits? Businesses? Philanthropy? From my perspective as the economic development specialist at Nebraska Public Power District, I have learned that some of our biggest challenges do not […]
text:
An employee at Cubby’s Childcare Center in Bridgeport, West Virginia, plays with two infants in July. A bipartisan group of state lawmakers say it’s time to rethink the nation’s fragile childcare system. (Photo by Amelia Ferrell Knisely/West Virginia Watch)When a community is facing a challenge as complicated as early childhood, it is easy to ask who is responsible for solving it. Do we look to government? Nonprofits? Businesses? Philanthropy?
From my perspective as the economic development specialist at Nebraska Public Power District, I have learned that some of our biggest challenges do not have one person or organization responsible for solving them. Sometimes the best place to start is simply by getting the right people around the same table and recognizing that everyone has a role to play.
That is one reason I am looking forward to joining hundreds of Nebraskans at the Thriving Children, Families, and Communities Conference in Kearney on Sept. 22. The people gathering there represent different communities, professions, organizations and perspectives from across the state. But we all have something in common. We want Nebraska’s children, family and communities to thrive. That is something we care about at NPPD, too.
At NPPD, we understand how important strong communities are to Nebraska’s future. Communities need families who can build their lives here. Employers need a reliable workforce. And Nebraska needs communities that are prepared to grow and compete. All of those things are connected in the interest of children and families.
That is why early childhood is not an issue that one organization or one sector can solve on its own.
It is a trickle effect that starts with families. Families need access to affordable, quality childcare. Providers need the employees and resources to operate their businesses and provide quality care. Employers need parents who can reliably participate in the workforce. Schools benefit when children arrive ready to learn. Communities need young families to stay, work and build their lives there.
When those needs are connected, our solutions need to be connected, too.
That means collaboration must be more than getting people in a room. It is more than exchanging business cards, sharing updates or agreeing that something needs to change.
Real collaboration means listening to people who may see the issue differently than we do. It means making room for parents, childcare providers, businesses and community leaders to help identify both the problems and the solutions. And sometimes, it means being willing to change the way our own organizations do things if it helps move a larger goal forward. 
Real collaboration means listening to people who may see an issue differently than we do. It means making room for parents, childcare providers, businesses and community leaders to share their perspectives and work together toward solutions that support children, family and our communities.
And sometimes, collaboration means being willing to change the way our own organizations operate if it helps move a bigger goal forward. That’s the kind of leadership Nebraska needs.
Leadership does not always come from the person with the biggest title, budget or organization. It can come from the childcare provider who understands what families in her community need. The parent who can explain why a program that looks good on paper is not working in real life. The business leader who recognizes that childcare is connected to workforce. The policymaker who brings people together around a solution. Or the community member who sees an opportunity others have missed.
Nebraska already has many of those leaders. Our opportunity is to connect them.
And that does not mean every community needs the same answer. Some of the best solutions start right in the community, with the people who understand the issue firsthand. What works in one community may not work in another. 
Communities can learn from each other. Organizations share what is working, and when we connect those local experiences, we have a better chance of finding solutions that can make a difference beyond one community.
This is why events and conferences like the Thriving Children, Families and Communities Conference are so important. The value is not just in what we hear that day, it is in the relationships we build and what we take back with us.
Nebraska’s future depends on strong communities, and strong communities depend on children and families having the opportunity to thrive.
No single organization can make that happen alone. But each of us has something to contribute.
And when we work together, Nebraska communities can accomplish things that none of us could accomplish on our own.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Lawmakers have ignored an Oklahoma constitutional edict for years. Kevin Stitt called their bluff.
description: Oklahoma’s Constitution requires that lawmakers give voters the right to consider calling a constitutional convention at least once every 20 years. Yet lawmakers last placed the referendum on the ballot in 1970 — 56 years ago. In 1994, the Legislature asked voters to repeal the 20-year requirement entirely; voters rejected it. After years of lawmakers […]
text:
House Speaker Charles McCall, R-Atoka, gives a farewell speech on the House floor to recognize his final days in the state Legislature on May 22, 2024, at the state Capitol. McCall is term-limited after 12 years in office. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)Oklahoma’s Constitution requires that lawmakers give voters the right to consider calling a constitutional convention at least once every 20 years.
Yet lawmakers last placed the referendum on the ballot in 1970 — 56 years ago. In 1994, the Legislature asked voters to repeal the 20-year requirement entirely; voters rejected it.
After years of lawmakers from both parties failing to comply with the constitutional requirement, Gov. Kevin Stitt’s patience has run out. He recently issued an executive order that sets a special election on April 6, 2027 where voters would at long last have the chance to decide whether to call a convention.
Critics argue Stitt lacks the authority to place a question on the ballot unilaterally. Stitt counters that the Legislature has abdicated its constitutional duty, and his oath of office compels him to enforce the requirement.
While attorneys debate the separation of powers, the underlying politics are simple: The Legislature systematically violated the Constitution because an independent assembly of Oklahomans threatens its power.
A citizen-led convention would give the people of Oklahoma the most realistic path to making constitutional reforms the Legislature won’t make on its own or its special interest allies won’t allow. Those could include adopting modern democratic best practices and other policies that ensure the people remain the ultimate authors of their government.
The concept of holding a constitutional convention was invented in Massachusetts in the late 1770s because lawmakers have an inherent conflict of interest when revising their own powers. Massachusetts’ innovation was to elect delegates independent of the legislature to propose constitutional changes, subject to direct voter approval.
The early state framers did not fully foresee how fiercely modern legislatures would protect their gatekeeping power. To prevent politicians from stonewalling needed reforms, 14 states, including Oklahoma, established the Periodic Constitutional Convention Referendum as a legislative bypass mechanism.
Over the years, I’ve examined and tracked how state legislatures across the country continue to undermine voters’ constitutionally protected right to call conventions.
Oklahoma stands out for its brazenness.
While lawmakers in other states use subtle maneuvers to undermine the process, Oklahoma’s Legislature has simply ignored its constitutional duty for more than half a century.
Oklahoma lawmakers often blame procedural gridlock between the House and Senate for their failure to comply with the Constitution. But American history shows that when a ruling party genuinely wants to pass legislation, procedural roadblocks vanish.
This institutional self-preservation also explains Oklahoma’s recent legislative attacks on citizen ballot initiatives. Like conventions, citizen initiatives bypass legislative control. In response to citizen success in getting measures before voters, lawmakers have consistently sought to raise signature thresholds and shorten petition windows to restrict grassroot access.
Tellingly, Oklahomans secured both the citizen right to place issues on the ballot and the periodic ability to call constitutional conventions through its original statehood convention.
Oklahoma lawmakers have demonstrated a preference for the standard legislative process over both initiatives and conventions because legislators get to control the agenda.
In the Capitol, leadership can pass favored bills while quietly burying popular reforms that would restrict their own influence — such as redistricting, term limits, transparency measures, and ethics oversight. They may also bury popular reforms — such as campaign finance, lobbying, administrative procedure, and legislative procedure — that would harm their special interests allies that have undue influence over Oklahoma’s government.
An open-ended constitutional convention strips away those legislative firewalls.
The political dynamics of an initiative petition versus convention differ for a minority party. With a ballot initiative, organizers can tightly narrow the agenda to a single popular issue that the majority party refuses to hear. A convention, by contrast, opens the entire constitutional agenda — inviting debates on popular reforms that face bipartisan opposition among political insiders.
Oklahomans should view legislative outrage over Stitt’s convention order with deep skepticism.
The stakes in this fight are clear: If this executive action is abandoned, the constitutional convention is functionally dead in Oklahoma. Modern legislatures simply will not call a convention that threatens their own power.
Putting this referendum on the ballot is the only plausible path to restoring a constitutional right that lawmakers have suppressed for decades and that courts in other states have often treated as a “political question,” meaning a matter the judiciary considers beyond its authority to resolve.
Even if Oklahomans ultimately reject calling a constitutional convention, putting the question on the ballot re-establishes a vital principle: The people, not entrenched politicians, hold the ultimate authority over the state’s foundational document.

name: WyoFile
title: The rattlesnakes of Sinks Canyon: Some lack rattles, others den alone but shed their skins with friends
description:
One of the most likely spots in Wyoming to spot a prairie rattler has never been studied until now, and an in-the-works scientific inquiry suggests that there’s a unique population full of quirky traits. 
The post The rattlesnakes of Sinks Canyon: Some lack rattles, others den alone but shed their skins with friends appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Sinks Canyon State Park Superintendent Jessica Moore was responding to a call that she’s quite familiar with — a snake was on the trail — when WyoFile rang on Tuesday, incidentally to inquire about rattlesnakes.
A colleague’s call had alerted Moore “that we need the bucket,” without specifying why. But she knew the drill. 
“We want to make sure, in case guests are overhearing, that they’re not going to the location where the snake is,” Moore recounted from her office a couple hours later. 
In what’s a routine operation at Sinks Canyon State Park, seasonal staffer Conner Gregory gently seized the venomous viper with a dedicated snake grabber along the trail leading to where the Popo Agie River goes subterranean. The snake in his grip looked to be about 8 years old, based on the beads on its rattle. It was pretty chill.
“It didn’t actually start to rattle,” Moore said, “until we were putting it into the bucket.”


Sinks Canyon State Park employee Conner Gregory moves a rattlesnake from the trail leading to the Popo Agie River sink on Sept. 1, 2026. (Skylar Sargent)


It was a low-drama affair, even with a handful of intrigued park tourists watching. The snake-moving crew carried the rattler a stone’s throw away from the trail, set it free and that was that. 
A couple years earlier, the snake would have been given a ride to the higher-elevation west end of Sinks Canyon State Park. But for the snake’s own well-being, they’re now moved much shorter distances. 
“That procedure has changed based on the research that Emily’s provided for us,” Moore said. 
Emily is Emily Martin, a Ph.D. candidate at the University of Idaho’s College of Natural Resources Idaho Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit. She just completed three years of field research on prairie rattlesnakes in Sinks Canyon, one of the more likely places to see a rattlesnake. Yet, little was understood about the population, which numbers in the hundreds. 
“No one had done any research in Sinks Canyon before,” Martin said. 
Moore encouraged Martin to dig in, and she did. For the next three years, the biologist visited the state park regularly searching for and capturing rattlers. Early on, she realized the snakes of Sinks have their quirks. 
“In a lot of places in Wyoming, you get these big dens where you’ve got hundreds of snakes,” Martin said. “In Sinks Canyon, they don’t really do that. It very much seems that they’re hibernating singly, or in very, very small groups, which is really unusual.” 
That wasn’t the only atypical behavior. Rattlesnakes are renowned for providing some level of maternal care.
“A rattlesnake will have her babies, and then often babies will hang out with mom until they have their first shed,” Martin said. “I never observed that in Sinks, which I thought was really odd.” 
Even in the immediately adjacent Sawmill Creek drainage, she said, communal dens and mothering behavior were much more common. From a research standpoint, the quirks were initially challenging. 
“I worked on rattlesnakes in California, and was used to being able to walk up to a den and sample 20 or 30 snakes,” Martin said. “Whereas at Sinks, I’m out there 10 hours a day for six months and I catch 100 snakes, which is pretty low return.” 
That’s not to say there are few snakes in Sinks. They’re everywhere, but just dispersed around the landscape, she said. Martin encountered rattlesnakes basking in the snow, and coiled up in pine needles. A few snakes even hibernated in the talus on the shady, north-facing side of the canyon, which isn’t typically thought of as good habitat. 
“I have no idea what they’re doing up there,” Martin said. “But it seems to be working for them.”

University of Idaho PhD candidate Emily Martin helps a Great Basin rattlesnake breathe while surgery is conducted for research. (Courtesy)

Moore, the park superintendent, confirmed that the snakes of Sinks are just about everywhere. Early this summer, which brought record-breaking heat, the park was fielding a lot of calls about snakes along trails that cut through the timbered slopes along the south side of the canyon.  
“We were speculating: Is it because it was so hot that they were using more of that shady side?” Moore said. 
Martin’s study also provided some clues about exactly what the Sinks serpents were up to. Although their reptilian body shape doesn’t lend itself well to exterior tracking equipment, researchers are able to embed transmitters into snakes’ body cavities using a minor surgery. 
“It actually sits underneath the rib cage,” Martin said. “I suture it to a rib, and then the antenna runs subcutaneously, just under the skin along the body wall.” 
During field seasons from 2024 to 2026, she implanted 31 Sinks Canyon prairie rattlesnakes with the transmitters. It was through this research that Martin learned that snakes particularly struggled when state park workers moved them long distances. 
“We found that they had decreased survival,” she said. “They weren’t doing well.”
Specifically, she found that three of the 11 translocated snakes died over the months and years ahead. Comparatively, only three of the 20 snakes that didn’t get moved died in the months ahead. 

Grant McCarger, a University of Idaho wildlife technician, relocates a prairie rattlesnake from near the Sinks Canyon’s sink in summer 2025. (Sinks Canyon State Park)
Over the course of the study, Martin also picked up some other oddities about the snakes of Sinks. About 3% she encountered didn’t have rattles. Although other studies have investigated rattleless rattlesnakes, the cause of the trait in Fremont County snakes seems to be different. 
“We found that it was associated with skeletal and reproductive abnormalities,” Martin said, “which is not something that’s been reported before.” 
An academic paper about those rattleless rattlers is in the works, and Martin’s aiming to publish it in the Herpetological Review. That’s not the only part of her research that she’s pushed through the peer-review process. This spring, the University of Idaho scientists published a research article about Sinks Canyon snakes’ proclivity to aggregate when they’re shedding their skins. 
“To my knowledge, it’s the first observation of shedding aggregations in prairie rattlesnakes, so that was exciting,” Martin said. 
An average of 2.4 snakes gathered together during periods of skin shedding, but a handful amassed during the largest groupings. Sometimes groups were all females, other times there were bisexual aggregations. 

About 3% of the rattlesnakes that University of Idaho researchers encountered during a 3-year study in Sinks Canyon lacked rattles. A reproductive abnormality likely explains the snakes lacking their telltale feature. (Emily Martin)

Why they gather when they slough their skin remains a bit of a mystery, Martin said. 
“As with a lot of science,” she said, “I think we’re not totally sure what they’re up to.” 
One behavior that the Sinks Canyon research did not document among the rattlers: conflict with people and their pets. Only one of the study subjects got into trouble. 
“I had one that we translocated after a dry bite to a dog,” she said. “She was set up under a picnic table, and unfortunately somebody had their little dog on a leash, and the dog came in and got tagged in the face. But luckily, the snake elected not to use any venom.” 
That fits with Moore’s experience managing a heavily recreated square-mile state park that’s squarely in dense prairie rattlesnake habitat. She’s only been aware of the one dog bite in four years, and hasn’t heard of a human being struck.  
“There are hundreds of rattlesnakes here in Sinks Canyon, and we see a couple dozen a year,” Moore said. “That speaks to the fact that we can all share this space, and for the most part, the snakes don’t really want to interact with people.” 
Presenting her research at the Saving Yellowstone conference hosted by billionaire Bondurant resident Joe Ricketts last month, Martin made her case for the value and importance of rattlesnakes. They help protect native vegetation from rodents, she said, and provide a food source for small carnivores and raptors.
“I think more importantly, rattlesnakes are emblematic of the things we really value about nature, about wild spaces like the Greater Yellowstone,” Martin said. “The strong feelings that rattlesnakes inspire, including fear for some people, is a good reminder of what we value about nature as a society.”

name: WyoFile
title: Waiting on s’mores until the danger subsides
description:
Our understanding of wildfires in the West grows as we live alongside them, writes columnist Walt Gasson.
The post Waiting on s’mores until the danger subsides appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
After almost 70 years, I still remember it quite clearly. We were on our way to the home place one evening when my dad told me about a forest fire nearby. For some reason, I concluded that if the people fighting the fire saw us, they would conscript my father into helping them. That scared me. I can still recall driving along the north side of Little Prospect Mountain in the dark, watching the glow from the fire above us and wondering if we were going to be OK.

Opinion

I guess you can’t grow up in a family like mine without having some consciousness about wildland fires. The country around the home place hasn’t had a major fire for a century. But you can still see the scars from the old burns. When we were riding or hiking, I thought about them and wondered what it must have been like when our part of the country burned. That was a little bit scary too.
Somewhere along the line, I discovered I wanted a career in wildlife conservation. In college, I learned about the role of fire in Wyoming ecosystems. I was pretty familiar with the effects of fire, and it all made sense to me because it was linked to science. Science took the fear factor out and made fire more of a natural process — just a part of the country, like rain or photosynthesis. But like most things academic, the real world turns out to be a little more complex.
I remember the first controlled burn I worked. It was in Sunlight Basin, just east of Yellowstone National Park. We were creating more winter habitat for elk, which was a great idea. But I was ill-prepared for the reality of being close to fire on that scale. I was part of a crew that set the first drip line. It was well-planned and well-executed. We carefully monitored all the conditions — wind speed and direction, humidity, soil moisture, etc. And then, drip torches in hand, we set the first fire line. Everything proceeded just like it should. The fire advanced slowly across a wide sagebrush flat. We followed it, and the teams with the fire trucks were close at hand. The perimeter was secure. It was kind of fun to watch until I saw a juniper tree explode. The fire line was still 20 or 30 yards from that old tree, but it must’ve increased the temperature remarkably. Long before the flames ever got near the juniper tree, it exploded with a sound like 50 gallons of gasoline going off. I was humbled and amazed.
The human response to the 1988 Yellowstone fire was uneven, at times verging on frenzied, but large wildlife, for the most part, executed an orderly evacuation. (Steve Henry, NPS)
Since then, I’ve been around other fires — some big, and some small. And the truth is, they still amaze me. In my head, I know that they’re an important part of landscape and that they have been so since the beginning. Our forests in the West evolved with fire, and they depend on it to propagate. Indigenous folks burned lots of places for a variety of reasons, from grasslands and sagebrush country all the way up to timber line. The country grew up with fire. I guess I did, too.
Kim and I now find ourselves in the position of wrangling hundreds of public land users in a Forest Service campground. Our campground is at elevation 10,500 feet. The trees are mostly Engelmann spruce and subalpine fir, and about 50% of the standing trees are dead — victims of an insect epidemic years ago. We came out of a very dry winter into a very hot, dry summer. There hasn’t been a major fire anywhere near us in my lifetime. So when it comes to fires in the campground, we’re very cautious right now. 
And that causes some consternation among the campers. Most of them are from someplace else, and a lot of them aren’t very connected to wild lands. 
They come to us with a bundle of firewood from a convenience store and the expectation that they will have a campfire. Many consider that campfire an absolute must, indeed a right. Only a few of them recognize the irony in coming here from the Front Range to escape the smoke, while feeling entitled to a fire in a tinderbox. But our job is not to win a popularity contest. It is to keep all of us safe. 
Recently, a good friend posed an interesting question when a big sagebrush fire burned thousands of acres near his place. He’s as Wyoming as you can be, and he’s not afraid of anything. He makes a living selling outdoor gear and supplies. But after a day of helping his neighbors move livestock out of harm’s way, he asked the rhetorical question, “What if we all just stayed home for a while, until we get some rain and the fire danger goes down?”
If we posed that question in the campground, we’d be the least popular campground hosts ever. Most of our campers come from urban or suburban places, comfortably disconnected from wildland fires. But that doesn’t change the fact that safety beats entitlement every time. Someone has to lead. So right now, the s’mores are going to have to wait for some rain.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: 2026 Tennessee state House election: Five races to grab attention of both parties
description: Five Tennessee state House races are likely to draw the most attention of both political parties this fall as Democrats look to pick up seats in the lower chamber for the first time in eight years.  Democrats hold two of the seats, while Republicans hold the other three. No matter the outcome, Republicans will maintain […]
text:
Tennessee Democrats are trying to flip a handful of legislative seats to pick up seats for the first time since 2018.  (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Five Tennessee state House races are likely to draw the most attention of both political parties this fall as Democrats look to pick up seats in the lower chamber for the first time in eight years. 
Democrats hold two of the seats, while Republicans hold the other three. No matter the outcome, Republicans will maintain their supermajority control of the state House, since the party holds a 75-to-24 advantage. 
The most flippable seat for Democrats is a Memphis district held by GOP state Rep. John Gillespie. The District 97 seat is the only one a Republican holds in the state legislature that former Vice President Kamala Harris won in the 2024 presidential election. 
Gillespie ran about 5 percentage points ahead of Republican President Donald Trump in that election, defeating Democrat Jesse Huseth by around 1,100 votes. The 2026 race is a rematch.
Republicans’ top pickup opportunity is a Clarksville seat held by Democratic state Rep. Ronnie Glynn. Trump carried the District 67 seat in 2024, but Glynn won a narrow 131-vote victory that same year. 
Other potential opportunities for Democrats include a district in Knoxville where Republican state Rep. Elaine Davis faces Democrat Bryan Goldberg. In 2024, Davis beat Goldberg by about 2,500 votes.
Democrats also plan to challenge a Clarksville seat, where Republican state Rep. Michael Lankford faces Democrat Allie Phillips. Phillips ran in 2024 against the late state Rep. Jeff Burkhart, who beat her by about 2,000 votes; Lankford was appointed in December to serve out the rest of Burkhart’s term. 
Republicans want to flip a seat in Nashville’s suburbs that Harris won with just over 50% of the vote. Democratic state Rep. Caleb Hemmer held the seat the past four years, but he chose not to run this cycle. Democrat Mark Proctor faces Republican Bill Hancock this year. 


The Tennessee House of Representatives has steadily moved in the GOP’s favor in nearly every election since it first gained control of the lower chamber in 2008. The party has held 75 seats since 2022, when the state last redrew House districts. 
State Rep. John Ray Clemmons, a Nashville Democrat who chairs the state House caucus, said the goal for now is holding all their seats.
“The map is so gerrymandered, flipping any seat would be a win,” Clemmons said.
The national political environment should favor the Democratic Party, as New York Times polling averages show Trump with an approval rating of 38% and the generic ballot polling shows the party leading Republicans by 5-7 percentage points. 
State Rep. William Lamberth, a Portland Republican and the majority leader for the House caucus, said the state GOP’s goal is to control all 99 seats, and they want to challenge “every race where a Republican is running against a Democrat.”
Hanging over the election is a threat of redistricting in 2027
Tennessee redrew its U.S. congressional map in May after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down a crucial part of the Voting Rights Act that required states with a history of racial discrimination to draw majority-minority districts to ensure Black representation. 
The decision allowed state lawmakers to further gerrymander the state’s U.S. House map so Republicans could hold all nine of the state’s congressional seats, despite Democrats winning between 35-40% of the vote in past elections.
State lawmakers chose not to redraw any of the state legislative maps because the 2022 redistricting helped the party reach its current level of 75 seats. But depending on the results of the 2026 election, that calculus could change.
Clemmons said he is “very concerned” about the possibility of Republicans drawing a new map if Democrats make any gains. 
“They will 100% redraw the map and try to rig it if they lose,” he said.

title: Civil rights group urges Alabama ban on criminal arrests for unpaid trash bills
description: A civil rights group is continuing to bring legal challenges against municipalities and counties that file criminal charges against residents with unpaid garbage bills, but wants state lawmakers to ban the practice. Rep. Tim Wadsworth, R-Arley, introduced HB 512, during the legislative session last spring that would have prevented local governments from brin[...]
text:
A trash can sits on the side of the road Wednesday, Aug. 2, 2023 in Lanett, Ala. The Southern Poverty Law Center has represented individuals who faced criminal charges for unpaid garbage bills and wants lawmakers to pass legislation to ban the practice. (Stew Milne for Alabama Reflector)A civil rights group is continuing to bring legal challenges against municipalities and counties that file criminal charges against residents with unpaid garbage bills, but wants state lawmakers to ban the practice.
Rep. Tim Wadsworth, R-Arley, introduced HB 512, during the legislative session last spring that would have prevented local governments from bringing misdemeanor charges against people with outstanding solid waste fees.
“We want legislation preventing cities, localities, and the state from arresting folks for nonpayment of trash fees,” said Ellen Degnan, senior staff attorney with the SPLC, in an interview Tuesday. “Right now, there is a state law that makes it a misdemeanor to fail to pay trash fees but does not actually permit counties and municipalities to prosecute those cases. And furthermore, the Alabama Constitution does not permit the use of the criminal system to go after civil debt.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
SPLC last Friday sent a letter to Winston County officials demanding they drop  70 active criminal cases tied to unpaid solid waste fees; repay fines and fees owed in the cases and stop pursuing criminal charges in the matter.
Multiple messages were sent to the Winston County Commission and the county attorney on Tuesday and Wednesday. A message was sent to Wadsworth on Wednesday seeking comment. Wadsworth’s district includes Winston County.
The SPLC letter included images of notifications sent by the Winston County Sanitation Department to residents with outstanding bills of over $1,000. The notices said that the county commission is “requesting an arrest warrant be issued for delinquent accounts,” and gave individuals 10 days from the date of the notice to contact the department for payment.
SPLC has targeted other municipalities engaged in the practice.
Degnan said SPLC has received some positive responses from the demand letters. The district attorney in Valley agreed to stop prosecuting people for their unpaid solid waste fees. Chickasaw placed a moratorium on additional prosecutions.
SPLC has yet to receive a response from officials in Fayette or Winston County, Degnan said. However, SPLC representatives believe it is an ongoing problem in the state, and they want a definitive answer from the Legislature to permanently ban the practice.
“What we need at the state level is clarity that these policies are illegal and unacceptable in Alabama.” Degnan said. “That is what we are hoping the Legislature takes up this session.”
Wadsworth’s legislation was sent to the House County and Municipal Government Committee, but never came up for a vote last spring. The Legislature did approve SB 32, sponsored by Sen. Wes Kitchens, R-Arab, that established an exemption for veterans who lived below the poverty line and whose sole income source is from veteran’s benefits regarding solid waste fees.
“We were trying to add that with the Military Stability Commission, the package of bills we do, trying to make sure we are one of the most military friendly states,” Kitchens said in an interview Wednesday. “Really, just as a way to support our veteran’s community too.”
Kitchens said he is open to expanding the exemption to include others but with caveats.
“There was a lot of concern about who was going to cover that cost because it still is a cost,” Kitchens said. “Is that passed on to all the other residents who are paying? Does the county, the city, the local governing body that is over the solid waste? All of these are conversations that got brought up.”

California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom departs after speaking about the Election Rigging Response Act at a news conference in Los Angeles. On Wednesday, Newsom visited Montgomery, Alabama as the first stop of a tour of the South. (Mario Tama/Getty Images)California Gov. Gavin Newsom Wednesday visited Montgomery as the first stop on a tour of the South.
Although the tour was announced in advance, Newsom, a Democrat considered a potential presidential candidate in 2028, did not have public events and did not make appear to make himself available to local or state media during the day. Newsom’s office did not respond to requests for comment Tuesday or Wednesday.
Newsom met with Montgomery Mayor Steven Reed as part of a tour of sites of the Civil Rights Movement. During a press conference Wednesday afternoon, Reed said he hopes Newsom has a better understanding of the state now that he’s visited.

“The road to prosperity comes through the South, and I believe it comes through Alabama, and certainly right here in Montgomery,” Reed said “And I think to make sure (we have to make sure) that leaders, again, from the political side to the private sector, understand what’s happening in the heartland, and they understand what’s happening in southern cities and communities like this.”
According to Reed, he and Newsom also had conversations about the Civil Rights Movement, the U.S. Supreme Court’s Louisiana v. Callais decision that significantly weakened the Voting Rights Act, and the Alabama Legislature redrawing the congressional map of the state in attempt to replace U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Mobile, with a Republican.
Reed said they also discussed “the history of the city of Montgomery and all the courageous men and women who fought for civil rights before it was popular, before it was cool, while it was very, very dangerous, life-threatening, and how they fought for the Voting Rights Act and many of the freedoms that are at risk today.”
This is not the first time the governor has visited Montgomery. Newsom in 2024 visited the city unannounced and made a video outside of Dexter Avenue King Memorial Baptist Church, which he visited again Wednesday.
Reed said in addition to visiting Civil Rights sites, Newsom also visited small businesses and Alabama State University to talk with students.
“(The conversation) was a student-led conversation around initiatives that he has brought on in California,” Reed said. “Things that he has seen there, both with college students, whether it’s the rise in the cost of higher education, whether it is where is AI taking the workforce and how to prepare for the world with AI and how they should prepare themselves to create change and to lead in their current spaces.”
Alabama State University Wednesday confirmed Newsom’s visit in statement, but declined further comment.

title: Let’s figure out affordability. Then we can talk about data centers.
description: One of my most vivid memories of moving to Silicon Valley in 2007 is walking my dogs through town one Saturday morning and stopping to watch a young couple, early 30s maybe, take delivery of a brand new Lamborghini.  It felt like I’d arrived in Oz, a fantastical land where a young person could make […]
text:
Tesla owner Elon Musk, right, was hardly alone in the tech sector in supporting the reelection efforts by Donald Trump, left. Many Silicon Valley investors and innovators were hoping for a lighter regulatory hand than they have seen under President Joe Biden. (Photo by Brandon Bell/Getty Images)One of my most vivid memories of moving to Silicon Valley in 2007 is walking my dogs through town one Saturday morning and stopping to watch a young couple, early 30s maybe, take delivery of a brand new Lamborghini. 
It felt like I’d arrived in Oz, a fantastical land where a young person could make millions at a startup or by being an early employee of Facebook or eBay or Google — companies that sold mysterious airwave connections — and where a man named Mark Zuckerberg was just one of the many young wizards with extraordinary powers. 
Today, most young people can’t afford to buy a starter house.
I thought of this as I watched Kentucky Senate President Robert Stivers, in a recent interview on WKYT, attempt to assuage the public’s growing fear of what data centers (new to us, like Facebook was back in 2007) might bring. 
“[T]hese can be economic development opportunities that have a huge financial tax base impact to the positive to a local community, if done right,” Stivers said, noting that concern about utility rates is legitimate. He then said there is also a fear of water usage but that this is not really a concern, and “you don’t want them placed where it ruins the fabric of the community.”
Correct. We do not want data centers to ruin the fabric of our communities. An interesting choice of phrase considering what social media firms — now needing to build massive data centers for their AI products — have wrought on the social fabric of our communities. 
In her 2025 book “Careless People” about her time working at Facebook, Sarah Wynn-Williams writes that she now thinks mostly about the worst of what they’ve done. “How Facebook is helping some of the worst people in the world do terrible things. How it’s an astonishingly effective machine to turn people against each other.”
Just a few days ago, Facebook’s parent company Meta agreed to settle a multi-state lawsuit for $17.1 billion — yes, that’s billion with ‘b’ — and make changes to its social platforms for children’s safety. In a press release, Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman indicated that Kentucky will receive $358 million. 
Which brings me to the data center debate. Are we to expect these same tech companies — one of which had to be sued in multiple states to protect our kids online — to tell us the truth about AI and data centers? 
I don’t remember when we started talking in billions vs. millions of dollars, but the word “billions” is in seemingly every story coming out of the Trump administration, and we’re not even two years in. 
His billion dollar ballroom. 
His Iran War quagmire that is costing, by some estimates, a billion dollars a day.
The billions the president and his family have made off crypto, while most ordinary investors have lost money.
Meanwhile the powerful elite, from Washington D.C. to Silicon Valley to Senate President Stivers insist we calm down about data centers and trust them, because they’re doing what is best for us and for our communities. If that’s the case, the next time Stivers trains his gaze on a TV camera he should explain why he let this year’s popular, bipartisan bill to restrict social media for kids, which easily passed the House, die in the Senate after Meta lobbied against the bill.
I no longer live in Silicon Valley, where I watched the 2007 ordinariness of a Lamborghini delivery. But contrary to popular GOP talking points, we did not leave California because of culture wars or politics, but because of the punishing cost of living. 
Today, that punishing cost of living is — thanks to a cult-like Republican Party and their leader’s Gilded Age ballroom, his Iran war, and his obsession with tariffs — leaching its way into Kentucky’s farms, bourbon industry, the local gas station, and more.
I don’t know if a data center would be good for my community or not. What I do know is that there is a cost for lies, and Americans have been swamped with so many years of lies from the president and his tech buddies — billionaires, all — and now the latter insists we roll out the Welcome Wagon for their massive data centers, post haste. 
What could go wrong?
I was filling up my truck at the Lawrenceburg Kroger when a woman with a child in her car pulled up on the other side of the pump. She walked over to my window and said, “I’m so sorry. I’m sorry to bother you, ma’am, but do you have a few dollars for one gallon so I can get home?”
We do not live in the land of Lamborghinis or crypto wizards or billion dollar ballrooms. We live in the real world where we need a reasonably-priced tank of gas and the truth. 
And we need our oh so powerful GOP supermajority to show us during legislative sessions, when it counts, that they are more than the obsequious vessel of a billionaire president and his billionaire tech buddies. 
Then we can talk about data centers.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: State lawmakers, road paving industry both concerned about lack of state road projects
description: Both state lawmakers and representatives of Kentucky’s road paving industry have strong concerns about the lack of road work that state transportation officials are awarding this summer compared to previous years.  Last month, the Kentucky Lantern reported the number of road work projects, particularly repaving, had dramatically fallen this summer compared t[...]
text:
Kentucky road paving projects have dropped dramatically in the summer of 2026. (Getty Images)Both state lawmakers and representatives of Kentucky’s road paving industry have strong concerns about the lack of road work that state transportation officials are awarding this summer compared to previous years. 
Last month, the Kentucky Lantern reported the number of road work projects, particularly repaving, had dramatically fallen this summer compared to the previous two summers. Representatives for the road paving industry presented data Wednesday to the Interim Joint Committee on Appropriations and Revenue showing the dramatic drop in projects. 
Rep. Jason Petrie, R-Elkton, the co-chair of the committee, pointed to data showing the lack of state road work in Warren County and Bowling Green, one of the fastest growing parts of the state. 
“If you’re in a fast-growing place that has transportation needs and you’re not keeping pace, you’re not just falling behind. You’re really falling behind exponentially,” Petrie said. 
Sen. Steve Rawlings, R-Burlington, at one point asked road paving representatives why there was such a drop off in road projects in his Northern Kentucky area given it was “high population.” 
“It just looks so sad,” Rawlings said about presented data showing the drop off in projects. 
Kentucky’s road projects down by more than 50% this summer

Representatives of the road paving industry told lawmakers the consequences of the lack of road projects this summer have meant road paving companies have had to cut back on hours offered to road crews with some companies working four-day work weeks. 
Brian Wood, the executive director of the Plantmix Asphalt Industry of Kentucky, said because of the seasonality and temperature requirements to do asphalt paving work, the state was quickly approaching a window to where it’s not possible to get repaving work done before winter. 
“When we have slowdowns like we have now, the end result is deferring maintenance, declining pavement conditions, increased backlog, higher cost — all the things that we’re very well aware of,” Wood said. 
Chad LaRue, the executive director of the Kentucky Association of Highway Contractors, told lawmakers Wednesday afternoon LaRue the cabinet has advertised more road repaving projects recently, but the overall number of projects is still down compared to previous years.
LaRue said he believes Kentucky Transportation Cabinet has concerns about the balance of an internal fund within the cabinet used to pay out road work projects as they happen.
“They’re kind of clipping the trees right now on their cash flow model, and so out of necessity, they feel like they’ve had to pull back in order to make sure they don’t zero out the account,” LaRue said.
Executives within the Transportation Cabinet also told another legislative committee Wednesday that the cabinet usually the internal cash fund for road work can fluctuate with money spent on active road projects, as much as $10 million a day spent. 
Those directors said the cabinet usually wants to have at least $100 million of cash on hand in that internal fund; that internal fund reached a low of $32.9 million as of Aug. 19, recently rising back to above $100 million.
Shaun McKiernan, the executive director of the cabinet’s Office of Budget and Fiscal Management, told the Budget Review Subcommittee on Transportation on Wednesday that the cabinet’s goal was “put to work all of the state dollars.” 
“But we also must maintain our sufficient cash level to pay for our obligations and pay our expenses,” McKiernan said. “We’re committed to advancing as many projects as we possibly can. We are constantly monitoring our cash situation so we can be in the best situation as possible to authorize additional project expenditures.”
Transportation Cabinet spokespeople did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment Wednesday about LaRue’s comments. A cabinet spokesperson previously told the Lantern that constraints enacted in the budget by the state legislature have been the main reasons behind the lack of road projects. 
LaRue told lawmakers the inflation of road construction costs have continued to outpace the state funding available for road projects, even with the state legislature adding one-time appropriations for road work.
“We’re probably at this point looking at some inflection points on the ability to properly deliver the program based on what we’re seeing from an industry side,” LaRue said.
