title: Bear attacks in Colorado are climate attacks
description: Last week, a black bear broke into a house in Estes Park and attacked a woman who is in her 80s, scratching her stomach and knocking her to the floor. The week before that, a bear attacked an angler in his 60s in Jefferson County. The bear knocked the man to the ground and bit […]
text:
A bear is seen in Colorado. (Photo courtesy of CPW)Last week, a black bear broke into a house in Estes Park and attacked a woman who is in her 80s, scratching her stomach and knocking her to the floor.
The week before that, a bear attacked an angler in his 60s in Jefferson County. The bear knocked the man to the ground and bit his legs until his friends managed to scare the animal away.
The number of bear attacks in Colorado this year is more than double the figure last year, and they come amid an extraordinary number of bear encounters as environmental pressures drive bears to food-finding extremes. Colorado Parks and Wildlife, the state’s wildlife manager, has broadcast bear safety awareness, and news outlets in the state have widely covered the unusual bear activity. But what has failed to come through official and media channels is the obvious, if uncomfortable, fundamental cause of this phenomenon: global warming.
These bear attacks are climate attacks.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to CPW, 6,129 bear “incidents” — including “sightings and conflicts” — occurred this year through mid-August. Just 3,115 were reported during the same period last year, and the state is on pace to record the most incidents since officials started keeping track.
These include unprecedented encounters, such as bears appearing in the middle of Denver.  Last week a bear showed up in the city’s Platt Park neighborhood, near Washington Park. This is not too far from the heart of the urban core. Never happened before.
Climate horrors in Colorado are no longer just a threat. They’ve arrived.

We’re in the time of year when black bears go on an eating spree to store up fat for the winter. But natural sources of food are especially scarce this year. Why? “Low mountain snowpack, wildfires and drought have reduced the availability of natural foods such as berries, fruits, nuts, plants and grasses in parts of Colorado,” according to CPW.
What the agency omits is that human-caused climate change, from the burning of fossil fuels, is a key contributor to low mountain snowpack, wildfires and drought.
“What we’re seeing are the unprecedented impacts of climate change right now on the environment, and bear behaviors reflecting that,” said Samantha Miller, senior carnivore campaigner with the Center for Biological Diversity and a Grand Lake resident. She noted in an interview with Newsline that increasing wildfires and hotter and drier conditions degrade bears’ ability to survive. “All of these factors are really contributing to decreasing habitat, less available food for bears, and bears becoming more desperate right now because of the climate impacts that they are navigating.”
Colorado saw a record-low snowpack this year, and a study from Colorado School of Mines researchers showed that global warming is almost certainly to blame. Wildfires in Colorado are becoming bigger and more intense, and researchers have established that climate change plays a role. A drought that’s gripping the Southwest is so severe and so prolonged that researchers call it a megadrought. What’s causing it? Yes, climate change. Now we can add to these expressions of catastrophic global warming the desperation of Colorado’s hungry bear families.
“With climate change, it causes a cascade of impacts on our ecosystems,” Miller said. “So it causes drought. It causes wildfire. All of that then causes less habitat, less food availability. Harsher winters can cause, you know, more like a weaker condition in animals, too, as they emerge. The longer summers are hard. Warmer springs are hard. All of these things impact not only wildlife like bears, but also food for wildlife like bears … It’s all from climate change, and it’s all interconnected.”
It’s important to be forthright about these things. When state officials can’t bring themselves to honestly acknowledge why bears are behaving in a way they’ve never seen before, they rob residents of understanding, which otherwise might spur them to demand new leaders. Saying the extraordinary bear behavior is due to drought without mentioning climate change is like saying the Pan Am Flight 103 passengers died in a plane crash without mentioning the plane was bombed.
Elected leaders in the United States, including in Colorado, have consistently failed to approach the climate crisis with the urgency it requires. CPW’s reluctance even to mention global warming in connection with this year’s bear attacks is part of an all too familiar pattern of half-measures and foot-dragging in state climate policy. If the depletion of water resources, loss of whole forests, and vanishing snow doesn’t get the attention of state leaders, maybe bear bites will.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Cumberland county residents split on proposed gas plant, slated to be second largest in the nation
description: In a crowded school cafeteria in Cumberland Monday evening, residents of the rural county  gathered to hear Dominion Energy representatives detail the gas plant the utility is pitching to the local leaders and state regulators.  The Cumberland Energy Center will be able to generate three gigawatts of power, making it the second largest gas plant […]
text:
Cumberland County residents meet Aug. 31, 2026 to discuss the proposed Dominion Cumberland Energy Center. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)In a crowded school cafeteria in Cumberland Monday evening, residents of the rural county  gathered to hear Dominion Energy representatives detail the gas plant the utility is pitching to the local leaders and state regulators. 
The Cumberland Energy Center will be able to generate three gigawatts of power, making it the second largest gas plant in the nation if it is approved. 
The gas plant is part of Dominion’s proposed fleet of energy generation projects to meet the increased demand for power, which is expected to more than double by 2045. If approved, the plant would take about ten years to come online, with construction slated to begin in 2029. 
The site plan is located off Duncan Store Road bordering the James River, lining Buckingham County. The project would generate local tax revenue of approximately $500 million in the first 35 years. 
Neighbors in the county shared mixed responses to the proposal, with some touting its potential harm to the environment and quality of life and others touting the economic benefits it could reap for the area.
“We have kids now that have to have car washes, they’re going to churches, civic organizations, begging for money, so they can buy band uniforms or whatever. This project would increase the tax base of this community, which desperately needs it,” resident Fred Shoemaker said at the meeting.
The Cumberland gas plant would be larger than Dominion’s Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind project that tops out at 2,600 megawatts and is in the process of powering on. Dominion representatives emphasized that the gas plant is just a portion of their energy profile, with renewable energy sources also in the pipeline. 
 Opposition rallies across counties

Residents from multiple counties rallied against the plant ahead of the meeting, citing air pollution as a major health risk, sound and light pollution as a disruption of the county’s rural character.
A resident’s T-shirt shows anti-transmission line sentiment at Cumberland County Planning Commission meeting, Aug. 31, 2026. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)
The plant’s opponents, some wearing  yellow shirts reading “Protect Cumberland” and “Rural Virginia is not for sale”, also criticized the plan for the power generated by the plant to be used in places far from Cumberland.
Dominion spokesman Jeremy Slayton said they selected this particular site in Cumberland County to develop the plant because “it’s near existing utilities and a reliable water supply, which is critical because it minimizes impacts to the community.”
Slayton said the company is finalizing the details for the natural gas and water and will share them publicly soon.
Muriel Miller Branch, a community advocate and former teacher whose family is from Cumberland, was one of the fiercest opponents of a large-scale garbage dump in the southern part of the county. Now, she is fighting to keep the gas plant out. 
Miller highlighted particulates that gas turbines release into the air as a potential health hazard for those who live nearby. The American Heart Association reports that air particulates can worsen existing conditions and have been linked to cardiovascular challenges.
“Is profit worth the displacement due to air, water, land, and noise pollution of families who have lived on this land for generations?” Branch asked the Planning Commission Monday. “Is profit worth the price of increased severe health problems? The moral question before you this evening, ladies and gentlemen, is what is the human cost of profit?”
The Southern Environmental Law Center recently commissioned a health impact study on the proposed plant that found exposure to fine particulate matter from burning fossil fuels will “result in 3–7 premature deaths annually, approximately 7 new cases of asthma, 2,430 minor restricted-activity days, 410 days of lost work, and other cardiovascular and respiratory illnesses, hospital admissions, and emergency room visits.” 
The study, conducted by EmPower Analytics Group, also analyzed atmospheric modeling, scientific health research and EPA health-impact methods. It found that residents of surrounding counties such as Powhatan, Amelia, Goochland and even the city of Richmond, 60 miles away,  could experience health impacts from the plant’s air pollution.
Dominion maintains that the turbines would follow state and federal regulations laid out in the air permit that the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality must grant in order to operate.
“Emissions will be monitored through various means and technologies to ensure we remain in compliance with permitted limits. This includes continuous emissions monitors, stack performance testing and engineering process calculations,” Slayton said.
Supporters say Virginia needs power, Cumberland needs jobs
A digital rendering for Dominion Energy’s proposed Cumberland Energy Center, a 3,000 megawatt (3 gigawatts) combined cycle natural gas plant planned to come online by 2033 or 2034. (Photo courtesy Dominion Energy)
Dominion said the plant will generate enough electricity to power 750,000 homes. Cumberland makes up just under 3,000 of Dominion’s customers. 
TheValley Link transmission line is proposed for development near the gas plant’s location, which is expected to carry more energy to Northern Virginia to meet major power demands driven by data centers. 
When asked if the plant would be connected to the Valley Link line, Dominion said that the regional grid operator PJM is studying the project to determine “what infrastructure is needed to maintain a reliable grid.”
Jenny Bales and her husband Gerald came to the meeting to support the project and hope the expected tax revenue will bring down property taxes. Their home is about 10 miles from the plant site but they’re not worried about the facility’s potential impact on their health. 
“Our son works for Dominion and he says it’s a clean plant,” Bales said. “A lot of the things people are concerned about are not going to be an issue.”
Members of the International Brotherhood of Boilermakers union, sporting stickers that promote reliable energy, said building the plant could help a generation of workers retire and give jobs to apprentices in the area – creating much-needed vocational opportunities for young workers.
Union member and Cumberland resident Jared Turner said the new plant would be the latest in the area, pointing to the Bear Garden gas plant in Buckingham that is operated by Dominion – a fraction of the new plant’s size at 628 MW – and the proposed 1540 MW Tenaska gas plant in Fluvanna County.
“The reality is, five miles down the road, there’s already a gas plant. So, it’s already happening whether they like it or not,” Turner said. “If Cumberland doesn’t want to have it, I bet you Powhatan, or Buckingham, or Goochland – one of them is gonna take it.  And then guess what? The same people are still gonna be affected equally by whatever the environmental impact is, yet Cumberland wouldn’t get any of the benefits.”
County commissioners would need to rezone the area where the plant is proposed, which is currently zoned as agricultural. It’s a necessary change, some residents said, denouncing concerns about development impeding on the county’s rural character. 
“(They believe) that’s what’s wrong with this podunk backward county, that we don’t embrace modern development,” Cumberland resident Luke Fleischman said. “Our county is rural and agriculturally based. We don’t even have a grocery store. We just got a small mom and pop grocery. But, you know, there are things that we can develop that are good for the county.”
Fenceline communities fight despite steep challenge
Annie Riddle, 88, wasn’t at the meeting but expressed apprehension about the planned gas plant. Riddle lives on the border of the project site in the home she and her husband built in the late 1960’s. Some of her children and their children live on the property with her. 
Annie Riddle on the porch of her home that will be across the street from Dominion Energy’s proposed Cumberland Energy Center. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)
She said the county did not alert her about the project that would be housed across the street from her, a key point of her opposition. 
“I only got my information out of the newspaper. You know, nobody stopped by to talk to nobody,” Riddle said.
A woman who refuses to sit still, Riddle spent the day of the meeting fixing up her lawn mower before doing some yard work. She said that the gas plant’s noise, construction trucks barreling down her small road, and the years of pollution yet to come are disheartening.
“I ain’t worried about me, ’cause, they talk about this thing won’t come in until the 2030s,” Riddle said. “Who said I’m gonna be here that long? But my grandchildren are here, and my great grandchildren are here. They are the ones that are gonna suffer.”
Some of her neighbors’ view of the plant as a source of revenue and jobs is understandable, she said. Still, she said she and others, like family friend and Protect Cumberland organizer Katie Hoffman, don’t believe it’s the right fit for their home. They will continue working to learn and illuminate the full impact it would have on the surrounding communities. 
After multiple hours of public testimony, the Cumberland Planning Commission voted to recommend approval of the conditional use permit for the power plant. Next, the county Board of Supervisors must approve or reject the proposal, and the State Corporation Commission will also have to determine if the plant is in the public interest.
Sign shows opposition to Dominion’s proposed Cumberland Energy Center. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Wittman voted 60 times to undo the Affordable Care Act. Then he backed extending its subsidies.
description: In 2017, U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman, R-Westmoreland, touted voting to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act 60 times. Nearly a decade later, he was one of just 17 Republicans nationwide to vote to extend expired ACA subsidies, before Congress ultimately let them lapse. The expired subsidies have spurred 94,000 Virginians to drop their insurance […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman, R-Westmoreland discusses housing policy in Henrico, Virginia on July 10, 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)In 2017, U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman, R-Westmoreland, touted voting to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act 60 times. Nearly a decade later, he was one of just 17 Republicans nationwide to vote to extend expired ACA subsidies, before Congress ultimately let them lapse.
The expired subsidies have spurred 94,000 Virginians to drop their insurance so far and is the latest healthcare issue congressional candidates in Virginia and elsewhere must contend with on the campaign trail.  
“Every House Republican in a competitive race is having to walk a tightrope on healthcare affordability,” said Erin Covey, a Cook Political Report analyst.
University of Virginia Professor Larry Sabato, who helms Sabato’s Crystal Ball, said that Wittman’s January ACA vote is “a recognition that his district is competitive enough that he can’t stick to (President Donald) Trump and GOP congressional positions 100% of the time.” 
With polling indicating healthcare affordability and access among top concerns for voters this year, Democrats have seized on the issue as a potentially winning platform and pushed Republicans on the defensive. 
 Why Wittman broke from the pack and how it could impact the VA-01 race

While Wittman still doesn’t fully embrace the ACA, he said he voted to extend the subsidy primarily because of how it would impact his constituents in Virginia’s 1st Congressional District.
“I did not believe families should face dramatic increases in their health insurance costs without a transition,” Wittman said this week. 
When asked if he would back future repeal efforts, he didn’t clarify, but  shared broad health policy goals if re-elected. 
“Going forward, I will continue working to make healthcare more affordable, accessible, and transparent by increasing competition, expanding patient choice, improving price transparency, and giving patients and families greater control over their healthcare decisions,” Wittman said. 
Data shows 94,000 Virginians have dropped their ACA insurance since last year

Of the 16 other Republicans to side with Democrats on the recent ACA vote, only four of them were in the House for the 2017 repeal attempt. 
Pennsylvania representative Brian Fitzpatrick and Ohio representative Dave Joyce voted against the repeal nearly 10 years ago, while California representative David Valadao joined Wittman in voting for it. 
Valadao then lost his reelection bid in the 2018 midterms, when Democrats made big gains in both congressional chambers. Both healthcare and the economy were campaign-year focal points.
Covey attributes some of Valadao’s ousting to his repeal vote, while Wittman was in a safer seat at the time, and less vulnerable to pushback for it. 
Though Virginia’s 1st District still has a Republican lean, it has grown more politically purple in recent years, so it’s unclear how voters there will judge his turnabout vote at the ballot box. 
Wittman’s Democratic challenger, prosecutor Shannon Taylor, doesn’t think he should get too much praise for his shift in stance. 
“Now, with an election around the corner and families facing higher premiums, he wants to try and change his tune,” she said. “We deserve a representative who will lower costs and expand care, not one who brags about their votes to rip it away.”
Recent KFF polling found that 55% of independent voters see healthcare costs as an important candidate discussion topic while courting their votes this year, while 60% of democrats say the same and 37% of republicans agree.
Democrats have hammered Republicans all year on their failure to renew the expired subsidies as well as their votes for H.R.1, the Trump-backed reconciliation bill that entails forthcoming changes to Medicaid. 
About 300,000 Virginians are at risk of losing that health insurance next year while 5,800 lawful immigrants are guaranteed to lose it next month. The bill’s changes to hospital funding mechanisms may also contribute to potential closure or reduced services of rural hospitals and a predicted $31 billion reduction in the state’s Medicaid funding over the next decade. 
As H.R. 1 was debated, Wittman — and incumbent U.S. Rep. Jen Kiggans, R-Virginia Beach, who is running in a competitive district — pushed back on aspects of the bill, before ultimately voting for it. 
As a compromise, Congress also created the Rural Health Transformation Fund, a $50 billion investment for states over the next five years. 
Republican National Committee spokeswoman Emma Hall said that Wittman and Kiggans had “put Virginians first and delivered a huge win for rural communities,” as $122 million in RHTF funding disbursements were announced last week. 
Wittman has also backed the “Lower Health Care Premiums For All Americans Act,” which passed the House last December but has not yet become law. That bill would expand association health plans by allowing small businesses and self-employed people to band together to purchase insurance. 
Health care fight intensifies as Congress weighs GOP-backed insurance changes

Some analysts describe it as a way to chip away at the ACA, but Wittman and others see it as a different pathway to help people access care. 
“(Small companies) just can’t band together in large enough numbers to get the advantages of these larger plans,” Wittman said. “Anything that you buy in bulk or in mass quantities, you get a reduction in price. That’s what the idea is here.”
Since the passage of ACA, insurers have not been able to use a person’s health risk to determine the premiums they pay. 
Wittman said that his issue with the current makeup of government-funded healthcare is that it is “a system based on reimbursement for treatment.”
Having healthier and less healthy people in the same insurance pools is meant to drive down costs broadly, Georgetown University researcher Sabrina Corlette said.
“We all get older and sicker,” she said. “(The Democrats’ approach) is recognizing that you might be subsidizing a sicker person today, but someone else will be subsidizing you down the road.”
As midterm elections draw nearer and candidate debates grow fiercer, campaign messaging to the public across party lines have honed in on affordability.  
Voters are experiencing inflation in gas, groceries and healthcare costs made worse by Trump’s war with Iran and his directives to Congress like H.R. 1, which will likely be reflected in the way they vote this fall.
 ”It’s all connected,” Saboto said. 
Though Wittman’s district “is not quite a tossup yet,” Sabato said, “if Shannon Taylor wins, it’s because this is such an anti-Trump year.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: As sports betting surges, Virginia weighs how to curb gambling harms
description: As college football season gets into full swing over Labor Day weekend, sports betting companies, public health experts and Virginia lawmakers are confronting a question that has grown more pressing since wagering moved into smartphones: How can the industry keep gambling from becoming an addiction? Representatives from those groups gathered Wednesday at the[...]
text:
State Sen. Mike Jones, D-Richmond, left, and Dr. Carolyn Hawley, director of the Virginia Partnership for Gaming and Health, participate in a Responsible Gaming Roundtable at the Hilton Richmond Downtown on Sept. 2, 2026. (Photo by Markus Schmidt/Virginia Mercury)As college football season gets into full swing over Labor Day weekend, sports betting companies, public health experts and Virginia lawmakers are confronting a question that has grown more pressing since wagering moved into smartphones: How can the industry keep gambling from becoming an addiction?
Representatives from those groups gathered Wednesday at the Hilton Richmond Downtown for a Responsible Gaming Roundtable hosted by the Sports Betting Alliance, an advocacy organization representing bet365, BetMGM, DraftKings, Fanatics and FanDuel — five of the nation’s largest online sports betting operators.
The discussion focused on tools that help customers control their betting, educating young people about gambling risks and connecting people with treatment when gambling stops being entertainment. 
“Responsible gaming is not a regulatory obligation to us; it’s the foundation of a sustainable, durable legal market,” said Joe Maloney, president of Sports Betting Alliance and one of the roundtable’s moderators, along with state Sen. Mike Jones, D-Richmond. “Getting this right takes more than one company working on its own.”
The industry has expanded rapidly in the commonwealth since Virginia lawmakers legalized sports betting in 2020. The law took effect that July, and the first online wagers were accepted in January 2021. Lawmakers also authorized casinos in certain cities, subject to local voter approval. 
Virginia now has five operating casinos and 11 approved sports betting permit holders. Casinos reported more than $102 million in adjusted gaming revenue in July 2026, while bettors wagered more than $589 million on sports in June, according to the Virginia Lottery. 
Maloney said legal sports betting has generated more than $400 million in state tax revenue since its launch. But a regulated market, he argued, should be judged not only by the money it generates but by how well it protects customers. 
Licensed operators verify betters’ ages and locations and allow customers to set limits on deposits and time spent gambling. Voluntary self-exclusion programs also let people block themselves from betting. Maloney said over half of online sports bettors use at least one responsible-gaming tool. 
 Technology offers both tools and new risks 

Industry representatives said licensed online platforms can monitor betting patterns and intervene when someone’s behavior suggests a potential problem.
Cameron Zuckert, senior manager of responsible gaming partnerships and programs at FanDuel, said customers are encouraged to decide ahead of time how much they are willing to spend. 
“We do a lot of work to drive awareness of not just what it means to play responsibly, but also the risks associated with problem gambling,” Zuckert said. “You don’t want to shy away from that topic. It’s a very real topic.”
Fanatics Betting and Gaming does not allow customers to wager on credit. Anthony D’Angelo, the company’s head of responsible gaming, said preventing harmful play is also in its business interest.
“We want a long-term, sustainable business, and we can’t do that if customers are on our platform playing irresponsibly, not getting the help they need and then never play again,” D’Angelo said. 
Research shows the risk can be significant, particularly for younger bettors. 
The National Council on Problem Gambling’s 2024 national survey found that 8% of American adults — nearly 20 million people — frequently experienced at least one indicator of problematic gambling. The rate was 17% among traditional sports bettors and 24% among fantasy sports players. 
Adults ages 18 to 34 faced substantially greater risk than older Americans. Online gambling participation also rose from 15% of adults in 2018 to 22% in 2024.
Keith Whyte, founder and president of Safer Gambling Strategies, said risky gambling behavior increased during the COVID-19 pandemic alongside depression, loneliness, isolation and job loss. 
The latest survey found overall indicators of problematic play had returned to 2018 levels, though Whyte cautioned that gambling expansion will always carry risks.
“You can’t expand gambling without risk, without additional casualties,” Whyte said.
He also argued that gambling education needs to reach children before advertising and celebrity endorsements begin shaping their views of betting.
“Everybody should have a conversation around gambling, especially with young people,” he said.
Adults should routinely use spending and time limits as well, Whyte added, “not because they think they have a problem, but because they want to prevent themselves from having a problem.”
 Treatment and other expansion debate

Virginia has built a statewide network offering treatment, peer-recovery support, support groups and financial counseling, said Dr. Carolyn Hawley, director of the Virginia Partnership for Gaming and Health at Virginia Commonwealth University.
The program also trains treatment providers and conducts prevention work in schools and universities. Hawley said addressing gambling addiction requires coordination among the industry, government and public health system, particularly as betting companies collect more data that could help identify customers at risk. 
But finding qualified clinicians remains a challenge, experts say.  
“It’s one thing to have money for treatment,” Hawley said. “It’s another thing to have capacity — providers who know how to deliver that treatment.”
Virginia directs portions of sports betting and casino tax revenue to the Problem Gambling Treatment and Support Fund.
New Jersey, which legalized online casino gambling in 2013, requires operators to analyze customer data for warning signs. Platforms must contact customers whose activity shows certain markers of risky behavior, beginning with automated outreach and escalating to direct contact from responsible-gaming staff.
In Virginia, lawmakers considered another gambling expansion this year through Senate Bill 118 and House Bill 161, which would have allowed licensed casinos to offer online slots, blackjack and other games. Both chambers passed versions of the legislation but failed to resolve their differences before adjournment. The issue is expected to return in 2027. 
Supporters of online betting argue that Virginians already gamble through offshore or sweepstake-style sites operating outside the state’s regulatory system. Maloney called the illegal market the most serious obstacle facing licensed operators, saying those sites offer no meaningful accountability, monitoring or statewide self-exclusion system. 
Virginia Secretary of Finance Mark Sickles, a former lawmaker who has long been skeptical of gambling expansion, said tax revenue should not determine whether the state legalizes another form of gambling.
“I would not support legalizing or keeping it illegal based on revenues to the state,” Sickles told The Mercury Wednesday. 
If Virginia does expand gambling, he said, lawmakers should ensure some proceeds support prevention and treatment. Sickles also endorsed including gambling in school lessons about addiction.
“I don’t think we will stop gambling by keeping it illegal,” Sickles said. “I think everyone needs to put on their work shoes and get out their pencils and figure out if there’s a way to make it happen — and everybody’s satisfied with it, and it has consumer protections in the law.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Lacking cash, Jackson is leaning into his ground game
description: Troy Jackson is focused on the ground game.  Wearing a Red Sox hat and jeans in a supporter’s backyard in Brunswick, the Democratic U.S. Senate nominee did not mince his words. “They’re gonna outspend us,” he told Maine Morning Star of incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins’ campaign and the dark money groups blanketing the […]
text:
Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Troy Jackson takes a selfie with supporters at a campaign event in Brunswick on Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)Troy Jackson is focused on the ground game. 
Wearing a Red Sox hat and jeans in a supporter’s backyard in Brunswick, the Democratic U.S. Senate nominee did not mince his words. “They’re gonna outspend us,” he told Maine Morning Star of incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins’ campaign and the dark money groups blanketing the airwaves with favorable ads. 
“There’s just no way around it. But, you’re seeing all across this country people are getting outspent and still winning because they have the right message. People know that they’re honest and sincere — what they’re fighting for.” 
That trend has largely been seen in primaries with progressive candidates challenging establishment Democrats. Jackson is banking on progressives like himself being able to replicate that success against Republicans in the fall.  
With a glaring financial disadvantage to Collins, Jackson is aiming to scale up the type of support that secured him the nomination in July, after Graham Platner’s late exit from the race following an accusation of sexual assault. 
Coming off of a recent loss in the Democratic gubernatorial primary, Jackson quickly consolidated support for his Senate bid, becoming the presumptive replacement before official votes were even cast at a nominating convention that the state Democratic Party pulled together in a matter of weeks. 
“We’re gonna do just like what we did for the convention,” Jackson said. “We’re gonna go out and organize people. I mean, we’ve got a ground game.” 
By the numbers
Jackson isn’t required to report his campaign’s full stockpile until October, but he raised $5.3 million through his party’s national fundraising platform, ActBlue, in July alone — largely on July 25, the day he was selected. 
He started essentially from scratch during a condensed campaign period, unable to transfer any money from his gubernatorial bid. But Collins had already been outfundraising Platner when he was still in the running. 
The Republican incumbent had $11 million cash on hand as of last quarter, which covered April 1 through June 30. Still, much of her financial might comes from outside groups. 
For example, the Senate Leadership Fund, a Republican super PAC, committed to investing over $42 million against Jackson the day Maine Democrats officially selected him as their nominee. While such super PACs must disclose their donors, they are beneficiaries of large contributions from nonprofits that aren’t. 
According to a New York Times analysis of advertising funded by dark money, Republican groups have spent $47.4 million in Maine’s Senate race so far, including on TV ads and mailers. 
In comparison, Democratic groups have spent $27.1 million, according to that analysis. Some of the liberal dark money being funneled to Jackson comes from the Government That Works PAC, which is spending $1.3 million on supportive ads, according to recent filings. 
Voters of various persuasions have told Maine Morning Star throughout the past year that negative ads focused on mudslinging do not resonate with them. 
“I can’t even watch baseball in peace,” said Judy Parker, a Democrat from Portland. 
Parker and other voters said they want ads to focus on policy. Ads of both types have been misleading this election cycle. Unable to escape them, Sophie Creamer of Portland said they try to fact-check claims in real time.
“It still doesn’t influence ultimately how I’m going to vote in the race,” Creamer said of ads, “because I think the best place for me to get my information about a candidate is going to be from their campaign website in terms of policies.” 
Studies have found that political ads don’t often change voters’ minds but can help boost voter turnout.
Attendees at Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Troy Jackson’s first town hall in Lewiston on Sept. 1, 2026. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)
The ground game 
While both money and a ground game matter, money doesn’t buy outcomes, said Mark Brewer, chair of the political science department of the University of Maine. Collins won reelection the last time even though her Democratic challenger, Sara Gideon, had outspent her. 
“I think money gives Collins an advantage, but I don’t think it debilitates Jackson in any way, shape, or form,” Brewer said. “Despite the modernization of campaigns and the professionalization of campaigns and all that other stuff, we know that boots on the ground still matter.” 
Money can matter in that, too, because it can be used to buy a ground game. Several Mainers have reported out-of-state canvassers knocking their doors to campaign for Collins.
“We know that a ground game based on enthusiastic volunteers and party workers is better than a hired-gun ground game, just because those people are more invested,” Brewer said. 
More than 1,000 Mainers joined Jackson for the Maine Democratic Party’s volunteer kickoff last month. But that’s far less than the approximately 15,000 volunteers Platner’s campaign said it had before he withdrew from the race. 
“There are more of us out there that are looking for a different government than the people that are holding us back,” Jackson told the crowd during his first town hall in Lewiston Tuesday night. 
Similar to Platner’s campaign events, attendees were encouraged to sign up to volunteer their time. 
“One conversation with any of you all, and those ads are toast,” said organizer Eva Kappas. “The billionaires are terrified because they don’t have what we have in this room and that is all of you.” 
One of the Mainers knocking doors and phone banking for Jackson is Diane Morin of Augusta, who first met him when she was helping a friend campaign for the state Legislature in 2012. With family in the logging industry, Morin recalled liking Jackson’s background and dedication to helping average workers, having formerly been a hairdresser with few benefits and no vacation.  
Given his late entry into the race, Jackson is tasked with constructing the plane while he’s flying it, as Brewer put it, “and Susan Collins is anything but. She’s got decades of construction experience. It’s almost turnkey-ready.”
That said, nationally this cycle Democrats have a massive enthusiasm advantage over Republicans, Brewer added. 
“Can Jackson take advantage of that?” he asked. “Can Collins somehow cut into that?”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana BMV plans mobile driver’s license
description: The Indiana Bureau of Motor Vehicles is launching an optional mobile driver’s license for Hoosiers who wish to limit what information bank tellers, bartenders and others see when asked to verify their age or identity. The digital license would not replace a person’s physical driver’s license, but would instead grant Hoosiers the ability to verify their […]
text:
Matt Kestian, general counsel for the Indiana Bureau of Motor Vehicles, addresses the Interim Study Committee on Roads and Transportation Sept. 2, 2026. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle) The Indiana Bureau of Motor Vehicles is launching an optional mobile driver’s license for Hoosiers who wish to limit what information bank tellers, bartenders and others see when asked to verify their age or identity.
The digital license would not replace a person’s physical driver’s license, but would instead grant Hoosiers the ability to verify their age or identity through a mobile application.
Popular uses include age verification to purchase alcohol or tobacco products, as well as identification for traffic stops or banking.
Hoosiers who opt in would download a mobile application, which uses digital biometrics like a face scan or fingerprint to verify the person on the phone matches BMV data on file to activate and use the license, according to Matt Kestian, BMV general counsel.
The mobile application functions similarly to tap-to-pay debit or credit cards, allowing users to share information with a mobile driver’s license reader.
“You wouldn’t be able to give your phone to your child,” he said.
Kestian told the Interim Study Committee on Roads and Transportation Wednesday the mobile driver’s license option should be ready within 18 months.
Lawmakers asked questions about a budget for the initiative but the agency said there is not currently a vendor or cost estimate.
Questions about privacy
Kestian described the mobile license as a “step forward for privacy,” as Hoosiers would be able to confirm their age or identity without sharing extra information like their home address.
“Why does the bar need to know that person’s home address?” he asked. “Right now, if they’re getting a physical driver’s license, that bar has access to that person’s address, date of birth, organ donation status, veteran status — all of the other things that may appear on a driver’s license. They don’t need it.”
Indiana state Rep. Jim Pressel, R-Rolling Prairie, presides over the Interim Study Committee on Roads and Transportation Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Lawmakers directed the BMV to comply with international data security standards in a 2023 law, authored by committee chair Rep. Jim Pressel, to prevent law enforcement, government agencies and commercial entities from using mobile driver’s license data to track Hoosiers.
“A law enforcement agency will not be able to send a subpoena to the BMV and ask for a list of this person’s purchases or visits to various establishments,” Kestian said. “It’s designed to not have that information. It’s also designed that the officer is not going to take the person’s phone and be able to go through it.”
The digital driver’s license is the latest example of the BMV’s efforts to modernize its systems in response to an executive order from Gov. Mike Braun last April.
The agency has implemented electronic car titles and liens in recent  years, Kestian said.
The mobile driver’s license will also be available for learner’s permits and state-issued identification cards.
Pressel praised the BMV’s modernization effort for giving Hoosiers “something that may be beneficial to them if they choose to use it and make their life a little bit simpler,” he said.
About 20 states offer a form of digital driver’s license and ID.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: COVID education blame game should include more than parents
description: In March 2020, schools across Indiana were thrust into the COVID pandemic. There was no play book for how to handle this situation. Everyone deferred to those above them in the chain of command and the advice given by medical professionals. Gov. Eric Holcomb and then-Indiana Superintendent of Public Education Jennifer McCormick led the state’s […]
text:
A student receives online instruction during the pandemic. (Getty Images)In March 2020, schools across Indiana were thrust into the COVID pandemic. There was no play book for how to handle this situation. Everyone deferred to those above them in the chain of command and the advice given by medical professionals. 
Gov. Eric Holcomb and then-Indiana Superintendent of Public Education Jennifer McCormick led the state’s efforts to send all kids home with technology and internet access as fast as possible during the mandated school closure and quarantine period. The governor released an executive order, the Indiana State Board of Education released guidance to schools and the Indiana Department of Education released more than $13.2 billion to schools in CARES Act funding and another $150 million in grants for community organizations to support schools meeting the new learning challenges due to the COVID pandemic. 
As schools rushed to get a laptop, with a camera, and full internet access in the hands and home of every student, an estimated $35.8 billion was poured into the EdTech industry. While every level of educational professional focused on getting kids online as quickly as possible, two groups of people were completely left out of the decision-making process, students and families.
Access without training
During the COVID pandemic my children were 8 and 2. With the best of intentions and no training for my 8-year-old or myself, a laptop fully loaded with apps, chat features, and a camera were sent to my home from the school. The expectation was that she would log on to an online meeting app that utilized the camera and chat to allow her to see her teacher and her classmates every day for online learning. Logging on with the camera on was required for her to receive credit for attendance. As a former professor that had previously taught online classes I felt really prepared to support her experience. 
Every morning we had her space prepared with her supplies, her laptop was charged up, and our high speed internet was ready to go. I would make sure she got through all the necessary login information and once her teacher could see and hear her, I would make sure she had a quiet place to work while class was in session. 
These steps were the easy part; the hard part was trying to keep her focused and on topic for multiple hours a day while also being available to answer all of her questions. She didn’t know how the apps worked, she didn’t know her username or password, and she didn’t know basic etiquette like the difference between mute and cameras off. 
One morning, after getting her going with online learning, I went to take a shower. About 10 minutes into the shower I hear her say, “Hey mom, what’s this word?” I turn around and realize she had brought her laptop into the bathroom and was holding it up in the shower to show me the word on the screen. In complete horror I could see that she was online with her class. Her entire third grade class was in my shower. I let out a scream and told her to get out of the bathroom with the laptop, to which she responded, “Gosh mom what’s your problem? It’s on mute.”
 Free cigarettes everywhere
Parents did not get to choose if technology, the internet, apps, chat features or cameras connected to the internet were brought into their homes; it was required by law and backed by billions of dollars during a global pandemic. 
As a mom, I was not given a choice as to whether my 8-year-old was given a laptop with apps and a camera. Neither of us received any training about what was on the laptop, the security features, or any other aspects of required and untethered online access. 
It happened to us, not with us. 
When I hear debates about who’s to blame about the social media crisis with teenagers, I always hear two arguments: addictive Algorithms lack of parental oversight. I often hear the analogy to smoking and that social media is as addictive as smoking and if parents would just parent their children we wouldn’t have this problem. 
This analogy would be accurate if we had handed out cigarettes in schools, required children to smoke them, made them readily available outside of school, and they were free everywhere. If we continue to only blame algorithms and parents, and forget the accessibility piece, we will miss any real opportunity to learn from this crisis.

name: Maryland Matters
title: How low should it go? Maryland regulators weigh energy efficiency program cuts
description: Maryland utilities are proposing cuts to the EmPOWER Maryland program, which could save customers $9 on their monthly bills. But advocates warn that there are long-term costs to shrinking the program.
text:
Protesters gathered outside the State House on March 30 to defend the EmPOWER Maryland program against temporary cuts proposed in the Maryland General Assembly. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)Maryland’s electric utilities submitted proposals Tuesday to reduce the size of EmPOWER Maryland, the state’s signature energy efficiency program, changes that could save residential customers up to $9 a month on their electric bills starting in January.
The proposals follow a temporary reduction of the program by lawmakers earlier this year to offset high electric bills, amid pressure on the grid from data centers, retiring power plants and more.
Now, regulators at the Maryland Public Service Commission are deciding how dramatically to cut the EmPOWER program. The commission in July asked asked each utility that offers EmPOWER to submit two options: a more aggressive cut to the program and a less aggressive one.
At Exelon, which owns Baltimore Gas & Electric, Pepco and Delmarva Power, officials said they’re hoping to see the commission approve the deeper set of cuts.
“Given where our customers are in terms of their bills, I think the most important thing that we can do is offer some relief — and we think that’s in line with the legislative intent,” said Lindsay North, director of strategy at Pepco and Delmarva Power.
But those cuts would come as Maryland’s Exelon utilities are proposing rate increases that may make any EmPOWER savings less noticeable.
An advocate holds a sign opposing Baltimore Gas & Electric’s rate increase request during an Aug. 11 news conference. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
Baltimore Gas & Electric in July put forward what it called a “bare bones” rate increase request that would raise the average residential customers’ monthly bill by $8, if approved by the PSC. Regulators recently cut a Pepco rate increase request in half, but Pepco customers will see, on average, a $3.94 increase in their monthly bills, the commission ssid.
And consumer advocates and environmental groups have warned that short-term cuts to the EmPOWER program would increase bills in the long run, as homes and businesses that are less energy efficient place greater strain on the electric grid. That would add costs to consumers and ultimately require new infrastructure such as substations and power plants.
“It’s really just shifting those costs into the future,” said Mike Specian, a senior research manager at the American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy. “Because if you’re not going to pay for energy efficiency now, you’re going to have to pay for additional generation later.”
Utility proposals differ
Under the plans submitted Tuesday, Potomac Edison’s residential customers in Western Maryland could see the biggest EmPOWER Maryland surcharge drop on their monthly bills. Its two proposals would cut either $8.79 or $8.06 per month compared to this year. (Some of that decline is because the company over-collected EmPOWER funds in 2026, said spokesman Will Boye.)
Delmarva Power’s residential customers could see a similar decline — either $7.86 or $8.39 a month — according to its plan. At BGE and Pepco, the monthly decrease would be more like $6 to $7.50.
Southern Maryland Electric Cooperative customers, meanwhile, would see a monthly decrease of 22 cents or $1.53. In total, the EmPOWER program would cost those customers $14 to $16 each month in 2027.
North, of Pepco and Delmarva Power, said she’s hoping customers don’t feel the effects of a shrunken program. She said the goal was to trim programs that customers are using less, and keep the most popular programs, offering similar-sized rebates as in years’ past — but fewer in number.
“I don’t know that our customers are going to notice that much of a difference,” North said. “It’ll be the same impactful EmPOWER where they [can] participate in the majority of programs that they know, or their neighbors have done.”
A worker from Total Home Performance, an Eastern Shore contractor, examines an air conditioning unit. Owner Matt Hargrove said many of his customers get rebates on costly energy-saving work from EmPOWER Maryland. (Photo Courtesy of Total Home Performance)
EmPOWER, which began in 2009, offers consumers free and reduced price energy efficiency services, including home energy audits, insulation and weatherization, HVAC upgrades, smart thermostats and more.
Under their plans for 2027, the Exelon companies plan to continue offering free “quick home energy checks,” which are considered a “gateway” to EmPOWER programs, wherein an energy efficiency professional visits a customer’s home and identifies possible improvements, installing LED light bulbs and weather stripping along the way.
But fewer rebates will be available. Homeowners seeking rebates for new HVAC equipment and other upgrades could encounter exhausted budgets if they apply too late, North said.
“The contractor who is running or helping to support that program would know when those budgets are getting close to being spent, and so they’d probably encourage the customer to get those applications in and sign up sooner so that they get those rebates and those incentive dollars before the budgets run out,” North said.
Some EmPOWER programs could end entirely. BGE’s lower-budget scenario would end a few EmPOWER initiatives, including an appliance recycling program and a budget for experimental energy efficiency pilot programs, said Jessica Yu, a senior manager of BGE’s energy efficiency portfolio.
The company believes the temporary cuts won’t be “too detrimental” to the state’s long-term energy demand.
“Like the appliance recycling program — that’s not really impacting peak demand,” Yu said. “We are taking the resources and budget that were used towards that program and actually shifting it towards the programs that provide the biggest reduction in peak demand.”
BGE has also proposed adding new resources for customers, including a dedicated staff member to help people who in multifamily dwellings, such as apartments and condos, access EmPOWER programming where eligible. The company also plans to better target marketing dollars for EmPOWER, Yu said, sending information to customers most likely to use it.
“In the past, because of how ambitious the goals were and because they were climbing at the degree that they were climbing at, it required us to basically have to throw everything at the wall to get as much GHG [greenhouse gas] savings as possible. Now that there’s a little bit more breathing room, we’re really able to focus and optimize our portfolio,” Yu said.
Maryland geothermal energy program faces delays amid cost concerns

Disputes over emissions goals
When the General Assembly decided to cut EmPOWER in this year’s Utility RELIEF Act, they did so by trimming the greenhouse gas emissions reduction goals associated with the program. The goals will decline in 2027, and then begin increasing again in 2029, reaching today’s goals by 2033.
But the legislature also allowed utilities to count solar energy in their territories toward their goals, effectively reducing the size of the EmPOWER program further — and adding some complexity to the calculations.
The utilities proposed a formula that would cut EmPOWER more drastically, said Specian, of ACEEE.
“The utilities took advantage of the RELIEF Act,” Specian said. “In my opinion, they used it as an excuse to try to lower the size of the program even further. But in doing so, it violates the law.”
ACEEE proposed its own formula, as did the PSC staff. Amid the disagreement, the commission asked the utilities to produce two plans for their EmPOWER budgets — one following the utility model and the other from the commission.
But a coalition of advocates, the Maryland Energy Efficiency Advocates, have appealed that decision, arguing that the two models approved by the commission wouldn’t meet the legislature’s goal. The advocates argue that the utility model would result in nearly $40 million less net benefit to utility customers, and the model from the commission’s staff would result in $13 million less net benefit.
The commission is accepting comment on the rehearing request, and has not made a decision.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Hunger Action Month brings renewed commitment to increasing food access in Rhode Island
description: Moving to Rhode Island from North Dakota, I often get asked about the differences between the two places. People say they’ve never met anyone from North Dakota before. They’ve never had a hotdish or a Scotcheroo. They’re curious about what would make me move from the Midwest to a coastal state that, on the surface, […]
text:
Clients at Good Neighbors Community Kitchen and Food Pantry in East Providence wait in line for food assistance on Wednesday, Oct. 22, 2025. The food pantry is one of the 140 agencies participating in the Rhode Island Community Food Bank's network.(Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)Moving to Rhode Island from North Dakota, I often get asked about the differences between the two places. People say they’ve never met anyone from North Dakota before. They’ve never had a hotdish or a Scotcheroo. They’re curious about what would make me move from the Midwest to a coastal state that, on the surface, couldn’t be more different from where I grew up.
It’s true — the beaches of Rhode Island look very different than the prairie grasslands of North Dakota. 
But as Hunger Action Month begins, and I just wrapped up my first year leading an extraordinary team at the Rhode Island Community Food Bank, it’s not the differences that stand out. It’s a universal truth for hunger relief advocates from Fargo to Foster: Hunger is something you experience; it’s not who you are. 
It can affect anyone, and it is affecting too many of our neighbors.
The latest RI Life Index, a survey conducted by Blue Cross Blue Shield of Rhode Island and Brown University’s School of Public Health showed that the number of households reporting food insecurity more than doubled between 2020 and 2024. Add in last fall’s SNAP crisis, steadily rising food costs, high cost of living, and ongoing policy changes that threaten food access for even more families, and the need is truly greater than ever. 
Those statistics aren’t just numbers; they represent real people and families. Hunger looks like people working full time who still can’t make ends meet. Young professionals who have no choice but to pay high rents. Seniors who have paid into Social Security, trusting that it would be there when they retire. Parents who skip meals, so their kids don’t miss dinner. Their dollars aren’t stretching as far as they used to, and an occasional trip to the local food pantry has become an essential monthly stopgap. The Food Bank and our network of 140 member agencies are struggling to keep up with demand. 
It’s an unstable, unpredictable time for many families, and for many of us working in hunger relief. 
And yet, it’s in these challenging moments that reveal what a community can accomplish together. 
Rhode Island Community Food Bank CEO Melissa Cherney speaks at a press event at the food bank’s Providence headquarters on Oct. 28, 2025. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
When SNAP benefits were delayed last fall, Rhode Islanders stepped up to help one another. Individuals donated, volunteers served, businesses and community organizations rallied, and the General Assembly increased funding for food purchases. Their response showed the compassion and collective strength of our state.
But responding to a crisis is not the same as solving it. We need a long-term solution that ensures reliable access to nutritious food, strong public policies, sustained investment, and action on the underlying pressures that force families to choose between groceries, housing, medicine and other necessities. Our response last fall showed what Rhode Island can do. Now, we must turn that spirit of collective action into a lasting commitment.



Quotation







It’s a universal truth for hunger relief advocates from Fargo to Foster: Hunger is something you experience; it’s not who you are.


Because if there is anything that 20 years in hunger relief has taught me, it’s that no one organization, no one state entity, no one policy can solve this significant and complex issue. As Feeding America says in this year’s Hunger Action Month campaign, “assembly is required.” Real solutions are never built alone. Yet hunger is solvable. 
And while I may still be a newcomer by Rhode Island standards, this past year has given me renewed optimism that it is here — 1,600 miles away from the farmlands where my work in this field began — where we can solve it.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: New Steelpointe apartments fuel affordability debate in Bridgeport
description: Residents reflecting on the new Steelpointe apartments said they want Bridgeport to grow. But they don't want to be left behind.
text:
Steelpointe Harbor, the waterfront development at the southern tip of Bridgeport’s East Side, has been touted for decades as a centerpiece of the city’s revival. Concepts proposed for the site over the years — including former plans for a luxury movie theater, hotel and a Dave & Buster’s restaurant — served as symbols of what Bridgeport hoped to become.
Now, some retail, a restaurant and, most recently, the first phase of housing is here, with more still to come.
Last month, residents began moving into The August, a 420-unit apartment complex across from Bass Pro Shops, Chipotle and Starbucks and next to the waterfront Boca Oyster Bar.
The apartment complex is the first residential phase of a larger transformation of Steelpointe, a peninsula that was once home to a United Illuminating power plant.
The August offers its residents a pool, fitness center, sauna, workspaces, parking and harbor views. Rents range from around $1,900 for some of the nearly 40% deed-and income restricted apartments to more than $9,000 a month for some of the market-rate three-bedroom units, an annual rent that totals nearly double the city’s median income.
For city residents, The August is more than a new apartment building. It is a sign of how Bridgeport is changing and who can afford to be part of that change.
The question is not whether Bridgeport needs development. Nearly everyone who spoke to The Connecticut Mirror said it does.
The question is who gets to participate in it. 

A pickleball court and outdoor spaces for residents, including a grilling station, are seen during a tour of The August apartment complex in the Steelpointe Harbor neighborhood of Bridgeport on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Mayor Joe Ganim says The August is part of a broader effort to increase Bridgeport’s housing supply. The city is pursuing a goal of 5,000 new units across the city by the end of the decade, he said, with more than 1,300 currently in active development. About 30% of those units are deed-restricted affordable housing, according to the mayor.
“Both market-rate and affordable housing production are necessary,” Ganim said in a written statement.
But “affordable” means something different to residents depending on where they stand.
The development is cut off from the East Side neighborhood it belongs to by Interstate-95. The median household income for that neighborhood was $45,754 in 2024, according to data from the U.S. Census Bureau.
The August has some apartments set aside for people with middle incomes. To qualify, a person’s income must fall within a certain range based on the size of their household. For example, a person living alone can earn between about $88,000 and $110,000 a year and qualify for some of these apartments. A household of five can earn as much as about $203,000 and still qualify for some units. Renters also must earn at least 2.5 times the apartment’s monthly rent to qualify.
Those numbers are based on regional income standards, while Bridgeport’s median household income was $57,394 in 2024, according to census data. That disconnect concerns Wayne Winston, who was a longtime city resident, activist and Bridgeport NAACP member and now lives in Trumbull.
“Affordable is basically what a person can afford,” Winston said.
Winston said he wants Bridgeport to attract investment, businesses and good-paying jobs. But he questions the value of expensive housing if the people living around it do not have the incomes to afford it.
He calls the jobs Bridgeport needs “feed your family jobs.”
“If we can’t benefit, it makes it very difficult to just say, ‘Hey, this was a good idea,’” Winston said.

Resident Lenny Grimaldi walks thorugh his one-bedroom apartment at The August apartment complex in the Steelpointe Harbor neighborhood of Bridgeport on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Lennie Grimaldi sees the development differently. The longtime Bridgeport political insider and founder of the Only In Bridgeport blog now lives at The August. Grimaldi, who worked for Ganim during the mayor’s first time running the city more than two decades ago, describes The August as a transformational project. He said its affordability should be considered alongside its amenities and the range of apartments available.
He points to the building’s amenities as well as the income-restricted units. 
Grimaldi acknowledges that some of the building’s highest-priced units are out of reach for many renters. But he said the conversation has focused too heavily on the most expensive apartments rather than the entire building.
“You really need a mix of housing,” Grimaldi said.
That mix is where Kelvin Ayala, a Bridgeport resident and business owner, sees both an opportunity and a problem.
Ayala, director of economic development at Led By Us & Associates, considers himself pro-development and pro-developer. He said Bridgeport needs housing at different income levels, including market-rate apartments like those at The August.
But Ayala said many residents cannot see how they move from the housing they have now into the new housing being built around them.
“We don’t see the tiers,” he said.
For Ayala, the issue is whether Bridgeport is creating a path for residents to improve their economic circumstances and eventually participate in the growth happening around them. He also said the city needs to improve its older housing stock so residents are not forced to choose between deteriorating apartments and expensive new construction.
“It’s OK to know you can’t afford it yet,” Ayala said. “But it doesn’t mean you can’t set your goals and want it.”

The pool is seen during a tour of The August apartment complex in the Steelpointe Harbor neighborhood of Bridgeport on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Alicia Carpenter-Cummings, a longtime North End resident who has worked throughout Bridgeport, including in her work with the American Red Cross, has seen firsthand the needs residents face. She questions whether adding housing without adding the stores, services and jobs people need actually creates stronger neighborhoods.
“You’re putting up more housing, but you’re not putting up grocery stores,” she said. “You’re not putting up drugstores.”
She points to the East End, the neighborhood just over the Yellow Mill Channel bridge on Stratford Avenue, where residents have waited years for a grocery store to be built. Many have also argued the neighborhood lacks many services within its borders, like a bank or pharmacy.
Carpenter-Cummings’ concern is that people can move into new apartments without ever becoming economically connected to the neighborhood around them.
Residents, she said, have opportunities to speak about development. What matters is whether anyone listens.
“I think residents always have an opportunity to speak,” Carpenter-Cummings said. “But the next question is: Is what they say going to get a response?”

Councilman Jorge Cruz, who represents the city’s South End, said Steelpointe is contributing to gentrification and worries that rising housing costs will make it harder for longtime residents to remain in Bridgeport.
But Cruz also said the city needs development. His concern is based on how he defines affordable housing: not by an income formula but by what is left after the rent is paid — enough to cover bills, buy food, save money and live without the constant fear of eviction.
“Affordable housing means where somebody feels content, feels that they’re established,” Cruz said.
Mercedes Alicea, an East Side resident, sees the issue through the condition of the neighborhoods surrounding the new development. She wants investment in infrastructure, small businesses and services in the communities where many Black and Latino residents have lived for generations.
For Alicea, it is difficult to celebrate expensive new apartments while longtime residents continue asking for better streets, neighborhood services and economic investment.
Her frustration reflects something that many others repeated to the CT Mirror: residents do not necessarily want Bridgeport to stop changing. They want to know whether they will be part of the change.
Ganim argues that the city is working toward that balance by producing housing across the income spectrum, from deeply affordable and supportive housing to workforce, mixed-income and market-rate apartments.

Views of the Steelpointe Harbor neighborhood of Bridgeport are seen from coworking spaces at The August apartment complex on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

But while the city counts units under construction, residents count their paychecks, rent, groceries, transportation and what is left at the end of the month, they said.
That is why The August has become such a powerful symbol in Bridgeport. 
Residents said they want Bridgeport to grow. They just don’t want to be left behind by that growth.
Longtime Bridgeport resident and former city librarian John Soltis grew up two blocks from Father Panik Village, a former East Side public housing complex that reported high levels of crime and poverty before its demolition began in the late 1980s.
Soltis has watched Steelpointe plans come and go for decades. He sees the opening of The August as progress. But he is skeptical that enough of the housing will reach the residents who need it most.
“I would have liked to see some more genuinely affordable housing there,” Soltis said.
He said successful development should bring people of different incomes, races and backgrounds into the same communities rather than separate them.
“We need a mix of people,” Soltis said. “But we don’t need gentrification.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Ahead of Labor Day, unions back Crowley
description: Days before Labor Day, and with just over two months before the November election, a coalition of labor unions announced Wednesday they were backing Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley’s campaign for governor.  Leaders from American Federation of Teachers-Wisconsin, the Service Employees International Union Wisconsin, the United Food and Commercial Work[...]
text:
Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley was endorsed by four labor unions on Wednesday. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)Days before Labor Day, and with just over two months before the November election, a coalition of labor unions announced Wednesday they were backing Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley’s campaign for governor. 
Leaders from American Federation of Teachers-Wisconsin, the Service Employees International Union Wisconsin, the United Food and Commercial Workers Local 1473 and the Wisconsin Education Association Council announced their organizations’ endorsements of Crowley — acknowledging that even if they don’t agree with the Democratic nominee on every issue, he’s preferable to Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany — who as a member of the Legislature voted for Act 10, the controversial law that stripped collective bargaining rights from most public employees. 
“For the future of labor, this election is incredibly important,” Jon Shelton, president of AFT-Wisconsin and a professor at UW-Green Bay, said. “We know that we just came out of a primary that was contentious, but we are showing the solidarity to work with your campaign to make sure that we don’t just win this election, but we win a trifecta, and we move the state of Wisconsin in the direction that every working person, every kid in our schools, every citizen in this state deserves.” 
At a virtual news conference to announce the endorsements, Crowley touted his family’s union membership and the work he’s done in the past to support Wisconsin labor. 
“Working people, we aren’t asking for a handout,” he said. “We’re asking for a seat at the table. We’re asking for a fair deal. That’s pro- worker, that’s pro-family, and that’s the Wisconsin that I absolutely believe in.”
Leadership from some of the unions touted the support Crowley has provided to them in previous fights. Pat Raes, president of SEIU Wisconsin Healthcare and a nurse at Madison’s Meriter Hospital, noted that Crowley joined her union’s fight when Meriter’s nurses went on strike last year and when Milwaukee commercial office workers were bargaining for a new contract in 2024.
Raes also pointed to Crowley’s support for raising Wisconsin’s minimum wage, overturning Act 10 and expanding access to child care and healthcare. 
But other unions throwing support behind Crowley are making some policy concessions. WEAC had endorsed state Sen. Kelda Roys (D-Madison) in the Democratic primary for governor — partially because of her plan for winding down the state’s private school voucher program. 
Private school vouchers
As Milwaukee County executive, Crowley represents the part of the state with the largest number of voucher school students and has said he doesn’t support ending the controversial program, though he has said he wants to increase oversight and transparency. 
On Wednesday, WEAC president Peggy Wirtz-Olsen said she’s “talked” with Crowley about the “damage caused by vouchers” and added “Wisconsin educators are convinced that David Crowley will be the best choice for governor.” 
“WEAC has met with David Crowley and engaged in extensive conversations about the issues that are affecting public school educators, my colleagues and I, students and families we serve, and public education in Wisconsin,” Wirtz-Olsen, who also teaches high school English and art in Marshfield, said. “We’ve talked honestly about the inadequate and unstable funding, the growing class sizes, educator shortages, mental health, special education, and all the damage caused by the vouchers. We’ve talked about affordability and about high costs and how that’s squeezing families, students, and our educators.”
Tiffany has supported voucher schools and cuts to public education funding as a member of the state Legislature and in Congress. If elected, he and his Republican allies are likely to further expand the state’s voucher programs, which draw from the same pool of resources as public schools. Wirtz-Olsen said that WEAC was supporting a candidate who won’t send more state money to private voucher schools. 
“When lawmakers send more taxpayer dollars into unaccountable private school voucher programs instead of fully funding public schools that serve every student, the direct result is fewer resources for students who need the support, larger class sizes, and continued delayed services,” she said. “It’s no wonder that about half of first-time teachers will leave the profession. These demands are unsustainable. That’s been a failure of state priorities. Wisconsin needs a governor who understands that public schools are not a chip for high-stake deals. Public schools are an investment in our children, our workforce, our communities, and our democracy.”
Data centers and trade unions
The early weeks of the general election campaign were dominated by the two candidates wrangling over the issue of data centers, which has become a hot button in elections across the country this year. 
Tiffany, who in ads has called Crowley “data center David,” has said he opposes data centers, along with wind and solar farms, on the grounds that they’re taking too much of Wisconsin’s prime farmland. Crowley has said he wants to enact additional regulations governing data center development, including requirements that they be powered by renewable energy and built with union labor. 
Wisconsin’s building trade unions have been more supportive of data center developments than the public at large. 
But once hyperscale data centers such as those currently under construction in Beaver Dam, Mount Pleasant and Port Washington are built, the artificial intelligence technology they support could potentially disrupt the jobs of thousands of Wisconsin workers, including the teachers, professor and nurses endorsing Crowley. 
At the Wednesday event, Crowley said he wanted to make sure Wisconsin is “being aggressive when it comes down to protecting our workforce, protecting our environment, making sure that not one single dime is being pushed off to ratepayers and taxpayers here.” He added that he believes AI should increase productivity rather than replacing it and noted that Tiffany was a deciding vote when the House of Representatives voted to ban states from regulating AI for a decade as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The provision was not in the version of the bill that President Donald Trump signed into law last year. 
“Artificial intelligence will never ever be able to compete with authentic intelligence, and that’s what people bring to the table,” Crowley said. “And so it is unfortunate that my opponent, Congressman Tom Tiffany, he actually was the deciding vote to actually put up a state ban on us being able to regulate artificial intelligence. But we have to do everything that we can to make sure that we’re protecting workers moving forward and make sure that workers have a seat at the table as it relates to how we use artificial intelligence in the field, no matter the industry.”
