name: Kansas Reflector
title: Why the rise in government debt is freaking out the bond market
description: Mortgage holders know interest rates have risen over the past year. But they’re not alone: governments and business borrowers are facing the same pressure. In the United States, 10-year interest rates sit around 4.7%, surging nearly half a per cent just this year, while the benchmark 30-year bond is near a two-decade high. In the UK, […]
text:
Rates in bond markets have been rising across much of the world as government juggle debt. (Photo by Angela Weiss/AFP via Getty Images)Mortgage holders know interest rates have risen over the past year. But they’re not alone: governments and business borrowers are facing the same pressure.
In the United States, 10-year interest rates sit around 4.7%, surging nearly half a per cent just this year, while the benchmark 30-year bond is near a two-decade high. In the UK, 10-year bond rates on Tuesday hit the highest level since the global financial crisis.
In Australia, the Reserve Bank of Australia also lifted the cash rate to fight inflation. That government now has to offer investors more than 5% on its 10-year bonds, which hit a 15-year high on Tuesday after a long period of low interest rates since the global financial crisis in 2008.
Higher rates mean higher interest payments for governments too, leaving less room for other spending or for tax cuts. This trickles down to state and local communities.
So what’s actually driving market interest rates higher?
 
Supply and demand
Governments issue bonds to raise money and finance spending that isn’t covered by tax revenue.
Like any asset, the price of a government bond depends on supply and demand. Less bond supply means issuers (governments or companies) don’t need to offer higher rates to attract buyers; more supply pushes rates up.
Bond issuance comes from three main sources:

Households – borrowing for mortgages, which the banks can then repackage into bonds and sell to investors.
Businesses – issuing bonds to fund operations. In the U.S., AI-sector firms such as Amazon and Microsoft have issued about $240 billion in debt to fund data centers. Even in Australia, Google owner Alphabet launched a huge A$5.5 billion bond last month.
Governments – governments often have large debts they have built up because of their past budget deficits. Like anyone, if you spend more than you earn, you need to borrow.

 
The main driver is government debt
The larger a government’s debt, the more bonds it must issue — and the higher the interest rates needed to attract investors.
U.S. national debt has grown to more than $40 trillion — more than 20 times the size of Australia’s entire economy — while Australia’s federal government debt recently passed A$1 trillion.

Funding debts of this size is pushing up interest rates worldwide. At the same time, bond investors are getting concerned by the high levels of U.S. government debt and the lack of plans to curb spending, so they are demanding higher interest rates on government bonds.
 
What central banks can do
The Reserve Bank of Australia manages interest rates through the “cash market” — short-term borrowing of less than a day — using the cash rate to influence demand for borrowing. Raising interest rates ultimately dampens economic demand and reduces inflation.
The RBA cash rate affects borrowing costs across the economy for all other forms of debt, including car loans and credit cards as well as mortgages, and corporate debt.
But the RBA can’t directly influence longer-term interest rates such as 10-year bonds, which are market rates and fluctuate constantly based on investor demand.
If the RBA cut rates sharply right now, for instance, bond investors would likely read this as inflationary — pushing up inflation expectations and, in turn, the interest rates demanded on longer-term bonds. The RBA’s action would end up being counterproductive.
 
America’s ‘exorbitant privilege’ — and its limits
The United States has long enjoyed a unique position in global markets: it can issue growing volumes of government bonds without needing to offer higher rates to attract buyers.
This “exorbitant privilege” stems from the U.S. dollar’s dominance in global trade and financial transactions, and the widespread trust that central banks and private investors place in U.S. government debt.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has tried to capitalize on this by intervening in the bond market, aiming to shrink supply and push market interest rates lower. That would reduce the interest bill for the U.S. government.
The U.S. Treasury increased the amount of debt it is buying back, but the buybacks only had a brief impact on the market.
Investors concluded the buybacks don’t change the underlying picture: increasing U.S. government financing needs, fears of rising inflation, as well as growing corporate bond issuance to fund AI and data centers. All these forces tend to push interest rates higher over the medium to long term, and no financial engineering can undo this reality.
 
Rates are rising around the world
Across many countries, bond market rates are rising because higher inflation is eroding the real returns for investors. They are demanding more compensation to protect their spending power.
This is compounded by rising bond issuance from both governments and companies. No amount of financial engineering from the U.S. Treasury can reverse these forces.
Central banks and governments can influence short-term interest rates to some degree. But longer-term debt such as 10-year bonds are ultimately priced on three things:

Expected inflation
The scale of government debt and financing needs
The level of corporate and household borrowing.

The best thing any central bank can do to keep market interest rates low is set policy so inflation remains low.
That’s the purpose of the RBA’s inflation target of 2–3%. As well as keeping a lid on consumer inflation expectations, it lets bond investors know inflation should return to that level in the medium term, and so market interest rates don’t get too high.
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.


Mark Crosby is a professor at Monash Business School, Monash University. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Somerset County schools book policy faces new State Board challenge
description: A Somerset County School Board policy that makes young adult books in school libraries unavailable to almost all students in county schools violates state law and the First Amendment, an appeal to the State Board of Education claims.
text:
A Somerset County schools policy that would place "young adult" literature out of reach of almost all K-12 students faces a new challenge from critics who say it violates state law and the First Amendment. (Photo by Terry Vine/Getty Stock Images)A Somerset County School Board policy that makes young adult books in school libraries unavailable to almost all students in county schools violates state law and the First Amendment, an appeal to the State Board of Education claims.
The appeal, filed by a county parent, the Somerset Education Association and the Maryland Association of School Librarians, targets board Policy 500-19, which requires that all young adult books be put in an adult section of the library and be prohibited for any student under age 18.
The updated policy, adopted by the county school board last month, also calls for discipline of school librarians for “insubordination” if they fail to follow the policy.
Besides violating free speech guarantees of the First Amendment, the appeal says the policy violates Maryland’s Freedom to Read Act, a 2024 law that prohibits books and other school library materials from being removed until a formal process is conducted. It also restrict disciplinary action against school employees who follow the law.
“Policy 500-19 nevertheless directs SCPS (Somerset County Public Schools) officials to favor materials that support the… beliefs and values endorsed by the Somerset County Board of Education,” according to the appeal. “While disfavoring materials associated with anti-religion, victimhood, rebellion, sexuality, and other ideas.”
Somerset County Superintendent David Bromwell declined via email to comment on the appeal Wednesday.
But Phaedra Spencer, president of the Somerset teacher’s union and a high school teacher and librarian, said the amended policy allows a majority vote of the school board to remove and purchase books in school libraries.
“Do I have to ask permission because the kids spilled Kool-Aid on their book [and] take it out of the library? Am I going to get in trouble because I didn’t ask you?” asked Spencer, who has a master’s degree in school librarianship. “That policy is really, really tying us down to be able to do anything.”
The appeal could extend a 60-day stay on the policy that was imposed last month by state Superintendent Carey Wright. The stay will remain in effect through Oct. 20, but can be dissolved sooner by the superintendent or state school board.
State Superintendent Carey Wright at Maryland State Board of Education meeting in April. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
The Freedom to Read Act was approved by the legislature two years ago, during a time of national conversations on the subject of book bans.
Among its provisions, the law requires local school officials to set policies and procedures to review objections to books made by a student, parent or guardian. Local officials must also create reasonable timelines to conduct and conclude a review, and it says that books and other materials must remain available for use by students and school personnel until the review process has ended.
Maryland became one of the first states in the nation with strong protections to preserve access to information in libraries, as well as penalties for those who attempt to thwart access. It also prohibits retaliating against employees for doing their jobs.
‘I don’t care what anybody thinks, except for Jesus Christ’
The five-member Somerset County board voted Aug. 18 to amend its library policy follow what it said was U.S. Supreme Court precedent “in applying the school/library policy to students. All library materials must be educationally suitable for minors.”
The policy defines a child as age “0-18” and young adults as those ages 18 to 26. It prohibits minors from accessing “adult library materials.”
In terms of discipline, the policy says “the superintendent shall immediately implement disciplinary procedures for insubordination of adults in charge of ensuring proper educationally suitable material is accessible for minor children in Somerset County Public Schools.”
Board Chair Matthew Lankford, Vice Chair Andrew Gleason and Mary Beth Bozman voted for the policy. John Robertson voted against it and William McInturff Jr. abstained.
Before the meeting ended, Lankford had some closing remarks.
“When I really read these books, how many people have read these books? I’ll tell you the truth, I read them and it disgusted me,” he said. “So we give them books that’s got a hundred F-bombs, and we don’t expect them to use it in the classroom at our teachers. These are the things that, I don’t care what anybody else thinks, except for Jesus Christ, I don’t think they should be given to our children.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
But critics said the policy would put books like “The Diary of Anne Frank” or “To Kill a Mockingbird” off limits.
A week before the vote, the state Librarians Association wrote that the policy “demonstrates that the board is giving itself standing to flag, review, pull, or veto books on its own motion.” The association noted that Somerset’s policy would restrict certain books from being read because the school district should have “classical literature with well-known authors should be the priority when selecting books and media materials.”
In addition, the association said standard industry practice identifies young adult books as those for ages 12 to 17, not 18 to 26. It said the policy would remove award-winning books such as “All American Boys” (which highlights police brutality through the eyes of two high schoolers, one Black and one white) and “All Boys Aren’t Blue” (an author’s memoir of growing up Black and queer).
The policy “starves students of different perspectives and viewpoints, while also failing to get them excited about reading by making books available far beyond the types they see in the classroom,” the library association wrote.
That letter and other letters opposing the policy are included in the appeal.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Nessel wins injunction against Kalshi as prediction market says Michigan lacks regulatory authority
description: In her lawsuit against the prediction market Kalshi, Michigan’s Attorney General has secured another block barring the company from offering sports betting services in the state of Michigan.  Attorney General Dana Nessel first filed suit against the company in March,  arguing the company was operating in violation of the state’s Lawful Sports Betting Act. Ka[...]
text:
Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel on July 30, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)In her lawsuit against the prediction market Kalshi, Michigan’s Attorney General has secured another block barring the company from offering sports betting services in the state of Michigan. 
Attorney General Dana Nessel first filed suit against the company in March,  arguing the company was operating in violation of the state’s Lawful Sports Betting Act.
Kalshi allows individuals to trade on the outcome of certain events, including sporting events, an operation which Judge Rosemarie Aquilina of the 30th Judicial Circuit Court of Ingham County called “a sports betting operation masquerading as an investment opportunity.”
In her suit, Nessel argues that the company is operating without the licensing approval of the Michigan Gaming Control Board. 
Aquilina previously granted a temporary restraining order demanding Kalshi cease offering event contracts on sporting events to Michigan residents. On Tuesday, she granted a preliminary injunction, barring the company from engaging in any activity tied to sports betting in Michigan.
“Kalshi long attempted to pass itself off as a legitimate gaming operation in our state, and I am relieved that this order further protects Michigan residents from its predatory, unlicensed practices,” said Attorney General Nessel. “My office will continue to defend Michiganders and enforce our gaming laws, which ensure gambling revenue is regulated and distributed back into our communities.”
In order to meet the requirements of the order, Kalshi must work with a third-party geolocation service to ensure it does not accept wagers from Michigan residents.
In this online ad, prediction market platform Kalshi advertises its sports betting products in California and Texas, both states that have not legalized sports gambling. States are increasingly targeting platforms like Kalshi, arguing they circumvent the protections and taxes of regulated gambling markets. (Image courtesy of Dustin Goucher/ Event Horizon newsletter)
In an email to Michigan Advance, Kalshi referred to a previous statement from its head of communications, Elisabeth Diana, issued in response to the temporary restraining order. 
“It’s no surprise that we disagree with the state’s decision and will fight it in court,” Diana said. “Kalshi is subject to exclusive federal jurisdiction. We won’t be bullied by interests that care more about protecting their monopolies than their consumers. In the meantime, we’re implementing restrictions.”
In a letter to the Department of Attorney General Friday, Kalshi Attorney Andrew Porter shared concerns that other states were pursuing enforcement actions against other competitors like Polymarket, Crypto.com, Robinhood and Coinbase.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“To be clear, it remains Kalshi’s position that event contracts traded on federally-regulated designated contract markets are subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. But we recognize that position is contested, and appreciate that Michigan, unlike states such as Nevada and Washington, is not seeking to favor some industry participants at the expense of others,” Porter said. “To that end, we note that Polymarket, Robinhood and Coinbase all sought, and were denied, federal court orders that would have prevented Michigan from taking action against them in state court.”
Porter noted that Aquilina’s decision to grant a temporary restraining order was based on alleged harm to Michigan residents ages 18 to 20, who can make trades on Kalshi but are not old enough to participate in legal sports betting in the state, which is limited to residents 21 and older.
“Kalshi disputes that harm, but recognizes that, if it exists, it is inflicted equally by other market participants that presently are allowed to operate in Michigan,” Porter said in the letter. “As such, Kalshi must reserve its right to move for dissolution of the Court’s forthcoming preliminary injunction order in the event Michigan does not seek to address the purported harms inflicted by Kalshi’s competitors.”
The Department of Attorney General did not respond to emails or a voicemail asking whether it plans to pursue similar sports betting lawsuits against Kalshi’s competitors. This story will be updated when a response is received.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Who works for whom? Ohio man’s podcast explores data centers, AI.
description: Data centers have emerged as a central battleground in the 2026 midterm elections. As they have, a Columbus man has spent many months traveling the country learning what the fuss is about: Complaints of noise and pollution, strain on the electricity grid, loss of local control to fabulously wealthy tech giants — and the possibility […]
text:
An aerial view shows a data center situated near single-family homes. (Photo by Nathan Howard/Getty Images)Data centers have emerged as a central battleground in the 2026 midterm elections. As they have, a Columbus man has spent many months traveling the country learning what the fuss is about: Complaints of noise and pollution, strain on the electricity grid, loss of local control to fabulously wealthy tech giants — and the possibility that a trillion-dollar speculative bubble is about to burst.
In addition, data centers power AI chatbots that have been accused of engaging in sexual conversations with minors and failing to discourage them from suicide. Even among adults, excessive use of chatbots is causing “AI psychosis.”
On the other hand are undeniable benefits. The technology is already enabling tremendous strides in things like medical research and the other sciences. It’s also creating millions of construction jobs, and it’s integrating itself into everyday life in ways that make it more convenient.
But other questions are more ominous.
Who will lose their jobs to artificial intelligence? And how many more will be forced to work as living, breathing AI drones, monitored by GPS and biometric cameras as computers make humans labor right up to the limits of their ability?
As he reported and produced the podcast series “The Data Centers are Coming,” Danny Caine tried to address those questions.
Working with the antimonopoly group the Institute for Local Self Reliance, the former Kansas bookstore owner interviewed people in places like Virginia’s Data Center Alley and Memphis, Tennessee, where Elon Musk is accused of using more than a dozen unpermitted gas-fired generators to power his massive xAI center.
Growing opposition
In those places and hundreds of others, residents fear that their lives are being profoundly altered by projects over which they didn’t get much of a say. That might explain why opposition is growing so fiercely across the political spectrum.
“Data center opposition is a remarkably bipartisan issue,” Caine told the OCJ.
An example: In Box Elder County, Utah, 70% of voters went for Donald Trump in 2024, while in Minneapolis, voters went for Kamala Harris by a similar margin.  
“Both passed data center moratoriums,” Caine said. “This is everybody. You’ve got farmers out west and you’ve got socialists in New York City organizing on the same issue. I think they’re doing a really good job making sure there’s room for everybody. A part of it is that this is local. It hasn’t been polarized by national political rhetoric like immigration. This is people talking about what gets built in their community and how they should grow economically.”
Caleb Max, president and CEO of industry group the National Artificial Intelligence Association, said it’s a misconception that data centers don’t have to go through the permitting processes that other projects do. He also said communities are given advance warning and a chance to have their say.
“Data centers file the same permits and go through the same county zoning and board processes as any other large development and those processes end in votes by elected local officials,” he said in an email. “Projects have been modified, relocated, and voted down outright across the country, including in Ohio.”
Max cited plans to build an OpenAI data center in Effingham County, Georgia, as an example.
“Before construction began, the company published its commitments, held a public open house where residents questioned engineers directly, and is building a community compact out of that feedback,” he said, later adding, “Was the meeting contentious? Very. That is the process working, not failing.”
However, the public appears to have been informed of the $20 billion project pretty late in the game.
OpenAI got local government officials to sign nondisclosure agreements regarding the project on Feb. 2, WTOC reported. Then, on July 21, they signed a memorandum of understanding and finalized a huge tax break for the project, the TV station reported.
With the county already committed to the project, it was publicly announced on July 22, with construction planned to start before the end of the year.
The open house Max cited was held a day after that, according to the Effingham Herald. Hundreds packed the meeting and are now forming an opposition group — to fight a project their county officials have already bound them to.
In addition, The Current reported that Gov. Brian Kemp met in May with OpenAI and Georgia Power “with no mentions of data center construction on its briefing memo.”
Opposition to such projects appears to be spreading.
An Economist/YouGov poll released last month reported that just 24% of Americans now believe data centers are good versus 47% who say they’re not. 
Democrats were most opposed, followed by independents. More Republicans were in favor than opposed, but only by five percentage points, and 29% were undecided.
In addition, Politico polls conducted in January and July found that opinion has been shifting against data centers rapidly, so opposition seems likely to grow.
Tax breaks
One reason why opinion is shifting might have to do with the belated discovery of massive tax breaks that were given in virtual secrecy to companies controlled by some of the world’s richest people.
In June, The Columbus Dispatch wrote that before he left office in 2019, Ohio Gov. John Kasich quietly gave Google, Amazon and Meta huge tax exemptions lasting 40 years. 
They were part of $2.3 billion in tax breaks the former governor handed out — supposedly to persuade companies to build in Ohio. However, they’re so desperate to build more “compute,” that Industrial Equipment News reports some are even looking at ways to build data centers in the ocean.
Max, of the Artificial Intelligence Association, agreed that the AI companies don’t need the tax breaks with which Ohio and other states have been so lavish.
“They do not need them,” he said. “Communities offer them because they want to compete for the investment, and Ohio has been good at it. Governor DeWine noted in May that previously exempted projects reported $27.2 billion in capital investment in 2025 alone.”
The investment is huge, but it will create relatively few jobs once construction is completed. Policy Matters Ohio estimates that the Google, Amazon, and Meta subsidies will cost Ohio taxpayers $1 million per permanent job created.
For Caine, news of the Ohio tax breaks came just as he and his team were finishing their podcast series. It might be part of a bonus episode, he said.
“That policy was basically a secret until somebody went and dug it up years later,” he said. “That’s one thing that really upsets people about this. Data centers are bad and people hate them. But they also hate that a lot of this is happening in secret. They don’t have any input. They feel like the first time they hear about this stuff, it’s a done deal.”
Affecting neighbors
When he traveled to Data Center Alley — a region in Northern Virginia containing about 300 of the facilities — Caine saw the effects they can have on people living close to them. Generators serving some are so loud that residents are spending thousands doing things like installing plexiglass over their windows to dampen the noise.
Caine said such noise forces people indoors — and away from the neighbor-to-neighbor organizing his group advocates. 
“One thing that’s really concerning is that if you make the neighborhood environment hostile via noise or pollution or whatever, people connect with each other less,” he said. “You’re driving people inside and away from connecting with each other. Big Tech people might not mind that. Instead of being outside connecting with people, you’re inside looking at your device. So just being outside organizing with your neighbors is a kind of rebellion against what Big Tech wants to build.”
Max, the AI industry spokesman, said focusing solely on those complaints ignores advancements in the industry.
“There is a vacuum mentality here, the assumption that data centers drain the water, the power supply, and the grid, and that often isn’t the case anymore,” he said. “On water, the industry has moved to closed loop cooling that recirculates water in a sealed system rather than evaporating it. New Central Ohio developments use air cooled closed loop chillers, Meta has committed to (be) water positive by 2030, and Amazon has a water neutral pledge.”
Max also touted a pledge by PJM, the electricity grid that serves Ohio and 12 other states, that data centers will pay for any additional generation they’ll require.
However, the Ohio Manufacturers Association and others are concerned that monopoly utilities are using data centers to inflate demand forecasts to justify construction from which they’ll profit. That can force up rates, and if they overbuild, ratepayers will be stuck holding the bag, critics say.
Many data centers are easing the strain on the electricity grid by generating their own power “behind the meter.”
But that comes with downsides of its own. The great majority burn fossil fuels and generate noise and greenhouse gasses.
And PBS and Floodlight report, they’re going up so fast that they’re overwhelming state and federal regulators that have been systematically starved of resources. In a separate investigation published last week, Floodlight and The Guardian reported that a Microsoft-backed data center in New Jersey fired up dozens of gas-powered generators without getting the required permits — an apparent violation of federal law.
Impact on average people
But perhaps the most important question is what will happen to Americans — especially the most vulnerable — once all these data centers are built and AI takes a central role in the workplace.
Many worry that it will make millions of jobs obsolete. Caine is also worried about the ones that will remain.
One need only look at the lives of the 1 million Americans who work for Amazon to get an  idea, he said.
“If you look at Amazon warehouse workers or delivery drivers, they’re completely at the mercy of the machines that control their rates,” he said. “Whether it’s all the biometric cameras in the Amazon vans, or the little GPS handheld things in the warehouse, they exist to make sure the machines keep running. It’s machines first, then humans.”
In other words, Caine is saying a dangerous line is crossed when AI doesn’t just work for people, but people also work for AI.
“When the human loses agency for the sake of the machine, it’s literally dehumanizing,” he said.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Bookman: Secrecy and tax breaks pave the way for surge of unpopular data center proposals in Georgia
description: This year, Georgia taxpayers will spend an estimated $2.4 billion in tax breaks to subsidize construction of data centers in our state.  I have several problems with that. You might too. First, and most obviously, that $2.4 billion could buy a lot of health insurance, or keep rural hospitals operating. It could pay a lot […]
text:
A protest sign pictured after DeKalb County residents gathered before a county commission meeting on Nov. 20, 2025, to protest a data center proposal in Ellenwood. Alander Rocha/Georgia RecorderThis year, Georgia taxpayers will spend an estimated $2.4 billion in tax breaks to subsidize construction of data centers in our state. 
I have several problems with that. You might too.
First, and most obviously, that $2.4 billion could buy a lot of health insurance, or keep rural hospitals operating. It could pay a lot of teacher salaries. But leadership in this state has decided those are not good uses for the money. Instead, they’ve decided it is better used to fatten the bank accounts and stock portfolios of people who are already some of the richest on the planet. 
Because really, that’s all state officials are doing. Even if you believe that data centers are necessary – and there’s a decent argument to that effect – billions of dollars of state tax subsidies remain a ridiculous waste of money. The usual justification for such subsidies is to encourage needed economic development projects that otherwise would not occur, and that is simply not the case here. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
To the contrary, this year the artificial intelligence industry is expected to draw $2.5 trillion in new private investment globally. The worry isn’t that the AI industry can’t attract enough investment, it’s that it is drawing too much investment, too quickly, to the point that many experts warn that the sector is creating a financial bubble that may soon burst.  
In short, we are subsidizing and incentivizing projects that almost certainly would have been built in Georgia anyway.
Second problem: We are using public money to subsidize something that the public does not seem to want. Nationally, poll after poll finds that more than 70% of Americans would oppose construction of data centers in their community. Here in Georgia, an Atlanta Journal-Constitution poll of primary voters back in April found that 53% of Republicans and 75% of Democrats would oppose data centers near them. Those numbers have probably grown since then.
Why? Data centers require huge quantities of water to cool servers. They require huge amounts of electricity, straining power plants and grids and potentially raising energy costs. They are noisy, and once operational they don’t generate many jobs. It is not irrational to wonder whether their drawbacks outweigh their benefit, particularly to communities forced to host them. 
That leads us to the third problem. In their headlong rush to cash in on the AI boom, data center proponents often have neither the time nor the patience for working with and reassuring communities about its impact. Instead, they attempt to get their way through brute force, deception, political power and money.
Take recent events in Effingham County, near Savannah, where a huge new data center was announced in late July. At full build-out, the facility will cover 1,400 acres and require 3.2 gigawatts of electricity, enough to serve 3 million homes.
That’s a project of immense public impact. Yet there had been no public input or even knowledge about the project before it was announced as a finalized deal. That happened by design, not accident. According to The Current, the CEO of the Effingham County development authority had signed a non-disclosure agreement with OpenAI, the company building the plant. In April, he even publicly denied that negotiations for a data center were underway, actively misleading the people he is supposed to represent.  
In late July, the county development board quietly approved the final deal in a hastily called meeting without proper public notice. Nobody in the community was in attendance. The local weekly newspaper had been told a deal was coming, but it agreed to embargo the news, withholding it from its readers and denying them the chance to weigh in, until after the deal had been approved. That’s a terrible journalistic decision.
That is not operating in good faith. It is a way of doing business that heightens rather than mitigates fear and suspicion. And the problem is, similar stories are playing out all over the country.
Outside Memphis, for example, Elon Musk is building another massive data center project and has installed dozens of natural gas generators to supply the needed electricity. However, he has done so without the legally required air quality permits and pollution-control systems, producing thousands of tons of unregulated pollutants.
And when local groups sought to sue Musk’s company for violating the federal Clean Air Act, the Trump administration declared the facility essential to national security, claiming that status meant Musk could ignore federal law and was immune to lawsuits.
Such high-handed action may work in the short term, but it will inevitably produce a backlash. It has done exactly that, which leads to my fourth and most important point:
AI is already a spooky technology to many people, including people intimately involved in its development. They warn of its impact on jobs and communities, of its propensity to “hallucinate,” to tell users what they want to hear, and in some cases to set its own agenda, independent of its human creators.
The companies and people championing the promise of AI reassure us that they will keep the public interest in mind, that they will be responsible and conscientious in implementing this powerful technology and will not blow through safeguards in a mad rush for profits. Yet these are the same people now bulldozing through environmental laws, compelling elected officials to keep secrets from their own constituents and ignoring community input in their gold rush to build AI data centers.
So color me skeptical.

title: More than 40% of Ohio school districts have active LifeWise Academy chapters, with more on the way
description: Ohio has the most chapters of Ohio has the most LifeWise Academy chapters, a Christian religious release time program for public school students. About 32,200 Ohio students are enrolled in 267 active LifeWise chapters across the state — about 43% of Ohio’s school districts, according to a LifeWise spokesperson.  There are 240 more LifeWise chapters […]
text:
A LifeWise Academy bus in Ohio. (Photo by Megan Henry). Ohio has the most chapters of Ohio has the most LifeWise Academy chapters, a Christian religious release time program for public school students.
About 32,200 Ohio students are enrolled in 267 active LifeWise chapters across the state — about 43% of Ohio’s school districts, according to a LifeWise spokesperson. 
There are 240 more LifeWise chapters in process in Ohio, according to a new map on LifeWise’s website. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Ohio is LifeWise Academy’s home state, so we have deep roots and strong community support here,” according to a LifeWise spokesperson. “Ohio also has a long history of released time religious instruction, including the program in Van Wert that helped inspire LifeWise’s creation.”
LifeWise’s founder and CEO Joel Penton is from Van Wert in Northwest Ohio.
LifeWise is a non-denominational Christian program based in Hilliard that teaches religion to public school students during the school day at a special release time. It currently has 531 live chapters and 4,377 chapters in process nationwide, according to the map. 
Religious release time instruction must meet three criteria: the courses must take place off school property, be privately funded, and students must have parental permission. The United States Supreme Court upheld release time laws during the 1952 Zorach v. Clauson case.
Mercer County in western Ohio is the only county in Ohio where a LifeWise chapter is not live, launching or in the planning stages, according to the map. 
In January 2025, Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine signed a law passed by Republican lawmakers that mandates public school districts create a policy allowing release time for religious instruction. Ohio is one of 18 states with such a law, according to LifeWise. 
States that have LifeWise Academy, a Christian religious release time program for public school students. (Photo from LifeWise Academy)
“LifeWise has been well received in Ohio communities as families see the positive impact it has on students’ behavior, academic performance and well-being,” according to a LifeWise spokesperson. 
But the program isn’t universally accepted in Ohio by any means. Some parents have said their students have been ostracized and bullied for not taking part in LifeWise, and some parents have said their child goes to a study hall in the school’s gymnasium while their classmates attend LifeWise.
“(LifeWise doesn’t) look at the effects of the Jewish students that are basically being forced into a gym, that are feeling punished because they don’t believe as such, and because they don’t believe, they don’t go,” said Kitty Schwanitz, an organizer for the Secular Education Association.  
She said LifeWise is spreading “very much almost the way that cancer spreads.” 
“(People) don’t realize what they’re getting, and that’s actually what we’re seeing a lot of,” she said. 
“Parents are coming to us and going, I didn’t understand or realize what I was getting my kids into, and now they believe these things, and I’m horrified. … Parents are getting the buyer’s remorse of what LifeWise is.”
Indiana has the second most live chapters LifeWise with 63, followed by Illinois with 28, and Michigan with 19, according to the map. 
Texas has more than 400 chapters in process, Pennsylvania has more than 350 chapters in process, and Indiana has more than 200 chapters in process, according to the map. 
Maine, Vermont, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Maryland, Rhode Island, Connecticut, Louisiana, Missouri, North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Utah, Nevada, and Hawaii do not have any live LifeWise chapters, but all are building up chapters, according to LifeWise.

title: ICE violence against women is largely untracked. One advocacy group is working to change that.
description: This story was originally reported by Candice Norwood of The 19th. Meet Candice and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy. No comprehensive, publicly available data exists tracking immigration agents who have a record of violence against women and children. One organization is attempting to fill some of that gap. The Ohio […]
text:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer's badge and weapon are seen during a vehicle checkpoint on Georgia Ave. in Washington, D.C., on Aug. 30, 2025. (Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
This story was originally reported by Candice Norwood of The 19th.  Meet Candice and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy.
No comprehensive, publicly available data exists tracking immigration agents who have a record of violence against women and children. One organization is attempting to fill some of that gap.
The Ohio Immigrant Alliance, a grassroots advocacy group, has compiled a list of 152 agents from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CPB) who have either faced administrative disciplinary action or criminal penalties for allegations of violent crimes.
The report, published Tuesday, is an expansion of findings released by the advocacy group in July. The organization identified cases involving the arrests of ICE or CBP personnel by looking at court documents, reports from the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Inspector General, the Department of Justice website, news reports and other publicly available records. The group then compiled a list of 152 ICE and CBP agents who have been accused, arrested, charged or convicted in connection to a range of violent crimes between 1982 and 2026. All but one of the alleged offenders on the list are men.
Critics have raised concerns about the vetting and training of immigration and border patrol officers as the administration continues a historic hiring spree.
The report notes that the dataset is not “a comprehensive review of every ICE or Border Patrol agent who has ever committed a crime,” adding that they “chose to focus on agents who committed sexual and violent crimes.”
An analysis by The 19th indicates that 73 percent of the people on this list were categorized by the Ohio Immigrant Alliance as being criminally charged or convicted and sentenced related to sexual offenses. Fifty percent were categorized as being criminally charged or sentenced related to crimes against minors. The alleged crimes include abduction and sexual assault of a minor, unauthorized access and use of intimate digital photos, possessing child sexual abuse materials, aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, domestic violence and strangulation.
One of the hopes in releasing this report is to get “law enforcement to start tracking data about family violence” among their officers, according to Lynn Tramonte, executive director of the Ohio Immigrant Alliance. During a call with reporters to discuss the findings, she also encouraged researchers and other organizations to get involved with collecting data and building on the work her organization has started.
“We’re giving you these 152 names,” Tramonte said. “We’re giving you the dates of their last activity — whether it was a charge, whether it was a conviction — and we’re giving you links to information about them. There’s so much you can do with this information that we didn’t get into in our report.”
In response to a 19th request for comment, a DHS spokesperson wrote via email: “the ICE Office of Professional Responsibility diligently applies the proper personnel vetting regulations, including guidelines for national security, and evaluates all available information for every applicant based on these factors.”
The statement continued:  “We take allegations regarding misconduct seriously and cherish the public’s trust. We work tirelessly to uphold the rule of law and hold ourselves accountable.”
Acts of violence, including sexual and gender-based violence by immigration agents, have received more attention during President Donald Trump’s second term. Though videos documenting use of force by ICE agents against women while on duty have flooded social media, comprehensive data tracking these incidents is basically nonexistent. Another key frustration for critics of the administration is the alleged history of violence committed by immigration agents.
In July, the Associated Press reported that ICE agent David Brouillette, who fatally shot 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero that month, had a documented history of domestic violence against two previous wives and his daughters.
His first ex-wife, Ashley Brouillette, told the Associated Press that in late 2025 — around the time David joined ICE — he left a three-minute voicemail in response to her filing for a restraining order against him. He also suggested that she and the other women and girls in her “bloodline” should die.
“And all of you should have your f——–g throats cut,” the voicemail said. “Yeah, you should. Am I threatening that I’m gonna do that? Nope. Nope. But do I think that you should have your f——-g throats cuts? Or should have had them cut? Yep.”
Federal law enforcement agents can be criminally prosecuted or sued in civil court for excessive violence while on the job. But in many instances, broader legal protections make it nearly impossible to win these cases. Organizations like the American Civil Liberties Union are working on legal avenues to hold the federal government accountable for alleged abuses. Law enforcement officers who face non-criminal disciplinary action or firings for misconduct can be rehired by other agencies, a pattern often referred to as “wandering officers.”
In its report, the Ohio Immigrant Alliance calls for the government to freeze ICE and CBP budgets and hiring, implement real accountability measures and vetting processes and to restrict the ability of immigration agents to carry weapons and wear disguises given that they  represent a civil rather than criminal sector of government.
“We need different paths for protection. We need a different system that doesn’t just protect agents,” Tramonte said in the conference call on Tuesday. “We need to make civil immigration enforcement truly civil, so that it won’t be an attractive job to people who want to run around carrying a gun.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio officials in state, Congress, need to step in after death of young Haitian student
description: This commentary discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is contemplating suicide, please call or text the National Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988. A promising, young Haitian immigrant in Ohio, fitted with an ICE ankle bracelet in July, threw himself in front of a semi on I-70 on Monday. Pierre Damas Bel, a […]
text:
Signs of support for Haitians in Springfield, Ohio after temporary protected status ended on July 27. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal).  This commentary discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is contemplating suicide, please call or text the National Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988.
A promising, young Haitian immigrant in Ohio, fitted with an ICE ankle bracelet in July, threw himself in front of a semi on I-70 on Monday. Pierre Damas Bel, a Springfield immigrant and new student at Wright State University, was pronounced dead at the scene. The 20-year-old, with big dreams of going to medical school, had been mocked by fellow students about the bulky ankle monitor he was forced to wear. On a July 30 Instagram post, Bel shared his pain.
“I came to this country to pursue my education. I didn’t come here to commit a crime or hurt anyone. Yet now I’m walking through the streets of the United States with a GPS monitor on my leg, carrying a feeling of shame and humiliation that I never imagined I would experience,” Bel wrote. “I came here to study, build my future and to live a better life, not to be treated like a criminal.”
Like Bel, dozens of Springfield’s Haitians have been fitted with ankle monitors or detained by ICE after their Temporary Protected Status was officially ended by the Trump administration on July 27. The extreme toll on the community— that had come to Springfield legally under TPS to work and raise families until it was safe to return to Haiti— was ironically the emphasis of the “Unshackle Springfield” rally held the day before Bel took his own life.
The protest at city hall drew hundreds of faith leaders from across Ohio and the country, immigration advocates, asylum-seeking Haitians, and supporters but notably no political leadership (local, state, federal) with an elevated platform to decry the dehumanization of terrified Ohio residents.
“They’re nowhere. They’re hiding. They’re afraid of the federal government. They’re afraid of masked federal agents coming into Springfield with guns, ramming their cars against people driving down Springfield roads,” said an exasperated Lynn Tramonte, executive director of the Ohio Immigration Alliance. “I mean, who’s protecting us? I can’t believe we’re in this situation where the only people standing up are the faith community and regular, ordinary people who are on the lookout for ICE and doing these patrols.”
“The city of Springfield went from embracing the Haitian population that helped it grow to abandoning them in their hour of need.”  
Tramonte also said “agents of the U.S. government are using our tax dollars to terrorize good people who deserve to live in a safe place” and city officials are accommodating and actively assisting ICE out of fear.
She argued that the people in power who could bring peace to Springfield would rather offer “thoughts and prayers” for better days ahead than lead through conviction. The inhumanity is happening in Ohio, and Springfield is offering city property to make it more efficient.
Mayor Rob Rue once urged Congress to find a permanent legal solution for hard-working, tax-paying Haitian TPS holders in Springfield, strongly rejected the dehumanizing lies spewed by JD Vance and Donald Trump about pet-eating Haitians, and blamed consecutive bomb threats in his town on that hateful rhetoric, demonstrating that he had a functioning moral compass before.
But now, Tramonte said he is not talking publicly, and his rote political statements about enforcing the law and deporting criminals who break it “is not what we’re talking about in Springfield.”
ICE is “enforcing paperwork violations” as if they were heinous crimes, with raids, detentions, deportations, and boxy electronic shackles, she said. City officials are missing in action on purpose.
So is Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, added the immigrant advocate. After being an ardent proponent “for Haitian-Ohioans settling into their new home,” Gov. DeWine seems to have turned the page, Tramonte said. He published an op-ed in the New York Times that tries to pass the buck to President Trump, naively calling on him to “lead an effort to reform our immigration system—to make changes that prioritize our workforce needs while respecting our history of welcoming people fleeing from oppression and humanitarian crises.”
Tramonte noted wryly that “no one has ever used the words ‘Trump’ and ‘welcoming people fleeing oppression’ in the same sentence for a reason.”
The lame-duck governor, concluded Tramonte, feels like he’s done all he can. Time to move on. The ball is in Trump’s court.
“But when it’s your family, you don’t give up, and I just want him to think about it as these (Haitian immigrants), this is your family. These are Ohioans. These are your people. Don’t give up.”
DeWine can pick up the phone today, she added, and tell U.S. Sens. Bernie Moreno and Jon Husted that Ohio needs them. He can tell Ohio law enforcement to focus on criminal activity not civil immigration enforcement.
“They should not help the Trump administration send Ohioans to a country where they will be killed,” Tramonte said. “That is not who we are and now is the time to lead.”
Maybe DeWine will surprise us, and maybe Ohio’s U.S. senators will grow a spine to save an Ohio city and the immigrant population that revitalized it. I wish somebody of either party would seize the moment with the moral courage it demands. Because, as Martin Luther King Jr. taught “there comes a time when silence is betrayal.”
A Haitian son who came to Springfield with his family legally and lost that status through no fault of his own, was bullied about the large, black tracking unit ICE slapped on the leg of the honor student who played soccer and wanted to be a doctor.
When Pierre Damas Bel died by apparent suicide this week, DeWine called it “a horrible, horrible tragedy.” It is also a grievous stain on the state that conceded defeat on his future without a fight.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: We are one rainstorm away from another public health crisis
description: New England’s infrastructure cannot handle more intense rainfall that overwhelms systems designed decades ago.
text:
When a 42-inch sewer main ruptured in Haverhill, Massachusetts, days before July Fourth weekend, millions of gallons of untreated sewage poured into the Merrimack River. 
Beaches closed. Shell fishing and oystering halted. Public health warnings dominated headlines. 
And unfortunately, it wasn’t until summer vacation plans were interrupted that residents paused to question how something this catastrophic could happen in 2026? The truth is, due to systemically underfunded, aging and inadequate clean water infrastructure, there’s an average of a dozen water main breaks every single day in New England. 
That should concern everyone.
The easy answer is to blame the city and the state for not doing enough or ignoring a problem. Not only is that untrue, but the real story behind the crisis is far more worrisome.
This wasn’t a failure of one pipe. It was the predictable outcome of a nation that has spent decades starving one of its most essential public services. One rainstorm was enough to shine a spotlight on a national crisis and expose the vulnerabilities of New England’s aging clean water systems.
New England’s infrastructure cannot handle today’s realities. Climate change is producing more intense rainfall that overwhelms systems designed decades ago. Population growth demands additional capacity before communities can build more housing. New environmental standards require advanced treatment technologies that cost millions to install and operate.

Mary Barry

Haverhill, Massachusetts is not a community that has ignored its infrastructure. In fact, it is one that has proactively been preparing for the future. Since 2016, the city has invested $50 million to make improvements, comply with federal guidelines and improve its infrastructure. The irony – city officials had already warned that this crisis was imminent. The 42-inch pipe that was overcome by the capacity of the torrential rainstorm on June 26 had already been identified by city officials as ‘insufficient’ and it is on the city’s five-year plan for expansion.
If Haverhill is vulnerable despite its notable investment, what does that say about the thousands of communities that simply cannot afford to keep pace? The answer should concern everyone.
Across America – particularly in New England, a region with some the oldest infrastructure, clean water professionals are fighting a losing battle against infrastructure built for another century. Pipes installed before World War II are expected to handle larger populations, more stringent environmental regulations, heavier rainfall fueled by climate change, and contaminants that engineers couldn’t have imagined when those systems were built.
America’s water infrastructure is in jeopardy because of insufficient funding. Federal investment has steadily declined since the 1970s, shifting the financial burden almost entirely onto local ratepayers. Communities are now expected to rebuild trillion-dollar systems through monthly sewer bills – a mathematical impossibility. In a 2022 report, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency estimates the nation needs more than $630 billion in clean water infrastructure investments over the next 20 years – an increase of 73 percent.
Water infrastructure isn’t glamorous, and when stacked against other priorities in Washington, it falls to the bottom of the list. Politicians don’t cut ribbons on buried pipes. Residents don’t think about clean water treatment plants until something breaks. When our systems work, rivers stay clean, neighborhoods don’t flood with sewage, beaches remain open, and drinking water continues to be safe. The invisibility of our water infrastructure has become one of the industry’s greatest challenges.
For decades, we’ve treated water infrastructure as something that can wait until next year’s budget. We’ve delayed maintenance, deferred replacement, and expected local utilities to solve a national infrastructure problem with local resources and creative problem-solving.
The lesson from Massachusetts isn’t that infrastructure failed. It is that, while we can’t predict where or when, the same public health crisis will happen in another community if we continue to neglect critically needed investments in water infrastructure.
Every million dollars invested in water infrastructure generates approximately $2.5 million in economic output. It creates jobs. Supports housing development. Protects businesses. Preserves tourism. Safeguards public health. And strengthens resilience against increasingly severe weather. This is not frivolous spending. It is one of the highest-return investments government can make.
Water is the foundation of every community, every economy, and every public health system in this country. Treating it as an afterthought is no longer an option.
Mary Barry is executive director of the New England Water Environment Association.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Education expert starting with the wrong question
description: Why are we so eager to scrutinize the spending decisions of districts that have significantly less money to spend in the first place?
text:
Based solely upon my reading of the Connecticut Mirror’s article on the last meeting of Gov. Lamont’s Blue Ribbon Commission on K-12 Education, one thing became abundantly clear: the governor’s hired expert is trying to reframe inequity as a management problem rather than a funding problem.
During the meeting, Marguerite Roza warned that some districts may “drag their feet” in responding to enrollment declines and could “get themselves in financial trouble.” She also argued that the real “villain” is declining birth rates and made suggestions ranging from mandated budget reserve requirements and mandatory budget projections to state intervention when districts face fiscal distress.
But before even entertaining stronger oversight, financial controls, or state takeovers, we should ask a more fundamental question: Why are we so eager to scrutinize the spending decisions of districts that have significantly less money to spend in the first place?
Connecticut is one of the wealthiest states in the country. It has been historically one of the most segregated by race and income and remains so today.
This results in wild fluctuations in spending.  For example, Bridgeport spends thousands of dollars less per student than Fairfield. Stamford spends substantially less per pupil than nearby Darien. Similar patterns exist when comparing Hartford and its suburbs, New Haven and neighboring towns, as well as Waterbury and much wealthier districts nearby.
These disparities are not occurring between states hundreds of miles apart. They exist right across the street.
Yet whenever districts have to advocate for more money,  the conversation changes. The blame shifts to local boards of education.
Imagine — one district gets thousands of dollars less per student than a district right across the street. Then concentrate higher levels of poverty in that district. Add much larger populations of English Language Learners. Add a pinch of newcomer students who require intensive language-acquisition supports.  Add a spoonful of higher concentrations of students requiring special education services.  Fold in half of pound of rising transportation, labor, and operational costs.  Let the mixture set in a cool dark place for 13 years and you have a recipe for disaster — one which our students must eat regardless of it’s nutritional value or the ability to keep from vomiting from the rot.
Then act surprised when the district experiences financial stress. Blame local leadership for the chef’s recipe that put education on life support.
That is not a serious analysis of educational finance and thankfully some on the commission pushed back directly.
Lisa Hammersley pushed back when Roza suggested that district comparisons reveal inefficiencies. She pointed out that districts serving different student populations cannot be meaningfully compared without accounting for factors such as multilingual learner populations and other student needs.
She was absolutely right. Districts serving immigrant students require family language specialists and additional instructional support. These services cost more money per pupil, not less. When accounting for spending one must look to need.
A district serving larger special education populations faces similarly significant obligations. Those costs are not inefficiency. They are the cost of serving students with severe needs.
What makes the discussion especially frustrating is that many urban districts have already done exactly what critics say they should do.
New Haven Mayor Justin Elicker reminded the commission that his district has already closed four schools and reduced staff. His argument was not that management doesn’t matter. His argument was that districts can make painful reductions year after year and still face structural financial problems when funding fails to keep pace with need.
That matters because districts cannot cut their way out of a funding gap forever. Bridgeport has cut all librarians. We cannot solve underfunding through efficiency. You certainly can’t compare outcomes while ignoring resource and demographic disparities.
Connecticut’s ECS formula foundation amount has been frozen since 2013.  Advocates such as myself have argued for years that education has lost hundreds of millions in today’s dollars while the state’s demands have continued to grow.
Connecticut continues to rely too heavily on property taxes to fund education. This after several lawsuits found this to be discrimination. Zip code remains one of the strongest indicators educational resources. And this brings us back to the central flaw in this premise.
Before lawmakers entertain intervention or accountability from others, they must first confront their own culpability, and be accountable for their shortcomings.
Of course districts should be accountable for spending, but the real question is whether accountability can be separated from equity. Districts cannot budget their way out of chronic disinvestment.
Connecticut’s real challenge is not getting districts to spend smarter.  It’s making certain that students are funded fairly regardless of where they live.
I feel this group of hardworking dedicated individuals were set up to fail as an election year ploy. I am sure after seeing the results of the last meeting that the commission will make some good recommendations.  My fear is that as soon as the election is over those recommendations will sit on a shelf gathering dust for the next 13 years.
Joseph Sokolovic is a resident of Bridgeport.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Hundreds of thousands of eligible kids in the US are waiting for childcare assistance
authors: Moriah Balingit and Lauren Coffey, Associated Press
description: Meygan Maloney poses for a portrait with her son Callum Wilson, 3, Friday, Aug. 28, 2026, at their home in Hartford City, Ind.
text:
INDIANAPOLIS — There’s the mother of two who needs a full-time job to keep up with the bills, but can’t afford full-time childcare. There’s the medical technician who stopped buying groceries and turned to food banks so she could pay for her infant’s care.  
There’s the baby who remained in foster care, even after his mother completed the steps to bring him home. She had found a job, as the state required, but couldn’t afford his childcare.  
It’s hardly news that childcare is expensive, straining the budget of even middle-class parents. But these families all qualify for government-funded childcare assistance, intended to drastically reduce the childcare bills of needy parents so they can work or go to school. Instead, Indiana’s program, which had run short on funds, waitlisted them.  
Hundreds of thousands of children were sitting on childcare assistance waitlists in 23 states and the District of Columbia as of this spring, according to an analysis by The Associated Press. In three more states, some eligible parents were turned away before they even applied because of enrollment freezes. 
Childcare assistance, funded by the federal government with help from states, is supposed to aid working parents who are low-income, homeless or caring for foster children. But waitlists have ballooned since 2023, when eight states had them, according to the AP analysis. Reporters collected waitlist and enrollment data from 47 states and the District of Columbia.  
Meygan Maloney looks through a toy with her son Callum Wilson, 3, Friday, Aug. 28, 2026, at their home in Hartford City, Ind.  Credit: AP Photo/Cara Penquite
Many of the waitlists first started after $28 billion in pandemic aid expired in the fall of 2024. The Republican-led Congress declined to extend the extra money. Some states have increased funding to try to fill the gap, but families’ need for childcare assistance has only grown, as they’ve faced mounting costs for food and gas. 
While eligible families sit on waitlists, untold numbers of adults are sidelined from education or the workforce because they can’t afford childcare. Those parents who remain in school or keep working make difficult tradeoffs. In interviews, parents described forgoing necessities, falling behind on bills or relying on acquaintances to watch their children. Unable to find viable childcare, some have resorted to bringing their children with them to work or class.  
For Meygan Maloney’s family in rural Indiana, waiting for childcare assistance means month after month of falling short financially. Maloney was working as a caregiver for disabled adults before she had her second child in 2023. Around the same time, the family took emergency custody of a close relative’s newborn daughter.  
The next three years were marked by deepening financial struggles. Maloney only received $300 a month to care for her foster daughter, and both toddlers were put on a waitlist when she applied for childcare vouchers for 2025. 
While the girl returned to her family in the fall, Maloney and her husband are still behind on bills. They recently refinanced their home, and her husband is working seven days a week as a tire technician and delivery driver. A local childcare provider gave her a steep discount, allowing her to leave her son four mornings a week to clean at a local hospital.  
“I felt useless as a stay-at-home mom. I felt like I wasn’t contributing to our household,” Maloney said, her voice cracking. “We’re trying to get out. But for us to get out, we need the assistance.”  
Foster parents left to pay for childcare in Indiana 
Indiana started its waitlist in December 2024, a few months after pandemic aid ran out and it became clear the state would struggle to support families already in the program. Until May of this year, it put virtually everyone who applied on the waitlist, including foster parents. By spring 2026, nearly 37,000 children were waiting for assistance. 
Maloney and other foster families feel like they were misled by the state, which had for many years paid for childcare for foster children. Malinda Cox, an Indianapolis mom who took in a newborn last year, said she was forced to dip into her family’s savings to pay for the baby boy’s childcare so she could return to work. At one point, she considered giving up custody of the boy because her family could not afford his childcare bill. 
In the meantime, the boy’s biological mother was completing the requirements she had to satisfy to take him home. She had taken parenting classes and gotten a job. But she could not afford daycare, and because the boy could not get childcare assistance, he had to remain with Cox. 
“We started to feel, like, guilty. He should be home with his mom, but (because of) this massive system upset, he’s not,” Cox said. 
Books, toys and a painting rest on a shelf in a corner with a sign reading “Callum’s Corner” in Meygan Maloney’s living room Friday, Aug. 28, 2026, at their home in Hartford City, Ind.  Credit: AP Photo/Cara Penquite
In April, Indiana Gov. Mike Braun, a Republican, announced the state would send $200 million in surplus funds to the state’s childcare assistance program, which would allow it to move roughly 8,000 children off the waitlist.  
Even before the recent growth in waitlists, federal funding for childcare assistance has always fallen short of providing for every needy family, only providing enough money to serve a fraction of those eligible. Experts say waitlists represent the tip of the iceberg, because many eligible families who need the help don’t know about the program or haven’t applied, daunted by tales of long waitlists. 
The origins of the funding shortfall are cultural, said Ruth Friedman, who headed the Office of Child Care under Democratic President Joe Biden. For decades, “childcare was the responsibility of the family,” she said. “The system is fundamentally broken, and if the government doesn’t help fix the system … it will not be affordable for families.” 
There are stark differences of opinion on whether the government should provide help — or how much. This year, 40 congressional Republicans called for “robust” funding of the federal program that underwrites childcare assistance. Instead, it received the same money as the year before. President Donald Trump said during his campaign that he could make childcare more affordable by using tariff revenue, but this spring he told a White House audience that paying for childcare should be up to states. 
“We’re fighting wars. We can’t take care of daycare. You got to let a state take care of daycare, and they should pay for it, too,” Trump told people gathered for an Easter luncheon.  
His administration has largely focused on allegations of fraud in the program, at one point halting funding to five Democratic-led states. After a lawsuit, a judge ordered Trump’s administration to restart the funding.  
Moms bring babies to college or work 
Without affordable childcare options, parents have resorted to bringing their children with them to work or school.  
In Minnesota, Deaira Gresham’s 1-year-old daughter Seaira has been on the waitlist for childcare assistance since birth, one of 9,000 children in her state awaiting aid as of this spring. Gresham, who works as an in-home health aide and takes a full load of classes at a chiropractor school, had some help with Seaira from her mother. But oftentimes, she was forced to take Seaira with her to class and to the homes of her clients. It took a toll — Gresham failed several classes juggling school and caring for a baby. 
This fall, she lucked out, getting a childcare grant for parenting students, allowing her to put Seaira in full-time care. 
“Parents are in desperate need,” Gresham said. “We need that break. We need to be able to go to school, go to work and know that our kids are in good hands.” 
It’s not just their work or college classes that parents worry about. Research has shown that high-quality childcare can boost a child’s social-emotional and academic development.  
Meygan Maloney plays with her son Callum Wilson, 3, Friday, Aug. 28, 2026, at their home in Hartford City, Ind.  Credit: AP Photo/Cara Penquite
Carmen Perez, who lives north of San Francisco, has applied for childcare help for all four of her children. Her eldest son never received it before aging out of the program. He struggled academically in ways that his sisters, who attended subsidized preschool, did not.  
Now her two-year-old son is on a waitlist. She fears he will face the same challenges as his older brother. “It makes me sick.” 
On a rainy May day in Indianapolis, Cox bundled up her foster son and delivered him to a social worker. She packed up her own car with the boy’s things — clothes, diapers and a small changing table. The boy’s biological mother still had not gotten childcare assistance, but Cox had negotiated a deal with a childcare provider to offer a massive discount. When even that was out of the mother’s reach, Cox agreed to pay half. 
She arrived at the boy’s new home to watch him reunite with his mother. She felt a mix of grief over parting with him and elation over seeing his delight with his mother.  
Three weeks later, the mother got notice: He had finally been approved for a voucher. 
____
