title: 3 dead and multiple injured, including police, in downtown Minneapolis shooting
description: Three people are dead and multiple, including three police officers, are injured after a shooting in an apartment building in downtown Minneapolis on Wednesday. Among the dead is the suspected shooter, from unknown causes, according to city officials. Minneapolis police Sgt. Garrett Parten said in a brief news conference that officers responded to reports of[...]
text:
A Minneapolis Police Department squad car. Photo by Tony Webster. Three people are dead and multiple, including three police officers, are injured after a shooting in an apartment building in downtown Minneapolis on Wednesday.
Among the dead is the suspected shooter, from unknown causes, according to city officials.
Minneapolis police Sgt. Garrett Parten said in a brief news conference that officers responded to reports of gunfire around 4:30 p.m. at 15 E. Grant St., a high-rise apartment building near Loring Park. Inside, police encountered victims and heard gunfire. They went to the upper floor of the building where they encountered “a haze” limiting their visibility.
Two officers were injured by gunfire and a third was injured by unspecified causes. Two of the officers were being treated at Hennepin Healthcare for injuries that were not life-threatening, and a third was in surgery. Multiple other people were also taken to the hospital, where one died.
“This is a tremendously tragic event,” Parten said. “Our thoughts and prayers are with the families and the loved ones of those who lost their lives.”
City officials are expected to provide more information later Wednesday.
For hours after the shooting, Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey urged people to avoid the area while the city received support from other law enforcement agencies including state patrol, the Hennepin County Sheriff’s Office and the Saint Paul Police Department.
Police have not offered a motive, but the shooting appears to have begun as a domestic violence incident.
A resident of the apartment complex, Shoreline Plaza, told the Star Tribune that the suspected shooter made earlier threats, saying earlier this week that he was going to shoot his ex-girlfriend and the two building property managers.
“He said, ‘I’m going to shoot people,’” resident Chris Miller told the paper.
Another bystander told FOX 9 the shooter grabbed her in the building and said he was going “kill my baby mama and you’re gonna witness it.”
“He had the look of doing what he was going to do in his face,” she said.
Gov. Tim Walz issued a statement thanking law enforcement for their work, saying “Minnesota is praying for our first responders.”
U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar and House Speaker Lisa Demuth, who are running for governor, also released statements praying for victims and thanking first responders.
The Minneapolis shooting comes less than two months after a man shot and killed three workers at an apartment building in St. Paul after arguing with apartment managers about his parking garage contract.
It was a chaotic scene outside the apartment building in Minneapolis on Wednesday with at least one police squad car significantly damaged, the back half ripped off from an apparent accident.
This is a developing story.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: New $20M loan recommended for Military Gallery to restart construction
description: North Dakota lawmakers on Wednesday advanced a funding compromise to restart construction on a stalled Military Gallery construction project, though several voiced concerns about increasing the state’s share of the cost. A joint House-Senate budget committee recommends a $20 million line of credit from the Bank of North Dakota and removing conditions attache[...]
text:
Dale Lennon, executive director of the State Historical Society of North Dakota Foundation, gives a tour of the unfinished Military Gallery to state lawmakers on Sept. 2, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota lawmakers on Wednesday advanced a funding compromise to restart construction on a stalled Military Gallery construction project, though several voiced concerns about increasing the state’s share of the cost.
A joint House-Senate budget committee recommends a $20 million line of credit from the Bank of North Dakota and removing conditions attached to $15 million in state funding already approved for the project on the Capitol grounds. The recommendation, approved in a 34-4 vote, will advance to the Senate for a vote on Thursday.
Rep. Glenn Bosch, R-Bismarck, said the line of credit included in Senate Bill 2407 is intended to serve as a construction loan to give fundraisers time to raise private donations. The goal is for the $20 million to be repaid with donations, keeping the cost of the $78 million project split evenly between state and private funding. If the loan is not repaid by March 2029, the bill directs the Legislature to evaluate whether to extend the repayment timeline or look for alternative funding sources.

More special session coverage

The solution followed several hours of testimony about the project’s development, the state of fundraising efforts and the impact of abruptly stopping construction. 
“We’re at the point where we decide whether we have a museum or we don’t have a museum,” said Rep. Jon Nelson, R-Rugby. “If we start construction again, I don’t want to see it stop at any point.”
Sen. Sean Cleary, R-Bismarck, one of the lawmakers who opposed the plan, said after the vote he is concerned taxpayers will end up being responsible for the new $20 million loan. 
“Frankly, the fundraising momentum hasn’t been good, so that was my main concern with that additional $20 million in the line of credit,” Cleary said.
Sen. Sean Cleary, R-Bismarck, speaks during a legislative committee meeting on Sept. 2, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
The bill would transfer oversight of the project to the Capitol Grounds Planning Commission, which includes four legislators in addition to other state officials. 
Sen. Jonathan Sickler, R-Grand Forks, who also opposed the bill, said he did not hear enough evidence there would be sufficient new oversight. 
“I think something that seems to have been a theme of this project is some rushed decision-making, and I think we’re being put in a position here where there is some potential rushed decision-making,” Sickler said. 
Sickler preferred an earlier version of the bill that did not include the $20 million line of credit and would have allowed the Legislature time to consider the problem in the 2027 legislative session. 
That version was abandoned after a short recess during the committee’s debate, in part because lawmakers want to ensure contractors and workers on the project have certainty moving forward. 
“I think we do need to take into account how we keep the project going without potentially having multiple starts and stops,” Bosch said. 
Military Gallery construction project stalls with fundraising lagging in North Dakota

The project has $5.3 million in unpaid bills through Sept 15, including $4.7 million to contractors, according to the Office of Management and Budget. 
The owner of a local contractor on the project, H.A. Thompson & Sons, said his company is owed nearly $1.9 million for unpaid work completed since April. He said he is worried about the impact a continued delay will have on his business.
“It will probably be very difficult to man the job. Every one of my employees has payments to make, and if they’re not getting 40 or not getting full time, they’re going to find another employer that isn’t on hold,” testified Mark Thompson, owner of H.A. Thompson & Sons. 
Patrick Pins of Mandan testified in support of action to resume construction on the project. 
“We have faith in you that you’ll make the right decision,” Pins said. 
Lucinda Johnson of Beulah said lawmakers’ spending of taxpayer money has gotten out of control and questioned why the gallery needs to be grandiose. 
“I am very appalled at the amount of money that is being put into a museum,” Johnson said. “It’s like you don’t care how much you spend on things.”
The military gallery project has been in development since 2022. 
The Legislature allocated $39 million of taxpayer money to the project during the 2025 legislative session. The state funding includes $15 million from an infrastructure fund that can be unlocked if the project receives nearly $12.8 in pledged private donations. 
That funding also included a $20 million Bank of North Dakota line of credit, with the intention that lawmakers would budget in 2027 to pay it back. 
Lawmakers were careful to stress that the new $20 million line of credit proposed during the special session should be viewed as a construction loan and the State Historical Society is expected to repay it with private donations. 
Construction began in August 2025. It was paused on July 3 when the project ran out of funds and the State Historical Society learned it could not legally obtain a construction loan to bridge the gap until additional donations were received.
Mark Thompson, owner of H.A. Thompson & Sons, speaks during a legislative committee meeting on Sept. 2, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
The project has $4.162 million in pledges and has collected about $800,000, Shannon Schweigert, managing partner of PACE Fundraising, said Wednesday. He has previously said most pledges are to be paid over five years. The project is a joint effort involving the State Historical Society, the North Dakota National Guard and their foundations.
Hogue pointed out that fundraisers have raised 11% of the goal in pledges and 2% of the goal in cash donations.
“That’s not a strong record,” Hogue said. “That does not inspire confidence in me.”
Schweigert has said one challenge for the fundraising campaign is that it overlapped with efforts to raise money for the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library. 
He told lawmakers he remains confident the fundraising goal can be met, and the only way they can fail is if they quit.
“I am asking for the opportunity to finish. We are fighters. We are problem-solvers,” Schweigert said.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jacob Orledge can be reached at jorledge@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Klobuchar, Demuth pledge to boost housing construction though neither commits to zoning reform
description: U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar and House Speaker Lisa Demuth, two candidates running for Minnesota governor in November, broadly agree that the state needs to build more homes to increase supply and slow rising costs. In-back-to-back interviews with KARE 11 on Wednesday at the Minnesota State Fair, Klobuchar and Demuth said addressing rising rents and mortgages […]
text:
Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth, R-Cold Spring, (left) and U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar (right) (Photos by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar and House Speaker Lisa Demuth, two candidates running for Minnesota governor in November, broadly agree that the state needs to build more homes to increase supply and slow rising costs.
In-back-to-back interviews with KARE 11 on Wednesday at the Minnesota State Fair, Klobuchar and Demuth said addressing rising rents and mortgages is a top concern and agreed that the state has too many regulations that are stymieing the construction of more homes.
Klobuchar said the red tape around construction was what was hurting housing supply, while Demuth took aim at labor policies like paid family leave implemented by the Democratic-Farmer-Labor trifecta a few years ago.
Klobuchar, the Democratic-Farmer-Labor nominee for governor, said she would work with the private sector to build 100,000 new housing units, cut construction regulations and streamline permitting processes and utilize federal funding to increase the supply of housing.
“If you want to take a job, you can’t if you don’t have a place to live. If you want to have kids, you can’t if you don’t have a place to put them, and that’s why I’m so devoted to this issue,” Klobuchar said, pointing to her affordable housing plan.
Demuth, the Republican nominee, said she would get rid of government mandates that are driving up costs for businesses, which are then passing those additional costs onto the price of homes. But she was light on specifics, pointing vaguely to “energy codes,” minimum sick leave and paid family leave.
“When you look at the energy codes and the energy things that have pushed up the cost of housing — yet it’s done just as safe, but less expensive in our bordering states — we really need to reimagine that. We want to take care of our environment. We want to make sure that energy is there and available, but we also have to bring down the cost and the regulation,” Demuth said.
The House speaker has not yet released an affordable housing plan though she said she intends to.
Klobuchar released an affordable housing plan in June which includes making permanent the state housing tax credit; launching a low-interest revolving loan fund for rural developers; protecting manufactured home owners from exploitative practices by corporate park owners; and banning price-fixing algorithms, which companies use to coordinate rents.
Both Klobuchar and Demuth were noncommittal about forcing local governments to allow more density by overriding local zoning control, a contentious issue at the Minnesota Legislature. A bipartisan coalition of housing advocates for years has sought changes to restrictive local zoning codes at the Legislature, but cities have fiercely pushed back on the legislation.
Klobuchar said she supports “many elements” of the legislation, but didn’t say whether she would support the bill that stalled earlier this year in the Legislature.
Demuth praised the bipartisan group of legislators, housing advocates and local government officials who were able to make progress on the legislation this year. She said every community is different and she’s heard that cities are worried about increasing the strain on water and sewer infrastructure if zoning reforms are implemented. The bill never came up for a vote in the Legislature earlier this year.
Klobuchar said she believes that more people are wanting to move to the state after witnessing Minnesotans’ resistance to the incursion of thousands of immigration agents earlier this year during Operation Metro Surge, which she called “one of the top five civil rights moments of the century.” She said this will be a good thing for Minnesota’s housing supply.
“We stood up for people. We stood up for strangers, and I believe, in the end, when you’re a beacon like that, that makes people want to move to your state. That makes them want to start businesses here. All of that is tied in with housing,” Klobuchar said.
Demuth said the state in recent years has put many millions into preventing homelessness and affordable housing but doesn’t have the increased number of housing units to show for it. She said she wants to analyze how many homes are built in a certain time period to make sure taxpayer dollars are being used appropriately.
“The way we bring that affordability back in check is less regulation, less mandates put on by the state across all sectors that are really hitting families really hard,” Demuth said.
The KARE 11 interview was put on in partnership with Family Housing Fund, Greater Minnesota Housing Fund and Housing First Minnesota.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Early detection is the most practical way to improve cancer outcomes in Alaska
description: Every August, Alaskans gather in Palmer for the State Fair. They come for the exhibits, the food, and the chance to see neighbors from across the state. On Thursday, Aug. 27, a good number of them also came for something less festive and more useful: cancer screening. That day was the second annual Cancer Screening […]
text:
A participant in the second annual Cancer Screening Day at the Alaska State Fair on Aug. 27, 2026 gets a blood draw for a prostate cancer screening. (Photo courtesy of the Aurora Integrated Oncology Foundation)Every August, Alaskans gather in Palmer for the State Fair. They come for the exhibits, the food, and the chance to see neighbors from across the state. On Thursday, Aug. 27, a good number of them also came for something less festive and more useful: cancer screening.
That day was the second annual Cancer Screening Day at the Alaska State Fair, organized by Aurora Integrated Oncology Foundation and a group of clinical and community partners. 
In six hours, 443 people received screenings or related preventive services. Staff and partners recorded 1,922 community engagements — conversations with fairgoers about prevention, risk, and how to get care. The weather cooperated. The lines moved. People left with information they did not have when they arrived.
The numbers are straightforward. Partners provided 181 skin cancer screenings, 146 PSA blood draws for prostate cancer, 52 mammograms, 22 oral cancer screenings, and two HPV vaccinations. In addition, 40 people began the process for at-home colorectal screening. Those are not program slogans. They are individual Alaskans who chose to do something about their health in a place they were already going.
Cancer is the leading cause of death in Alaska. It accounts for about one in five deaths in the state. Breast, prostate, lung, and colorectal cancers make up roughly half of new diagnoses. For several of those cancers, screening finds disease earlier, when treatment is more effective and less burdensome. That is not a slogan. It is how medical evidence works.
Alaska makes this harder than it should be. Distance, weather, work schedules, insurance status, and a thin health workforce all get in the way of routine preventive care. A substantial share of women who should be current on mammograms are not. Colorectal screening still lags recommended levels. Late-stage diagnosis remains too common, and late-stage care is harder on patients, families, employers, and the health system. Anyone who has worked on infrastructure or economic development will recognize the pattern. Deferred maintenance is expensive. The same is true of deferred screening.
That is why the Foundation exists. Aurora Integrated Oncology Foundation is a nonprofit that operates radiation oncology centers in Anchorage, the Mat-Su Valley, the Kenai Peninsula, and Juneau. Our purpose is to improve the quality of, and access to, cancer prevention, treatment, and supportive care for Alaskans — regardless of insurance status. Treatment is essential. So is finding disease before it requires the most intensive treatment. Screening Day is one way we put prevention in front of people instead of waiting for them to navigate an appointment they may never make.
We did not do this alone. The Alaska State Fair gave us a setting where thousands of Alaskans already gather, and the Fair staff were steady hosts. Clinical partners brought the equipment, the clinicians, and the follow-up capacity. Our team handled the unglamorous work that makes a public event function: scheduling, supplies, patient flow, and problem-solving when something did not go as planned. Events of this kind succeed or fail on logistics. I am proud of the efforts of our staff and community partners. It was a resounding success.
Those partners include: Alaska Breast & Cervical Health Check, Alaska Health Fair, Alaska Men’s Run, American Cancer Society, American Lung Association, Anchorage Neighborhood Health, ANTHC, Breast Cancer Detection Center, Let Every Women Know, Connect Mat-Su, Mat-Su Public Health, Providence Imaging Center, Abbott Cancer Diagnostics, Mat-Su Dermatology, Palmer Fire & Rescue all alongside Aurora Integrated Oncology Foundation.  
I have spent most of my working life on questions of investment and return in this state — in energy, infrastructure, workforce, and civic institutions. Health belongs on that same ledger. A screened population is a more productive population. Early treatment keeps people at work and at home. It reduces the travel and lodging burden that so often accompanies a late diagnosis in Alaska. It is also simply the responsible thing to do.
Screening Day will not, by itself, change statewide cancer statistics. One afternoon at the Fair is not a substitute for a primary-care relationship or a regular mammogram schedule. It is a demonstration that if you remove friction — cost, travel, time, and uncertainty — Alaskans will take the test. The task now is to keep removing that friction the other 364 days of the year.
If you were among the people who stopped between Raven Hall and the farm exhibits last Thursday, thank you. If you were not, the invitation still stands. Talk with your clinician about the screenings appropriate for your age and risk. Do not wait for a fairgrounds booth to appear. And if you are in a position to support screening access in your community — as an employer, a clinic, a borough, or a neighbor — do that. Early detection is not complicated. It is work. Alaska is capable of the work.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Lacking federal funds, local groups press to continue legal aid for immigrant children
description: The Trump administration's decision to pull funding for a network of nonprofits that represent children who crossed the border without parents or legal papers has left immigrant and legal aid groups in Maryland scrambling to continue providing service.
text:
A migrant child sits in the back of a border patrol vehicle after being apprehended near Ruby, Arizona, in June 2024. The Trump administration's decision to cancel a contract for legal representation for unaccompanied immigrant minors has left local legal aid groups scrambling. (Photo by Brandon Bell/Getty Images)A legal motion filed in late August, begins this way:
“On the morning of August 6, 2026, in an immigration court in Los Angeles, an unaccompanied child appeared before an immigration judge – facing a Department of Homeland Security attorney and the possibility of removal. The child had no legal representation and appeared on their own.”
This is no anomaly.
That child is one of thousands of unaccompanied immigrant children across the country fighting for the legal services they are guaranteed by law, along with the right to shelter, healthcare, education and screening for human trafficking.
But the Trump administration has pulled funding to a nationwide network of nonprofits that represent children who have crossed the border without parents or legal papers. That has left groups like the Amica Center, based in Baltimore and Washington, to try to continue representing children without funding.
“No child should be forced to face immigration court alone,” said Michael Lukens, the executive director of the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, which was a party to the August court filing in California. “Yet that is exactly what the Trump administration is trying to do. Every day without legal representation puts unaccompanied immigrant children at greater risk.”
Scott Bassett, a managing attorney of Amica’s Children’s Program, said its staff of lawyers, paralegals and social service professionals is currently monitoring more than 700 unaccompanied immigrant child cases.
Legal aid for immigrant kids in question after Trump administration pulls contract

While the Amica Center has been able to continue providing services, smaller nonprofits have had to cut back assistance or close altogether. Other groups, like the Chacón Center for Immigration Justice at the University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law, are trying to build net networks to reach unaccompanied minors.
But advocates say they are up against an immigration system that is not working in the child’s best interest and badly in need of reform.
“Personally, I think that it needs to come from Congress,” said Chacón Center Program Director Francisco Flores. “At the bare minimum, representation, specifically for children, if someone has an attorney, it gives them a better fighting chance.”
Federal government moves to end funding
Unaccompanied immigrant children are not held by the Department of Homeland Security but are placed in the custody of the Department of Health and Human Services, which is supposed to provide for their care and legal representation if there is no adult relative who can take them in.
But in December, HHS stopped paying the Acacia Center for Justice – which distributed funding to a network of some 100 providers, including Amica – in a dispute over access to sensitive client data. “We told them that ethically we could not provide it to them,” Bassett said. “They claimed that was non-performance and stopped paying us.”
On July 31, HHS allowed the contract with the Acacia Center to expire without renewal, leaving no plan for how these children would continue to receive representation.
HHS designated the nonprofit U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants to temporarily take charge. But in the August court filing, Amica and three other legal service providers said USCRI attorneys frequently fail to show up at hearings “in any capacity, arriving late or leaving early, and remaining silent at moments when friend of-court services would have been valuable,” as in the California case.
The filing asked the U.S. District Court for Northern California to intervene to enforce the law.
Officials with HHS did not respond to requests for comment.
Maryland Hispanic student enrollment declines amid immigration fears

Expediting cases, compromises due process
Meanwhile, Bassett said, immigration judges have been under pressure to expedite cases, and tighten up any extensions, moves he says compromise the due process rights of unaccompanied minors.
“The immigration removal proceedings are just outrunning the few years you’d have to otherwise wait for access,” or the legal journey to a green card. He said advocates “are seeing a lot of kids with approved Special Immigrant Juvenile Status or pending status” who are being pressured by judges to take voluntary departure.
The Chacón Center trains future lawyers in its clinics, and represents immigrant clients in court. Faced with the lack of representation for unaccompanied minors, center Director Maureen Sweeney says one new initiative seeks to ensure that immigrant children in foster care are properly screened.
“We want to work with the state and the counties and the lawyers who represent these children to make sure that the immigration piece is being taken care of, and part of that will also be recruiting pro bono attorneys who would be willing to take on those cases and support these kids,” she said. “It’s a vulnerable group, but [the project] feels doable.”
It is not known how many of the 3,800 abused, neglected or abandoned children and teens in Maryland’s foster care system are also unaccompanied immigrants, but Flores said the center will seek to identify them.
Building a network
“Right now, we are focusing on creating this referral [and] training network, seeing what is already happening, that [attorneys] have everything they need to take on one of these cases using connections we have developed over the years with the pro bono, the nonprofit and the private bar,” Flores said. “We want to make sure that no child is ever overlooked or that they always have access to representation.”
For Flores, the mission is personal. Born in the United States to Salvadoran immigrants, he said he turned to a career in immigration law after witnessing the struggles his parents and his community faced to gain legal status.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
For the last 13 years he has worked as an advocate for immigrant children, until recently as a senior attorney at the Amica Center.
“It makes me feel that if I can help them, give them the opportunity that I had, then I know that they are going to take that chance, run with it and do amazing, great things for this country,” he said.
A ray of hope
As for that child described in the August filing, it said that, “Without legal advice and almost certainly unaware of their rights – to the extent any children could understand the concept of legal rights – the child requested voluntary departure from the United States.”
“An attorney from the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants was in the court room … and said nothing as this child asked to waive all rights to seek asylum, likely not knowing whether the child qualified for asylum, Special Immigrant Juvenile Status, or any other relief,” the court document said.
But another lawyer with experience with unaccompanied minors, witnessed the scene and spoke up as friend-of-the-court.  He asked the judge to continue the case to give the child a chance to consult an attorney.
The judge granted the request.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho Supreme Court to weigh if ballot language on abortion rights initiative could mislead voters
description: As the deadline to print ballots looms, the Idaho Supreme Court will decide whether state officials’ descriptions of the effects of voting for or against a proposed abortion rights initiative will appear on ballots in November.  The justices questioned the state officials’ attorneys and the legal challengers Wednesday about how best to ensure voters are […]
text:
The exterior of the Idaho Supreme Court building in Boise as seen on Jan. 14, 2026. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)As the deadline to print ballots looms, the Idaho Supreme Court will decide whether state officials’ descriptions of the effects of voting for or against a proposed abortion rights initiative will appear on ballots in November. 
The justices questioned the state officials’ attorneys and the legal challengers Wednesday about how best to ensure voters are informed about the ballot measure that would repeal Idaho’s abortion bans if passed. 
Idaho Secretary of State candidate Phil McGrane talks with a supporter during the Idaho Republican Party primary celebration on May 17, 2022. (Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun)
Attorneys for supporters of the initiative argued before the court Wednesday that the “yes” and “no” effect statements drafted by Republicans Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador and Secretary of State Phil McGrane were misleading and confusing. 
Attorneys for Labrador and McGrane said the two elected officials did their due diligence to comply with the state law requiring “clear and concise” ballot statements to tell voters what effect their votes would have. 
The proposed, voter-led ballot initiative would legalize abortion until fetal viability or in cases of emergency, and enumerate reproductive rights, including access to contraception and IVF, and rights to privacy in medical decision-making. 
 What does the draft ballot language say? 

The effect statements, as drafted by state officials, are: 
“A YES vote would create reproductive rights, including a right to abortion before a fetus’s ability to survive and after a fetus’s ability to survive in cases of a medical emergency, and provide liability protections for healthcare providers.”
“A NO vote would make no change to Idaho’s current law, which protects the life of the unborn while allowing abortion in reported cases of rape or incest, or when necessary to protect the life of the mother.”
Melanie Folwell, lead organizer for the ballot initiative in Idaho to restore abortion access, speaks to supporters at the Idaho Capitol in July. (Photo by Kelcie Moseley-Morris/Stateline)
Idahoans United for Women and Families, the nonprofit organization that drafted the initiative — now called Proposition 1 — filed the lawsuit challenging the ballot language on Aug. 27, Stateline reported. The lawsuit argues the proposed language is confusing, especially the description of the existing abortion ban, which the attorneys say is incomplete. 
The deadline for the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office to mail printed ballots and voter information pamphlets is Sept. 18 and Sept. 25, respectively, according to court filings. 
“The top priority is making sure that there is clear language on the ballot, that is what we have fought for since the beginning,” Melanie Folwell, lead organizer for the initiative proponents Idahoans United, told the Idaho Capital Sun following the hearing. 
Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador addresses attendees during the Idaho National Guard’s Cyber Discovery 2026 conference at the state’s Chinden campus in Boise on June 9, 2026. (Photo by Sgt. Rusty Rehl/U.S. Army National Guard)
Labrador in a statement said the statements followed the requirements of the law.
“Our duty under the law is straightforward: to provide a clear and concise statement of the effect of a vote on an initiative,” Labrador said in an emailed statement. “We do not tell Idahoans how to vote; we tell them what their vote will do. The Yes statement reflects the sponsors’ own initiative language, and the No statement reflects Idaho law as it stands today. The sponsors are entitled to advocate for their initiative, but they are not entitled to dictate the official ballot language. Idaho voters deserve a fair description of both choices so they can decide for themselves. That is what we provided.”
 Justices question if the statements are complete without noting existing abortion penalties 

Supreme court justices at Wednesday’s hearing questioned whether the “no” statement fully explained the effect when it omitted the penalties in Idaho’s abortion ban. 
Doctors who perform abortions in Idaho face felony charges with prison time and revocation or suspension of their medical license, unless the procedure is performed to prevent the death of the mother or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester if a police report has been filed.
“How does not telling a voter a ‘no’ vote would leave felonies and licensing discipline in play, how does that inform them what the effect of a ‘no’ vote is?” Justice Colleen Zahn asked the attorney representing McGrane. 
Yvonne Dunbar, Idaho attorney general’s office chief counsel, said McGrane and Labrador took a “balanced approach to try and get as much information” into a concise statement as they could. 
James Craig, a division chief in the attorney general’s office, said it would be “impossible” to summarize all of Idaho’s laws dealing with abortion into a clear and concise statement. 
“My guess is that there are well over a dozen laws, perhaps dozens of laws, affecting abortion,” Craig said. 
He said the discretion for how to summarize the effect lies with two elected constitutional officers, the attorney general and secretary of state, who are members of the executive branch. He argued the court lacks authority to override their judgement. 
He argued that the yes and no statements when read together offer a complete picture. 
“You have to look at them together,” Craig said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 What can the court do?  

Idahoans United’s attorney Jennifer Aiko, partner at the Boise law firm Holland & Hart, proposed the statements say, “A NO vote would make no change to Idaho’s current law” and “A YES vote means Proposition One will become state law.”
However, Zahn questioned Aiko on if the court had the authority to choose the statements, and can only determine whether the statements “substantially comply” with the requirements under the law. 
Aiko agreed the court couldn’t require certain language, but said they believe their proposed statements would be in compliance. 
Justices questioned Aiko on whether such simple statements would fulfill the requirements of the law, which was created after the 2002 to address voter confusion over a ballot measure that included a double negative, making it unclear what a yes or no vote would do. 
“What is the purpose of the short statement if all it says is a vote ‘yes’ means it passes and a vote ‘no’ means it fails? It seems to be just a waste of time,” said Justice Gregory Moeller 
Aiko argued there was sufficient information in the ballot titles, which are the explanations of what the initiative would do that appear on the ballot. The supporters of the initiative in April 2025 filed a separate lawsuit challenging the proposed ballot titles, and the Idaho Supreme Court at the time unanimously ruled that Labrador’s office must revise the short ballot title. 
 Aiko said the language on the ballot after the 2025 decision would be appropriate to use if the court decided some further description would be required. 
Chief Justice G. Richard Bevan said the justices would take the case under consideration and issue a ruling later.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Patagonia, environmental groups revive old legal fights against new cuts to Utah monuments
description: Opponents of Trump’s sharp downsizing of two Utah national monuments are re-upping their argument that he didn’t have the authority.
text:
The Bears Ears buttes, namesake of the Bears Ears National Monument, are pictured on Friday, Sept. 19, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Opponents of President Donald Trump’s decision to sharply downsize two Utah national monuments in July are re-upping their argument that he didn’t have the authority to do so.
Retailer Patagonia, environmental groups and tribal organizations waged legal battles against Trump in 2017 after he ordered prior reductions of Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante national monuments. The cases went dormant when former President Joe Biden restored the boundaries in 2021. 
Now that the president has redrawn the boundaries even smaller than he did almost a decade ago, the environmental groups said Wednesday they requested permission to file two updated lawsuits in federal court in Washington, D.C. Retailer Patagonia also filed a new suit over the Bears Ears reductions.
‘Zero consultation’: Tribal reps say they were left out of monument reduction decisions 

The new court filings say Trump’s orders leave the landscapes open to hard rock mining and oil, gas and coal leases. And they note mining claims have been filed in recent weeks on lands cut out of the new boundaries. 
Steve Bloch, legal director at the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, called the reductions unlawful and said in a prepared statement that “we intend to make sure Trump doesn’t have the final word over the fate of these treasured landscapes.”
White House spokeswoman Taylor Rodgers did not directly respond to the allegations in a statement to Utah News Dispatch, but focused on actions by Trump’s Democratic predecessors.
“The Obama and Biden administrations abused the Antiquities Act to lock up millions of acres of Utah’s public lands,” Rodgers said in a prepared statement. She went on to say that Trump “rightsized the Bears Ears National Monument to allow for common sense land use in these areas.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In his first term in the White House, Trump slashed Bears Ears from roughly 1.35 million acres to roughly 228,000 acres, and Grand Staircase-Escalante from about 1.87 million acres to roughly 1 million acres. In the more dramatic cuts in July, he cut Bears Ears to about 121,000 acres and Grand Staircase-Escalante to about 182,000 acres.
Other presidents have whittled down boundaries. In the biggest change prior to 2017, President Woodrow Wilson shrunk Mount Olympus National Monument in Washington state by about half in 1915, cutting out more than 313,000 acres. 
Conservationists say when Congress approved the Federal Land Policy and Management Act in 1976, it required congressional review for cuts of more than 5,000 acres. The law didn’t change the Antiquities Act of 1906, which allows presidents to proclaim national monuments but doesn’t say anything about canceling or shrinking them. 
The view from a primitive road in Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument (U.S. Bureau of Land Management).
The U.S. Department of Justice sees it differently. In a legal opinion last year, the department concluded a president who finds sites “never were or no longer are deserving of the Act’s protections” can in fact eliminate the land from a national monument.  
State leaders have long condemned the Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante as unnecessarily big and restrictive. Utah’s Republican governor, House speaker and congressional delegation joined Trump in the Oval Office as signed the orders. 
Former President Bill Clinton designated Grand Staircase-Escalante in 1996. Bears Ears, established by then President Barack Obama in 2016, was the first monument in the nation created at the urging of Native American tribes to whom the land is sacred. 
It’s been managed jointly by the U.S. government and the Bears Ears Commission made up of five tribal nations: the Hopi Tribe, Navajo Nation, Ute Mountain Ute Tribe, Zuni Tribe and Ute Indian Tribe. But Trump’s order on Bears Ears is ending that partnership, terminating the federal agencies’ agreement with the commission.
The environmental groups want the courts to order the monuments restored to full size and void any mining claims or mineral leases that were based on Trump’s proclamations in 2017 and 2021.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Cassandra Wilson, Jackson native who earned international acclaim as a jazz singer, dies at 70
description: Cassandra Wilson performs at the JVC Jazz Festival in Newport, R.I., on Aug. 10, 2003.
text:
Tributes are pouring in for Grammy-winning jazz singer, songwriter and producer Cassandra Wilson of Jackson, whose “sultry, honey-toned voice” brought her international fame. She died Tuesday at age 70.
Singer Cassandra Wilson attends the 48th Annual Songwriters Hall of Fame Induction and Awards Gala at the New York Marriott Marquis Hotel on Thursday, June 15, 2017, in New York.  Credit: Evan Agostini/Invision/AP
“Cassandra Wilson transitioned peacefully at home, surrounded by family, close friends and her manager,” the longtime manager, Robert Torre, said in a statement published by WGBO. “Her family and close friends respectfully ask for privacy during this difficult time as they grieve her loss.”
Wilson, who grew up as Cassandra Fowlkes, graduated from Jackson’s Murrah High School. 
During her career, she was known for a style that infused her jazz performances with influences of country, folk, blues and pop.
Grammy-winning singer/songwriter Dee Dee Bridgewater shared her condolences, writing on social media: “Cassandra was unique in every way, blessed with a sultry, honey-toned voice. I will miss our occasional phone conversations and rare times in the same space.”
Questlove, the Grammy-winning drummer and producer who leads The Roots, posted online: “Cassandra/The Siren of Sirens/That Voice, That GiftDamn.”
Malcolm White, a longtime Jackson music promoter who once served as director of the Mississippi Arts Commission, was a friend of Wilson’s. He told Mississippi Today she will be remembered as an international icon.
“Her records, performances, her awards will stand the test of time as a giant in the American music field of jazz,” White said.
He noted that even after Wilson found success, she stayed connected to the jazz scene in Jackson.
“I always thought it was cool that she came back and was a part of her home community,” White said. “She could have lived anywhere, you know.”
Jackson Mayor John Horhn said in a statement: “Jackson has lost an extraordinary native daughter, and the world has lost a singular musical voice.”
Horhn added, “She built a remarkable career rooted in jazz, blues, gospel, folk and the many traditions that shape our state’s musical identity. Her work had rare depth of character and a profound understanding of how music moves people, tells stories and connects generations. Through every performance and recording, she carried forward the legacy of jazz, blues and gospel.”
Fellow Grammy-winning musician Jon Batiste, former band leader of “The Late Show with Stephen Colbert,” posted a clip on social media of himself interviewing Wilson on a Brazilian talk show. The caption reflected on the time he spent touring with her as a young musician. 
“She sounded like the south,” he wrote. “Her Mississippi heritage was always present in everything no matter how expansive her artistry evolved.”
Terence Blanchard, left, and Cassandra Wilson perform at the MusiCares Person of the Year tribute honoring Neil Diamond on Friday, Feb. 6, 2009, in Los Angeles.  Credit: AP Photo/Matt Sayles
Born in December 1955, she was inspired by her parents’ love of music. Her father, Herman B. Fowlkes, was a music teacher, guitarist and bassist who loved jazz, while her mother, Mary Fowlkes, was a teacher who loved Motown. Cassandra began taking classical lessons at a young age. By age 6 she began playing piano, and at 12 she started working as a vocalist.
Singer Cassandra Wilson performs at the 48th Annual Songwriters Hall of Fame Induction and Awards Gala at the New York Marriott Marquis Hotel on Thursday, June 15, 2017, in New York.  Credit: Evan Agostini/Invision/AP
She attended Millsaps College and Jackson State University, earning a degree in mass communications. While in college, she sang with multiple cover bands in Jackson’s local music scene. Alvin Fielder, drummer and founding member of the Black Arts Music Society, encouraged her to sing modern jazz.
She moved to New Orleans in 1981 and performed jazz with Earl Turbington and Ellis Marsalis. She moved to New York City in 1982, where she became a founding member of the jazz collective M-Base. She also signed with an independent German record label in 1986, where she released her first album.
In 1992, she signed with Blue Note Records. She released several albums, including the Grammy-winning albums “New Moon Daughter” in 1997 and “Loverly” in 2009.
Wilson was named Female Jazz Vocalist of the year by Downbeat magazine in 1995-96, received the Miles Davis Prize from the Festival International de Jazz de Montreal in 1999 and was dubbed “America’s best singer” by Time Magazine in 2001.
She received the Mississippi Governor’s Award for Artistic Excellence in Music in 2009 and was added to the Mississippi Blues Trail in 2010. In 2022, she was named a jazz master by the National Endowment for the Arts.
Jazz musician Cassandra Wilson poses during an interview in Cologne, Germany on Sept. 25, 2003. Credit: AP Photo/Hermann J. Knippertz

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi pediatricians recommend vaccines against flu, COVID and RSV this fall
description: A certified medical assistant holds a syringe for a flu vaccine at a clinic in Seattle, on Wednesday, Sept. 10, 2025.
text:
Mississippi pediatricians are backing fall vaccination recommendations from a coalition of leading medical groups as the nation’s traditional federal vaccine advisory system remains in limbo. 
Historically, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and its vaccine advisory committee have issued guidance on seasonal immunization. But the vaccine advisory committee is no longer functioning after a federal judge ruled in March that Health Secretary Robert Kennedy Jr. unlawfully altered vaccine policy and improperly replaced all members of the committee.
In August, against advice from medical organizations, President Donald Trump signed an executive order advocating for spacing out childhood measles, mumps and rubella vaccines into three separate visits, and calling on the nation’s health department to present a plan offering this regimen to families.
In the vaccine advisory group’s absence, several major U.S. medical associations released guidance on flu season vaccine recommendations Wednesday. Mississippi pediatricians have voiced support of the coalition’s efforts. 
“The bottom line is we recommend that all children and adults ages 6 months and up get their fall flu vaccine,” said Dr. Anita Henderson, a Hattiesburg pediatrician and former president of the Mississippi chapter for the American Academy of Pediatrics. “And then for the pediatric population in particular, it’s really important to protect your baby against RSV,” or respiratory syncytial virus. 
Henderson said the lack of national leadership is “100% contributing to the problem” of declining childhood vaccination rates across the country. Only 10 states have kindergarten vaccination rates above 95%, the threshold needed to prevent outbreaks of measles, a highly contagious and life-threatening virus. Mississippi is one of those states, but vaccination rates in the state fell nearly half a percentage point during the 2025-26 school year. 
Henderson’s message to parents is to seek the advice of their physicians and tune out the noise of influencers on social media taking advantage of an increasingly politicized issue. 
“Nothing has changed as far as what your pediatrician is recommending,” Henderson said. “We will continue to follow evidence-based medicine and science. We are pediatricians, we’re not politicians.”
Recommendations from four major medical associations – American Academy of Family Physicians, American Academy of Pediatrics, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the Infectious Diseases Society of America – include:

Annual flu vaccines for adults and children 6 months and older; 


One-time RSV antibody shots for newborns, as well as RSV vaccines for adults 75 and older and those who are immunocompromised; 


Annual Covid-19 vaccines for adults 19 and older, especially those who are at an increased risk for severe disease. 

Before the Trump administration’s overhaul of the CDC and federal childhood vaccine policies, Mississippi’s childhood vaccine rates have been declining for the past three years. In 2023, the state started granting religious exemptions for school vaccine requirements. 
Overall, Mississippi’s rates are still high compared to the rest of the nation. But eight counties have fallen below a measles vaccine coverage rate of 95% among kindergartners. Those counties include Franklin, George, Jackson, Lincoln, Pontotoc, Tate, Tishomingo and Webster. 
This fall, doctors say parents should pay attention to RSV, a leading cause of infant hospitalizations that can cause long-term consequences, such as lung damage and asthma. Additionally, severe cases of the flu can cause long-term consequences, including organ damage and heightened risk of heart attacks and strokes. People often forget how dangerous the flu can be, said Dr. Patricia Tibbs, president of the Mississippi chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics. 
Despite what she calls an uphill battle to keep vaccine rates up, Tibbs said it’s “been so awesome to watch” the way that medical organizations have banded together so quickly to fill a void left by more than a year of disruptions to federal infrastructure. She hopes that the groups’ recommendations hold the same weight for parents that recommendations from the CDC historically have.
“Let us not go back to the dark ages when these vaccine-preventable illnesses were killing children,” Tibbs said.

title: Trump's newest order on birthright citizenship blocked in federal court
text: A federal judge in Maryland Wednesday blocked President Donald Trump’s second attempt to redefine birthright citizenship. In a preliminary injunction, U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman barred the Trump administration from carrying out the president's executive order that would deny citizenship to babies born in the United States to parents deemed part of a designated terrorist organization or to parents who purposefully came to the U.S. to gain citizenship in what critics call “birth tourism.” The executive order also aimed to deny citizenship to children born to foreign diplomatic staff and children born in U.S. territories where Congress has not passed a law granting citizenship, which is only American Samoa.In her order, Boardman said this summer's Supreme Court ruling affirmed the country’s long understanding that babies born on U.S. soil were guaranteed American citizenship. “The 2026 Executive Order is almost certainly unconstitutional as applied to the certified class for the simple reason that the Supreme Court in Barbara already decided that the children in the class are citizens at birth,” she wrote, referring to the earlier case. “This Court must, once again, preliminarily enjoin enforcement of the President’s most recent attempt to strip the right to citizenship from them.”The White House did not immediately respond to States Newsroom's request for comment.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: FEMA to reimburse eight South Dakota counties, three tribes for storm-related infrastructure fixes
description: The federal government will reimburse up to 75% of public infrastructure repair costs from storms that hit eight South Dakota counties and two Native American reservations in late June and early July, the Federal Emergency Management Agency announced Wednesday. The Oglala Sioux Tribe, meanwhile, is in line for the same level of reimbursements for repairs […]
text:
Matilyn Kerr, left, and sister Brittany Kerr watch as a skid-steer loader pulls a tree from Brittany Kerr's yard in Highmore, South Dakota, on June 29, 2026, after a severe storm that morning. (Photo by Meghan O'Brien/South Dakota Searchlight)The federal government will reimburse up to 75% of public infrastructure repair costs from storms that hit eight South Dakota counties and two Native American reservations in late June and early July, the Federal Emergency Management Agency announced Wednesday.
The Oglala Sioux Tribe, meanwhile, is in line for the same level of reimbursements for repairs to public infrastructure caused by storms in early June, and individual tribal members will be eligible for financial aid to cover some property losses from that incident.
Gov. Larry Rhoden requested a presidential disaster declaration from the Trump administration in late July, in a letter laying out $4.5 million in public property damage from a storm system that moved through the state between June 28 and July 3. 
Governor of South Dakota seeks federal help for damages from summer storms

Rhoden said, first in a Tuesday evening social media post and again in a press release on Wednesday, that President Donald Trump called him directly to tell him about approving the state’s request for a disaster declaration. 
On X, Rhoden shared a post from Trump in which the president wrote “South Dakota is a special place, which I won by Historic margins, three times, and I will always deliver BIG for them.”
The disaster declaration for the state as a whole will reimburse public property repair costs in Beadle, Bennett, Buffalo, Day, Hand, Hughes, Hyde and Stanley Counties, along with the Crow Creek and Lower Brule reservations. Roads, power systems, parks, recreation areas and public facilities were damaged in the storm, with the heaviest impacts in Hyde and Beadle counties.
Lower Brule Sioux Tribe President Boyd Gorneau told South Dakota Searchlight on Wednesday that the tribe lost some center-pivot irrigation systems on its agricultural land in the storm. 
FEMA sent a press release on disaster declarations for South Dakota on Wednesday, but the release did not include dollar figures. 
A FEMA spokesperson told Searchlight the reimbursement isn’t limited to the $4.5 million in damage cited in Rhoden’s request to President Trump, whose post said he’d “approved” $3.4 million — a figure that would cover 75% of the cost to repair that damage.
The actual amount paid in reimbursement will be based on the cost to repair infrastructure, the spokesman said, provided local governments and state officials adhere to FEMA guidelines and protocols.
The same will be true for the Oglala Sioux Tribe’s public infrastructure. The tribe, which requested a disaster declaration separately, was hit with flash flooding June 2-4 after a heavy rain and hail storm.
During the first round of storms, according to the National Weather Service, “6 to 7 inches of rain fell in a short period, causing streets and ditches to fill extremely quickly,” in addition to strong winds and hail. A tornado touched down near Ideal in Tripp County the following day, damaging mostly agricultural land.
The individual assistance program, part of the FEMA announcement for the tribe, will allow residents to work with FEMA to obtain “grants for temporary housing and home repairs, low-cost loans to cover uninsured property losses and other programs to help individuals and families recover from the effects of the disaster,” the spokesperson wrote in an email.
A separate press release from FEMA on the tribal disaster declaration said that tribal members who experienced losses in the storms “should document their damage, keep any receipts for repairs, and file a claim with their insurance provider.”
“Information on how individuals may apply for federal disaster assistance will be announced when it is available,” the press release said.
The FEMA spokesperson said the tribe has not requested a disaster declaration for a more recent hailstorm, which dropped baseball-sized hail on some areas of tribal land, damaging school buses and homes and forcing a delayed start to the school year.
The tribe’s public information officer did not immediately return calls and emails seeking comment on Wednesday.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Yellowstone’s ‘thumping’ hot springs
description: Yellowstone National Park is rightly famous for spectacular geysers. It also has hot springs that create thumps you can hear and feel. Black Sand Pool, in Yellowstone National Park’s Upper Geyser Basin (near Old Faithful), is a hidden gem.  Although it is not far from a road and is very accessible via an easy trail, few […]
text:
Black Sand Pool, in Yellowstone National Park's Upper Geyser Basin. The hot spring is known for it's thumping behavior, which occurs every few minutes due to collapse of bubbles within the spring.  The thumping is strong enough to be heard and felt by anyone nearby. (USGS photo by Mike Poland)Yellowstone National Park is rightly famous for spectacular geysers. It also has hot springs that create thumps you can hear and feel.
Black Sand Pool, in Yellowstone National Park’s Upper Geyser Basin (near Old Faithful), is a hidden gem.  Although it is not far from a road and is very accessible via an easy trail, few people visit the hot spring.  Those that make the short walk and stay a few minutes are rewarded with a special treat—every several minutes the pool starts to thump, and it is strong enough to feel and hear. It’s as if a giant in an underground cavern is striking the cavern’s ceiling with a hammer.
Another famous “thumper” is Doublet Pool on Geyser Hill, also in Upper Geyser Basin.  The thumping at Doublet Pool varies over time, lasting up to a few minutes with intervening quiet times that have varied between 13 and 35 minutes in recent years.  The thumping is so strong that you can see the water in the spring “jump.”
Doublet Pool, fringed by geyserite, in the Upper Geyser Basin of Yellowstone National Park. (National Park Service photograph by Jacob Frank)
One of best places in Yellowstone National Park to see this process in action is Firehole Spring, which is along Firehole Lake Drive in Lower Geyser Basin.  This small one-way side road off the main highway is often closed due to bear management and also poor road conditions (the road lies on very hot ground and so the asphalt tends to melt), but when it is open, Firehole Spring is along the north side of the road just before Great Fountain Geyser.  The spring’s water is very clear, providing a view of bubbles that rise from the vent at the bottom of the pool.  The bubbles often collapse as they rise, creating an audible “thump” as they implode.
Many other hot springs in Yellowstone also thump—for example, pools in Norris Geyser Basin.  But what causes this activity?
The collapse of the bubbles is due to the variable temperature and pressure conditions within the hot springs. As bubbles rise within a thermal pool, their volumes increase and internal pressures decrease.  At the same time, the cooler temperatures near the tops of the pools cause the steam in the bubbles to condense back into liquid water, and this, combined with the decreasing internal pressure, causes the bubbles to implode. If the bubbles are large enough, the thump can be felt.  The components for thumping are not that common, which explains why only a few hot springs in Yellowstone demonstrate that behavior.
Scientists investigated the thumping at Doublet Pool by deploying seismometers around the area to record how the thumping changes with time. They found a number of interesting correlations.  For example, when strong winds blew, the time between thumping was longer than on calm days. This is because the wind cooled the pool by removing heat from the surface.  There were also changes that corresponded to activity at nearby features.  In September 2018, Ear Spring, a short distance from Double Pool, erupted for the first time in decades. At that time, the interval between thumping periods at Doublet Pool was only about 13 minutes—a very short time period that may have been due to an overall increase in thermal input to Geyser Hill.
Firehole Spring, located along Firehole Lake Drive in Yellowstone National Park’s Lower Geyser Basin. The spring is characterized by a thumping behavior that is caused by the implosion of bubbles rising from the base of the pool due to changing temperature and pressure conditions within the pool. The bubbles can be seen in this picture as the whitish mass in the center of the pool. (USGS photo by Mike Poland)
That the rate of thumping seems to change due to heat input indicates that monitoring the thumping interval could be a useful way to track hydrothermal activity in a region. For instance, if interval between thumping at Doublet Pool suddenly starts to decrease, it might be a sign of deeper variations in heat input that could impact other thermal features in the region, perhaps even leading to the formation of new thermal features as occurred in 2023.
If you have a chance to visit Yellowstone National Park, be sure to check out one of the thumping springs—Doublet Pool, Black Sand Pool, and Firehole Spring are easily accessible. You can literally hear and feel the changes that are happening in one of the most spectacular hydrothermal systems on Earth.
Yellowstone Caldera Chronicles is a weekly column written by scientists and collaborators of the Yellowstone Volcano Observatory. This week’s contribution is from Michael Poland, geophysicist with the U.S. Geological Survey and Scientist-in-Charge of the Yellowstone Volcano Observatory.

name: WyoFile
title: Pitching 940-acre data center, Prometheus Hyperscale asks Natrona County to bypass state review
description:
Data center developers pitch local control to a packed room during discussion with county commissioners regarding proposed $500 million campus near Casper. 
The post Pitching 940-acre data center, Prometheus Hyperscale asks Natrona County to bypass state review appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
CASPER—Natrona County commissioners took no action Tuesday after developers of the proposed Prometheus Hyperscale data center asked them to consider an industrial park zoning designation, which would speed up build time by exempting the $500 million project from state industrial siting review.
At the Natrona County Courthouse, Prometheus founder Trenton Thornock and Build Wyoming Director Eric Schlidt presented the request during the workshop portion of the board’s meeting — during which no decisions are made — in front of a packed house of supporting and skeptical residents alike. Per the presentation, Prometheus intends to apply for a planned unit development to zone 940 acres south of Interstate 25 on the Falls Ranch property situated between Casper and Glenrock.
Eric Schlidt with Prometheus Hyperscale’s Build Wyoming, left, and Prometheus founder Trenton Thornock sit among the Natrona County Board of Commissioners audience just prior to their workshop discussion about plans to build a 1.5-gigawatt data center campus to the southeast of Casper. (Greg Hirst/Oil City News)
Thornock told commissioners that an industrial park designation allows developers to seek an exemption from the Wyoming Industrial Siting Council while keeping county-level oversight. He described industrial siting processes as “cumbersome and time-consuming,” adding the exemption would not remove “any applicable environmental or regulatory requirements.”
State agencies like the Department of Environmental Quality and the Wyoming Department of Transportation would still regulate air, water and roads, Thornock said, adding that the DEQ’s Industrial Siting Division has three employees and the seven-person siting council meets quarterly, which slows project reviews.
“Local control in my opinion is much better than state siting oversight,” he said. “You, the county commissioners and local officials, know your community and their needs better than a state siting council.”
Thornock added that county-level permitting allows local officials to negotiate directly with developers for road maintenance and infrastructure funding rather than waiting on state formulas from Cheyenne.
Project background and design
Prometheus announced plans in late 2025 to build a 1.5-gigawatt data center campus on Falls Ranch property — owned by Texas billionaire Russell Gordy — north of Interstate 25. Plans at the time would have placed the data center portion in Converse County and the power generators in Natrona County. 
County officials said after pushback from neighbors regarding noise, heat and traffic, developers shifted the site to other Falls Ranch property south of the interstate, bringing the $500 million campus entirely within Natrona County. 
Converse County commissioners previously adopted a policy to streamline industrial park designations for the project in April, but rescinded it a month later after the Wyoming attorney general found the county lacked the statutory authority to create independent exemption procedures outside standard zoning rules. 
Thornock previously said the proposed data center relies on a closed-loop cooling design using a blend of water and food-grade propylene glycol. The blend is used for five to six years before being hauled off by a supplier for recycling, requiring no ongoing water draw or wastewater discharge for cooling.
On Friday, Prometheus announced a partnership with Evansville-based Mesa Power Solutions to supply natural gas generators. Previously, the company had said it would deploy Jenbacher generators to power the first phases of development. Either arrangement would allow the center to produce its own power on-site without drawing electricity from the public utility grid. 
Friday’s announcement added to the announced partnerships with Spiritus, which says it develops carbon-negative power infrastructure, and Casper Carbon Capture, which agreed to provide land and access to permitted underground carbon storage wells. 
Schlidt estimated the data center portion of the project would support roughly 3,000 temporary construction jobs at peak build-out and 150 permanent positions, and generate between $80 million and $115 million in recurring annual property taxes.
It seems that the county loses a part of its leverage in those negotiations if things have been fully permitted.Commissioner Peter Nicolaysen
Thornock said the campus footprint requires 300 acres for on-site power generation and 640 acres for data center halls west of Big Muddy Creek. He told the board that prospective tenants need a clear path toward local permits, warning that delays could push the company to move resources to alternative project sites in Texas. 
During the meeting, there were no other details provided regarding a site plan, project timeline or potential customers.
Uinta County advances project
Prometheus pointed to its work in southwest Wyoming as a model for how it plans to work with Natrona County.  
In June, the Uinta County Board of County Commissioners approved a zone change from agricultural to industrial use for the Atlas Industrial Park Subdivision. That decision cleared the way for Prometheus to plan a 640-acre campus on Thornock’s family ranch outside Evanston.
Thornock told commissioners that Uinta County placed rules directly onto the company’s conditional use permits. The county handled the project through two separate permits, dividing rules between power generation and the data halls.  
“These are the kind of good-neighbor things that have very specific conditions around how we have to operate our facility both during the construction phase and later on,” Thornock said. 
Before making decisions on those permits, Uinta County planning staff traveled to the Nova data center in Jordan, Utah, Thornock said. The visit allowed staff to see closed-loop liquid cooling systems in person. 
He offered to arrange a similar tour for Natrona County officials.  
Thornock said the company also met with Evanston and Uinta County fire agencies to establish safety rules for on-site backup batteries.  
Natrona County commissioners listen to a presentation by Prometheus Hyperscale founder Trenton Thornock and Build Wyoming Director Eric Schlidt on Tuesday during their workshop meeting at the Natrona County Courthouse. (Greg Hirst/Oil City News)
Natrona County commissioners question developers
Commissioner Peter Nicolaysen questioned the timing of potential community agreements. Thornock said Prometheus prefers negotiating community benefit agreements after county permits are finalized. The company faced accusations of bribery in Uinta County when talks ran during the permitting process, he said.
“It seems that the county loses a part of its leverage in those negotiations if things have been fully permitted,” Nicolaysen said, “and so I would prefer that those things work in tandem, go through the permitting process, but also be moving forward and making progress on the community benefit agreement.”
Nicolaysen also pressed the developers on road access, utility impacts and cooling fluids. Thornock said primary access for construction and operations would come from a newly constructed Interstate 25 interchange, with Hat Six Road reserved as a secondary emergency route.
Commissioner Dallas Laird asked audience members to raise their hands to show whether they supported or opposed the development, then addressed the developers.
“Opinions are different than facts,” Laird said. “And agreements, in my opinion, if they aren’t in writing, they don’t mean anything. So, we’re going to take a really hard look at this.”
Natrona County Board of Commissioner meeting attendees who are against the proposed Prometheus Hyperscale data center project near Casper raise their hands Tuesday at the request of Commissioner Dallas Laird. (Greg Hirst/Oil City News)
Public comment split over landscape, local control
The commissioners took more than an hour of public comment from the dozens of residents packing the courtroom.
Katherine Dvorak of Casper questioned how initial water use would affect area wells and raised concerns about heat output from generators during hot summers. Sherry Johnson, a lifelong Casper resident, urged commissioners and audience members to drive out to Hat Six Road before supporting rezoning efforts.
”Please go take a look at that land because you people need to understand once you allow that behemoth, our landscape will never look the same,” she said. “We’re talking what, 150 jobs? It’s not worth our landscape. We can’t get it back. Once it’s gone, it’s gone.”
Erika Cook said she lives downstream and downwind from the site. The natural gas power plant was her primary concern.
“Gas generators on this scale would turn our rural prairie into a polluted industrial nightmare,” she said. “We would hear and feel the noise from this power facility 24–7, 365 days a year in our home. This is not what we bargained for when we invested our life savings in our peaceful family home.”
Casper resident Sherry Johnson speaks to the crowd about her concerns regarding the proposed Prometheus Hyperscale data center during the public comment portion of the Natrona County Board of Commissioners meeting on Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026, at the Natrona County Courthouse. (Greg Hirst/Oil City News)
Brad Isner, a neighbor of the project’s initial site, said company officials have not provided answers to questions about construction camps, traffic and emergency services.
Meanwhile, supporters urged the board to keep project reviews under local control rather than handing oversight to state boards in Cheyenne.
“What we need to ask is if we have the potential as a community to welcome business development, handle it locally, or do we want to let Cheyenne determine our fate and the impacts and be in charge of the money that comes back to this community?” Casper resident Tassma Powers said. “Because that’s what industrial siting does.”
Keegan Fox of Casper told commissioners that public officials should base decisions on verified facts rather than fear or unverified promises.
“A responsible ‘yes’ doesn’t ignore legitimate concerns and it doesn’t allow speculation to become a substitute for evidence,” he said. 
Colton Dillion, who lives off Hat Six Road, said the development would sit near his home, but he welcomed the opportunity to attract advanced technology jobs to Wyoming.
“Data centers are very efficient businesses in terms of space, in terms of noise, in terms of negative externalities of pollution,” he said. “I would really invite you to think about what is the alternative and what are these other opportunities that we could give to our children.”
The first thing that has to happen is if we pass an industrial zoning matter so that it can be handled by us.Commissioner Dallas Laird
Fred Fichtner, chief operations officer for Mesa Power Solutions, said large infrastructure projects help local suppliers and trade workers compete for work, while geologist JoAnn True said that Natrona County has experience with big projects as it manages oil fields, pipelines and refineries. She urged commissioners to vet the project while creating jobs that give younger residents reasons to stay in the state. 
Commissioners balance property rights, community impacts
In their closing comments, Nicolaysen and Chair Jim Milne said the board must balance community concerns with the rights of private landowners. Laird framed the current technology infrastructure race as an issue of national defense. He said that domestic computing facilities keep American technology out of foreign hands.
“[President Donald] Trump has said it too,” the commissioner said. “He says we have a war going on with China and Russia over who’s going to take over with this AI business. And that’s what this data center is all about. … Do you want China running your AI or Russia running your AI or do you want Natrona County commissioners and the state of Wyoming and America running AI?”
Commissioner Casey Coates, who in June said he had no interest in industrial parks, cautioned against reacting with panic instead of focusing on tangible facts. 
“When we ask for the protection of the government, we really ought to be careful because government at times can be overreaching and those protections that we ask for can be overly applied to ourselves,” Coates said. “Do we not like something because of what it is, or do we have real impacts? If we have real impacts, let’s address those.”
Commissioner Dave North said that state environmental regulators handle water rights and industrial pollution under state statutes.
“The state engineer is the one that takes care of the water,” he said. “That is not our responsibility. That’s not our job. That is up to the state. The DEQ takes care of a lot of stuff. That’s their job. That is not our job.”
Potential county timeline
Commissioners told residents that any formal vote on the Prometheus project remains months away.
Laird said the county can’t set a firm schedule because the developer hasn’t submitted an application. Once filed, any proposal must go through multiple public steps before the commission can act.
“The first thing that has to happen is if we pass an industrial zoning matter so that it can be handled by us,” he said. “This has to go through our zoning board first and they have to decide whether it’s something we should be doing, and then we have to have another meeting where you all come down and we hear from people again, and then we make a vote.”
Laird added that even if the board approves a zone change, Prometheus would still have to apply for separate conditional use permits and meet state rules.
“This isn’t something you’re even going to see a building for for a couple years, I wouldn’t think,” Laird said.
North said the county will demand answers before taking any action.
“That’s a totally different process that takes a lot of time, and there’s a lot of hard questions that we’ve been asking and we will continue asking,” North said. “And before it comes before the commission, those questions are going to have to be answered. That’s the way that works.”
