name: VTDigger
title: Harwood district leaders eye Cabot Creamery’s Waitsfield complex as a possible future school site
description:
The corporate office building may be suitable to convert to an elementary school that would serve Waitsfield, Warren, Fayston and Moretown students.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Harwood district leaders eye Cabot Creamery’s Waitsfield complex as a possible future school site.
text:
Students arrive at Brookside Primary School this morning for the first day of the school year. School district leaders are considering a consolidation scenario that would close the Waterbury school in the future. Photo by Lisa Scagliotti/Waterbury Roundabout Credit: Lisa Scagliotti/Waterbury Roundabout

This story by Lisa Scagliotti was first published in the Waterbury Roundabout on Aug. 26, 2026.
DUXBURY — The recent listing of Cabot Creamery’s company headquarters in Waitsfield for sale for $2.95 million has caught the attention of Harwood school district leaders who are mulling a major school consolidation effort.
The Harwood Unified Union School District School Board at its first meeting of the school year on Aug. 26 agreed to explore a significant consolidation of its seven schools to just three. It also directed its Building Use and Visioning Committee to draft a request for proposals to explore whether Cabot’s corporate office building adjacent to Mad River Park might be suitable to convert to an elementary school that would combine schools currently operating in four of the district’s six communities: Waitsfield, Warren, Fayston and Moretown. 
The building committee met Aug. 18 for the first time since June and discussed the news that Cabot is looking to vacate and sell its office complex in Waitsfield. Several school board members and the superintendent had already toured the property and came away interested.  
“It’s a nice site,” said Superintendent Mike Leichliter. “It’s not built as a school. It’s built as an office building, but structurally it’s a very good structure — primarily steel — a lot of light, a lot of windows. There would need to be some additional space consideration for things like a gymnasium, cafeteria, large group space and potentially some other classrooms.”
School Board Chair Ashley Woods of Waitsfield said the need to modify the facility should not be an obstacle to the district exploring this well-timed opportunity. 
“Definitely not perfect, but it’s a standing building in a really central location in the (Mad River) Valley, which — that right there was very exciting,” she said. “I don’t want to get ahead of myself, but I thought it was a really great thing that we should be looking at pretty thoroughly.”
Cabot officials say the company is seeking to consolidate its administrative staff, and moving its 115 or so employees from the Waitsfield site is part of that plan. The company has not yet said where that would be. Owned by the Agri-Mark farm cooperative, Cabot Creamery employs over 1,000 workers in multiple production plants in Vermont, New York and Massachusetts, retail stores and a Vermont distribution facility. 
Cabot has occupied the 32,000-square-foot Waitsfield office complex adjacent to the Mad River Park playing fields on Home Farm Way since 2014. The building on 7.5 acres originally was owned by Northern Power Systems. Vermont Public reported on the Cabot news in July. 
Likewise, Harwood leaders this year have begun looking for ways the district might combine schools as a way to curb operating costs as pressure from the state increases. The state’s ongoing push to slow growth in education costs has resulted in multiple new laws passed in the past two years. Those measures have put into place new efforts for districts to explore merging and to find ways to collaborate to find operational savings. 
Separate from the state-level steps, Harwood’s administrators and school board have been discussing how the district on its own might revamp operations to run on tighter budgets in the future. Cuts in the past few years have eliminated more than 10% of the district’s jobs, and district leaders say that trend cannot continue without education quality suffering. 
The school board’s building committee in June floated a proposal to downsize from seven to three schools. That would mean replacing elementary schools in Moretown, Fayston, Waitsfield and Warren with one school. The scenario also would close Brookside Primary School in Waterbury, shifting those elementary students to Crossett Brook Middle School. Harwood Middle-High School would continue with additional middle-schoolers from Crossett Brook added.  
At its Aug. 18 meeting, the building committee further dug into the consolidation concept. Committee Chair J.B. Weir, of Waitsfield, noted that the three-school scenario is very similar to one of a long list of options that the district received from Burlington architects at TruexCullins in 2025. One proposal at that time suggested the valley elementary schools combine at Waitsfield Elementary School. That location has since been ruled out, Weir said, due to building constraints and site issues including the potential for future flooding. 
Still, the committee’s latest recommendation otherwise was very similar, with a location to be determined.
Seeing potential 
The superintendent said that Nick Managan, chief of staff at Cabot Creamery, approached him in July to discuss Cabot’s plans to sell the Waitsfield building and move staff out. “If the school district has any interest in having conversations, they would certainly be very interested in selling that building to the school district,” Leichliter said. 
Given that the school board was not planning to meet until late August, Leichliter said, he contacted board leaders and a site visit was arranged. He and several board members — Weir, Woods and Vice Chair Cindy Senning, of Duxbury — visited the Waitsfield facility for a first look. 
Woods said she was “totally surprised” to get the news about the Cabot building. “It was really exciting to go through it and see the potential,” she said. 
Senning agreed. “The central location piece of it is excellent. And the building’s quite lovely. There’s a lot of light. … It’s like an office building, but it’s not like an office building,” she said.
The superintendent said that combining four elementary schools into one would require a new school that could accommodate about 450 students. 
Weir stressed that no one has begun to estimate any costs connected with using the Cabot property as a future school. 
Analysis needed
The committee members acknowledged the long road ahead for decision-making on whether and how to consolidate district schools. Analysis is needed to compare the costs of merging schools and upgrading the facilities that would remain against the costs of continuing to operate the current facilities. Other factors such as class sizes, staffing and logistics all need review. 
Along the way, the board members and administrators stressed the importance of involving community members by sharing information and getting feedback. 
Weir said that if the full board agrees to pursue the committee’s recommendation, the building committee would work with the board’s public outreach committee to schedule public meetings. “Certainly it is the goal to get out there as much as possible and work this through with our towns,” he said. 
School board member Macon Phillips of Warren, who was attending the committee meeting, commented on the challenges ahead in keeping the public informed and involved. “The public interest isn’t focused on the feasibility of a new site particularly,” he said. “It’s about the necessity of this kind of change.”
Before the community can debate details of a significant consolidation, people will need more information, Phillips said. “I don’t fully understand the cost of the status quo. … We should be able to show people why this is a better option than doing nothing.”
Harwood Finance Director Lisa Estler said she is prepared to put together financial forecasts using known data and current state policy that dictates tighter restrictions on how much district budgets may grow before they trigger financial penalties. 
Community feedback 
At least a dozen members of the public logged into the Aug. 18 building committee meeting via Zoom. Viewer Robert Perry said he’s a property tax payer in Warren, Waitsfield and Burlington who supports the current push to slow down the growth in education costs in the state. 
“The people of Vermont want this change. Vermont is increasingly unaffordable, and the education costs are driving that unaffordability,” Perry said. “While the board should have acted years ago to deal with this structural problem of too much infrastructure and too few students, I’m really happy that now you’re actually paying attention to this and making some plans.”
Perry, however, questioned the proposed three-school scenario before the Cabot facility was discussed. “Building a new school for a declining population — that doesn’t seem to make any sense either. So, I don’t know why you don’t pick a more incremental approach.” 
Matt Lillard asked about the status of needed repairs and upgrades at Harwood Union High School. He requested that any proposals for future consolidation also address building needs there. After a failed bond in 2021 that would have paid for major upgrades at Harwood, a renewed effort in 2023 to focus on renovations in excess of $60 million at the middle-high school was shelved after voters rejected the district’s annual budget, prompting multiple revotes in spring 2024. 
Board member Steve Rosenberg from Moretown chairs the school board’s outreach committee and shared feedback from local residents that he’s received over the summer with the building committee. Comparing costs of merging schools with the status quo was high on the list, he said. Other concerns he’s heard include whether bonding to pay for consolidation will trigger state financial penalties and whether consolidating will allow the district to bring back programs it has recently cut. Local residents want to know the impact on bus ride times and staffing levels if schools are combined, Rosenberg said. 
There’s also “worry that towns that no longer have elementary schools will be less attractive to the young families we want to move into our towns — where there’s one winner town and several loser towns as a result of consolidation,” he said.
Committee Chair Weir nodded as he listened to the list. “Those are all questions that we hope to have answers to sooner rather than later. I would at least add that our overarching goal, no matter what, is to make sure we’re providing our kids with the best education we can get them both in and out of the school, whether it’s on the soccer fields, on the stage, in the music room, or in the classroom.”
The Harwood school board held its first regular meeting of the 2026-27 school year on Aug. 26. Several members of the public attended to plead that the board consider cost-cutting measures that don’t involve closing schools. 
Moretown resident, former school board member and educator Peter Langella challenged the notion of closing schools, asking, “What if we treated our community schools as assets instead of liabilities?” He suggested an overall redesign of the district’s programming before closing schools. “There are so many intelligent and compassionate people in this room, and throughout this district, so please don’t say there are no other options,” he said. 
“Help me understand how outfitting an entirely new giant elementary school building fixes our current budget crisis,” Moretown resident Sasha Bianchi told the board. “We have to think outside of this box that we’ve been bouncing around in for almost a decade.”
Board members in their discussion later in the meeting acknowledged that exploring the Cabot facility is just the first of what will likely be multiple options they will consider going forward. But board Chair Woods said that the potential to improve an existing building rather than start from scratch gives the elementary consolidation proposal an attractive starting point. “This building has opportunity that we can’t ignore,” she said.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Uncounted late ballots jump in WA as fears of Postal Service delays intensify
description: SEATTLE — Over 20,000 ballots in Washington’s primary election last month were rejected because they came in too late, thousands more than in 2024.  This comes as election officials have raised the alarm over the U.S. Postal Service not postmarking mail-in ballots on the day they’re received due to reduced service and faraway processing centers. […]
text:
Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs speaks about the importance of returning ballots early alongside U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell, right, and leaders from the Seattle King County NAACP and the League of Women Voters of Snohomish County on Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026, in Seattle. (Photo by Jake Goldstein-Street/Washington State Standard)SEATTLE — Over 20,000 ballots in Washington’s primary election last month were rejected because they came in too late, thousands more than in 2024. 
This comes as election officials have raised the alarm over the U.S. Postal Service not postmarking mail-in ballots on the day they’re received due to reduced service and faraway processing centers. Officials here have encouraged Washingtonians to use ballot drop boxes or mail their ballots at least a week before election day to ensure they’ll be counted.
Late last year, the Postal Service finalized a rule saying that a piece of mail’s “postmark date does not inherently or necessarily align with the date on which the Postal Service first accepted possession of the mailpiece.”
Statewide, the number of ballots not counted because of late postmarks increased 32%. 
In the 2024 primary, 16,131 votes were uncounted because of this. This year, it was 20,267, despite lower turnout overall at about 37%. Over two-thirds of ballots were returned via drop box this year, up a tick from 2024.
Rural counties appeared to be affected the most, according to state election data. Lewis, Pend Oreille, Franklin, Okanogan and Yakima counties saw a tripling of late ballots that couldn’t be counted. In Mason and Stevens counties, the number quadrupled. In about half of Washington’s counties, it doubled.
Meanwhile, the state’s most urban areas went the other direction, with fewer ballots rejected for not coming in on time. King, Spokane, Pierce and Clark counties all improved.
The rejected ballot total equals a small fraction of the nearly two million votes cast in this year’s primary. 
Washington has over five million registered voters. But just a few votes can make a difference in individual races. In one legislative district, two Democratic state Senate candidates were separated by four votes to advance out of the primary. They were running to represent part of Whatcom County, where 615 votes were rejected for lateness, 179 more than two years ago.
Secretary of State Steve Hobbs and U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell presented the data Wednesday in Seattle.
Cantwell, a Democrat, said President Donald Trump and the Postal Service are “disenfranchising voters across the United States with policies that are leaving them with a ballot that was cast but never counted.” She called on her Republican colleagues in the Senate to hold hearings on the issue.
“This is what makes our country great: the fact that we have free and fair elections,” Cantwell said. “But right now, the U.S. Postal Service is not making it too fair.”
They attributed the rural-urban divide to less access to drop boxes, forcing voters to rely on the unreliable mail system to return their ballots.
The Postal Service also recently changed policy so that mail dropped off more than 50 miles from a distribution center is picked up the next day, instead of at the end of the day. The mail, including any returned ballots, is transferred to these facilities and postmarked there. This process, especially important in rural areas, could take multiple days. 
This year, election officials also saw delays in transferring ballots returned in drop boxes in one county that needed to be counted by another. In Island County, for example, ballots mailed over by neighboring Skagit County were postmarked on Aug. 7, but weren’t delivered until after election certification, which was Aug. 18, according to the secretary of state’s office.
These votes aren’t counted among the tallies of ballots that came in too late.
Hobbs’ office says it has spent $400,000 to educate voters on the importance of using drop boxes, instead of the mail, and over $350,000 reimbursing counties for new boxes and reprinted ballot envelopes.  
The Postal Service didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
The first ballots will go out in a matter of weeks for the Nov. 3 general election. Most ballots will be mailed to voters Oct. 16.
Tensions between the state and federal government are rising ahead of Election Day.
This week, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security reportedly launched a surge in voter fraud investigations in Washington and other states in its crusade for noncitizen voters. 
The state is also litigating the future of its mail-in ballot system with the Trump administration, which is seeking to tighten federal control over it through the Postal Service. A federal judge has blocked the federal government’s moves, but the case is likely headed to the U.S. Supreme Court with just two months until the election. If upheld, officials here think it could sow chaos for the midterms.
“I don’t have time to depend on the Supreme Court,” Cantwell said. “I have to depend on Washington voters and the rest of America to get out and vote and do it in the most prudent fashion, so that we can have our voices heard in an election.”

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Hobbs said the Postal Service “is trying to do everything they can to ruin vote by mail in the state of Washington.”
Washington is also awaiting word from a federal judge in Seattle on whether the state needs to hand over its voter rolls to the Trump administration. The administration has been unsuccessful in numerous similar cases across the country. The state and feds argued the case last month and are waiting for a ruling. 
On the ballot will be three statewide initiatives dealing with Washington’s new income tax on high earners, parental rights of public school students and transgender students’ participation in school sports. Also decided will be five closely-watched state Supreme Court races, over 100 state legislative races and every member of the U.S. House.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska schools set to receive $115M in war-driven oil revenue bonus, state announces
description: The Alaska Department of Revenue announced on Monday that Alaska’s K-12 public schools will receive an additional $115 million in state funding this year, prompted by a boost in oil revenues driven by the U.S. war on Iran. Legislators earmarked the additional oil revenue for schools as part of the state budget approved by Gov. […]
text:
A school bus passes in front of the Alaska State Capitol on Wednesday, May 20, 2026. (James Brooks photo/Alaska Beacon)The Alaska Department of Revenue announced on Monday that Alaska’s K-12 public schools will receive an additional $115 million in state funding this year, prompted by a boost in oil revenues driven by the U.S. war on Iran.
Legislators earmarked the additional oil revenue for schools as part of the state budget approved by Gov. Mike Dunleavy in June. 
The additional funding is a relief to school districts statewide. Many districts have faced severe budget shortfalls in recent years due to funding not keeping pace with rising costs. This year, a record 12 elementary and middle schools closed across the state.
Following the announcement, Luke Meinert, superintendent of the Fairbanks North Star Borough School District — the state’s third-largest district by student count — welcomed the news, and said the district is appreciative of the Legislature for making it a priority.  
“(We’re) very excited that the projected numbers came through and that we will see a sizable increase in funding for our school district through the one-time funds that are being allocated,” he said in an interview Tuesday. 
Officials with the Department of Revenue announced the state had collected sufficient revenue funds to meet the special appropriation of nearly $600 million. 
Lawmakers designated funding for four priorities areas, in sequential order: nearly $128 million to the Permanent Fund to allocate one-time energy relief payments of $200 per eligible Alaskan along with dividend checks; $115 million to K-12 schools through the Alaska Department of Education and Early Development; $15 million to the bulk fuel loan program; and $341 million to the state’s budget reserve account.
According to the announcement, the Monday revenue estimates are expected to be revised and finalized this fall. The revenue amounts are expected to “change slightly,” impacting the exact amount that will land in the budget reserve fund, the state’s savings account, officials said. 
The $115 million will be distributed to school districts according to the state’s education funding formula, which is based on student enrollment counts in October.  
For Fairbanks, that’s estimated to be roughly $10.2 million this year. Meinert said the district designed its budget this year anticipating about half of that amount, and the additional funding will go toward teachers and staff, as the district is currently in union contract negotiations are ongoing, and other areas. “So that will help us in our negotiation discussions for this school year,” he said. 
“Student activities have been an area that’s been cut pretty hard over the past several years,” he continued. “So potentially adding some funding there to ensure that families aren’t having to pick up a bigger burden of paying for student activities. And then, additionally, I think there may be some smaller investments for teacher mentoring, teacher coaching, and possibly some funding in our nutrition services department.”
School board members with Fairbanks and Anchorage called on the state in June to release estimates earlier, ahead of the school year — “the earliest practical information available,” they wrote in an op-ed for the Anchorage Daily News. They asked the state to announce whether “funding is likely, unlikely or still uncertain,” to help districts plan, particularly for hiring teachers. 
But the Department of Revenue did not change its scheduled announcement.
Lisa Parady, executive director of the Alaska Council of School Administrators, said they were “elated” and “grateful” at the announcement. But she said it underscores Alaska schools’ needs for prior notice and consistent state funding. 
“We do have to get to the place where we have predictable, reliable funds in advance of needing to extend contracts. That’s the biggest issue,” she said Tuesday. 
“Because we’re in the greatest education shortage in the history of Alaska and in the nation, it allows for the recruitment and retention of quality educators and that ability to lock in those contracts sooner,” she said.
Among the state’s largest districts, the Anchorage School District is expected to get $32 million. The Matanuska Susitna Borough School District is expecting $16.1 million, the Kenai Peninsula School District is expecting $7.6 million. Both districts closed schools this year. 
Parady said it’s difficult to say if the additional funding earlier in the year would have prevented school closures.
Districts cited surging costs of operations, as well as declining enrollment as more families opting for homeschool programs or leaving the state. 
“Each school district is in their own unique place in terms of overall education funding in their budgets,” Parady said. “Having a long term fiscal plan that allows for timely, reliable, and predictable revenue for schools … is the only way that school boards and our school district leaders can have the tools they need to make the best decisions as they’re managing their budgets. And school closures are obviously a piece of that, and so I can’t say for sure that it could have changed an outcome, but it’s certainly possible.”
Anchorage Democrat Sen. Löki Tobin, who chairs the Senate Education Committee expressed her reaction Tuesday as “mixed.” “We know that our schools are in desperate need of resources,” she said. 
“We have nonpartisan financial memos from our Division of Legislative Finance that says to adequately address the years that inflation has eroded the purchasing power of our base in funding, we need to appropriate significant financial resources per student to our schools, and while $115 million is a significant amount of dollars, it’s clearly not enough. And one-time funds do not create stability nor predictability.”
Tobin also acknowledged the moral dilemma of the upswing of Alaska oil revenues and state funding driven by the U.S. war on Iran. 
“It is gut-wrenching to know the reason that Alaska has been able to receive these resources,” Tobin said. “It is not without contemplation or thought that I have been thinking about the children that were bombed in these recent years in a place that is very far away from us, but is no less important and nor no less critical for the health and well-being of all of our kids, and how those choices are driving the record increases in the price of a per barrel of oil.”
With the boost in state revenues, Tobin also credited the efforts of lawmakers across political divides in designating funding for schools. “Folks who work to get this funding into our budget not only crossed the aisle but also were bicameral in nature, and that is absolutely critical,” she said.
Lawmakers allocated roughly $144 million in one-time additional funding for K-12 schools, plus $148 million for school repairs and construction this year to address an extensive maintenance backlog. They approved $29 million to offset districts’ rising energy costs beginning in 2028 and subject to future lawmakers approving the funding.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pennsylvania labor agency launches initiative targeting wage violations in home care industry
description: The state will preemptively investigate Minimum Wage Act violations in the home care industry and sent agency notices Wednesday.
text:
Union members with SEIU Healthcare Pennsylvania support a state initiative to preemptively investigate Minimum Wage Act violations in the home care industry. (PACast)As a wheelchair user who’s relied on home care services since breaking his neck playing high school football decades ago, Theo Braddy knows the importance of getting good assistance.
“You’re hearing from someone who knows the difference attendant caregivers and direct care workers bring to the table,” he said. “Unfortunately, Pennsylvania’s home care system is already fragile. We lost a lot of small- and middle-sized providers during the (COVID-19) pandemic, and we have not been able to recover from that.”
As the executive director for the National Council on Independent Living, he helps advocate for others with disabilities, including two phone calls last week from people who couldn’t get out of bed or use the restroom without assistance. Neither could secure home healthcare. 
Theo Braddy, the executive director of the National Council on Independent Living speaks about the importance of well-aid home care workers at a state press conference on Sept. 2, 2026. (PACast)
But the industry, already struggling with low wages, is also vulnerable to wage theft. According to state Secretary of Labor and Industry Nancy Walker, nearly 40% of the agency’s Minimum Wage Act complaints come from home care workers. 
“Behind every single one of those complaints is someone who showed up to work, who cared for someone else’s parent or spouse or family member or child or loved one, but was not paid,” added Walker. 
In response, Walker’s agency is establishing a new initiative to affirm pay across independent home agencies, sending legal demands for wage and hour information to businesses throughout the commonwealth. 
In a Wednesday press conference, Walker didn’t specify how many agencies would be subject to review or if there was a timeline. 
“We will not wait for new complaints, but we will be proactive and strategic within an industry where people are often isolated, where they’re often underpaid and where they fear if they speak up they’ll be retaliated against,” Walker continued. 
Mia Haney, the CEO of the Pennsylvania Homecare Association, emphasized that the organization supported “holding bad actors accountable,” but added that “they should not define an industry overwhelmingly made up of providers committed to their workers and the people they serve.”
Pennsylvania Secretary of Labor and Industry Nancy Walker announces an initiative to “proactively” investigate Minimum Wage Act violations in the home care industry on Sept. 2, 2026. (PACast)
“Pennsylvania’s home care industry has been a focus of the Department of Labor & Industry for years, and responsible providers take seriously their obligation to follow wage and hour laws,” Haney told the Capital-Star. 
Haney and others have long pushed for the state to increase reimbursement, saying it lags behind other states.
“Strong enforcement protects workers from employers who break the law. Adequate Medicaid funding gives responsible employers the resources to raise wages and strengthen the workforce. Pennsylvania needs both,” she added.
The National Institute for Worker’s Rights claims that employers violate minimum wage laws every day to the tune of $15 billion annually, a cost higher than losses from “all forms of property crime.”
“Wage theft should not be tolerated. And we cannot talk about addressing Pennsylvania’s home care worker shortage while allowing workers to go unpaid,” said Braddy. “Fair treatment and fair pay have to be a part of our workforce strategy.”
 How will the initiative work?

An agency release described the initiative as “proactive” investigations in collaboration with partners like union leaders and advocates, rather than waiting for a worker to file a complaint. The state started sending notices to agencies, who collectively employ an estimated 100,000 home care workers, on Wednesday. 
‘I hope you can live with your consciences’: Pa. minimum wage proposal blocked by Senate GOP

“Minimum Wage Act complaints often involve unpaid overtime, unpaid hours worked, improper overtime calculations, inaccurate records or other pay practices that prevent workers from receiving the wages they are owed,” read the release. 
For example, an employee who worked 30 hours with one client and also spent 20 hours with another client is entitled to 10 hours of overtime, as described by the state’s Home Care Workers’ Rights. On-duty hours include times when the client is sleeping and employers cannot deduct “sleep time.” 
Workers must also be paid for time spent traveling between clients. 
“Employee status under the (Minimum Wage Act) is determined by the economic realities of the working relationship, not by labels, tax forms or employment contracts,” said another state website geared toward home care workers. 
Employers aren’t allied to retaliate against employees who file complaints under the law.
 Low wages stifle fast-growing industry

Roughly 200,000 Pennsylvanians, both aged or disabled, rely on Medicaid to cover the pay for home care workers, also known as direct care workers. This workforce assists with activities of daily living, such as bathing, eating or toileting.
“Home care workers make it possible for our fellow Pennsylvanians to live, to work, to love, to go to school and participate in the communities of their choice amongst their loved ones and friends,” said Juliet Marsala, the deputy secretary for the state Office of Long-Term Living. “They provide people with the dignity and independence they deserve, so they can live their lives and reach their goals.” 
Most state payments filter through agencies, though a small number of enrollees pay their home care workers directly. But industry demand is growing.

Speakers added that approximately 25% of Pennsylvanians are age 60 or older, a number that is projected to increase to 33% by 2030. Receiving care at home, rather than in an institutional setting like a nursing home, is the preferred option for aging adults across the country. 
“But making that possible depends on having a strong, stable and respected direct care workforce,” said Gabrielle Szymanski, a deputy secretary at the state Department of Aging. 
Matt Yarnell, the union president of SEIU Healthcare Pennsylvania, noted that the average hourly wage for workers was $13.50 and turnover at agencies topped out at 104%.
“That is way too low. Nobody, doesn’t matter what corner of Pennsylvania you live in, $13.50 an hour does not cut it,” Yarnell said. “These are high stakes. We’re caring for humans. We’re not making cereal, we’re caring for humans in their homes and that’s a big deal.”
‘We can’t wait any longer’: Latest Pa. budget lacks home health nurse funding increase

Haney and others point to low state reimbursements for care, noting that all of Pennsylvania’s neighbors pay home care workers at a higher rate. According to the group, more than 112,500 home care shifts go unfilled each month.
“The reality is that (home care) agencies agree with the (Shapiro) Administration’s comments that we have to pay workers more,” Haney added. “Direct care workers deserve higher wages, but the (state) Department of Human Services Medicaid rates that largely fund those wages have not kept pace despite significant advocacy efforts to prioritize this workforce.”
In the last budget cycle, workers directly employed by their Medicaid enrollee got a boast, but Braddy said more steps are needed. 
“We cannot continually demand that providers pay better wages, provide better benefits, recruit more workers and meet additional requirements without asking whether or not the system is adequately funding and accomplishing those things,” he continued. “Accountability and adequate funding have to go together.” 
Other speakers emphasized the difficult work required to be a home care worker, adding that sometimes they’re the only face a client sees that day.
When Wanda Carroll-Russell first started as a home care worker in Philadelphia two decades ago, she didn’t have any training or union backing. 
“This work isn’t simple, it’s complex. Isolating conditions inside someone’s private home, usually with no coworkers or anyone watching us, this isolation makes workers vulnerable,” said Carroll-Russell. 
“So many” other workers don’t have the protections she says she has now as a union member with SEIU Healthcare Pennsylvania, she continued, specifically when it came to getting paid fair wages. She credited them with securing a raise last year from $15.49 to $17.21, an amount she said allowed her to keep her insurance. 
“The demand is growing fast. The workforce isn’t keeping up because the pay and the support haven’t kept up either.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Another interim superintendent chosen for Canton schools
description: The Canton Public Schools district office will work throughout the year to prepare for the curriculum change during the 2027-28 school year.
text:
Veteran educator Bonita Coleman is the new temporary superintendent of Canton Public School District. 
Coleman comes to the district after more than three decades of working in schools in Mississippi and Maryland. Most recently, she served as superintendent of Ocean Springs School District for a decade before retiring in 2023. 
According to a Canton schools press release, Coleman’s tenure in Ocean Springs was “characterized by a disciplined focus on student achievement, leadership development, organizational effectiveness, fiscal stewardship, safety, and continuous improvement.”
Bonita Coleman, pictured here in 2017. Credit: Kayleigh Skinner/Mississippi Today
She previously worked in the Clinton and Jackson school districts, led instructional development and early childhood education at the Mississippi Department of Education and served as a professor at Tougaloo College and Jackson State University — both her alma maters. 
“It is an honor to be selected to serve the students and families of Canton Public School District,” Coleman said in a statement. “I look forward to working with leaders and teachers to continue to assess Canton Public Schools’ organizational needs and maintain a strong focus on teaching and learning and operational efficiency.”
The district celebrated Coleman’s hire on Wednesday, immediately after announcing the departure of interim Superintendent Dwight Luckett. Luckett led the district for more than a year, after an initial commitment of five months. He was Canton’s district superintendent from 2006 to 2014. He also served as interim superintendent in 2018.
He gave the school board three weeks’ notice that he was leaving, the release said.
Beverly Luckett, the district’s spokesperson and Luckett’s wife, said Coleman’s appointment is temporary, and the district continues to search for a permanent superintendent. The last permanent superintendent left the district in July 2025.
The district serves roughly 3,100 students, the majority of whom are Black, and is rated a C by the Mississippi Department of Education’s standards.

title: Why the rushed Postal Service plan for mail-in voting has states in a panic
text: President Donald Trump’s executive order placing new restrictions on mail-in voting would assign state officials a Herculean task to reach compliance before the crucial midterm elections.The order directed the U.S. Postal Service to strictly regulate the envelope design of mail-in ballots and to collect voter data from each state through an online portal, among other things. The Postal Service has argued in court that its rule is not an election regulation, but is within the agency’s purview as a standard for a specific type of mail.But some state officials tasked with fitting their systems to the new regulations say it presents massive — if not impossible — challenges to reach compliance for the November midterms, when voters will decide whether to continue Republican control of the U.S. House and Senate. Ballot designs and printing are typically done months in advance of ballots being sent to voters, which begins this week. North Carolina is set to mail out ballots for the Nov. 3 general election on Friday. “In some States, it would be impossible at this point to comply with the last-minute rollout of USPS’ novel ballot-verification program,” more than 20 Democratic-led states suing to block the order said in a Wednesday court filing. “In other States, there will be chaos.”The states presented a list of tasks state and local elections administrators would have to complete. That list includes: redesigning ballot envelopes and obtaining USPS approval “on an unprecedented timetable,” purchasing new envelopes, developing technological systems to meet barcode standards in the rule, uploading voter-specific information to the USPS portal that they have not yet received access to and training state and local officials and voters on the new standards.“Each step of this process is fraught with an extreme risk of error,” they said.‘Courts will stop it’Because of the unworkable timeline and a general principle not to change voting policy too close to an election, officials believe courts will ultimately block the rule from going into effect for this year.“There's a pretty universal feeling that the courts will stop it from happening,” Katy Owens Hubler, the director of elections at the National Conference of State Legislatures, said in an interview.“In general, you don't want to be changing things right before the election. So in a lot of ways, it is already too late. Part of the rule relates to the absentee ballot envelopes themselves. And … almost universally, those have already been designed and printed.”A Massachusetts federal judge has paused the rule from taking effect through Sept. 11 while multiple legal fights play out.Tammy Patrick, the chief programs officer at the National Association of Election Officials, a nonpartisan industry group for state and local elections officials, said in a court declaration filed Aug. 28 the timeline was unworkable for the midterms.“None of the Rule’s requirements can feasibly be implemented before the November 3, 2026, General Election,” she wrote. “Administration of the 2026 election is already well underway, with timelines, budgets, and staffing already set, many of which are unmovable or unchangeable.” The rules requirements “will place new and heavy burdens” on election offices whose budgets are “already constrained,” she added.Election officials and USPS began preparing for the 2026 election months ago, she said. And states already set funding levels.“The infeasibility of the Rule for election officials is obvious when you consider the calendar and preparation for the 2026 general election next to the Rule’s requirements and implementation,” she wrote.The rule would force states to push through in a matter of weeks what should take a year, Matthew Weil, the vice president for democracy and bipartisanship at the Bipartisan Policy Center, a Washington think tank, said.“A year of lead time is the best practice before any new policy,” he said.Envelope designSome of the requirements themselves are not objectionable, according to experts. The standards for envelope design, for example, largely codify best practices the Postal Service has recommended for years.But the rule also requires that USPS approve each design, possibly through an online portal that has yet to be introduced and has reportedly seen major problems in development.Nationwide, there are about 40 mail design analysts who would be qualified to judge mail ballot designs. Asking every state, and many counties that have their own designs, to submit them at the same time would be unworkable.“If even a fraction of election offices has to submit their new envelopes and materials … before the 2026 election, it would take weeks for USPS to work through the sudden volume,” Patrick wrote.A similar problem could face election offices seeking to order printing of new ballots and envelopes, she said. The turnaround time for new envelopes could stretch 12 to 16 weeks, she said.Despite those obstacles, the rule would mean any ballots that do not fit the new specifications would be rejected, possibly stopping many voters from casting ballots.IT problemLike the implementation of ballot envelope standards, the rule’s requirement that states electronically share voter files with the federal government has suffered from a rushed process, according to an explosive whistleblower complaint published Tuesday.The Postal Service lacks the capacity to implement the executive order, David Becker, the executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, said in a statement Tuesday.“They secretly rushed development of the technology the order demanded, trying to piece it together in a few months rather than taking the time required for a proper rollout,” he said. “This slapdash effort is guaranteed to result in significant problems just weeks before the election, potentially disenfranchising thousands of voters.”Owens Hubler said states have not yet gained access to the portal.“It’s a pretty big (information technology) project to have done very quickly,” she said. “And I don't know that anybody's actually seen it yet. So, that's another aspect of putting it into place before the election that could be pretty tough.”The Bipartisan Policy Center predicted the difficulty in building the portal in a July 6 comment on the notice of proposed rulemaking by the USPS. The center noted that state and local officials would have difficulty complying.“Whether election officials can meet this burden at all depends on the successful deployment of a tool that does not yet exist,” the group wrote. “Building, testing, deploying, and training election officials to use a portal before October 4 (the beginning of the 30-day window during which election officials will be supplying lists to USPS) will be an enormous undertaking, and the risk of delay in the deployment of this portal is significant.”The Postal Service did not respond to a message seeking comment Wednesday.In a Tuesday statement, a spokesperson said the agency was finalizing the portal’s development, and called it “just one part of a broader, year-round effort” to ensure election mail is properly handled.“The Postal Service is now finalizing the portal and will soon make it available to election officials who voluntarily wish to familiarize themselves with the platform,” the spokesperson said. “USPS will also provide tools, presentations, and other resources to help election officials understand the platform and make informed decisions about whether and how they wish to use it.”Universal mail statesStates that already mail ballots to every registered voter, and the large jurisdictions within those states, may have an easier time meeting the standards, Owens Hubler said. If they are not already in compliance, they likely have a relationship with a commercial printer that could possibly handle a short order.But smaller, less-resourced counties and states that don’t have a robust mail-in voting program may have more trouble finding last-minute fixes.The eight states that have universal mail voting — California, Colorado, Hawaii, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Vermont and Washington — “will be affected, but everyone's affected,” Owens Hubler said. “And I think it is important to think of the ones that just don't have to do this as often. They may, in the end, be more affected.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Crow Creek tribal member to be South Dakota’s next Missing and Murdered Indigenous People liaison
description: A Fort Thompson resident and member of the Crow Creek Sioux Tribe who has more than two decades of experience working with crime victims will serve as South Dakota’s Missing and Murdered Indigenous People specialist.  Marlys Big Eagle will fill the role vacated earlier this summer by Allison Morrisette, who in 2022 became the first […]
text:
A mural in Eagle Butte on the Cheyenne River Reservation in South Dakota raises awareness about Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)A Fort Thompson resident and member of the Crow Creek Sioux Tribe who has more than two decades of experience working with crime victims will serve as South Dakota’s Missing and Murdered Indigenous People specialist. 
Marlys Big Eagle will fill the role vacated earlier this summer by Allison Morrisette, who in 2022 became the first to serve in the position. 
Attorney General Marty Jackley, under whose office the liaison serves, announced Big Eagle’s hiring in a press release Wednesday. 

Marlys Big Eagle, Missing and Murdered Indigenous People specialist for South Dakota. (Photo courtesy of South Dakota Attorney General’s Office)

“Marlys has spent her career helping victims of violence and families looking for missing loved ones,” Jackley said in the release. “Her credibility with tribal communities, law enforcement, and prosecutors makes her an outstanding choice.”
Big Eagle worked with crime victims for the U.S. Department of Justice for 27 years. For 23 of those years, she worked as the supervisory victim witness coordinator for the U.S. Attorney’s Office in South Dakota. For the past four years, she’s worked for the department’s Washington, D.C., executive office as the agency’s first Native American outreach services liaison for Missing and Murdered Indigenous People cases occurring in tribal areas.
The job of state-level liaison was created by the Legislature in 2021 but not funded. Initially, Morrisette’s salary was paid by a nonprofit organization. Jackley successfully lobbied to make the position permanent and state-funded shortly after she was hired.
The liaison works to connect family members to resources and the law enforcement agencies investigating their loved ones’ cases. In June, Morrisette told South Dakota Searchlight that serving as the first MMIP liaison for the state was an honor, but that the new position she accepted, working with juveniles for the Unified Judicial System, was a better fit for her growing family. 
In the press release on her hiring, Big Eagle said she’s “deeply honored” to have been selected to work with families “as they seek answers and confirmation about what may have happened to their loved ones.”
“I look forward to working alongside other MMIP stakeholders and partners to help bring answers, support, and justice to these important cases,” Big Eagle said.
Nationwide, Native Americans are more likely than non-Natives to die by homicide. In 2023, homicide rates for Native Americans were nearly five times higher than for non-Hispanic whites, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Q&A: South Dakota’s Missing and Murdered Indigenous People liaison reflects as she departs

Native Americans are also disproportionately represented in missing people cases. South Dakota maintains an online clearinghouse for all people reported missing to a law enforcement agency within the state’s borders. Consistently, 60% of the cases involve Native Americans, while around 8.5% of the state’s population is Native. 
As of Wednesday afternoon, 58 of the state’s 93 missing people were Native American. Thirty of the 48 missing women were Native American.
The South Dakota liaison position was created the year after state lawmakers voted to create that public-facing missing people site in 2020. A few months later, Congress passed the Not Invisible Act, which created a commission to investigate the underlying causes and identify improvements to help address the overrepresentation of Native Americans in missing people cases and violent crimes.
Nine tribal nations share borders with the state of South Dakota, which has one of the highest per-capita populations of Native Americans in the U.S.
