name: Maine Morning Star
title: Lobstermen buoyed by US House passage of Golden bill to pause right whale protections until 2035
description: The U.S. House of Representatives Tuesday passed a bill to extend the pause on federal lobster rules in a 219-196 vote.  If passed by the Senate, the bill — introduced by Reps. Jared Golden (D-Maine) and Michael Lawler (R-New York) in June — would continue shielding lobstermen from new regulations to protect North Atlantic right […]
text:
A lobster waits to be thrown back into the waters of Little Bay after researchers evaluate it on Monday, Aug. 10. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)The U.S. House of Representatives Tuesday passed a bill to extend the pause on federal lobster rules in a 219-196 vote. 
If passed by the Senate, the bill — introduced by Reps. Jared Golden (D-Maine) and Michael Lawler (R-New York) in June — would continue shielding lobstermen from new regulations to protect North Atlantic right whales until 2035.
In a statement, Golden described it as a win not only for the Maine fishing industry, but also for bipartisan work in Congress. 
“While the threat of unnecessary, industry-killing regulations is a matter of survival for lobster harvesters in Maine, the issues at play affect fishermen across the Northeast,” Golden said. “Building bridges across party lines is essential for a functional Congress, but unfortunately, it’s a skill that has been lost for far too many members.”
Golden worked with the rest of the Maine delegation to insert a provision in a 2022 federal omnibus funding bill to restrict new whale-related regulations on the lobster industry through the end of 2028. Because of their dwindling population, the government has sought to impose certain regulations to protect right whales, such as fishing restrictions in certain areas of federal waters during seasons when whales are present.
Lawler similarly noted the bipartisan effort, and said he was proud to see the bill pass in the House.
“While this legislation is particularly important to Maine’s fishing communities, the Northeast lobster industry supports small businesses and hardworking families far beyond the coastline, including restaurants here in New York,” Lawler said. “Fishermen have spent years adapting to conservation requirements and deserve regulatory certainty instead of constantly shifting rules that threaten their ability to operate and plan for the future.”
Golden introduced an earlier version of the bill in April, and in May, the Trump administration announced its strong support of the bill and said the president would sign the legislation if Congress sends it to his desk.
The Maine Lobstermen’s Association celebrated the bill’s passage. In a statement on Facebook, Executive Director Patrice McCarron called it a “major step forward for Maine lobstermen.”
“Extending the pause through 2035 will give scientists the time needed to build a meaningful body of data so future whale regulations are based on sound science, not assumptions, while protecting fishing families and coastal communities from needless economic harm,” McCarron said. 
But some conservation groups are raising concerns about the legislation. In a statement, Erica Fuller with the Conservation Law Foundation called for the Senate to vote down “this terrible bill.” 
The futures of right whales and lobstermen are entangled. Could high-tech gear help save them both?

Found along the East Coast, right whales’ migratory paths overlap with highly productive lobster fishing areas in Maine and Massachusetts, making entanglements in fishing gear one of the major threats for the animals. With a population of less than 400 and even fewer reproductively active females, right whales are approaching extinction with more than half a dozen threats to their existence, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Fisheries. 
“Entanglements in fishing gear are a leading cause of death for these critically endangered whales,” Fuller said. ”Punting crucial protections almost a decade down the line will condemn many whales to preventable and painful deaths.” 
Fuller said that if the Senate passes this bill, “they will be sacrificing whales’ lives to provide short term economic benefits to an industry that could be participating in solutions that benefit both.”
Supporting Maine’s fishing industry has been a major priority for Golden in the House. The congressman is not running for reelection this year, and will be replaced by either Democrat Matt Dunlap or Republican Paul LePage in November. 
Both candidates voiced their support for Golden’s bill after the Tuesday vote. 
“Matt supports the extension, in order to protect Maine lobstermen,” Dunlap campaign advisor Matt Herdman said in a statement Wednesday. “Thousands of families in the district rely on the lobster industry for their livelihoods, and Matt will always fight to help them succeed.” 
In a post on Facebook, the former governor thanked Golden and Lawler for their work on the bill. 
“When I was made aware of the bill and the need to gain more support to get it across the finish line, I was proud to step up and urge Republican leaders to get this to a vote,” LePage said. “This bipartisan legislation will protect Maine fishermen, their families and the coastal communities that depend on the lobster industry.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: Newly formed New Mexico ‘abundance’ housing coalition lays out legislative priorities
description: A new housing coalition including homebuilders, lawmakers, nonprofit leaders and state agency officials on Wednesday previewed an agenda for January’s legislative session that includes streamlined zoning, expanded funding options, reduced taxation and increased building in rural areas.
text:
The newly formed Housing Abundance! Coalition, which seeks to remove regulatory or financial barriers to housing construction, announced its priorities on Sept. 2, 2026, ahead of the 60-day New Mexico legislative session beginning Jan. 19, 2027. Above: Homes sit under construction in Albuquerque, pictured Aug. 26, 2026. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)A new housing coalition including homebuilders, lawmakers, nonprofit leaders and state agency officials on Wednesday previewed an agenda for January’s legislative session that includes streamlined zoning, expanded funding options, reduced taxation and increased building in rural areas.  
Housing Abundance! Coalition spokesperson Miles David Conway, who is also CEO of the New Mexico Home Builders Association, told Source NM on Wednesday that the group’s goal is to arrive at New Mexico’s legislative sessions with consensus on housing solutions. 
Different interest groups often arrive at legislative sessions on the first day only to find out they have “competing or contradictory” legislation or a repeat of past bills. 
“I think that is very frustrating for everybody,” he said.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
New Mexico is currently experiencing a housing shortage, recently estimated at roughly 58,000 units, as well as sharp increases in home prices and rent. Conway said his group aims to spur as much production as possible, with the help of tax code changes and state funding to both developers and homebuyers. 
The group’s four main “pillars” released Wednesday include offering incentives to local governments to modernize their zoning and permitting processes; expanding the use of state-funded mortgage rate buydowns and down payment assistance; eliminating gross receipts tax on market-rate and affordable housing construction; and building more housing infrastructure in rural areas.
Nonprofit Homewise, earlier this month released a report that identified obstructive local zoning ordinances and permitting processes as the main barriers to reducing the state’s housing shortage
The New Mexico Legislature and state agencies have tackled related measures in recent sessions, including a bill that eliminated sales tax on labor or supplies for affordable housing developers. Housing New Mexico, the state’s mortgage finance authority, also launched a pilot program earlier this summer that uses state funds to reduce low-income homebuyers’ mortgage rates. 
The term “abundance” used in the group’s name, Conway said, references a book New York Times columnist Ezra Klein co-authored that argues administrative burdens like zoning codes and parking requirements artificially limit the housing market and constrain the housing supply. In New Mexico, it also refers to the many different types of housing, both in rural urban areas, that the group aims to help build, Conway said. 
New Mexico Dem governor nominee Haaland touts permitting ‘shot clock’ in visit to housing project

“When we looked at the abundance of housing opportunities that we wanted to stimulate, that word arrived,” he said. 
The coalition lists multiple state lawmakers as helping shape the group’s platform, including Albuquerque Democrats state Sens. Heather Berghmans and Moe Maestas, House Speaker Rep. Javier Martínez and Rep. Cristina Parajon, as well as Rep. Rebecca Dow (R-Elephant Butte). 
State agencies like the Department of Workforce Solutions, which oversees the new Office of Housing, and the Economic Development Department are also listed as founding members.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Voting groups file federal challenge against Florida’s ‘SAVE’ Act
description: Two voting advocacy groups filed a federal lawsuit Wednesday, challenging Florida’s new law requiring proof of citizenship to vote.  The law passed the Legislature this year on a near-party-line vote and was signed by Gov. Ron DeSantis in April. It goes into effect Jan. 1.  The two groups are Black Voters Matter Fund and the […]
text:
The challenge comes in advance of the law's 2027 effective date. (Photo by Jim Neuger/Maine Morning Star)Two voting advocacy groups filed a federal lawsuit Wednesday, challenging Florida’s new law requiring proof of citizenship to vote. 
The law passed the Legislature this year on a near-party-line vote and was signed by Gov. Ron DeSantis in April. It goes into effect Jan. 1. 
The two groups are Black Voters Matter Fund and the League of United Latin American Citizens, represented by the Southern Poverty Law Center and Democracy Defenders Fund. 
“This is a political ploy to determine who wins our elections by picking who votes,” Tianna Mays, legal director for DDF, said in a news release. “This scheme targets Black and Brown communities by erecting barriers to voting for hundreds of thousands of eligible voters, including naturalized citizens and other Floridians who don’t have a passport.”
HB 991  appeals to the same sentiment as the federal SAVE Act, which has passed the U.S. House but not the Senate.
“Florida lawmakers are reviving a bill that couldn’t survive Congress and dressing it up as state law,” said Matletha Bennette, senior staff attorney for the SPLC. “This purposely manufactures a crisis for people who have done nothing wrong, and it does so on the backs of naturalized citizens, Black families, and working Floridians.”
A group of voting rights advocates filed suit against the law in federal court minutes after the bill was signed. That suit is is scheduled for a trial in late 2027.
The later suit lists Secretary of State Cord Byrd and supervisors of elections in Broward, Palm Beach, Miami-Dade, Orange, and Osceola counties. 
The groups are asking the court to declare the law in violation of the National Voter Registration Act and the Fourteenth Amendment and permanently enjoin Byrd and the supervisors from implementing or enforcing the provisions the lawsuit challenges.
Those include “conditioning federal voter registration on requirements prohibited by federal law, removing registered voters on unauthorized grounds or without constitutionally adequate procedures, conducting nonuniform or discriminatory list maintenance, or conducting systematic voter removal activities during the 90 days preceding a federal primary or general election.”
Proving citizenship
In 2020, Floridians voted in favor of a state constitutional amendment that allows only U.S. citizens to vote in state elections.
The new law requires all voting to be done on paper. Voters would show their status with a driver’s license, and the law removes student IDs as acceptable for voting purposes.
The suit bemoans that voter registration will be conditioned on the “state’s ability to independently verify citizenship through government records.”
“Naturalized citizens are particularly vulnerable because government records may reflect their prior noncitizen status while failing to reflect their subsequent naturalization,” the suit claims. 
“H.B. 991 likewise permits eligible applicants who timely submit valid registration applications to remain unverified and unable to cast a regular ballot. The consequence of incomplete, outdated, or inconclusive government records thus falls on the eligible citizen rather than the State.”
DeSantis signs bill requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote — voting rights group sue

Black Voters Matter, which works to encourage people to vote, says the law “frustrates BVM’s ability to carry out its existing programs and forces BVM to expend resources it would not otherwise expend.”
The law requires a voter to prove citizenship by providing, among other things, a birth certificate, passport, driver’s license that indicates citizenship, or an order from a federal court granting citizenship.
Obtaining the most common forms of identification “can impose meaningful costs” in time and money, the suit argues, noting the cost to obtain a passport ($130 to renew and $165 for a first-time issuance).
A birth certificate may be less expensive to obtain, the suit acknowledges, “but obtaining one still requires navigating the vital-records system of the jurisdiction in which the voter was born.“
During a debate on the Senate floor, Sen. Erin Grall, R-Vero Beach, cited statistics from the state showing that in January 20.6 million people in Florida held REAL-ID-compliant driver’s licenses and 872,408 did not.
The legislation was sponsored by Rep. Jenna Persons-Mulicka, who has since been appointed by the governor as Lee County’s supervisor of elections.
“I sign it, they sue us,” DeSantis said while signing the bill. “They go to a liberal judge. The liberal judge sides with them. Then we appeal, and then we win. So, that’s probably what will happen on this — I’ve just seen it enough.”
During the Legislature’s consideration of the legislation, Democratic Rep. Ashley Gantt shared the story of her aunt, who was born in the Jim Crow era and not issued a birth certificate.
“The burden of locating and replacing citizenship documents also carries a history that cannot be separated from race,” the suit notes. “Rep. Gantt explained that the problem was not hypothetical for Black families whose births occurred during the Jim Crow era, when access to hospitals and formal systems of birth documentation was not equal.”
The suit cites a U.S. Department of Homeland Security report that shows Florida had the second highest population of newly naturalized residents during 2024, at 93,240 new citizens.
“The Florida SAVE Act upholds the Florida Constitution by ensuring only citizens can vote in Florida elections,” Byrd said in a news release after it became law.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC students show gains in testing, graduation rate reaches record high
description: North Carolina’s graduation rate reached a record high last school year as overall test proficiency climbed to its highest level in three years. The four-year graduation rate reached 88.8%, up from 87.8% the previous year and marking the fourth consecutive annual increase, according to results the North Carolina Department of Public Instruction released Wedn[...]
text:
North Carolina’s graduation rate reached a record high last school year as overall test proficiency climbed to its highest level in three years.
The four-year graduation rate reached 88.8%, up from 87.8% the previous year and marking the fourth consecutive annual increase, according to results the North Carolina Department of Public Instruction released Wednesday. 
Overall, 59.2% of students were proficient on state end-of-grade and end-of-course tests, up from 55% in 2024-25 and the highest level in three years. Grade-level proficiency reached a three-year high on 14 of 15 reading and math tests.
“These academic achievement results are a testament to the incredible work happening across North Carolina’s public schools,” North Carolina Superintendent of Public Instruction Maurice “Mo” Green said. “While I am pleased to see these results trending positively, including our highest graduation rate ever, I look forward to continued progress.” 
The percentage of students who reached the state’s college- and career-readiness benchmark also increased, from 34.7% to 37.5%.
The two measures capture different levels of performance. Students need to score at level 3 or higher to meet the state’s grade-level proficiency standard. The college- and career-readiness benchmark requires a level 4 or 5.
“Although 59.2% of students are grade-level proficient, only 37.5% are college and career ready. That is an area that we will focus on,” Dr. Stacy Wilson-Norman told the State Board of Education.
Proficiency increased across every racial and ethnic group, as well as among English learners, students with disabilities and economically disadvantaged students.
North Carolina had 523 low-performing schools last year, down from 685 the year before. The number of low-performing districts fell from 23 to 10.
The percentage of schools receiving a D or F rating fell to 23%, from 31% the previous year, according to DPI.
NC families face higher back-to-school costs as school year begins

In Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools, 136 schools earned an A, B or C, up from 124 the previous year. Superintendent Crystal Hill said the district has focused its leadership meetings on analyzing student data and used the information to identify areas for improvement and direct support to schools.
“School leaders, coaches, and teachers now collaborate to isolate areas for improvement and deploy resources immediately,” Hill said during a press conference.
Robeson County came off the state’s low-performing district list for the first time since 2017-18. Its overall grade-level proficiency increased by 7.6%, while the number of schools that met or exceeded expected growth rose from 23 to 28.
“For us, this is about much more than coming off a list,” Assistant Superintendent Windy Dorsey-Carr said. “It represents intentional work, changes in practices, and a collective belief that the children of Robeson County can achieve at high levels.”
Carr said the district did not rely on a single program. Instead, it focused on core instruction, used student data to identify gaps and adjust instruction, and provided schools with support based on their individual needs.
“We don’t want data to simply tell us what happened. We want it to tell us what we need to do next,” Carr said.

title: Kentucky courts filing system part of ‘cybersecurity incident,’ judicial branch officials say
description: The Kentucky Administrative Office of the Courts said the system used for files for the Kentucky Supreme Court and Court of Appeals “experienced a cybersecurity incident.” AOC said it was notified by the company Thomson Reuters Court Management Solutions about the incident within the company’s C-Track system files. The company said an unauthorized third part[...]
text:
The Administrative Office of the Courts office in Frankfort, Kentucky, on March 26, 2026. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd)The Kentucky Administrative Office of the Courts said the system used for files for the Kentucky Supreme Court and Court of Appeals “experienced a cybersecurity incident.”
AOC said it was notified by the company Thomson Reuters Court Management Solutions about the incident within the company’s C-Track system files. The company said an unauthorized third party accessed and obtained court data from multiple states, including Kentucky Appellate Court data. 
As of Wednesday, the number of individuals and organizations affected is not known, the statement said. 
“Kentucky Appellate Courts were not functionally impaired by this incident,” the AOC statement said. “The AOC has no indication at this point that the unauthorized third party distributed the Kentucky data to any other party or entity. Thomson Reuters CMS is working with third-party experts and law enforcement and has assured each affected jurisdiction that it has taken significant mitigation steps to prevent unauthorized access to the data in the future.” 
As Kentucky does not use third-party vendors for trial court e-filing, trial information not in an appeals case is not affected by this, AOC said. Any person determined to be affected by the incident will be notified by Thomson Reuters CMS with further information and a year of credit monitoring and identity theft protection. 
Thomson Reuters CMS is leading the investigation and AOC is cooperating with it to identify Kentucky data involved.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Auditors: Millions given to Blue Hills Civic Assoc. unaccounted for
description: One of the largest recipients of state funding through Blue Hills Civic Association, Sonserae Cicero, refused to provide records to auditors.
text:
After poring through records for eight months, a team of auditors and forensic accountants was unable to find documentation to account for $2.4 million in taxpayer money distributed to businesses and nonprofits through the Blue Hills Civic Association, according to a new audit.
The audit was commissioned by the Department of Economic and Community Development after state officials learned that Sen. Doug McCrory, D-Hartford, used the Blue Hills Civic Association as a passthrough to subgrant millions of dollars to other organizations, including several businesses that are now the subject of an ongoing FBI investigation.
The 128-page audit highlights how little oversight the state had over the money that McCrory directed through the BHCA in recent years, and how poor the recordkeeping was at some of the organizations that received those funds.
The auditors from CliftonLarsonAllen noted that several of the organizations that received money from BHCA could not document how they used tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of dollars, despite a requirement that they keep such records for at least three years.
“As a result of these conditions, in many instances CLA was unable to fully substantiate the allowability, timing, or purpose of expenditures reported by subrecipients,” the auditors wrote. 
“These limitations increase the risk of unallowable costs, misuse of funds, and undetected instances of fraud, waste, or abuse,” the auditors wrote. 
Meanwhile, one of the largest beneficiaries of the state grant funding refused to cooperate with the  auditors entirely, citing the ongoing FBI investigation. 
Sonserae Cicero, who is being investigated because of her alleged relationship with McCrory, declined to turn over any records to auditors even though her companies, which operate under different versions of the name SHEBA, received $1.2 million through the Blue Hills Civic Association.
“In response to document requests, legal counsel for Ms. Cicero indicated that, based on publicly available information suggesting a potential ongoing federal investigation into related matters, SHEBA would not provide any documents or information absent a legal obligation to do so,” the auditors wrote. 
Cicero did not respond to a phone call seeking comment for this story. 
The auditors noted that Cicero signed a contract that granted the state and its auditors access to the company’s records “upon request.”
Asked if DECD would pursue legal action to force SHEBA to open its books, spokesperson Jim Watson said, “DECD has taken all reasonable steps through available mechanisms to recover and/or hold any funding allocated to entities identified in the audits and will continue to evaluate whether any additional action is merited or likely to lead to the recovery of funds.”
The audit findings are the latest twist in a ongoing political scandal that has destroyed the Blue Hills Civic Association, contributed to McCrory losing his senate seat and forced state lawmakers to rethink how they hand out money.
McCrory, who had served in the legislature for two decades, did not respond to a phone call on Wednesday. 
The auditors attempted to trace more than $6.5 million that was subgranted to 31 organizations in the North End of Hartford and other parts of Connecticut.
Auditors also sought records from RH Realty Services, a company that Blue Hills paid $225,000 over two years to provide mortgage coaching to low-income households.
Roberta Hoskie, who previously served on the state’s Minority Business Initiative Advisory Council with McCrory, gave auditors bank statements that they say suggested she may have used portions of that state funding for personal expenses.
The auditors noted multiple instances in which Hoskie’s company paid for meals, hotel stays and payments to a Jaguar-Land Rover dealership. There were also expenses for Edge Fitness, Mondovi Dental and Pearl Vision, as well as multiple ATM cash withdrawals.
The auditors questioned how those expenses related to the homeownership coaching program that Hoskie was supposed to be providing.
“The available documentation does not demonstrate how these expenses are directly related to program delivery, raising concerns that some may represent personal or mixed-use expenditures,” the auditors wrote. 
Hoskie did not respond to an email sent to her business on Wednesday, and DECD officials said she stepped down from the state Minority Business Initiative Advisory Council in April. 
The General Assembly passed a law in May that will set new limits on so-called legislative earmarks — money that individual lawmakers can direct to favored organizations.
That law will mandate additional documentation and reporting requirements from any entity that receives such funds. It also requires nonprofits, like the Blue Hills Civic Association, to obtain state approval before subgranting any money to other groups.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lawmakers could subpoena CT Children’s over gender care deal with Trump
description: Democrats Matt Lesser and Jillian Gilchrest say CT residents deserve to know details of the hospital’s agreement with the Trump administration
text:
The Democratic co-chairs of the state legislature’s Human Services Committee say residents deserve to know the details of a Connecticut hospital’s deal with the Trump administration to end gender-affirming care for children. And they’re willing to exercise their subpoena power to get it, according to a Tuesday press release.
Last month, the U.S. Department of Justice announced it had reached an agreement with Connecticut Children’s to resolve the agency’s investigation into the hospital’s gender-affirming care services for children. The deal included a “commitment” to stop providing gender-affirming care to minors, including hormones and puberty blockers, as well as a monetary penalty and an additional $500,000 in medical care to people “living with the harmful consequences of ‘gender affirming care,’” according to the DOJ announcement. 
Human Services Committee co-Chairs Matt Lesser, D-Middletown, and Jillian Gilchrest, D-West Hartford, sent a letter to Connecticut Children’s earlier this week requesting copies of the agreement and all correspondence between the hospital and the Justice Department, according to a press release from Democratic legislators.
State law gives legislative committee chairs the power to subpoena witnesses and require the production of documents related to matters under investigation by their committees.
“We have an obligation to the people of Connecticut,” Gilchrest said. “We’ve said that we are a safe state to be able to receive these services, and so I think it is incumbent on myself as a lawmaker to understand what this agreement is.”
The lawmakers’ press release also accused the hospital of violating its legal requirement as a Medicaid provider not to discriminate against patients. 
Gilchrest said lawmakers have a meeting with hospital leaders next week. She said she’s hoping to get more details on the deal and the hospital’s motivations for entering into it. 
In an emailed statement, Connecticut Children’s spokesperson Monica Buchanan said, “Throughout this extraordinarily difficult process, protecting our patients and their private health information has been our first and most important obligation.” 
Buchanan added, “Connecticut Children’s did not turn over any patient protected health information to the federal government during this investigation or settlement process. Protecting that information was a line we would not cross, and safeguarding the privacy of our patients will remain non-negotiable.”
Politics vs. policy
House Minority Leader Vincent Candelora, R-North Branford, said he agrees it’s reasonable for Connecticut lawmakers to discuss the deal from a policy standpoint, but that publicly threatening the hospital in a press release is “blatantly political.”
“We shouldn’t be leading with threats of subpoenas. I think Connecticut is better than that,” Candelora said.
Candelora took issue with the timing of the release as well, saying the Human Services Committee co-Chairs sent a letter to Connecticut Children’s, received a response from the hospital agreeing to a meeting, but sent out a press release anyway.
“It reeks of politics,” Candelora said.
Buchanan of Connecticut Children’s also took issue with the lawmakers’ actions, saying hospital leaders “welcome the conversation,” but the letter was the first correspondence they’d received from either legislator about the settlement, and that the hospital responded immediately.
“We are disappointed that serious conclusions about Connecticut Children’s and the circumstances surrounding this settlement were made publicly before Senator Lesser or Representative Gilchrest had an opportunity to speak with our leadership and understand the facts,” stated Buchanan. 
Last summer, in the wake of federal policy changes, both Yale New Haven Health and Connecticut Children’s made changes to the gender-affirming services offered to children. 
Yale stopped providing medication treatment, but continued to provide mental health services as part of its gender program. Connecticut Children’s shut down its program altogether (though Buchanan specified that the hospital continues to provide mental health services to all children, including those diagnosed with gender dysphoria).
Last month, the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services announced that Medicaid and CHIP funds could no longer be used to pay for youth gender-affirming care. But a document obtained by NPR in July showed the federal Department of Health and Human Services would likely not be following through on its most serious threat to finalize a proposed rule that would have blocked all federal funding for hospitals that provide gender-affirming care to children.
Lesser said he’s been trying, with limited success, to engage in meaningful conversations with Connecticut Children’s leadership since the announcement last year. He said he believes it’s important for state residents to know about what’s going on. 
“I could have sent a threatening letter and not publicized it, but I think it’s a matter of significant public interest,” Lesser said.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ wants US Supreme Court to review Kalshi’s sports markets
description: New Jersey wants the U.S. Supreme Court to review whether states can regulate prediction markets' sports bets.
text:
New Jersey wants the U.S. Supreme Court to review whether states can regulate prediction markets' sports bets. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey asked the U.S. Supreme Court on Wednesday to review an appellate ruling that found a federal 2010 law bars states from regulating sports bets offered on prediction markets, arguing the high court should step because lower courts have split on this issue.
In a voluminous 332-page filing, the state argued a recent 2-1 decision from the U.S. 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals would effectively kill all state regulation of sports betting — including for casinos — and expose existing sports book operators to violations of federal law. That decision found sports bets offered by platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket can only be regulated by the federal government.
New Jersey Attorney General Jen Davenport (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
“Companies like Kalshi claim to offer legal sports betting in all 50 States, but they refuse to follow the gambling laws of any State,” said New Jersey Attorney General Jen Davenport. “These companies have no right to offer their sports bets without following state law, which is why dozens of States across the ideological spectrum have opposed them.”
In April, a divided 3rd Circuit panel ruled that sports bets offered by prediction markets were swaps, a type of financial derivative that can only be regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission as a result of amendments made by the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act.
That decision, which for the moment bars New Jersey, Delaware, and parts of Pennsylvania from regulating prediction markets’ sports bets, is at odds with a ruling the 9th Circuit issued last month.
The 9th Circuit, which covers Nevada and other states, was dubious that Congress had intended to overhaul decades of gambling regulation “based on broad definitions of the words used in a Wall Street Reform Bill.”
In a statement, a spokesperson for Kalshi said the 3rd Circuit’s decision is the correct one and argued state regulation would be unfeasible for a business that operates across the country.
“Kalshi is an open, nationwide financial exchange. It cannot be regulated by 50 different regulators,” said Dani Lever, the spokesperson. “Both the 3rd Circuit and the District of New Jersey sided with Kalshi because the CFTC’s exclusive jurisdiction preempts state law. While New Jersey points to a recent decision in the Ninth Circuit, that decision agreed with that key principle.”
While the 9th circuit agreed the Commodity Futures Trading Commission has exclusive jurisdiction over swaps, it said the agency lacks the clear congressional authorization needed to treat sports bets as swaps. Kalshi advertises that it offers “legal sports betting in all 50 states.”
The disconnect between the two circuit courts demands that the U.S. Supreme Court step in, New Jersey argued in legal filings, adding more than 40 states had been opposed to Kalshi’s view of the legality of its sports bets.
“Given the volume of litigation cascading through the federal and state courts on this issue, and the Ninth Circuit’s explicit disagreement with the Third Circuit, there is no prospect that this disagreement will resolve itself absent intervention by this Court,” New Jersey said in court filings.
The state said allowing the 3rd Circuit’s decision to stand would effectively kill regulatory powers over sports betting the U.S. Supreme Court granted to the states in Murphy v. NCAA, which found a 1992 law unconstitutionally outlawed sports betting in most states.
Operators, including casinos, could escape state regulation just by self-certifying their sports bets with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, New Jersey argued.
Further, because the Dodd-Frank law bars companies from offering swaps unless they are registered with the commission, accepting the prediction market’s reading would expose state-licensed sports books to nearly a decade of violations of federal law, the state said in filings.
“Kalshi does not abide in any way with our state’s gaming laws,” said Mary Jo Flaherty, interim director of the state’s gaming enforcement division. “This is a states’ rights issue. In New Jersey, gaming is prohibited by its Constitution, other than for exceptions approved by New Jersey voters. In this case, the State is upholding the will of New Jerseyans regarding the manner in which gaming can be conducted.”



Quotation







Companies like Kalshi claim to offer legal sports betting in all 50 States, but they refuse to follow the gambling laws of any State.


– Attorney General Jen Davenport


Sports betting has a particular nexus in New Jersey. The state led litigation that ended a ban on sports betting under the Professional and Amateur Sports Protection Act of 1992.
Former Gov. Chris Christie, who signed laws legalizing sports betting here and whose administration opposed the federal sports betting ban in court but left office before the case concluded, predicted New Jersey would again prevail before the Supreme Court.
“It’s betting. It’s not an investment. It’s not a commodity. The Supreme Court has ruled that states have the right to regulate sports betting. I think that it’s going to go to the Supreme Court, and I’m confident [the prediction markets] will lose,” he told the Philadelphia Inquirer earlier this week.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Animal-welfare group expands lawsuit over puppy laundering, USDA enforcement
description: An animal-welfare organization that is suing the federal government over an alleged failure to enforce regulations against dog breeders in Iowa and elsewhere is now seeking to expand its lawsuit. The American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals filed its original lawsuit against the U.S. Department of Agriculture in September 2024, challenging t[...]
text:
Steve Kruse's Stonehenge Kennels in West Point, Iowa, has been repeatedly cited for failure to provide adequate veterinary care. The two dogs pictured here were suffering from bleeding foot injuries and an eye disorder, according to federal inspectors. (Aerial photo courtesy of Bailing Out Benji. Inset photos taken by USDA inspectors courtesy of Bailing Out Benji.)An animal-welfare organization that is suing the federal government over an alleged failure to enforce regulations against dog breeders in Iowa and elsewhere is now seeking to expand its lawsuit.
The American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals filed its original lawsuit against the U.S. Department of Agriculture in September 2024, challenging the USDA’s decision to license three Iowa dog breeders — Steve Kruse, Brian Lichirie and Wuanita Swedlund.
The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, alleges the USDA has failed to enforce the federal Animal Welfare Act by repeatedly renewing Kruse’s license, despite a history of animal-welfare violations, and by licensing two of his associates, Lichirie and Swedlund.
According to the ASPCA, the USDA’s own inspection reports detail “horrific treatment of breeding dogs kept caged in Kruse’s massive West Point, Iowa operation, which typically holds more than 700 dogs.” The inspectors’ reports document observations related to dogs limping and suffering from open, bleeding wounds; dogs with untreated eye infections or severe dental issues; painful fur matting; and a lack of veterinary care.
The USDA reports also allege Kruse poured hot sauce on one dog’s open wounds to keep the dog from licking them, and housed other dogs in cages so small they restricted the animal’s freedom of movement. The dogs also had fecal matter on their coats and in their food bowls, the USDA inspectors alleged.
During one inspection, Kruse was alleged to have thrown a bag of dead puppies at a USDA official, but he continued to operate his dog-breeding business under USDA licensure.
USDA seeks to have lawsuit dismissed
In addition to licensing Kruse directly, the ASPCA lawsuit alleges, the USDA has knowingly and unlawfully issued separate licenses for commercial kennels on properties owned by Kruse.
As a result, the ASPCA claims, hundreds of Kruse’s dogs have cycled through those affiliates as part of a puppy-laundering scheme intended to conceal the role Kruse plays in supplying puppies to out-of-state retailers.
The ASPCA’s lawsuit has proceeded at an extraordinarily slow pace, with no scheduling orders issued and no discovery or depositions taking place. Recently, the USDA filed a motion seeking dismissal of the lawsuit, arguing the case is now moot because Kruse, Lichirie and Swedlund are no longer licensed.
The ASPCA is resisting the motion for dismissal while also seeking to amend and expand its lawsuit against the federal agency.
In court filings, the ASPCA notes that within days of canceling Kruse’s license in September 2025, the USDA approved a license for another individual, Christine Snakenberg, at 2345 Highway 16 in West Point — the same address as Kruse’s Stonehenge Kennels, which he still owns.
The ASPCA said in the lawsuit this follows a previously established pattern in which Kruse installs a newly licensed operator on property he owns while retaining full control of the business.
The ASPCA’s lawsuit cites the licensing of Snakenberg as evidence that the USDA’s “ongoing policy of non-enforcement persists to this day,” and so the lawsuit should not be dismissed as moot.
Iowa breeder faces criminal charges
In the two years that have passed since the lawsuit was initially filed, the ASPCA argues, every claim it initially made about the federal agency’s alleged failure to enforce the Animal Welfare Act “has been vindicated, tragically, at the expense of the animals that this statute was designed to protect.”
As evidence, the ASPCA cites ties between Kruse and Swedlund.
As the Iowa Capital Dispatch reported in 2024, a USDA inspector visited a dog-breeding kennel in the Van Buren County town of Cantril in late 2023. The business was located on property owned by Kruse but was operating under a license held by Swedlund. During the inspection, USDA officials reported six puppies at the facility appeared to have frozen to death.
USDA records showing that in 2025 and 2026, Swedlund repeatedly denied federal inspectors access to her Van Buren County facilities.
On June 25, 2026, the U.S. Department of Justice obtained a temporary restraining order against Swedlund and then inspected her business, cataloging 20 violations. A few days later, the Van Buren County sheriff seized Swedlund’s 32 dogs.
On July 10, 2026, U.S. District Judge Stephen Locher found that Swedlund’s noncompliance with the federal Animal Welfare Act “goes well beyond bureaucratic handwringing. The evidence shows that Swedlund has housed hundreds of dogs since acquiring her USDA license in 2023. She has consistently failed to provide her animals with adequate facilities, access to water, or access to medical care. It is evident that the animals in Swedlund’s care suffered needlessly — precisely the type of harm that the Animal Welfare Act sought to prevent.”
In separate state-court proceedings designed to determine to the fate of the 34 animals taken from Swedlund, District Court Judge Joel D. Yates transferred ownership of the animals to the PAW Animal Shelter in Fort Madison for eventual adoption.
In his ruling, Yates said the evidence showed the “animals were neglected by not having access to appropriate food, potable water, sanitary conditions, proper ventilated shelter and necessary veterinary care.”
Swedlund, whose USDA license expired on July 14, 2026, has since been charged with 34 counts of animal neglect. She has pleaded not guilty to all of the charges. A trial date has yet to be scheduled.

name: VTDigger
title: Oil or babies, Vermont?
description:
While the state clings to costly imported oil, birth centers and rural health services are being left to wither.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Oil or babies, Vermont?.
text:
Dear Editor,
It is obvious to most that children are essential to our state’s future well-being. Children will become the future workforce, paying taxes and contributing in myriad ways to build and guide our communities. They will also be the next generation of parents. 
In contrast, imported oil drains a ridiculous amount of money out of the Vermont economy because we have no petroleum resources here. Money spent on oil leaves the state. So why does our governor go to the mat to protect the home heating oil industry while apparently turning his back on supporting family health services?
Affordability is not just about the cost of things; it is about the viability of our communities. Saying that Vermont moms can simply drive over to New Hampshire or Massachusetts ignores the financial and staffing pressures in those states. Massachusetts and New Hampshire are closing birthing centers, too.
The clean heat standard, which Vermont abandoned this year after Gov. Phil Scott vetoed it and lawmakers later let it die, was designed to steer Vermont toward a better long-term economy. Closing schools and reducing health services seem designed to diminish the future self-reliance of our communities.

READ MORE

Currently, the most profitable parts of the U.S. healthcare system are pharmaceuticals, medical equipment, specialty surgery and insurance. Where do people fit into this? While billions are made by cherry-picking the profit points, we are starving resources for primary care. And what is more primary than healthy births and healthy moms? Meanwhile, we spend millions on imported oil wasted on heating under-winterized buildings and driving at excessive and horribly inefficient speeds on our roads. 
It is time for new ideas that will do more than just reduce the rate of downward trends. Invest in Vermont’s birth centers and stop wasting resources on yesterday’s energy systems.
Andy DavisBrattleboro, Vt.

(West Virginia Legislative Photography)West Virginia Supreme Court Justice Bill Wooten had a “medical incident” on the bench while the court was in session Wednesday, leading the court to cancel oral arguments for the day, a spokesman for the court said in a statement. 
Justice William R. Wooton
The court stopped arguments and alerted emergency services, said Jared Hunt, the court’s communications director. 
“Justice Wooton was conscious, alert and conversing with first responders as they treated him,” Hunt said in the statement. “He was then taken to a local hospital for evaluation.”
Wooten will turn 82 later this month, Hunt said. He was elected in 2020 to a 12-year Supreme Court term that started in 2021, according to his Supreme Court biography. He previously served a total of 26 years in the West Virginia Legislature, as a member of both the House of Delegates and Senate. 
Hearings planned for Wednesday will be rescheduled, Hunt said.

title: Data center nondisclosure bill lacks support in committee
description: A legislative committee on Wednesday recommended rejecting a bill that would add repercussions to North Dakota data center developers that enter into nondisclosure agreements with public agencies or officials.  Senate Bill 2406 will advance to a vote by the full Senate with a do-not-pass recommendation from a joint House-Senate policy committee. The committe[...]
text:
Rep. Todd Porter, R-Mandan, speaks during a policy committee meeting on Sept. 1, 2026, ahead of a special session of the Legislature. Porter has been critical of a special session bill addressing nondisclosure agreements. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)A legislative committee on Wednesday recommended rejecting a bill that would add repercussions to North Dakota data center developers that enter into nondisclosure agreements with public agencies or officials. 
Senate Bill 2406 will advance to a vote by the full Senate with a do-not-pass recommendation from a joint House-Senate policy committee.
The committee approved an amendment to the bill that clarified that state agencies are still able to enter into confidentiality agreements to protect sensitive information for data centers and other industrial projects. 

More special session coverage

But the committee recommended dismissing the bill, with some arguing that the topic is too complex to deal with in a three-day special session. 
Rep. Jonathan Warrey, R-Casselton, who brought the amendment and is one of the sponsors of the bill, was among those who voted for rejecting the bill. 
Rep. Todd Porter, R-Mandan, argued that the state’s existing transparency laws are sufficient. 
“I don’t know what we’re chasing,” Porter said. 
Rep. Austin Foss, D-Foss, called the penalties under current law “a slap on the wrist.” 
He supported the bill because it includes the possibility that an industrial developer could have a permit revoked if a nondisclosure agreement is in place.
“The crux of this bill is basically saying it’s not all on the public official, that both parties are in violation of that law,” Foss said.
Rep. Austin Foss, D-Fargo, speaks during a policy committee meeting on Sept. 1, 2026 ahead of a special session of the Legislature. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Two amendments offered by the primary bill sponsor, Sen. Tim Mathern, D-Fargo, were not considered. One, which granted municipal power providers the ability to negotiate potential service agreements in private, was deemed unnecessary with the adoption of Warrey’s amendment. 
Mathern’s other amendment sought to repeal a state sales tax exemption for data center developers. It was deemed not germane to the bill topic.
North Dakota has several data centers proposed or in the works, including one under construction near Harwood being developed by Applied Digital. 
Nick Phillips, executive vice president of external affairs for Applied Digital, testified Tuesday that the company used nondisclosure agreements, also known as NDAs, for that project, but said it did so in compliance with state laws.
A separate committee, chaired by Warrey, is evaluating the impact of data centers and artificial intelligence. The committee’s work could lead to legislation in the 2027 regular session that starts in January.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont Conversation: Historian Jill Lepore on the threat of authoritarianism and how to counter it
description:
Lepore’s new book, “The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State,” frames the current state of artificial intelligence in a larger — and longer — historical context.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Conversation: Historian Jill Lepore on the threat of authoritarianism and how to counter it.
text:
The Vermont Conversation with David Goodman is a VTDigger podcast that features in-depth interviews on local and national issues. Listen and subscribe for free on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube or wherever you get podcasts.
Author and historian Jill Lepore. Photo by Richard Renaldi Credit: Photo by Richard Renaldi
Is technology killing democracy and destroying communities?
Yes, argues acclaimed historian Jill Lepore in her new book, “The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State.” She writes that the artificial state is “the rule of humans by machines manufactured by corporations.” It is the fantasy of tech billionaires. And its goal is the end of liberal democracy.
The artificial state is a “replacement of the liberal nation state, a constitutional democracy in which we are governed by our own consent, with a government by machine, in which many of the functions of democratic governments are automated, in which humans are replaced by bots as the predominant participant in public life,” she told me.
When the titans of Silicon Valley sat behind President Donald Trump at his inauguration in January 2025, it marked “the coming out of the tech right,” said Lepore.
Lepore is one of the country’s most acclaimed historians. She is a professor of American history at Harvard University, a professor of law at Harvard Law School and a staff writer at The New Yorker. Her many books include the bestsellers “These Truths: A History of the United States,” which Time magazine named one of the top 10 nonfiction books of the 2010s, and “We the People: A History of the U.S. Constitution,” which won the 2026 Pulitzer Prize in history. She hosts the podcast “The Last Archive.” She lives part-time in Brattleboro, which is where she spoke to me.
Lepore said that efforts by the Trump administration to sanitize American history are “a form of McCarthyism.” 

Book cover for “The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State” by author and historian Jill Lepore. Courtesy photo.

She said that skewed versions of history have evolved that have deepened social divisions. These range from the “far-right version of American history in which everything is a march of freedom and progress and prosperity and America has never done anything wrong at home or abroad” to the “far-left account in which American history is a litany of atrocities, in which the United States has never done anything good at home or abroad.”
“There was nothing that recognized there was plenty of truth in both of those accounts, and there was also unbelievable distortion in those accounts.” 
Lepore said history affirms that “the power of ordinary citizens working together has managed to defeat” forces like the artificial state and its techno-authoritarianism. 
“But the idea that we can sit in our living rooms and browse the news on our smartphones and post a few thoughts on social media, and that constitutes meeting our obligations as citizens is a false one.”

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming stops housing inmates in Mississippi prison thanks to improved staffing
description:
Legislature’s state employee pay boosts helped department “be more competitive in the regional job market.” 
The post Wyoming stops housing inmates in Mississippi prison thanks to improved staffing appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Improved staffing across Wyoming correctional facilities allowed the Wyoming Department of Corrections to bring inmates back from a Mississippi prison, where they were sent in 2023, agency Director Dan Shannon said. 
The corrections department announced last month that it had returned to Wyoming all 240 inmates who had been housed at the Tallahatchie County Correctional Facility in Tallahatchie, Mississippi. 
“Bringing these individuals back home to their families has always been a top priority,” Shannon said in the announcement. 
Citing staffing shortages, the department had sent the prisoners in 2023 to the Mississippi prison. At the time, Shannon noted concerns about this arrangement. “Keeping them away from home with no home visits and limited family interaction — they do have access to video conferences and things like that — it does have a negative impact on the rehabilitative mindset,” he said.
At the time, about 25% of the department’s uniformed staff positions were vacant. Those staffing shortages were particularly severe at the Wyoming State Penitentiary in Rawlins. In September 2023, when the inmates were sent out of state, uniform staffing at the state penitentiary was about 65%. Since then, the department has managed to close that gap, with uniform staffing now sitting at a little over 83% at the facility, Shannon wrote in an email. 
Staffing across other correctional facilities in Wyoming has also “improved significantly” over the past two years, according to Shannon. 
Shannon credited these staffing improvements to three factors: salary increases, “aggressive” recruitment and staff retention. 
Wyoming lawmakers voted to increase state employee salaries during the last legislative session, allowing state agencies like the corrections department to boost pay for current and potential staff. These pay increases allowed the corrections department “to be more competitive in the regional job market,” Shannon wrote. 
Combined with “aggressive recruitment strategies,” these salary incentives have led to “an increase in qualified candidates applying for correctional roles,” according to Shannon. 
“Equally important is our focus on retaining the dedicated staff already serving our agency,” Shannon wrote. To this end, the department prioritizes workplace safety and has expanded career development opportunities, he said.  
Whether the corrections department can continue housing all inmates in Wyoming is uncertain. That depends on facility capacity and continuing to maintain and improve staffing levels, Shannon wrote. 
“Given the unpredictability of future court commitments alongside existing staff vacancy rates, long-term operational needs remain subject to change,” he wrote. “Should the need for out-of-state transfers arise in the future, any decision will be made with one primary priority: safety. The safety and security of our staff, the inmates in our custody, and our facilities will drive these determinations, not financial costs.” 
The department’s facilities are now “operating at full capacity,” according to Shannon. 
In addition to the inmates sent to Mississippi, the corrections department transferred 40 inmates to the Lincoln County Detention Center in Kemmerer and eight others to the Sublette County Detention Center in Pinedale. Now, about 24 inmates are housed at the Lincoln County Detention Center. All female inmates who were temporarily placed at the Sublette County Detention Center have returned to the Wyoming Women’s Center in Lusk, Shannon wrote. 
The department also has “active housing partnerships with other local county jails across the state,” Shannon said. “Because all state-operated WDOC facilities are presently operating at full capacity, the department continues to actively seek out and evaluate additional county housing options in anticipation of ongoing capacity demands.” 
WyoFile reporter Maggie Mullen contributed to this story.

title: New work requirements could affect 250,000 Oklahomans on SoonerCare, agency warns
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Over 250,000 Oklahomans have been sent letters warning that new federal work requirements may put them at risk of losing their Medicaid health coverage.   The Oklahoma Health Care Authority on Wednesday said yellow letters were sent last week and any Oklahoman who receives one should follow the enclosed instructions to ensure they […]
text:
New federal work requirements could affect eligibility for a quarter of a million Oklahomans on SoonerCare. (Photo via Getty Images)OKLAHOMA CITY — Over 250,000 Oklahomans have been sent letters warning that new federal work requirements may put them at risk of losing their Medicaid health coverage.  
The Oklahoma Health Care Authority on Wednesday said yellow letters were sent last week and any Oklahoman who receives one should follow the enclosed instructions to ensure they maintain their eligibility. 
The letters were sent to only people who received coverage as part of Oklahoma’s voter-approved Medicaid expansion, an agency spokesperson said. 
As of July, there were over 1 million Oklahomans on SoonerCare, the state’s Medicaid program, and new work requirements passed by Congress as part of the “One Big Beautiful Bill” could affect nearly a quarter of them when they take effect Jan. 1, the spokesperson said. 
Under the requirements passed by Congress last year, adults ages 19 to 64 must either work 80 hours a month or demonstrate a minimum monthly income of $580 to maintain their eligibility for Medicaid. 
Hours can be through employment, community service and work or educational programs, according to the Health Care Authority. 
There are some exemptions to these requirements, including for people with specific disabilities, those who have dependents, pregnant and postpartum women, and some veterans. 
Receiving one of the yellow letters from the Health Care Authority means the individual may need to take action to stay eligible for Medicaid, according to a news release. The state agency will use information on file to determine who meets the requirements and will send follow up notices if more information is needed. 
The Health Care Authority is recommending that members update their contact information and watch for communications in their mail or email.
More information about the work requirements and exemptions are available on the Health Care Authority’s website.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri vote on initiative protections now before the state Supreme Court
description: Whether Missourians will vote on a measure making voter-initiated laws and constitutional amendments harder to change is in the hands of the Missouri Supreme Court. The court on Wednesday heard arguments to overturn the decision of Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, who on Aug. 4 declared the initiative that would be Amendment 6 to be […]
text:
Attorney Chuck Hatfield argues Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026, for the Missouri Supreme Court to order two measures to be on the November ballot over the objections of Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).Whether Missourians will vote on a measure making voter-initiated laws and constitutional amendments harder to change is in the hands of the Missouri Supreme Court.
The court on Wednesday heard arguments to overturn the decision of Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, who on Aug. 4 declared the initiative that would be Amendment 6 to be insufficient. Hoskins said it improperly covers more than one subject and changes more than one article of the Missouri Constitution, a decision upheld late last month by Cole County Circuit Judge Daniel Green.
The court is being asked to rule that Hoskins was wrong in his analysis and that he lacked the authority to use the final signature certification process to declare that a proposed measure has constitutional flaws.
“This is the first time I can find that a secretary has decided an initiative insufficient on this basis,” said Chuck Hatfield, the attorney for two plaintiffs representing the political action committee Respect MO Voters. WHOEVER THE PLAINTIFFS ARE.“I don’t think the certificate sufficiently explains the reasons.”
The arguments come just about a month after voters buried a measure designed to make initiatives more difficult to pass. If the court agrees that the initiative proposed by the political action committee Respect MO Voters should go on the ballot, voters will be asked if they want to make measures they pass more difficult for lawmakers to change.
The court also must decide whether Hoskins can revise the ballot language he wrote in 2025 before signatures were gathered. In the pre-argument brief prepared by the attorney general’s office, Hoskins said the language was deceptive.
Kathleen Hunker of the Missouri attorney general’s office argues against allowing a state vote on an initiative to limits legislative power to change measures initiated by voters (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
“Frankly, the prior ballot title would have defrauded Missourians and violated the law,” attorney Kathleen Hunker of the attorney general’s office wrote in her pre-argument filing.
Amendment 6, if passed, would put heavy restrictions on the ability of lawmakers to alter state laws and constitutional amendments proposed by initiative and approved by voters. Any changes would have to receive 80% support in the General Assembly and be ratified in a statewide vote.
Currently, there are no restrictions on lawmakers altering or repealing laws passed by initiative. That happened in 2025, when Republicans forced through a bill that repealed paid sick leave for Missouri workers and inflation adjustments to the minimum wage.
A majority of lawmakers in both chambers can propose changes in constitutional amendments but those changes must also pass statewide. 
That happened in 2020, when voters approved changes to the terms of a legislative redistricting proposal passed by initiative in 2018. Amendment 3 on the Nov. 3 ballot seeks to overturn the abortion rights measure approved in 2024.
The proposal would apply not only to measures approved in the future but also to laws and constitutional amendments previously enacted through the initiative process. 
For example, lawmakers left the $15 per hour minimum wage approved in 2024 in place when they passed the bill repealing sick leave. If Amendment 6 is ultimately approved by voters, changing that minimum wage in the future would require an 80% vote in the General Assembly and statewide voter approval.
To achieve that majority, a bill would have to have broad bipartisan support. Republicans won 111 of 163 seats in the Missouri House in 2024 and hold 24 of 34 seats in the state Senate. An 80% majority would require 131 votes in the Missouri House and 28 in the state Senate.
In arguments before the court, Hatfield defended the initiative from charges it is too broad and said Hoskins’ ballot language shows it. After reading the ballot title — and the one Hoskins has proposed to replace it — Hatfield said the secretary’s language proves his point.
“Every provision of this initiative has to do with initiative and referendum by the secretary’s own document,” Hatfield said. “I just don’t understand how there could be any doubt about it.”
Hunker said the initiative would unconstitutionally limit the power of lawmakers and the people to change state law or the constitution. 
“Amendment 6 is a profoundly anti-democratic proposal,” Hunker said. “It insulates itself…from reconsideration by the people in the future.”
Along with setting standards for changing anything presented by initiative in the future, Hunker said, “it smuggles in numerous subjects unrelated to the initiative process.”
Some of the questions being raised about the initiative are not ready for the courts, Chief Justice W. Brent Powell said as he questioned Hunker.
“Don’t we have to wait to take up those challenges if the initiative passes?” Powell asked. “Even if we are examining this through the eyes of the secretary of state, it is not law yet.”

 Roth faced pressure from fellow Democrats to clear way for independent candidate 

Roth announced he was ending his campaign on July 28, the Idaho Capital Sun reported. He had faced strong pressure from supporters of independent candidate Todd Achilles, who argued an independent had a better chance of defeating the longtime incumbent in a head-to-head race. Roth did not endorse Achilles. 
Roth told the Sun he didn’t want to drop out, but he felt like he didn’t have a choice. He’d also received a letter from leaders of Ada County Democrats asking him to drop out, the Spokesman-Review reported. 
“Without support from Ada County, I mean that really hindered fundraising or campaign ability,” Roth told the Sun in a phone interview. “And when you have so many people who hold leadership positions in the party advocating for a candidate besides their nominee, it makes it really just impossible.” 
Roth’s most recent federal election filing shows he garnered about $14,600 in contributions but that his campaign had about $10,100 in debts and loans to be paid back, as of June 30. 
Roth ran for federal office in 2022 and 2024 and for the state Legislature in 2020. He said this run was “probably the worst experience I’ve ever been through in my entire life.”
“And I’ve been through a lot,” he said. 
He expressed disappointment in his party leaders for not supporting the Democratic nominee in the race after he won his primary contest in May. 
“It’s an unfortunate situation,” he said. “I think the Democratic voters of Idaho have really lost their opportunity to have a voice, and I think it just goes to show how broken our whole system is.” 
Achilles’ most recent campaign finance filing shows he’s raised nearly $700,000, although his campaign has recently advertised he’s collected over $1 million. Risch’s warchest was more than $4.4 million as of June 30. The Federal Election Commission requires quarterly reporting on campaign contributions and expenditures, and the next filing deadline is Oct. 15. 
Without Roth’s formal withdrawal, his name would’ve still appeared on the Nov. 3 general election ballot. Achilles’ campaign has repeatedly said his odds are better if the contest is between him and Risch. 
“I respect Roth running and making the decision that the campaign just didn’t have the resources it needed to be competitive,” Achilles said in an interview. “I think it’s all about being competitive.”
After Roth’s withdrawal, Achilles said his campaign’s plan is to, “keep doing what we’re doing, which is just being out there talking Idahoans and you know working hard on a campaign.”
Risch in an interview for an August story told the Sun he was not concerned after Roth announced his departure from the race. 
“I know people are getting excited all of a sudden because I was running against two Democrats, and now I’m running against one Democrat,” Risch said, referencing that Achilles previously was a Democratic state legislator. “I’ve done that all my life.” 
Risch, Achilles, independent Natalie Fleming and Libertarian Matt Loesby will appear on ballots for the U.S. Senate race.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Legislature rejects Dem-led attempts to add childcare, data center moratorium for special session
description: North Dakota Democratic lawmakers tried to introduce bills on childcare funding and a moratorium on data center permitting during the special session Wednesday, but the attempts were voted down or blocked by each Republican-led chamber. House Minority Leader Zac Ista, D-Grand Forks, urged lawmakers to consider debating a proposal to add $9 million for childc[...]
text:
House Minority Leader Zac Ista, D-Grand Forks, speaks on the House floor during a special session of the Legislature on Sept. 2, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota Democratic lawmakers tried to introduce bills on childcare funding and a moratorium on data center permitting during the special session Wednesday, but the attempts were voted down or blocked by each Republican-led chamber.
House Minority Leader Zac Ista, D-Grand Forks, urged lawmakers to consider debating a proposal to add $9 million for childcare assistance to get low-income families off of a growing waitlist. 
Senate Minority Leader Kathy Hogan, D-Fargo, had pushed for the bill ahead of the session, but a panel of legislative leaders did not advance it. About 1,900 North Dakota families are on a waitlist to receive state childcare assistance.
Grand Forks Dems blast special session priorities, call for focus on families

Ista told House lawmakers that childcare needs affect every legislative district, family and the state’s workforce. Childcare providers are also being strained financially, he said.
“This is an urgent issue that cannot wait until January 2027,” Ista said. 
House Majority Leader Mike Lefor, R-Dickinson, said the bill was debated during Legislative Management prior to the special session, including discussion about a recent significant increase in state spending on childcare. In addition, an interim legislative committee that meets Sept. 9 is studying the programs.
“The interim committee is looking at what is the effectiveness of different programs within childcare, and I’d ask you to continue to allow the interim committee to continue to do their work,” Lefor said.
House Majority Leader Mike Lefor, R-Dickinson, speaks on the House floor during a special session of the Legislature on Sept. 2, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
House lawmakers rejected a motion to introduce the childcare funding bill on a 72-21 vote.
Hogan tried to introduce the childcare bill in the Senate, but Majority Leader Sen. David Hogue, R-Minot, objected. A voice vote to override the objection failed. 
Rep. Gretchen Dobervich, D-Fargo, attempted to introduce a data center permitting moratorium bill, but that motion failed on a 68-25 vote. The proposal led by Sen. Tim Mathern, D-Fargo, called for a temporary pause to data center permitting through June 2027.
“Data centers are not a black and white issue,” Dobervich said. “There are benefits and legitimate concerns that are being raised across North Dakota.”
In the Senate, Sen. Ryan Braunberger, D-Fargo, attempted to introduce a similar data center moratorium, but Hogue objected to the motion to introduce the bill. There was no motion to overturn Hogue’s objection.
North Dakota lawmaker eyes data center transparency, temporary moratorium for special session

During a press conference Friday morning, Sen. Jamie Selzler, D-Fargo, said the lawmakers were attempting to introduce the bills for discussion. 
“We just wanted to talk about it,” Selzler said. “Republicans are not listening, because if they were listening, they’d be willing to talk about these things.”
Lawmakers have five bills to consider during the special session, which is expected to take three days.
After the votes in the House, Rep. Matthew Ruby, R-Minot, co-chair of the Policy Committee during the special session, said Democratic lawmakers exercised their rights within House rules.
“At this point, we just don’t have the time to dig into it,” Ruby said. “And simply throwing money at it (childcare) might not be the best way to go about it.”
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling can be reached at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com.
