name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Republicans need a new approach
description: A former New Mexico Republican official addresses the state party with an assessment and advice for the future.
text:
The swag table at the 2026 New Mexico Republican Pre-primary Convention as seen on March 6, 2026. (Danielle Prokop/Source NM)My boys, Bryce and Taylor, have spent more Saturdays in a rodeo arena than anywhere else. Team roping is their primary event; however, they will enter in whatever involves a horse and a rope. Out there, the lesson never changes. The clock doesn’t care whose fault it was. You miss your loop, rope a leg, bobble your tie, and you don’t get to blame your horse or the cow. You go back to the trailer, figure out what went wrong, and fix it before your next run. That’s the whole code out here: accountability, honor, respect, humility, honesty. No excuses. Just miles to relive those costly mistakes, lessons learned and corrections made.
I can’t help but wonder where the Republican Party of New Mexico would be if we got rid of the excuses. It’s September, and excuses are about all we’ve got for an organization that’s supposed to represent roughly one in three voters in this state.
This year has been riddled with embarrassment for the conservative movement here. Our House caucus chair nearly didn’t make her own ballot. A governor candidate spent most of his campaign proving he actually lived in New Mexico, and a sitting party chair was removed from office by a judge. Our state party treasurer is in jail, and nobody’s formally filled the treasurer’s post either, at least not that I’ve heard. On top of that, we nearly failed to field candidates for U.S. Senate, state treasurer, and state auditor, leaving Republican primary voters with only write-in candidates for all three statewide offices.
Here’s the deeper problem, and it’s the one nobody wants to say out loud: We haven’t given people a real plan they can see five years from now, backed by values instead of slogans. Without that, you don’t get new voters, new donors, or good people willing to put their name on a ballot and take the hits that come with it. What you get is exactly what we have: 378,000 New Mexicans who’ve looked at both parties and picked neither, and a bench so thin we’re begging people to run as write-ins weeks before a deadline.
Until this party turns the page, the people with something real riding on New Mexico don’t have the luxury of waiting for it to sort itself out. That means the job creators and people investing capital in the industries that sustain this state: energy, oil and gas, construction, agriculture, and tourism. It means the businesses that helped build the way of life many of us grew up with. And it means the parents who simply want their kids to have a future here instead of a reason to leave.
We make do. We run our operations, raise our families, and hope the people we vote for eventually catch up to the seriousness of the moment.
Turning the page doesn’t require a rebrand or a new slogan. It takes three things, and none of them are complicated. First, integrity — leaders who own a bad quarter instead of blaming someone else for it. Second, leadership that is not fearful of hiring someone better than they are. Third, reigniting the Christian values that embody the principals necessary to promote lasting change. If our principles are fleeting, our influence will be short lived.
Until we have all three, we’ll do what New Mexicans have always done. We’ll play the hand we’re dealt.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana’s new anti-homelessness law punishes people already living a sentence
description: A new Louisiana law creates the crime of unauthorized camping, which could punish the homeless with fines they can't pay or unpaid labor.
text:
A homeless encampment in Paterson, N.J. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Throughout my life, I have seen my share of homeless people. Some of my own relatives have been homeless, and it saddens me to see men, women and children without shelter. 
On June 9, Act 788 went into effect in Louisiana. It creates a new crime, unauthorized camping, defined as intentionally using a tent, shelter or bedding overnight in a public space not designated for camping. It’s punishable by a fine of up to $500, up to six months in jail or both. 
The law also allows local homelessness court programs, meant to steer people toward treatment instead of a cell. To be eligible, defendants must agree to waive their right to a trial, and their case may be dismissed if they complete the program. If they fail, they would go on to sentencing. If they cannot afford the cost of their own treatment, the court might order them to perform unpaid labor instead.
A homeless person could be fined money they don’t have. To have them serve time for the condition they are already in is absurd.
Research shows homelessness is already a psychological trauma similar to being in prison. A University of Kentucky study found that older homeless men described “feeling imprisoned by the systemic issues around homelessness,” the isolation, the mistreatment, the constant exposure to danger, long before any of them ever saw the inside of a jail cell.
For the homeless already enduring trauma, this legislation will serve only to intensify their suffering. 
Many are former veterans. A Yale University study determined that those with a history of homelessness had significantly higher rates of post-traumatic stress disorder, depression and anxiety than veterans who were never homeless. More than 80% became homeless only after their military service ended. 
A significant portion of the unhoused population consists of domestic violence survivors, specifically women and children. A University of Hawaii at Manoa review consistently labeled domestic violence as a leading cause of homelessness for women and children, not merely a contributing factor. 
This is who Louisiana’s new law reaches: People who have escaped violence and now face punishment for having nowhere else to go.
Researchers from Columbia and Boston universities connected housing insecurity after a person is released from to lost earnings, and they tied lost earnings federal “one-strike” policies that can bar people with certain criminal records, drug convictions especially, from public housing. 
Findings from the University of California at San Francisco put it plainly: Mass incarceration and homelessness are driven by the same structural factors, and they exacerbate one another in a feedback loop. People experiencing homelessness face a heightened risk of justice-system involvement simply for engaging in survival behaviors in public. 
This is almost a direct description of what Louisiana’s new law does.
So the person coming out of jail, having served time or performed labor because they couldn’t pay a fine, goes back on the streets. They are still homeless. Now they also have a fine or a debt. They have no job, no income and are still without shelter. 
Why does Louisiana always seem to be pushing to go in the opposite direction from other states? Why is incarceration always the first tool that our policymakers reach for in their toolbox when it comes to social problems in our community? 
There is a proven alternative: A joint federal agency study examined the housing-first model, where the homeless are provided with permanent, independent housing without them first needing to stop using substances, complete treatment or show they are “ready.” Support services — including mental healthcare, addiction assistance and job support — are offered once they have housing, not used to block them from getting it. 
Instead, our lawmakers chose the treatment-first model, one that requires someone to get sober or stabilize their mental health before they’re considered ready for housing. 
Louisiana does not have to look far for a different path. Pennsylvania and Illinois have introduced bills that would make it illegal to enforce camping bans without adequate shelter available. California, even amid its struggles, passed legislation protecting people who help the unhoused. 
Finland’s national housing program — offering permanent housing first with no requirement to be sober or “treatment ready” before receiving it — cut long-term homelessness 72% over a decade. 
In Vancouver, Canada, housing-first approaches have reduced criminal sentences among people with mental illness who received housing instead of an ultimatum.
Louisiana keeps choosing everything that will bring it down rather than reaching for what has already been shown elsewhere to lift up people.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Governor urges permanent ban on all kratom in North Dakota
description: North Dakota Gov. Kelly Armstrong called on the Legislature Wednesday to prohibit kratom “in all its forms,” a boost for efforts to ban the substance as lawmakers deliberate what action to take. The Republican governor’s roughly nine-minute State of the State address came at the start of the special session he called last month for […]
text:
Gov. Kelly Armstrong gives a speech to a joint session of the Legislature on Sept. 2, 2026, during a special session. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota Gov. Kelly Armstrong called on the Legislature Wednesday to prohibit kratom “in all its forms,” a boost for efforts to ban the substance as lawmakers deliberate what action to take.
The Republican governor’s roughly nine-minute State of the State address came at the start of the special session he called last month for restricting kratom. A House-Senate policy committee is deliberating two bills to ban synthetic kratom products and to strictly regulate natural kratom with licensing and labeling requirements and various penalties for violations. 

More special session coverage

Armstrong cited moves to restrict or ban kratom and synthetic derivatives such as 7-OH by the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration and other states, as well as recommendations from public health officials and Republican Attorney General Drew Wrigley. Kratom is unregulated and the issue can’t wait months until the regular session next year, he said.
“People were overdosing and dying from a product that they could buy off the shelf without any regulations or any age restrictions. That’s why we took it off the shelves until you all could be convened,” Armstrong told lawmakers.
Public, lawmakers debate kratom regulation versus full ban in North Dakota

Last month, he banned all kratom products for 30 days, called the special session and approved an emergency pharmaceutical rule to ban 7-OH on the same level as LSD and heroin. Armstrong said his moves aligned with the DEA temporarily classifying 7-OH and related compounds as controlled substances.
Some people say natural kratom has helped them relieve pain, boost energy and combat opiate withdrawals. Others, including medical professionals and private citizens, have urged lawmakers to ban natural kratom and synthetic products across the board, calling kratom dangerous and addictive.
“I’m not really interested in anecdotal ‘wonder drug’ testimonials. I’m interested in verifiable data, and the problem with this product is there is none,” the governor said.
Armstrong cited comments by the DEA and U.S. Food and Drug Administration that kratom products are unregulated, lack data on quality control and bring risks such as liver toxicity and seizures. 
Since 2021, kratom or related substances have been part of the primary cause of 23 deaths in North Dakota, and a contributing cause in one additional death, according to the State Epidemiology Office. 
The governor outlined the state’s addiction resources, including eight behavioral health clinics around the state, online resources at hhs.nd.gov and help by calling 988.
He also specifically urged the Republican-led Legislature to ban the sale, possession and distribution of synthetic kratom, clarify enforcement authority of that ban and enact “reasonable criminal penalties” for buying and selling those synthetics.
What to know about the ban on kratom in North Dakota

“Getting the criminal policy correct on this is especially important. I don’t want to make someone a felon in September for something they could buy easily over the counter in July,” said Armstrong, a former criminal defense attorney. 
House and Senate Democrats, who unsuccessfully sought Wednesday to propose bills for more childcare funding and a moratorium on data center development, called the special session a missed opportunity to address affordability for families.
Armstrong pointed out the looming November general election and encouraged people to resist the urge for a little political grandstanding.” House Minority Leader Zac Ista, D-Grand Forks, said the special session gives lawmakers a chance to address issues they’re hearing about from voters on the campaign trail.
“It will be an egregiously wasted opportunity if all that’s accomplished this week is that we increase controlled substance regulation and we bail out a grossly mismanaged construction project,” Ista told reporters, referring to the stalled Military Gallery project on the Capitol grounds, which paused construction in July due to a fundraising shortfall.
Senate Bill 2407 proposes a $35 million line of credit and increased oversight for that project. 
The Legislature’s Joint Policy Committee was meeting after Armstrong’s speech to take up four bills, including the two kratom proposals: Senate Bill 2408 to ban synthetic kratom products, and House Bill 1628 to allow but regulate natural kratom.
Lawmakers have a goal of finishing the special session Friday, in three days.
Reach North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Video of 2 Mississippi County traffic stops prompt calls for Arkansas State Police investigation
description: The Democratic Party of Arkansas and the NAACP Arkansas State Conference are calling for a review of state police’s use-of-force policy after a video released over the weekend showed an officer pulling a man by his dreadlocks and punching him through a car’s broken backseat window. This is the second video of August traffic stops […]
text:
Rep. Tracy Steele, a North Little Rock Democrat, speaks at the Arkansas Legislative Black Caucus meeting on Tuesday, August 25, 2026 at the Arkansas State Capitol in Little Rock, Arkansas. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)The Democratic Party of Arkansas and the NAACP Arkansas State Conference are calling for a review of state police’s use-of-force policy after a video released over the weekend showed an officer pulling a man by his dreadlocks and punching him through a car’s broken backseat window.
This is the second video of August traffic stops in Mississippi County that have gained national attention and shown an Arkansas State Police officer striking Black civilians. 
The first incident, which involved an officer punching an 18-year-old during an Aug. 1 traffic stop near Manila, resulted in a civil rights lawsuit. 
Col. Mike Hagar, Arkansas State Police director, last week canceled his appearance at an Arkansas Legislative Black Caucus to discuss the incident citing the lawsuit.
Black lawmakers frustrated by Arkansas State Police head’s absence from meeting about traffic stop

Hagar defended State Police’s use of force in a statement Tuesday, but did not address the specific incidents.
Black lawmakers expressed frustration with Hagar’s absence from last week’s meeting, and repeated their concerns after the release of footage showing a second violent traffic stop in northeast Arkansas. 
“There are broader concerns regarding Arkansas State Police policies, training, use-of-force practices, de-escalation, accountability, community trust, and public safety that members of the Caucus have a responsibility to address on behalf of the Arkansans we represent,” Caucus Vice Chair Sen. Jamie Scott, a Democrat from North Little Rock, said in a statement Monday. “Those issues do not disappear simply because litigation is pending in a particular case.” 
The Aug. 19 incident occurred following a high-speed chase, according to NEA Report, who obtained video that shows Trooper Theodore Henderson breaking a rear passenger window, then pulling Tedrick Washington Jr. by his dreadlocks and punching him in the face. 
The State Police Highway Patrol Division documented 939 uses of force during the more than 1,026,000 Officer Violator Contacts made between January 2023 and Aug. 28, 2026, Hagar said. That’s less than 1% of all contacts, he said. 
“Recently released videos of use-of-force incidents are being sensationalized and monetized on social media,” Hagar said. “When streamers determined these videos would generate revenue, they scoured archives and re-released older videos, presenting them as new and creating a false narrative.”
Hagar reiterated that State Police would not comment on specific incidents involving use of force that have active criminal and civil cases pending, but said “any use of force by an ASP Trooper is a regrettable last resort and reviewed carefully.”
Barry Jefferson, president of the NAACP Arkansas State Conference, said officers “must meet high standards of professionalism, constitutional compliance, and respect for the dignity and rights of the people they serve.” 
Conclusions about an officer’s conduct must be based on verified evidence, he said. 
“Reports of repeated encounters have raised community concerns about the Arkansas State Police’s use-of-force practices, training, supervision, transparency, and accountability,” Jefferson said in a statement Monday. “Whether these incidents reflect a broader pattern should be determined through a thorough review of reliable evidence and relevant records.”

title: Severe weather hampers State Fair attendance
description: The Indiana State Fair drew 800,641 people over its 15-day run — a 7% drop in attendance from last year caused by significant weather events. Severe storms required multiple temporary closures and periods of sheltering throughout the fair to prioritize the safety of guests, exhibitors and staff, a news release said. “We are incredibly grateful […]
text:
The Indiana State Fair Midway welcomes patrons during the 2026 State Fair. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The Indiana State Fair drew 800,641 people over its 15-day run — a 7% drop in attendance from last year caused by significant weather events.
Severe storms required multiple temporary closures and periods of sheltering throughout the fair to prioritize the safety of guests, exhibitors and staff, a news release said.
“We are incredibly grateful to every Hoosier who chose to spend part of their summer with us at the Indiana State Fair,” said Ray Allison, the Indiana State Fair Commission’s executive director. “This year reminded us that the Fair is about much more than rides, concerts, food and exhibits. It’s about people. It’s about coming together, making memories and celebrating what makes Indiana special. When Mother Nature challenged us, our fairgoers, employees, vendors, exhibitors and partners showed incredible patience, understanding and still had a great time.”
This year’s theme was “Always a Hit,” carrying baseball across attractions, food and entertainment around the fairgrounds. It also dovetailed with celebrations of the nation’s 250th anniversary by pairing two long-standing American summer traditions — baseball and fairs.
The State Fair and Indianapolis Indians also announced they have entered into a long-term agreement to install a permanent wiffle ball field at the State Fairgrounds. While details are still being finalized, Schumacher Stadium will ensure a new experience for fairgoers, to build new traditions and make more memories throughout their summertime visit.
“Our partnership with the State Fair brought two great Indiana traditions together,” said Randy Lewandowski, Indianapolis Indians president and CEO. “The response to the Schumacher Stadium Wiffle Ball field was tremendous, and we’re proud it will now have a permanent home at the Fairgrounds.”
Here are some overall numbers and data about the 2026 Indiana State Fair:

The fair recorded its strongest final week since expanding to the three-weekend format in 2009, setting attendance records. The final Sunday, Aug. 23 set the second-highest final-day attendance since 2009.
Record breaking crowds attended the newly renovated Hoosier Lottery Free Stage concerts, including an estimated 9,000 concertgoers to see Josiah Queen — the largest crowd in Hoosier Lottery Free Stage history.
Five days of gate closures and sheltering in place.

Next year’s fair will run Aug. 6-22 and will be the 170th edition.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: As hemp’s future hangs in the balance, NC policymakers look ahead to regulate cannabis
description: When members of the North Carolina House and Senate reconvene in November, they will be faced with having to decide how to regulate intoxicating hemp products. The two chambers were at odds in July over House Bill 328, which would ban hemp with more than 0.4 milligrams of THC and prohibit the sale of any […]
text:
North Carolina lawmakers are trying to navigate how to best protect minors from hemp-derived cannabinoids, while also preparing for a future that could include some form of legal cannabis.(Photo: Amanda Watford/Stateline)When members of the North Carolina House and Senate reconvene in November, they will be faced with having to decide how to regulate intoxicating hemp products. The two chambers were at odds in July over House Bill 328, which would ban hemp with more than 0.4 milligrams of THC and prohibit the sale of any hemp consumables, including CBD, to anyone under 21.
House members opted to wait until after November’s midterm elections, not wanting to upset a $4 billion industry that employs 16,000 people in North Carolina.
In Washington, the hemp industry received a one-month reprieve this week from a national ban on intoxicating hemp products as part of a short-term funding bill. The U.S. House delayed the ban from taking effect until Dec. 11, as the White House pushes to delay or somehow fix the national ban. At the same time, the Trump administration has called on the U.S. Department of Justice to reclassify marijuana as a Schedule III drug, the same class as Tylenol.
While the outlook is hazy, the end of the year could bring big changes for both the hemp and cannabis industries.
Hemp consumables are largely unrestricted in our state, but North Carolina is in the unique minority of states in which marijuana is fully illegal for both recreational and medicinal purposes.
State lawmakers are trying to navigate how to best protect minors from hemp-derived cannabinoids, while also preparing for a future that could include some form of legal cannabis.
39 states, 39 approaches
The North Carolina Advisory Council on Cannabis, appointed in June 2025 by Gov. Josh Stein, has been meeting for months to develop a comprehensive approach to regulate cannabis sales and create a safe, legal market for adults that protects kids.
Nearly 40 states have already enacted cannabis regulations, but no two are the same.
Yasha Kahn (Photo: MCR Labs)
Yasha Kahn, co-founder of MCR Labs, has been involved in cannabis testing for more than a decade. Kahn was invited to offer his expertise to the advisory council last week, as that group explores a framework for legalization.
North Carolina policymakers will have to decide on an endless number of variables in regulating cannabis, including who should handle testing and at what point in the process the product should be tested.
Kahn said each state has unique testing requirements with no real consensus. And each state may have its own approach to testing batch sizes, packaging, total THC definitions, and regulatory audits.
“Instead of looking at this as a huge mess, it really is 39 individual experiments on policy with much of the data available that we can analyze,” said Kahn. “We can see which policies have worked, which ones haven’t.”
Kahn said cannabis has the potential to be a multi-billion-dollar industry for North Carolina.
Balancing testing and oversight
The advisory committee will also have to decide whether to use private labs or state labs to test the purity and potency of cannabis if it should become legal. Either way, Kahn recommended the state should require all lab results be made public and shared with state agencies.
“How long would it take to have a testing lab to be up and running and producing results?” asked council member Pat Oglesby.
Kahn said there are hemp labs that would likely be willing to take on the testing for a slice of a booming industry, but establishing an accredited lab from scratch would take time.
NC House delays vote on hemp ban until November as advocates pack hallways

“A lot of instruments have months of delays just to be delivered. You have to have capital and good talent,” said Kahn. “I’ve heard of labs opening within maybe nine months. In my experience, it’s closer to a year and a half.”
Privatizing testing, however, comes with risk, Kahn said, as consumer fraud has been documented in multiple states.
A store owner, for example, may find a low THC product is not selling well and urge the cultivator to produce a stronger product. The cultivator may then call the lab and suggest they provide higher THC results, or they will find a new lab to deliver those results.
“This happens in every market that has more than one lab,” Kahn cautioned.
Kahn said this deception becomes easier to trace when the labs are required to share data with the state and those results are made public.
In Colorado, THC potency inflation and the failure to identify mold and other contaminants has legislators considering shifting their cannabis testing to the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment. Lawmakers there are also considering having state regulators collect the samples to be tested from dispensaries, rather than samples being provided by the producer or cultivators.
Will the industry bloom in North Carolina?
Dr. Larry Greenblatt, state health director and chief medical officer (Photo: NCDHHS)
Dr. Larry Greenblatt, state health director and co-chair of the advisory council, said while it may appear that North Carolina is marching toward some form of cannabis legalization, it’s by no means a foregone conclusion.
“We are not in any way convinced that we are definitely moving to be a marijuana-legal state,” said Greenblatt. “It could happen, but it may not.”
The advisory group’s final recommendations, including a detailed look at lab testing, will be included in a report to the governor at the end of this year. It would then be up to the legislature to decide if they want to use the information as the foundation or guidance for a cannabis market in North Carolina.
Stein has said he supports legalization for adults, but Republican lawmakers are divided. Recent attempts to legalize medical marijuana have died in the state House, despite the backing of Senate leaders. And neither chamber has ever voted to legalize the drug for recreational use.
Meantime, other states are moving ahead. In neighboring Virginia, regulators will begin accepting applications for regulated recreational cannabis dispensaries in February, with a retail launch set for July 1, 2027.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Rio Grande in Albuquerque reaches historic dryness level
description: Amid historic dryness, 615 million gallons of water will course through the Rio Grande in Albuquerque this week to help dying vegetation and also provide scientists with data about the ongoing drought.
text:
More than 112 miles of the Rio Grande in Albuquerque were dry as of Aug. 30, 2026, which marks the most dry miles in at least two decades. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)Amid historic dryness, 615 million gallons of water will course through the Rio Grande in Albuquerque this week to help dying vegetation and also provide scientists with data about the ongoing drought.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
As of Sunday, a total of 112.4 miles of Rio Grande between the Cochiti and Elephant Butte Reservoir was dry, Sharon Wirth, Middle Rio Grande bureau chief with the Interstate Stream Commission, told Source NM on Tuesday. 
That’s the highest number of dry miles since at least 2007, according to the River Eyes Rio Grande Monitoring Program, and far more than the previous record of 78.9 miles set in 2025. 
The Albuquerque-Bernalillo County Water Authority announced Tuesday that it had released the 615 million gallons of water Monday from the Abiquiu Reservoir and expects it to reach the city by Thursday. 
“This one-time release will allow us to gather important data about how water flows through the river following a period of extended dryness, the relationship between the river and groundwater, and the effect of such a water release on plants and trees,” Water Authority Board Chair Barbara Baca said in a statement. “It’s also our hope that this will aid vegetation and wildlife affected by the ongoing drought.”
The pulse of 2,000 acre-feet of water down the river will also, at least temporarily, stop a drying pattern that has already reached historic levels. 
The “temporary re-wetting,” as Baca called it, comes amid uncertain weather forecasts from meteorologists about the remainder of the monsoon season and upcoming winter. September is a notoriously difficult month to predict in New Mexico, National Weather Service meteorologist Matt Demaria told Source NM on Tuesday, and the impacts of a strengthening El Niño remain to be seen in the Southwest. 
Still, even if the state experienced normal or slightly above normal precipitation the rest of this season, record low snowpack last winter means the river will likely remain mostly empty of water in Albuquerque this year, DeMaria said. 
Aridification is here

“It kind of doesn’t really matter what happens during the monsoon season when we have record-low snowpack,” he said, especially in the mountains in northern New Mexico and Colorado that feed the river’s headwaters. 
The drying river has taken its toll on plants and wildlife. DeMaria reviewed satellite data Tuesday capturing what he described as “pretty significant degradation” of vegetation along the river.
“But most people can probably tell by just looking down in the bosque, how stressed it is with the lack of water,” he said. 
The drying river has impacts beyond trees and wildlife. Middle Rio Grande water managers told lawmakers on the interim Water and Natural Resources Committee earlier this week that they need additional funding to help address the buildup of sediment from low or non-existent flows.
“We aren’t seeing those high flows pretty much anymore, and even when we do, it’s not able to do the work of scouring and cleaning the river channel,” the Interstate Stream Commission’s Wirth  said. “So the river now requires us to take human mechanical intervention to help improve that.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Livingston County sheriff temporarily removes Flock cameras after repeated vandalism
description: Livingston County Sheriff Mike Murphy said that the county has temporarily removed all of its Flock cameras — the controversial automatic license plate readers that have stirred bipartisan pushback across Michigan and the country — in the wake of a repeated string of vandalism incidents targeting the cameras.  “We took them down just to avoid any […]
text:
A Flock license plate reader camera in Southfield. July 3, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. Livingston County Sheriff Mike Murphy said that the county has temporarily removed all of its Flock cameras — the controversial automatic license plate readers that have stirred bipartisan pushback across Michigan and the country — in the wake of a repeated string of vandalism incidents targeting the cameras. 
“We took them down just to avoid any more vandalism,” he said. “Frankly, we’re trying to figure out how we can best protect our investment, and how we can hold those accountable that do the vandalism because it’s a felony. You can voice opposition against something all you want, but destroying property’s not the way to do it.”
He said that the county does not have a timeline for when they will put the cameras back up, but that they do intend to return the devices to operation once the sheriff’s office has determined how best to prevent future vandalism.
The county had about 25 cameras active prior to their temporary removal, Murphy said. 
But while Livingston County plans to maintain a Flock presence, jurisdictions around the state — from Menominee in the far western part of the Upper Peninsula to Westland in the Detroit suburbs — have canceled or rejected contracts with Flock entirely in recent months. Most recently, on Tuesday night, Monroe County voted to end its Flock program. 
Livingston County Sheriff Mike Murphy at roundtable discussion in Detroit featuring Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem. June 20, 2025 | Photo by Wali Khan/Michigan Advance
Murphy defended the use of Flock cameras as an investigative tool — emphasizing that, while some believe that the cameras have capabilities like facial recognition, all the cameras can actually do is take a photo of the license plate. The argument of the investigative importance of the cameras has been cited by other police departments around the state in defending their own contracts with Flock. 
Murphy also emphasized that in today’s “data-driven society,” technology including cell phones and even vehicles also collect extensive amounts of personal information — so he does not understand the specific pushback against Flock. 
“If you’re that worried about your privacy, instead of not going by a camera location, you’re gonna go out there and destroy it,” he said. “That, to me, doesn’t make any sense. But that’s where we’re at as a society today, unfortunately.”
Grassroots groups in the county have expressed opposition to the cameras — Stand Against Extremism LivCo launched a petition to remove Flock cameras from Livingston County permanently.  
“We don’t want to give the federal government tools that can surveil our community,” the petition reads as among the group’s reasons for the cameras’ removal. “Police nationwide can search the same database, this has already been abused for unrelated investigations.”
Among the group’s concerns are a lack of public oversight on the management of the data collected, as well as the amount of taxpayer dollars being spent on the cameras.

title: AI could upend the headquarters economy that made Minnesota rich
description: Several years ago, I spoke to Jawed Karim, a former St. Paul resident who co-founded YouTube before Google purchased it in 2005. text:
(David Espejo/Stock photo via Getty Images)Several years ago, I spoke to Jawed Karim, a former St. Paul resident who co-founded YouTube before Google purchased it in 2005.
A soft-spoken computer engineer who is part Bengali and German, Karim somehow escaped the celebrity spotlight of the early internet entrepreneurs who made their fortunes during the first decade of the 21st century.
Karim was in town to promote his new venture capital fund when he said something about Silicon Valley and the Midwest that has stayed with me ever since.
“In Silicon Valley, if people hear that you’re working for Oracle or Cisco, they will feel bad for you and say, ‘Hey, I can help you get a job at a startup,'” Karim told me. “In Minnesota, if people hear you’re working for a startup, they will feel bad for you and say, ‘Hey, I can help you get a job at 3M.'”
At the time, I took his observation as a critique of the Midwest’s lack of risk tolerance, one reason Minnesota has struggled to attract venture capital and launch tech startups in significant numbers. But over the years, I began asking a different question: What if Minnesota’s economic model wasn’t broken? What if it was simply different?
Rather than producing hundreds of venture-backed startups, Minnesota built one of the nation’s strongest headquarters economies. An unusually high concentration of Fortune 500 companies has generated high-paying jobs, billions in investment and a remarkable tradition of corporate philanthropy.
That model has served the state extraordinarily well.
However, Minnesota’s greatest economic strength could also become its greatest weakness.
The rapid emergence of generative artificial intelligence, including ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude, threatens many of the white-collar professions on which Minnesota’s headquarters economy depends: lawyers, engineers, communications professionals, accountants, market analysts and sales representatives.
“AI represents a particular vulnerability to our economy,” said Aaron Rosenthal, research director for North Star Policy Action, a local left-leaning think tank. “We tend to have a disproportionate number of white-collar jobs that’s more susceptible to AI.”
Rosenthal, along with researchers at the University of St. Thomas, recently authored a report estimating that one-third of Minnesota’s labor force — roughly 800,000 workers — are employed in occupations with “high levels of exposure” to AI.
So far, there is little evidence that AI is replacing workers in significant numbers. But given the speed and scale of the technology, it would be naive to assume the state can indefinitely resist its disruptive pull.
“This is the Second Industrial Revolution sped up to the max,” Rosenthal said.
That raises a larger question: If AI dramatically increases productivity, who will capture those gains? Will Minnesota’s corporate giants use AI primarily to reduce costs and boost shareholder returns? Or will they use it to launch new products, create new business lines, invest in new ventures and generate the next generation of Minnesota jobs?
Headquarters economy
That Minnesota has been home to so many Fortune 500 companies remains something of a mystery, even to experts who have studied the issue.
“It’s not like we were just gifted all of these headquarters,” Myles Shaver, a professor of corporate strategy and strategic management at the University of Minnesota, said in an interview. “It was a confluence of different things.”
In his book Headquarters Economy, Shaver points to the Twin Cities’ location along the Mississippi River and its proximity to Canada, advantages that helped give rise to the state’s mining, agriculture, and milling industries.
But even Shaver acknowledges that geography alone cannot explain why Minnesota became home to such a diverse collection of industries, including retail, food, health care and financial services.
In addition to publicly traded corporations like Target, 3M, General Mills, U.S. Bancorp and UnitedHealth Group, the state is home to some of the nation’s largest private companies, including Cargill and Thomson Reuters. Non-proft Mayo Clinic, one of the country’s largest hospital and medical centers, is based in Rochester. Locally grown firms that were later acquired, such as Medtronic and Supervalu, still maintain major operations here.
How Target lost its nerve — and then lost its business

That diversity helped Minnesota avoid the fate of manufacturing-dependent Midwestern cities like Detroit, St. Louis and Cleveland. It also made the Twin Cities an attractive destination for generations of white-collar professionals despite its famously harsh winters.
One thing, however, is clear, Shaver said. As more headquarters clustered in one region, they created an ecosystem of administrative and managerial talent that could move easily across companies and industries.
Over time, Minnesota’s comparative advantage shifted from producing goods to producing organizational capability. A state that began with farmers and millers gradually developed a workforce skilled at planning, coordinating, allocating resources, solving operational problems and executing strategy across increasingly complex organizations.
Resilience vs. creativity
As a result, Minnesota’s economy has come to reward managerial excellence perhaps more than entrepreneurial risk-taking.
Last year, Minnesota startups in their first year of existence created just 3.91 jobs per 1,000 people, according to the Kauffman Foundation, compared with the national median of 4.8 jobs. Only seven states performed worse. Minnesota also ranks a modest 20th in attracting venture capital.
Not every state needs to resemble Silicon Valley, of course.
Minnesota may not create as many new companies as other regions, but “we build businesses that last,” said Cameron Macht, regional analysis and outreach manager for the Labor Market Information Office at the Minnesota Department of Employment and Economic Development.
However, resilience is not the same thing as growth. For decades, Minnesota’s greatest strength has been its ability to execute — to build durable organizations that continually improve and adapt.
Over the past decade, Minnesota’s economy has grown about 1.7% annually, compared with 2.4% nationally. Since the pandemic, yearly job growth has averaged just under 1%.
The challenge is that AI is becoming increasingly capable of performing many of the very functions that headquarters have historically existed to perform: scheduling, forecasting, writing reports, synthesizing information, coordinating workflows, drafting plans and tracking projects. These are the kinds of execution-oriented, managerial tasks that have long defined Minnesota’s headquarters economy.
What AI has yet to consistently master are some of the functions at the other end of management: deciding which opportunities are worth pursuing, inspiring people around a common vision and creating entirely new businesses. In other words, strategy and leadership.
Built to last
Minnesota companies have displayed plenty of those traits — when circumstances demanded it. New technologies have disrupted industries before, but local companies have consistently endured and even flourished.
“Minnesota is the story of companies constantly reinventing themselves,” Shaver said. The state may lack outside entrepreneurs, but there’s “plenty of innovation that happens within companies,” he said.
Moreover, Minnesota companies know how to adapt without losing continuity with the very things that made them special and successful in the first place. But such situations have been messy.
A sign is posted on the exterior of a Best Buy store on August 27, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
Take Best Buy. As detailed in my book Rebuilding Empires, the Richfield-based consumer electronics giant in 2011 was in deep trouble due to market share losses to Amazon. Rival Circuit City had filed for bankruptcy, and it looked like Best Buy would soon meet a similar fate.
At the time, Best Buy fired its CEO and replaced him with a board director who wanted to quickly close stores and shrink the retailer’s footprint. That prompted founder Richard Schulze to launch a bid to take the company private.
Eventually, Best Buy hired Hubert Joly as CEO. Joly realized the company’s problem wasn’t store space but how the retailer used it. So rather than close stores, Joly introduced buy-online, pick-up-in-store service and store-within-a-store concepts from major vendors like Sony and Samsung. He also matched Amazon prices and reduced lower-margin items like DVDs.
The internet was supposed to wipe out physical shopping. Instead, retailers like Best Buy and Minneapolis-based Target held their ground and became formidable e-commerce players on their own.
Different game
Some local experts believe AI will cause upheaval in Minnesota’s headquarters economy but, just like the internet, the state has the necessary leadership and managerial talent to adapt.
I’m less optimistic. Yes, technologies have come and gone throughout history, and we’re still here. I’m sure some horse lovers in the late 19th century thought the world was going to end when the first cars started to rumble across American streets.
But AI is different for two reasons. The first is that we’re not exactly sure what it is capable of becoming. Programs like Claude and ChatGPT remain something of a black box. It took corporations years to figure out nonphysical abstractions like the internet, and some are still struggling.
The second is what truly frightens me: the speed at which AI capabilities are improving. The internet was enormously disruptive, but it was fundamentally a tool operated by humans. Today’s AI systems are increasingly capable of completing complex sequences of work with less human intervention.
One nonprofit research organization that has gained increasing attention among AI researchers is Model Evaluation & Threat Research, which seeks to measure what the latest AI systems can actually do. METR evaluates whether AI can successfully complete increasingly long and complex real-world tasks with minimal human intervention. The organization refers to this as an AI system’s “task horizon” — the amount of work it can reliably accomplish on tasks that would take a skilled human a given amount of time.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
METR’s findings suggest that frontier AI systems are improving at a striking pace. According to the organization’s research, the length of tasks that leading AI models can complete has roughly doubled every seven months since 2019.
While that doesn’t mean AI is becoming twice as intelligent every seven months, it does suggest that the systems are steadily acquiring the ability to perform longer, more sophisticated sequences of knowledge work — from tasks measured in minutes to those requiring hours of sustained reasoning and coordination.
Corporate response
A lot of people are naturally worried about AI eliminating jobs, especially politicians. Earlier this year, Gov. Tim Walz proposed a tax on social media companies and using the proceeds to help workers impacted by AI. Another bill proposed requiring companies to provide 90 days’ notice before deploying technology that could displace jobs. During this transitional work period, employees would continue to receive regular pay and would be offered a chance to reskill or upskill.
Luke Greiner, regional analyst for Central and Southwest Minnesota at DEED, thinks AI will actually help address a perennial problem in Minnesota’s economy — the lack of workers — by helping the current workforce become more productive.
“We don’t have enough people to grow the economy,” Greiner said.
In fact, he suggests the primary issue will be how workers individually adapt to AI.
Some kind of safety net and training assistance for workers makes sense, but these are purely defensive measures. What about the scenario in which businesses use AI to create new markets, industries and jobs, just as the printing press, steam engine and internet have done?
Unfortunately, this is where not having more Jawed Karims and well-funded high-tech startups willing to take big risks really hurts. Minnesota may still produce breakthrough technologies through institutions like the University of Minnesota and Mayo Clinic. But most startups fail, which is why an economy needs a lot of them to increase the chances that some will succeed.
No, Minnesota’s future with AI will largely depend on the Fortune 500 companies of the headquarters economy.
“Can companies drive more revenue without driving workers out of jobs?” Rosenthal said. “Or do they focus on ‘how do I squeeze more profits from automation?’ We don’t know.”
Minnesota companies are certainly trying to figure it out. UnitedHealth plans to invest at least $1.5 billion in technology and AI this year and again in 2027 to “help make health care simpler, more affordable and easier to navigate,” the company said in an email.
“We are using AI-enabled modernization to help make health care simpler and more connected, improve experiences for consumers and care providers, increase productivity and reduce administrative burden,” it said.
Jeff Shelman, a spokesman for U.S. Bancorp, referred me to the company’s annual report.
“We’ve increased efficiency and enhanced client experiences by investing in AI and machine learning,” the report said. “For example, our engineers use AI tools to write and review code faster and to automate processes. Our GenAI-powered code-review assistant reduces review time by 75%, so our engineers can focus on higher-value work.”
So there is a lot of discussion about AI improving customer experience and boosting efficiency. But there are not many clues to the larger question Minnesota needs to answer: Will AI become primarily a tool for cutting costs, or will companies use those productivity gains to create something new?
Because the future of the headquarters economy may depend on the answer.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Markey’s unvarnished liberalism ages well
description: In what became practically his campaign mantra, Markey repeated the line to all who raised the issue: “It’s not your age, it’s the age of your ideas that are important.”
text:
TIME AND TIDE, Chaucer told us, wait for no man. Except, it seems, Ed Markey.  
Against the backdrop of a national electorate increasingly fed up with the old ways of Washington and the aging politicians who dominate its halls of power, Massachusetts voters rejected a challenger campaigning on the theme of generational change and delivered a resounding victory to an 80-year-old incumbent who arrived on Capitol Hill when Gerald Ford was in the White House.  
Markey, a five-decade fixture in Congress – with the long-winded, stentorian speaking style to prove it – easily defeated US Rep. Seth Moulton in Tuesday’s Democratic primary, piling up a nearly 2-to-1 margin over the 47-year-old one-time Marine platoon leader.  
Markey, who came late to statewide office, winning the Senate seat in 2013 after serving more than 35 years in the House, has fashioned himself into the Bernie Sanders of Massachusetts politics – an avuncular, gray-haired champion of impatient, young progressives.  
Markey played the card brilliantly six years ago against another young Democratic congressman, Joe Kennedy III, becoming the first person to beat a Kennedy in a Massachusetts election. 
Fast forward to this year’s race and Markey – who turned 80 during the primary campaign against Moulton – managed to convince voters again to leave aside any concerns about his age.  
In what became practically his campaign mantra, Markey repeated the line to all who raised the issue: “It’s not your age, it’s the age of your ideas that are important.”  
Markey has not been in complete denial over the inevitable facts of life. He said during the race that, if reelected, this would be his last six-year term.  
In other words, while he has insisted that he is not too old to do the job, he seemed to tacitly admit that he almost is.  
One problem with Moulton’s call for generational change was that Markey didn’t fit the part of a one-time contender well past his expiration date. He exhibits none of the sharp decline Joe Biden showed toward the end of his presidency, or the somnolent eyelid droop that Donald Trump can’t seem to fight off in White House meetings, even with a bank of cameras in front of him.  
Markey still has a youthful bounce to his step and energetic manner. That made it hard for Moulton to get much traction from the issue, even when Markey showed signs of his age, such as his fumbling answer to a debate question about the artificial intelligence software powering search functions in his cellphone and iPad.  
Massachusetts voters have not been entirely immune to the call for fresh voices, even when they don’t come with a dramatic shift in positions on major issues. Eight years ago, Ayanna Pressley upended a 20-year Democratic incumbent by arguing she brought a different lens, not necessarily wholly different views, to the issues facing Congress. “Change can’t wait” was her campaign theme.  
Yesterday, voters decided it can.  
* * *  
For Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, the primary delivered a harsh lesson in the limits of transferring mayoral might to other contests.  
Angry over the state Senate’s refusal to go along with a Boston home-rule plan to shift more of the tax burden onto commercial property owners, Wu decided to go all in on behalf of two challengers to incumbent Democratic senators representing parts of Boston who defended the Senate stance. While the final outcome of one of the races is still unclear, it’s possible that she will have gone 0 for 3 when also considering a third state Senate contest where Wu weighed in.  
In the South Boston-Dorchester district, incumbent Nick Collins beat Latoya Gayle by roughly 10 points. Meanwhile, incumbent Will Brownsberger, who represents Belmont, Watertown, and parts of Cambridge and Boston, was in a nail-biter with former Wu aide Daniel Lander, but was holding onto a 61-vote lead, according to the latest AP tally with all precincts reporting.  
It turns out the real voter frustration with Beacon Hill incumbents representing Boston may have come despite Wu’s positioning, not because of it: Sen. Mike Rush, a moderate from West Roxbury who had the mayor’s endorsement, appears to have been toppled by progressive challenger Persis Yu, a Hyde Park attorney who had the backing of a long list of left-leaning groups.

name: Delaware
title: Meyer signs maternal health bill requiring safe discharge plans
description: New law requires hospitals to document clinical justification, transportation and backup care for pregnant patients discharged with signs of labor DOVER — Delaware hospitals must create formal discharge plans for pregnant patients sent home before delivery after Gov. Matt Meyer signed Senate Bill 301 into law Monday. The legislation applies when a pregnant p[...]
text:
New law requires hospitals to document clinical justification, transportation and backup care for pregnant patients discharged with signs of labor
DOVER — Delaware hospitals must create formal discharge plans for pregnant patients sent home before delivery after Gov. Matt Meyer signed Senate Bill 301 into law Monday.
The legislation applies when a pregnant patient experiencing signs or symptoms consistent with labor is discharged from inpatient care or observation status. It does not require hospitals to admit every patient who may be in labor, leaving the discharge decision to the documented clinical judgment of the treating health care professional.
However, when a patient is discharged, the hospital must provide a written plan intended to ensure the patient understands what to do next and has a safe way to obtain additional care.
“When a mother is in labor, ‘good luck’ is not a plan,” Meyer said. “Any pregnant woman who shows up to a hospital in Delaware should feel seen, heard and cared for until she and her baby are safe.”
The ceremonial signing was held at Josie’s Grace, a Newark-based nonprofit that provides maternal mental health support during pregnancy, after childbirth and during the transition to parenthood.
What hospitals must provide
Under the new law, a discharge plan must include:

Aftercare instructions and confirmation that they were explained to the patient, the patient’s representative or a caregiver;
An assessment of the distance and travel time between the patient’s primary residence and the hospital;
Verification that the patient has reliable transportation between the residence and hospital;
Identification of a backup hospital or facility where the patient could receive labor and delivery services; and
The clinical justification for discharging the patient.

The plan must be discussed with the patient, the patient’s representative or a caregiver and included in the patient’s medical record. If the patient or representative declines to participate, the hospital must document that refusal.
The Department of Health and Social Services may adopt regulations and enforce the discharge-planning requirements. The full bill is available through the Delaware General Assembly.
Bill received unanimous support
The legislation was sponsored by Sen. Marie Pinkney, D-Bear, and House Speaker Melissa Minor-Brown, D-New Castle. It passed the Senate 20-0 on May 20 and the House 40-0 on June 24.
“As a nurse, I know that discharge is not simply the moment a patient walks out of the hospital; it is a critical part of their care,” Minor-Brown said. “A pregnant patient who seeks help because she is in pain or experiencing labor-like symptoms deserves to leave knowing what is happening, what warning signs to watch for, what steps to take next and when to return for immediate care.”
Pinkney said the measure is intended to address gaps in maternal care, including concerns that Black women are more likely to have their symptoms or concerns dismissed by medical professionals.
The Delaware legislation was modeled after the federal Women Expansion of Learning and Labor Safety, or WELLS Act, advanced in Congress by U.S. Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and U.S. Rep. Robin Kelly of Illinois.
The federal proposal is named for Mercedes Wells, an Indiana woman who gave birth along a roadside shortly after being discharged from a hospital while experiencing labor symptoms.
“From the first trimester to the fourth trimester, we want to make sure moms and families have the support they need to be healthy,” Blunt Rochester said. “The signing of Delaware Senate Bill 301 will save lives while building on the work we’re doing in Congress to end the maternal health crisis.”
Hospitals supported goal, questioned mandate
During the legislative debate, the Delaware Healthcare Association supported the bill’s patient-safety goals but took a neutral position because of concerns about placing additional clinical requirements into state law.
The association said Delaware hospitals already operate under federal emergency-care standards and other regulatory oversight and maintain protocols for responding to pregnant patients showing signs of labor.
It recommended that the state also collect and publish annual county-level information about births that occur while a patient is traveling to a hospital or unintentionally at home. Such reporting, the association said, could help determine whether inappropriate hospital discharges are occurring in Delaware.
The law’s unanimous passage suggests lawmakers ultimately viewed the additional planning requirements as a reasonable safeguard. Implementation will now determine how hospitals document transportation, identify backup facilities and incorporate the requirements into existing discharge procedures without unnecessarily delaying care.
TO GO BOX

Law: Senate Bill 301
What it does: Requires Delaware hospitals to create a documented discharge plan when a pregnant patient experiencing signs or symptoms of labor is sent home before delivery.
Required information: Clinical justification, aftercare instructions, travel assessment, reliable transportation and a backup labor and delivery facility.
Who oversees it: Delaware Department of Health and Social Services.
Learn more: legis.delaware.gov/BillDetail?LegislationId=143227

title: Two Florida Democrats join every Republican in Congress in voting to condemn socialism and the DSA
description: Two Florida Democrats who are fighting for their political lives after seeing their congressional seats redistricted voted Tuesday for a resolution denouncing “socialism in all of its forms.” Kathy Castor and Darren Soto joined six other Democrats in supporting the resolution. The final vote was 220-192, with two Democrats voting present. The resolution “den[...]
text:
The U.S. Capitol on the evening of Sept. 30, 2025. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)Two Florida Democrats who are fighting for their political lives after seeing their congressional seats redistricted voted Tuesday for a resolution denouncing “socialism in all of its forms.”
Kathy Castor via U.S. House
Rep. Darren Soto, via his Facebook page
Kathy Castor and Darren Soto joined six other Democrats in supporting the resolution. The final vote was 220-192, with two Democrats voting present.
The resolution “denounces socialism in all of its forms, including the Democratic Socialists of America.”
Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidates have seen success in high-profile primary races across the country this summer, including in Florida, where Jacksonville state Rep. Angie Nixon defeated the vastly better-funded Alex Vindman in the primary for U.S. Senate last month.
Colorado Republican Rep. Jeff Crank, who sponsored the resolution, said last week that it was a “simple up or down vote” on the platform of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA).
Castor has represented a district in the Tampa Bay area for 20 years, but her re-election hopes are in question after her district was redistricted to one that Donald Trump won by more than 10 points in 2024. Soto’s Central Florida district was completely wiped out, and he now is running in an area that supported Trump by more than 18 points in 2024.
Florida Republicans have seized on the momentum of the DSA nationally this summer to paint Florida Democrats as socialists, and they received a gift of sorts when Nixon defeated Vindman.
“The DSA has infiltrated the Democratic Party at all levels of government and has never been more apparent than here in the state of Florida with the election of Angie Nixon for U.S. Senate,” Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia said Tuesday during a Republican Party of Florida event in Tampa. “It has never been more apparent that the Democratic Party of Florida is the DSA.”
Most Democrats opposed the resolution because it included language urging passage of the SAVE America Act.
“House Resolution 1490 explicitly calls for enactment of the so-called SAVE America Act, which is the top legislative priority of far-right extremists. Accordingly, I will vote No on the latest MAGA effort to rig the midterm elections,” House Democratic Leader Hakeen Jeffries said.

text:
Delaware voters have multiple days to cast ballots before the Sept. 15 primary, providing greater flexibility and another opportunity to participate in decisions that often shape state and local government.
Early voting for Delaware’s 2026 primary election begins Wednesday, Sept. 2, and continues through Sunday, Sept. 13, with a two-day pause for the Labor Day holiday.
Unlike absentee voting, voters do not need to provide a reason for voting early. The process is essentially the same as voting on Election Day: Election officers verify the voter’s eligibility, the voter signs the electronic pollbook and then casts a ballot on an accessible voting machine.
A Delaware voter may use any early-voting center in the county where the voter lives. Voters do not have to use their assigned Election Day polling place during early voting. Delaware Department of Elections

The primary election will be held Tuesday, Sept. 15. Election Day polling places will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Delaware primary-election information
Who can vote in the primary?
Delaware conducts closed primary elections:

Registered Democrats may vote in the Democratic primary.
Registered Republicans may vote in the Republican primary.
Unaffiliated voters and voters registered with minor parties generally may not participate in either major party’s primary.
Not every voter will have a contested race on the ballot.

The regular deadline to change political parties for this primary was May 29.
There is a special exception for some voters automatically registered through the Division of Motor Vehicles who were not previously given an opportunity to select a party. Those voters may affiliate with the Democratic or Republican Party through Sept. 15, including at an early-voting center. Delaware voter-registration guidance
Voters should use the state’s iVote portal to confirm their registration and review their voting information before leaving home.

The Fairfield Inn location is designated for the primary only. Voters should confirm locations before traveling through the state’s official early-voting list.
What should I bring?
Poll workers will ask voters to show identification, and presenting it generally speeds up check-in. However, Delaware does not require photo identification to vote in state and federal elections.
A voter whose name appears on the poll list but who does not present identification may complete an Affirmation of Voter Identity and then vote.
Before going to the polls:

Confirm your registration and party affiliation.
Review your sample ballot.
Select any early-voting center in your county.
Bring identification if available.
Leave candidate clothing, buttons and other campaign materials outside the voting room.

Voters may bring children age 17 or younger with them. Cellphone conversations are not permitted inside the polling place. Delaware voting FAQ
Why participation matters in Delaware
Primaries can be decisive
In districts where one party has a substantial registration advantage, the winner of that party’s primary may enter the general election as the strong favorite. That gives primary voters considerable influence over who ultimately holds office.
Local decisions affect everyday life
Many primary ballots include candidates for the General Assembly, county government and other offices responsible for decisions involving state spending, taxes, schools, land use, roads, housing, public safety and business regulation.
Smaller elections magnify each vote
Delaware is a small state, and legislative and county contests involve much smaller electorates than presidential races. A relatively modest number of votes can therefore determine a nomination.
Broader participation produces a more representative result
When only the most committed political voters participate, a small portion of eligible voters may choose the nominees presented to everyone in November. Greater turnout gives candidates and elected officials a clearer picture of the priorities of the broader community.
Early voting removes Election Day uncertainty
Work demands, family responsibilities, illness, traffic and weather can interfere with Election Day plans. Voting early gives residents several opportunities to cast a ballot while allowing Election Day polling places to serve voters who need or prefer to wait.
Looking ahead to November
Delaware’s general election is Tuesday, Nov. 3. Every eligible registered voter may participate regardless of party affiliation.
General-election early voting is scheduled for:

Oct. 28-Nov. 1, 11 a.m.-7 p.m.

The deadline to register for the general election is Oct. 10. Delaware general-election information

title: Kansas primary yields second-highest voter turnout in history
description: TOPEKA — The Aug. 4 primary election, which featured contentious races and a hot-button ballot question, had the second-highest primary voter turnout in Kansas history, according to the Secretary of State’s Office. More than 650,000 Kansans cast ballots on and leading up to the election, making it second only to turnout in the 2022 election, […]
text:
Kansas Secretary of State Scott Schwab has overseen the two highest voter turnout primary elections in state history in 2022 and 2026. He appears on May 19, 2026, at the Docking State Office Building in Topeka. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — The Aug. 4 primary election, which featured contentious races and a hot-button ballot question, had the second-highest primary voter turnout in Kansas history, according to the Secretary of State’s Office.
More than 650,000 Kansans cast ballots on and leading up to the election, making it second only to turnout in the 2022 election, when more than 922,000 people voted.
Kansans in both elections were voting on pivotal ballot measures. This year, voters rejected a measure that attempted to turn Kansas Supreme Court seats into elected positions. In 2022, voters similarly rejected a measure that would have taken away abortion protections.
Kansas Secretary of State Scott Schwab announced the turnout total Tuesday after state officials certified the results.
“Today’s certification reflects the hard work and dedication of election officials across Kansas,” Schwab said in a news release. “I am grateful to the 105 counties and the thousands of election workers who administered this election and ensured the results were accurately reported.”
Nearly 224,000 people voted in advance of the primary election. Schwab announced on Aug. 14 that all Kansas counties completed post-election audits, a process that ensures hand counts match ballot tabulation machines.
He said county election officials are preparing for the midterms in November. Voter registration is open through Oct. 13.

title: Sayge is on her way to becoming a pediatric occupational therapist
description:

text:
Sayge Bohannon is confident that this will be a great school year. Having done well in college-level classes last year, now she’s feeling far less nervous about taking four classes online at the Community College of Vermont (CCV) through Vermont’s Early College program, while enrolled in Richford High School.
Sayge is also president of her school’s National Honor Society chapter and stays active in soccer and track. Between the coursework and her other activities, Sayge feels ready for senior year, with just the right amount of challenge to prepare her for college.
“Of all places,” TikTok inspired Sayge’s research into her career focus
Sayge will be applying to colleges this fall as well. The oldest of six siblings (including two sets of twins), she’s been around kids her whole life and loves working with them. She knows she doesn’t want to be a teacher or in a classroom setting, although a career where she can help people appeals to her. 
She’s put those passions together and will be applying to programs to prepare her to be a pediatric occupational therapist. “Of all places, I actually found out about the career on TikTok, believe it or not,” she laughed. “At the time, I thought I wanted to be a nurse but have also always loved working with kids. I saw a ‘day in the life’ on TikTok and I was so interested in the opportunity to be able to work with kids living with disabilities.” As she researched it more, she became even more invested in the option for her future. 
To make sure it was what she wanted, Sayge shadowed an occupational therapist at the University of Vermont Medical Center. While the experience was mostly focused on older patients, she says she got a lot out of her time there, and it affirmed her interest in working with kids. 
Putting the puzzle together: preparing for college
As she’s started to put the pieces together to apply to college this year, Sayge is relying more and more on Matt Mitchell, a VSAC outreach counselor in VSAC’s GEAR UP college and career readiness program. She describes her school as a place where she feels like she always has access to the resources she needs to get help with college-related questions. Sayge started working with Matt a few years ago. 
“I meet with him every other week to work through my questions. I’ve had so many, and I want to make sure I’m on the right track,” she says. 
Her school counselor helps as well, and together, they’ve helped Sayge navigate her college-level curriculum, and now college applications. “I worked with Matt on my Common Application, and he’s always there helping to guide me and making sure that the colleges I’m looking at are aligned with my goals,” she shares. 
Matt also helped Sayge find a scholarship that will cover the cost of some of her textbooks and course materials for the CCV classes she is currently taking. She needed some financial help to make it work out, and he was able to guide her to the scholarship that would eventually cover it. 
They’re now working on the list of where Sayge will apply to college. She’s winnowing her list down to exactly what she wants, but it’s tough. She toured two colleges this summer and may be doing some more tours this fall. She had to do the FAFSA financial aid forms for her CCV program, and feels good that it’s already familiar to her, now that she’s completing it again for this fall’s college applications. 
Sayge dreams big, but trusts her instincts
“I always knew I wanted to go to college,” Sayge notes. “I’ve always enjoyed school and learning and college is something my mom always wanted for me and supported as she didn’t have that opportunity.” Sayge shares that the big goals she has for herself also make her mom proud. 
As she gets everything organized for fall applications, her essay, FAFSA, other scholarship applications, and everything else on her big list, Sayge is learning to trust her instincts, working through her questions to clarify that she’s heading in the right direction. “When I’ve done the work, I’ll know it’s the right fit,” she says. 
It’s something she learned through her CCV application process, and she’s applying that same work ethic this fall to her next steps. With hard work and a little guidance, Sayge is ready to trust the process—confident that wherever she lands, it’ll be exactly where she’s meant to be.
