name: Alabama Reflector
title: Tommy Tuberville outlines new data center approach as opposition to facilities mounts
description: Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville Tuesday laid out a new stance on data centers in Alabama after weeks of championing them and denouncing their critics. In an opinion column published in Alabama Political Reporter, Tuberville said as governor he would work to give communities the power to reject data centers and put them in the […]
text:
U.S. Sen. and Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville speaking at the Alabama Republican Party's Summer Dinner on July 31, 2026, at the Renaissance Hotel in Montgomery, Alabama. Tuberville Tuesday published an opinion column in Alabama Political Reporter detailing his plans for addressing data centers in the state after weeks of touting them and denouncing their critics. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville Tuesday laid out a new stance on data centers in Alabama after weeks of championing them and denouncing their critics.
In an opinion column published in Alabama Political Reporter, Tuberville said as governor he would work to give communities the power to reject data centers and put them in the state’s highest property tax bracket, though he was not clear on details. 
“Here’s my message to data centers: If you want to use our resources, you pay full taxes, cover the total cost of your energy, and replace what you take,” the article said. “We’ll welcome you with open arms, but keep your hands out of our pockets.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The announcement came as data center development around the state draws opposition over concerns about energy use and potential impacts on the environment and the communities where they reside, and differs slightly from previous statements Tuberville has made about data centers. In July, AL.com reported that Tuberville said people who are opposed to data centers and artificial intelligence are being influenced by China and called concerns about the environmental effects of data centers “bullcrap.” 
Tuberville’s column did not directly address environmental concerns. He wrote that he wants to give local communities the option to determine if they want a data center.
“A project that works in one community may be wrong for another,” Tuberville wrote. “Local residents understand their roads, water, schools and neighborhoods better than bureaucrats or corporate executives. Private property rights matter, but so do the rights of neighboring property owners.”
Tuberville said in the column he would make data centers pay for the total cost of substations, transmission lines and water systems needed to run the facilities; “replace the power and water capacity they take” and impose higher taxes on data centers. 
Tuberville also said he would want to put them in the highest property tax bracket in the state. Under a constitutional amendment passed in 1978, the highest taxed properties are utility properties providing utility services, taxed at 30% of fair market value. Owner-occupied homes and agricultural properties are taxed at 10% of fair market value. 
Tuberville’s campaign team did not respond to questions Tuesday about how he would implement his ideas. Alabama’s constitution severely limits county governments’ powers, and giving them more could require a constitutional amendment, a potentially years-long process in which the governor has no direct role. The Association of County Commissions of Alabama has called for giving county governments more comprehensive use of land control. 
During a policy speech in July, Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones called for a one-year data center moratorium to have “guardrails and policies in place to protect our people and our communities.” Messages seeking comment were left with the Jones campaign on Tuesday.
Ryan Anderson, a staff attorney with Southern Environmental Law Center, said in an interview Tuesday the recommendations in Tuberville’s column were a step in the right direction.
“We’ve seen a huge data center boom in the state of Alabama over the past year, and you know we really need our elected officials to start stepping up to the plate and doing something to protect communities,” Anderson said.
In Lowndes County, an 800-acre data center known as Project Red Clay, has received backlash from residents for lack of transparency from county officials.
Ann Burgwin Faulkner, a resident of Lowndes County who has opposed putting the center in the county, said in an interview Tuesday afternoon Tuberville’s current stance is “wonderful.”
“I don’t think that anyone is opposed to data centers,” Faulkner said. “The opposition is to the wrong developments coming to the wrong place with no transparency.”
Anderson said the one thing Tuberville’s recommendations lacked were clear guidelines on transparency.
“Another key piece that’s missing from this is required government transparency, whether that’s banning the use of NDAs (non-disclosure agreements), reforming the Open Records Act, something needs to be done to make sure that these decisions are made in a transparent manner,” she said.
Earlier this year, Bessemer City officials including Mayor Kenneth Gulley, signed a NDA for Project Marvel, an 18-building data center project.
Anderson said the difference between Jones’ moratorium and Tuberville’s proposal is that a moratorium could give communities more time to plan than Tuberville’s plan. 
“I think about it like a temporary pause, less than you know a blanket prohibition on these things,” Anderson said. “And a big issue here is what are we going to do for the communities that are facing data center developments with none of these protections right now, like the people in Lowndes County. We don’t have time to spare before good policies, protective policies, get implemented here in Alabama.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Alpha-gal syndrome is spreading rapidly. Arkansas may hold clues to what comes next.
description: Standing under an eastern hemlock tree near a thicket of lizard’s tail in her backyard — a tick’s dream — Casey Hamaker had flashbacks to the day she first contracted alpha-gal syndrome, a mysterious illness spreading rapidly across the United States. “This is the scene of the crime,” she said. As she was clearing brush […]
text:
The lone star tick, responsible for most U.S. cases of alpha-gal, aggressively pursues humans and other hosts in search of a blood meal. (Photo Courtesy of Lauren Bishop/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)Standing under an eastern hemlock tree near a thicket of lizard’s tail in her backyard — a tick’s dream — Casey Hamaker had flashbacks to the day she first contracted alpha-gal syndrome, a mysterious illness spreading rapidly across the United States.
“This is the scene of the crime,” she said. As she was clearing brush in her garden in the spring of 2024, three ticks — likely lone stars, the aggressive hunters known for causing most cases of alpha-gal — latched onto her. She reached up and found them drawing blood just behind her ear.
Within a few weeks, Hamaker, 49, was consumed by outbreaks of huge, red welts that crept across the tops of her feet, the backs of her knees and enveloped her torso — sometimes dotting her scalp, eyelids and ears. She downed handfuls of allergy medications. She would later find out they contained trace amounts of mammalian products to which she’s now allergic. 
“I was really uncomfortable in my own body, and I would just find myself itching like a dog with fleas,” Hamaker said.
Hamaker lives in Fayetteville, a picturesque college town nestled in the Ozark Mountains that’s emerging as an alpha-gal hotspot. Arkansas’ suspected cases have nearly doubled from 1,331 in the first half of 2025 to 2,833 over the same period this year, a significant number in a small, rural state. Northwest Arkansas, with its dense woods and outdoorsy lifestyle, is leading most other regions of the state in positive results. 
Arkansas is a bellwether for much of the country, which is just now waking up to this severe allergy that mostly went undetected for decades. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, as many as 450,000 people have contracted alpha-gal syndrome since 2010 — and given most states began counting cases just in the last few years and the CDC isn’t actively tracking it, that may be a gross underestimate. The condition has been diagnosed in large numbers in tony enclaves like the Hamptons and Martha’s Vineyard, where the tick was barely present 50 years ago.
The Tennessee Department of Health has received around 484 reports of AGS cases since July 2025, when AGS became a reportable condition in Tennessee. This is preliminary data for first year of the State’s AGS reporting and the total is pending final confirmation.
Alpha-gal syndrome is also rapidly expanding, alongside many other tick-borne illnesses, owing to a perfect storm of climate change, expanding white-tailed deer populations and massive historical shifts in land use and development. The lone star tick — which carries the alpha-gal molecule in its saliva — is on the march, and it’s taking alpha-gal syndrome with it. 

As more people test positive, the profound strangeness of alpha-gal syndrome is also moving to the forefront. Once simply referred to as a “red-meat allergy,” the confounding experiences of people like Hamaker — who can be triggered by trace amounts of mammalian ingredients as well as other substances, like seaweed — show that its impacts are more wide-ranging than originally imagined.

We also know that alpha-gal is dangerous. As many as three-quarters of people who test positive experience anaphylactic shock. There have now been a handful of deaths linked to alpha-gal syndrome. 
And yet as the condition spreads rapidly and positive tests pile up, scientific understanding is lagging far behind. Researchers are still unraveling the disease, public health agencies are struggling to track it, and there’s little federal funding or coordination driving efforts forward. But that may be changing as awareness — and a little panic — spreads. The challenge now isn’t just understanding the disease; it’s figuring out how to stop it. Arkansas researchers and residents may hold some clues. 
 An age-old disease?

Cresting the verdant foothills of the Ozarks on the drive into Fayetteville, outdoor lovers of the human variety see paradise. Ticks see heaven, too. The lone star tick— so named for the white marking on the adult female’s back — is at home in Arkansas, as it thrives in dense forests and humid climates. Needing animals to feed on — known as blood meals — the creature has once again come to the right place. Arkansas is lousy with wildlife.
While it isn’t the only tick that carries the alpha-gal molecule, the lone star spreads the syndrome more than any other because of its unusually aggressive hunting style. It actively chases after animals — and people — following vibrations and the trail of carbon dioxide. 
The syndrome takes its name from a sugar known as alpha-gal. When lone star ticks are born with the sugar molecules in their bodies, and when they bite humans, they pass it into their victims’ blood. 
This same molecule is found in the bodies of most mammals, but not humans. For some people, exposure to the molecule causes the immune system to mount defenses whenever they encounter alpha-gal in food or other products (mostly made from mammals), with symptoms ranging in severity from vomiting and hives to anaphylactic shock.
A big question — the one on everyone’s mind — is, how many are destined to get this? It’s thought that only a small percentage of the tick-bitten will go on to develop alpha-gal syndrome, but it’s impossible to say with certainty without more comprehensive studies. In 2013, researchers estimated that less than 10% of those with alpha-gal antibodies (known as sensitization) go on to develop the allergy, but University of North Carolina School of Medicine researcher Scott Commins is convinced the number is far lower. Recent research he contributed to may underscore his theory: 31% of a sample population from Arkansas tested positive for alpha-gal antibodies, a far larger portion than have gotten sick. 
“I think the tick-bitten number is incredibly large, so the percentage of people who go on to develop the allergy in that scenario, in my mind, is really small,” Commins said. Martha’s Vineyard, he said, would be a good place to run a more controlled trial to finally solve the riddle. 
Some Arkansans have tales of a distant cousin or a granddad suffering from a mysterious red meat allergy — decades ago. Alpha-gal syndrome has likely been lurking in the Ozarks for generations, but few would deny that something is making it far worse. That something, new research shows, is climate change. 
According to Dalton Williams, a researcher at the University of Arkansas who studies the relationship between tick-borne illnesses and ecological shifts, ticks are far more active year-round in Arkansas than they were just 15 years ago. While residents once could depend on a reprieve in cooler months, when lone stars would freeze to death or go into hibernation, warmer winters mean tick season stretches on much longer. “Now we’re seeing a lot of cases through the fall and steadily going through the winter,” Williams said. 
Using satellite climate data and thousands of tick samples, Williams produced research in May showing that the increasing humidity in June and July — peak tick season in Arkansas — is pushing ticks into more pockets of the state, as ticks depend on humidity to survive. Their hosts also seek out moist plants for food. “Not only are ticks endemic across essentially the whole state, but they are also more inclined to feed and breed,” he said. 
Climate change is also extending tick season across the country — and pushing the lone star into the upper reaches of the Midwest and New England. 
Martha’s Vineyard, an island escape for the well-to-do off the coast of Massachusetts, now has established lone star tick populations and has seen positive alpha-gal case rates explode from two cases to 523 in the last few years. New York’s Suffolk County, which includes the ultra-wealthy Hamptons, has the highest case numbers in the country.
There’s even evidence of lone star sightings in Central Park in Manhattan. The good news is that, lacking deer, the ticks are unlikely to settle there.
But climate change is just part of the story. The spread of alpha-gal syndrome is also one of nature rebounding — and then running amok. There’s evidence that the lone star tick was once found across much of the eastern United States, but as settlers replaced forests with farmland and factories, the creature was nearly annihilated by the early 20th century in the outer reaches of the tick’s range. 
The white-tailed deer has also helped expand the lone star tick population, as one of the creature’s preferred hosts, able to support all four phases of its life cycle. As parasites, lone stars need hosts to survive and thrive. They take a blood meal, engorging themselves, in order to molt and advance to each stage of development. Deer unwittingly play a key role in this process, carrying an average of 200 adult lone star ticks and 1,500 larvae per season. 
White-tailed deer, hunted nearly to extinction across much of the U.S., including in Arkansas, have made an extraordinary comeback in the past century. In the 1920s, Arkansas began to develop its economy around big game hunting. Today, there are an estimated 1 million white-tailed deer in the state, up from about 1,000 in 1947, something the Arkansas Game and Fish Commission touts with great pride. Across the country, there are 30 million white-tailed deer.
Williams, the University of Arkansas researcher, said that deer and other host animals like raccoons and squirrels are common within Fayetteville’s city limits. “Some people think it’s really wholesome, but every time I point at them, I say they’re dropping off ticks.” 
Ticks don’t wander far from their hosts, and thus it takes the combination of hosts, humans and ticks to produce a tick bite that leads to alpha-gal. That’s more likely to happen where humans are pushing into nature. While Arkansas is well-known for its pristine natural landscapes, Northwest Arkansas is rapidly developing, with hundreds of miles of mountain bike trails recently cut into the Ozarks; that, too, could be playing a role. A 2025 study of those living with alpha-gal in Virginia and the Carolinas found that cases were associated with areas where homes and lawns border wooded land or break up woods, indicating that urbanization and development into forests might be linked to contracting the disease. 
In 2023, Arkansas became the first state to make alpha-gal syndrome a reportable disease, with doctors and labs required to turn over positive results to the state Department of Health. Once the agency receives a positive test result, the department independently verifies it to separate out the people who are simply positive for alpha-gal antibodies versus those who are symptomatic.
But the agency has not moved beyond information collection and some modest public education. When asked if the health department operates, funds or coordinates any tick-control programs or has plans to, public health veterinarian Dr. Laura Rothfeldt said, “There are no resources or staff specifically designated for mosquito and tick control.” 
 Not just a red-meat allergy

As Hamaker suffered with all-consuming bouts of hives, it never occurred to her that it was alpha-gal syndrome. She has friends who had the condition — they would throw up from eating pork, for example, but none of them had hives. “Never in a million years would I have thought that it was alpha-gal,” she said. Her doctors missed it, too. She saw five different doctors over nearly a year and a half before finally being diagnosed. 
Alpha-gal syndrome was first recognized by the American scientific community in 2009, and thought then to be strictly a red-meat allergy largely confined to the Southeast. That it took until then to be identified in the American scientific literature is a testament to its strangeness. Since then, the symptoms have only proven to be even weirder and far-reaching. 
Unlike other food allergies, which prompt an immediate reaction, most alpha-gal victims’ first reaction occurs about one to two months after a tick bite and about four to six hours after eating a mammal or other allergen, often striking in the middle of the night. “You have to think back, like, what was I doing? Where was I? What did I eat?” Hamaker said. 
Casey Hamaker cooks in her home in Fayetteville, Arkansas, July 24, 2026. Alpha-gal forced her to prepare meals at home and vet ingredients. (Photo Courtesy of Novo Studio)
Because it’s delayed, alpha-gal syndrome is often confused for food poisoning or, in Hamaker’s case, anxiety. “Every doctor I went to was like, ‘Oh, it’s just stress,’ and that was very frustrating,” she said. 
Covered in hives and nearly driven mad from sleepless nights, Hamaker finally landed in the offices of Dr. Tina Merritt, a leading authority on alpha-gal syndrome, with a bustling practice in nearby Bentonville. Hamaker is one of Merritt’s 1,200 alpha-gal patients, up from zero two decades ago, including those who see her via telemedicine from as far away as New York and Florida. 
Merritt is a legend in the alpha-gal world. She helped identify the condition two decades ago — and has lived with it herself ever since she was bitten by about “a hundred seed ticks,” tiny newly hatched ticks smaller than a grain of sand, at a summer camp in north Louisiana when she was in third grade. “I think because I’ve had the allergy, I understand that the symptoms can vary and they vary all the time,” she said.
Merritt is currently studying more bizarre manifestations of alpha-gal syndrome. One patient’s voice gets hoarse at the mere smell of pork; another patient gets brain fog. Some have severe cardiovascular events similar to heart attacks. In August, she co-published a national survey of 3,000 alpha-gal patients showing that it affects many systems of the body, including the skin, brain and heart. More than 70% of those surveyed reported experiencing hives.
Merritt’s poison is gelatin, typically made from the bones and skins of pigs and cows and found in foods, cosmetics and pill capsules. If she accidentally ingests it, she can get dizzy and lose consciousness. The last time it happened, about eight years ago, Merritt was boating with friends on Beaver Lake in the Ozarks. After taking a Jell-O shot, she started to feel queasy and fainted on the floor of her boat. She came to hours later, to her friends asking, “Is Tina dead?” The national survey indicates she’s not alone — 16% of respondents reported losing consciousness from alpha-gal exposure.
As for what protects some from the syndrome, there aren’t great answers there either, Merritt said. It could have something to do with genetics or having type-B blood. Other conditions, such as an autoimmune disease or a vitamin D deficiency, are thought to make it worse.
Not every allergist thinks alpha-gal is responsible for such a plethora of maladies. Joshua Kennedy, an immunology and allergy researcher and doctor at the University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences in Little Rock, believes alpha-gal syndrome is being misdiagnosed in some cases because a positive test only indicates sensitization — not that certain foods or products are causing a patient’s allergies. His goal, he said, “is to be more aggressive in how we get foods back into people’s diets, if necessary.” Kennedy does that through highly controlled food challenges, where patients consume what they’re allergic to in a supervised setting. 
Determining who’s right will take more research — and lots of it. Commins, the researcher at the UNC School of Medicine, said that alpha-gal research has too little federal attention. “The funding of this is really limited, and there seems to be a big disconnect,” he said. As of now, much of the literature that exists on alpha-gal syndrome is based on patients who come through specialists’ doors.
 Detective work

Hamaker’s home is transformed in subtle ways. Her bathroom drawers, once full of makeup and face creams and the trappings of female-dom, are spartan. All that remains are a stick of Tom’s deodorant, a single tube of mascara by e.l.f. (the only brand she’s found that doesn’t cause her eyelids to erupt in hives) and alpha-gal-friendly allergy medication. Her toothpaste, shampoo and lotion are all absent of any mammalian ingredients. Her refrigerator and pantry are stocked with simple ingredients, like rice, produce and chicken, a meat she can safely eat.
Hamaker’s diagnosis was just the beginning of months of detective work, as she toiled to understand each flare-up. She discovered a mind-boggling number of ingredients contain trace amounts of the alpha-gal molecule, including the lubricating strip of her shaving razors (some are made with lanolin from sheep), dry-roasted peanuts (some of which contain gelatin) and even some brands of bottled water (which is filtered using bone char sourced from mammals). 
Navigating alpha-gal is challenging considering how many products have trace bits of mammalian products in them — and poor labeling. The CDC does not maintain a comprehensive list of products that may contain alpha-gal molecules, nor does the Food and Drug Administration recognize alpha-gal as a major food allergen, although some advocates are trying to change that.
Hamaker, who works as an accountant for a charitable foundation, now fears client dinners and work conferences. “I am terrified of buffets. I don’t eat catering. I don’t eat at luncheons,” she said. If a restaurant promises her the food is alpha-gal friendly, she often doesn’t risk it: A small amount of cross-contamination on the grill could send her body into a full-blown reaction. 
Casey Hamaker and her boyfriend, Matt West, in their yard in Fayetteville, Arkansas, July 24, 2026. Hamaker has alpha-gal syndrome. (Photo Courtesy of Novo Studio)
Even well-intentioned hangouts can spell trouble. A friend invited her over, promising an alpha-gal-friendly meal. Hamaker broke out into hives a few hours later. She later pieced together why: “I learned about my friends’ dogs that ate red meat. I couldn’t pet them because I was allergic to their dander and saliva,” she said. 
Another hidden danger for alpha-gal syndrome sufferers is medications that contain the sugar molecule. Acetaminophen, supplements like vitamin D, some vaccines and even medical devices like heart valves and sutures can have animal ingredients and can be administered to patients without their knowledge. 
Researchers are puzzling through more sensitive cases like Hamaker’s. But Merritt’s survey seems to indicate that many of Hamaker’s own seemingly odd reactions are quite common: 40% reported reactions to mammalian ingredients in personal-care products and prescription drugs; about 67% of people report an allergy to dairy. And her earlier research showed that 10% are allergic to carrageenan in red seaweed, which also contains the alpha-gal molecule. 
Hamaker’s allergy to carrageenan ruined rotisserie chicken for her when she found out some — but not all — store brands use it to keep the meat moist. “I just like almost started crying because on the ingredients it said carrageenan, and I was like, ‘You’ve got to be kidding me!’” Hamaker said. 
For now, people with the syndrome lean heavily on third-party apps like Fig, which has a barcode scanner that will flash X if a food isn’t safe, and Pill Clarity, which started out catering to vegans but is now relied on by alpha-gal patients to find pills and medical devices that don’t contain allergens. It also helps to live in an alpha-gal hotspot like Fayetteville, where there are numerous support groups, a few alpha-gal-friendly restaurants and other alpha-gal-afflicted people to commiserate with. 
Hamaker’s boyfriend, Matt West, eats alpha-gal-friendly meals, at least at home, and has supported her in making changes to her lifestyle (although he still sneaks off on occasion to down a hamburger on his own). As more people get alpha-gal syndrome in the area, Hamaker and her family are finding themselves in good company. 
“In the last year, it went from, ‘You have what?’ to, ‘Oh, my cousin has that or my daughter-in-law has that,’” West said. “And just the way that it kind of shows itself, too. There are so many variations of it.”
 All-out war on ticks?

There may be another effective treatment for managing severe alpha-gal symptoms, called Xolair, an injection approved in 2024 by the FDA for food allergies. While it won’t let alpha-gal victims feast on hamburgers again, for some it seems to cool their reactions from accidental exposure.
Some members of Congress have advocated more research, while other lawmakers have proposed classifying alpha-gal as a major food allergen for labeling purposes. Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced in May a multimillion-dollar pilot program between the CDC and the Department of Health and Human Services to, among other things, evaluate new drugs that could prevent people from developing alpha-gal syndrome following a tick bite.
But an all-out war on ticks is where the mind goes when contemplating a blood-sucking parasite that can potentially kill people — or steal away their favorite foods. “I hear people say all the time, ‘Why don’t we just kill all the ticks?’” said Williams, the University of Arkansas researcher. 
Calls for authorities to do something drastic are growing. The syndrome is spreading on the heels of other tick-borne illnesses like Lyme disease, which is severe in some parts of the Northeast. Martha’s Vineyard is considering a proposal to cull 70% of the white-tail population.
But going after the deer could be a nonstarter in many wildlife-loving places like Arkansas. Catherine Love, a wildlife veterinarian for the Game and Fish Commission, put it bluntly: “You couldn’t cull them at a rate in Arkansas without pissing off every hunter,” she said. Love is convinced the ticks would simply relocate to other hosts and warns it could be our pets instead. 
RFK Jr.’s May announcement also included commitments to develop new products to eliminate ticks on wildlife. Some have suggested simply treating deer with insecticides, either on their coats or via bait. It could work but makes ecologists like Williams nervous. “I’m always kind of iffy on putting ecosystems in flux,” he said. 
Going to war on ticks would be harder than fighting mosquitoes — a biting insect whose disease-spreading habits we’ve largely wrangled. While mosquitoes breed in standing water, making killing off larvae easy, ticks drop their eggs anywhere they topple off a host, said Emily McDermott, a vector ecologist at the University of Arkansas who researches how ticks spread pathogens and move through their environment. “You can’t just walk around the woods and say this is where the larvae are — here and not there,” she said. 
Culling the ticks will require many different strategies rolled out in conjunction, McDermott said, from better land management techniques like keeping tall grasses cut back and brush cleared, to novel treatments like insecticides applied to deer. 
To push alpha-gal out of the realm of personal problem into public responsibility will require coordination — across wildlife management, medical professionals and local and federal governments — at a time when trust is low. It will inevitably involve bumping up against contentious issues like vaccines, pesticides and government intervention. While federal help is needed, local solutions are wise, McDermott said. 
The good news is ticks aren’t everywhere, all the time. Lone star ticks, for example, prefer edge habitats between forests and grasslands or the borders between a suburban lawn and woods.
It might also help humans to understand the creatures hunting them. Ticks are not on an endless quest for blood. They eat just a few times in their lives. After they feast, engorged nearly until the point of popping, ticks lie nearly motionless, digesting for months. If the weather gets too dry or hot, lone stars dry out and dessicate — transforming into tick mummies. “They’re not just vindictive, evil creatures bent on destruction. They’re animals doing animal things,” McDermott said. She also noted that basic tick protection, like wearing permethrin-treated clothes and doing thorough tick checks after an outdoor escapade, is quite effective. 
The good news is that for some people, alpha-gal goes into remission eventually, typically within three to five years, as long as patients avoid red meat and other substances they are allergic to and, most importantly, avoid getting other tick bites.
Nowadays, Hamaker still experiences small outbreaks on her ears and eyelids, but gone are the sleepless nights and scratching until her skin bleeds. She has no regrets about learning how to cook unprocessed foods using whole ingredients. “So much of these things, like red meat and cheese, are inflammatory anyway toward your joints, so maybe it’s not a bad thing,” she said. 
The one thing Hamaker refuses to do is move. Her home is nestled into two and a half acres planted in huge magnolias, eastern hemlocks and leafy garden beds. She has no plans to give up mountain biking, hiking or hanging out in the yard with her partner and her three dogs.

“I pulled a tick off of me last Friday,” she said. “It’s like, I don’t know how I can avoid it. Move into an apartment in the city?” Alpha-gal syndrome has made its way to bigger cities, anyway. Nowhere is safe. 
How to keep the creepy crawlies at bay
In a region where outdoors is a way of life, there’s no need to cede territory or fun to ticks. Basic precautions can go a long way to avoiding alpha-gal. Here’s what you need to know: 
Practice basic precautions. Wear long socks tucked into pants; avoid rubbing up against tall grass and brush. Stay on trails. Consider wearing permethrin-treated clothing and tick repellents labeled for skin application. And stay on guard, as ticks are now more active year-round due to climate change.
Conduct a thorough tick check. Check for ticks on clothes and skin while outside. Once inside, remove clothes and closely check armpits, genitals and scalp. Dry clothes on high heat to kill undetected ticks and take a shower to help detect ticks and wash them off of skin. 
Remove ticks quickly and carefully. Try to pluck off ticks before they bite. If attached, remove quickly to decrease changes of getting a tick-borne illness. Using tweezers, pull carefully near the head. Once removed, clean the bite area.
Evaluate your landscaping. Eliminate piles of leaves and brush. Consider avoiding plants that attract deer and other host animals, like raccoons and rabbits. Do not feed wildlife, as this can lead to hosts lingering and dropping ticks. 
Consider precautions for pets. Tick-control medication is shown to reduce tick bites in their human owners. 
Get tested if you have symptoms. Alpha-gal syndrome is diagnosed by a blood test and can only be confirmed when symptoms are present. There’s currently no cure for alpha-gal, but it is manageable with proper medical care and, for some, goes away within three to five years.

title: Prayer, dynamite and leadership: 60 years of West Virginia water worries
description: The sight of a family on the shores of Summersville Lake, adults cooking on a fire while scattered children explore an inlet, is a common and relatable scene for many West Virginians over the last 60 years.  The scene is slightly different and more historical when the observer is Lady Bird Johnson swooshing in via […]
text:
President Lyndon B. Johnson and his wife, Lady Bird, attend the dedication of the Summersville Dam in Summersville, West Virginia, on Sept. 3, 1966. (West Virginia State Division of Culture and History photo)The sight of a family on the shores of Summersville Lake, adults cooking on a fire while scattered children explore an inlet, is a common and relatable scene for many West Virginians over the last 60 years. 
The scene is slightly different and more historical when the observer is Lady Bird Johnson swooshing in via helicopter to mark the newly man-made wonder of West Virginia water.
The then-First Lady was accompanying her husband President Lyndon Baines Johnson to the dedication ceremony of the new Summersville Dam. The first couple were joined by legendary U.S. Sen. Jennings Randolph and up-and-coming politicos like Sen. Robert C. Byrd and Congressmen Ken Hechler, John Slack, Harley Staggers, James Kee and a young Arch Moore, Jr. among others participating in the presidential festivities. Sept. 3, 1966, saw thousands gather at Charleston to greet the Convair version of Air Force One and thousands more anywhere they could fit around the 390 foot high and nearly half-mile long earth fill dedicated to keeping the Gauley River specifically and Kanawha River basin generally at bay.   
Lady Bird’s personal audio diary for the day noted several things about her brief trip to West Virginia. She found the scars of strip mining viewed from the air ghastly, noting “It is just as though some heedless child had been turned loose with a giant crayon on an enormous mural of forested hillsides and soft green valleys with creeks — the broad ugly scars of the strip mining laid bare to the hillsides, crawling around the mountains and on and on into the distance — ugly, brutal, dramatic.” 
She preserved into the official record the long-running joke locally of the naming of the lake, dam, and the speech LBJ was to give dedicating it all under the nomenclature of “Summersville,” despite the post office town of Gad having been relegated to the depths by eminent domain and the greater good. The wisdom of not naming such a feat of engineering the “Gad Dam, West Virginia” was as amusing to the First Lady then as it has been to locals ever since. And she noted the family in the inlet on the blanket ignoring the pomp, politics and policy to just enjoy the time on the water. 
For his part, LBJ delivered a speech that, after the usual acknowledgements of present persons of note, was an impressive mix of history and forethought. The president used his remarks to trace water as a constant challenge of mankind throughout history. Notorious for editing and “flavoring” his speeches from prepared text, Johnson put quite a bit of himself and impressive perspective into what could have easily been a low effort appearance. He talked of frustration at seeing flooding as president from aircraft and the devastation wrought, and touted the dam behind him — where workers had spelled out a nearly 400 foot long “Summersville Dam” into the earthwork itself as background — for its potential flood control abilities. 
The president related to being from the arid parts of Texas where water was scarce and valuable. The long-time congressman and U.S. senator before becoming vice president and then president touted his legislative pushes throughout his career across the country. He spoke of pollution control while still fueling industries and protecting water quality
Then the president zoomed out. He talked of the entire world, and how no water meant no peace. He listed seven points his administration was looking to work towards. He announced a forthcoming international conference on the subject. He talked about the entire history of humans being a struggle to get, use and keep water, and his desire “to get people to think of this most important subject before it is too late.” He punctuated his remarks with a quote from Texan historian Walter Prescott Webb on how humans had “resorted to every expedient from prayer to dynamite” to win the war for water. Webb concluded, “The story of their efforts is, on the whole, one of pathos and tragedy, of a few successes and many failures.”
President Johnson added his own piece to the quote, motioning to the dam he was dedicating behind him and to the already recognized elected officials standing beside him. “You not only have the prayer and the dynamite, you have the leadership of men in the Congress. You have the leadership of the great Corps of Engineers who participated. You have leadership in the state level with your great governor — to build projects like this that millions in years to come will enjoy, and millions today will thank you for.”
Sixty years after that visit to Summersville Dam finds West Virginians still waging wars over water. 
The long hot summer of 2026 has brought flood after flood to the state. Over the last 60 years, hundreds of West Virginians have died and untold thousands more affected by various floods, from the industrial massacre of Buffalo Creek to the Election Day floods in 1985 to the “thousand year” flooding of 2016. A renewed political debate over water policy, the kind of water for drinking and using for things, have renewed cries from the affected to “do something” to the political leaders. Leaders who have to solve the old problem of too many needs and not enough money and political will to tend them all but needing to show activity to keep their positions regardless of the issue at hand being solvable.
In the gaps where dynamite and engineering cannot or will not be used, prayer is substituted. Thoughts and prayers to mourn the dead. Crying out for relief when the building block of all life doesn’t come out of the tap clean and usable. Forlorn hoping a loving God can overcome bureaucratic limitations and infrastructure realities. The “thoughts and prayers” phrasing can also turn into cynical prayer-coded condescending buzzwords from more privileged outsiders aimed at their perceived lessers who they think should not be so. Unlike engineering and dynamite, the results of prayers answered and otherwise are more nuanced and hard to define as successful or not. 
By any measurement Summersville Lake and Dam has been a great success. During the already historically deadly 2016 flooding the US Army Corps of Engineers estimated the massive earth fill dam on the Gauley shouldered 42 feet of floodwater that otherwise would have caused Biblical destruction to downstream areas, including Charleston. 
Tourism has been a hallmark of the area, since impounding the mighty Gauley River for summer leisure on the lake also means world class white water in the fall when winter pool drain means rising river rapids. Rafters put in for the Gauley run right below where LBJ spoke that day 60 years ago, even as a hydroelectric plant made the outflow less visually stunning but more useful to the area. More recently Summersville Lake State Park formalized what many already knew, that this particular corner of the wild and wonderful was worthy of specific attention. 
All that success is because of leadership seeing through plans dating back to the 1930s to control water in West Virginia. Whether for power, for recreating, for preventing death and destruction, for 60 years Summersville Lake and Dam harnessing water has shown what can be done. The ability to dynamite and engineer such things is well established. The hopes and prayers of the citizens for better in the future are constants. 
The variable is leadership. 
While Lady Bird Johnson was visually processing the mining scars across the West Virginia hillsides she felt so deeply, she asked the governor of West Virginia’s wife Mrs. Smith if there was any sort of legislation requiring the mines to do something about what they had created. “Yes” she noted in her audio diary the reply. “That’s the business on the agenda. It involves mostly some sort of terracing because they are an erosion problem.”
Quite the summation in Lady Bird Johnson’s September sojourn to Summersville in 1966. She sees a massive, ugly, glaring problem on the way in and gets only a vague answer in return. Enjoys a ceremony set up with maximum pomp and circumstance to mark a real achievement that will make an everyday, mundane, under-appreciated difference. Flying over a family oblivious to it all because their focus is enjoying family time along a lake that months before didn’t even exist but would become one of thousands of stories. Pretty good West Virginia experience as highly choreographed official visits go.  
Meanwhile, the fight for and over water in West Virginia continues, with three fewer congressional districts. We still have the dynamite to get things done and prayers to see us through. Have a bit of a leadership issue, though. It mostly involves some sort of terracing because there is an erosion problem.

name: Michigan Advance
title: The ‘show-your-papers’ measure failed to reach the ballot. That’s good for Michigan’s newest voters
description: At a time when media is reporting on Gen Z’s lack of political engagement (prompting unfair accusations of apathy), many colleges and universities, along with nonprofit partners, such as the Fair Elections Center’s Campus Vote Project, are working to instill feelings of civic agency and lifelong voting habits in our nation’s newest voters. After all, […]
text:
A sign welcoming voters outside Thompson Middle School in Saginaw, Mich. May 5, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. At a time when media is reporting on Gen Z’s lack of political engagement (prompting unfair accusations of apathy), many colleges and universities, along with nonprofit partners, such as the Fair Elections Center’s Campus Vote Project, are working to instill feelings of civic agency and lifelong voting habits in our nation’s newest voters. After all, the future health of our democracy depends on the constant generational renewal of civically engaged citizens.
But in Michigan, anti-voting operatives are trying to advance policies that would silence young voters before they’ve even had a chance to find their political voices. After a “show your papers” bill requiring documentary proof of citizenship (DPOC) for voter registration stalled twice in the Michigan legislature, anti-voter groups responded by trying to gather enough signatures to have the question of whether DPOC should be required included as a ballot initiative in the upcoming 2026 elections.
The State Board of Canvassers deadlocked on whether the signatures met the state’s legal requirements, meaning the measure is not currently on the ballot. If it remains off, that would be a win for voters.
Board of State Canvassers deadlocks on citizens-only voting measure, setting up court fight

But the anti-voter forces behind the bill have vowed to turn to the courts to break the tie and force the issue to the ballot. If ultimately voted on and passed, this bad-faith anti-voter policy, rooted in demonstrably false narratives of noncitizen voting, would silence the voices of thousands of eligible Michigan voters—not just young people—and needs to be stopped in its tracks.
The problem? Many eligible Michigan voters, like thousands of eligible voters across the U.S., do not have or cannot access the required documents—such as a passport or birth certificate. Many more who have changed their names do not have documentation that matches their birth names (a category that includes millions of married women).
For students, the barriers that DPOC requirements would impose are clear. According to a recent Institute for Responsive Government study, 24% of 18–29-year-olds reported lacking the necessary documents. In several of the states covered by the study, voters in this age group were two to three times more likely to have trouble accessing proof-of-citizenship documents than those aged over 30.
The solution is not as simple as obtaining the necessary documents—for many, getting a passport or tracking down a birth certificate can be prohibitively costly and time-consuming, often taking weeks or months.
Students who live on campus are particularly vulnerable to being stopped from voting by these laws. Even those who have obtained a passport or a birth certificate often do not keep those sensitive documents on campus with them in dorms or group houses. As a result, requiring students to show documents to register severely hampers on-campus voter registration opportunities. These critical student engagement efforts cannot operate effectively when potential voters have to show paper documents to sign up.
Arizona provides a real-world example of whom DPOC requirements will disenfranchise. According to a 2024 Votebeat analysis, of the roughly 32,000 people excluded from voting in state elections in Arizona because they lacked DPOC, a disproportionate number were geographically concentrated in areas that included college campuses, most of them likely young voters: 18–24-year-olds in the state were nearly three times more likely to be excluded from voting in state elections because they lacked proof of citizenship.
The red tape that DPOC requirements force on voters is entirely unnecessary and will stop thousands of eligible citizens from voting for absolutely no good reason. Existing law already safeguards our elections to ensure that any instances of a noncitizen casting a ballot are extremely rare and usually a mistake. Noncitizen voting is already illegal under state and federal law, and state-level reviews of Michigan’s 2024 election cycle found that just .00028% of the more than 5.7 million ballots were cast by non-citizens.
Voting is habit forming: Michigan should continue to increase opportunities to start a life-long voting habit, not set up red tape that makes it harder to become an engaged citizen. We must work to ensure every eligible voter, no matter their age or background, can participate fully and fairly. Failure (so far) of the 2026 DPOC initiative is a win for voters that protects our elections and strengthens our democracy.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Wendell Berry asked: What do we owe to the place that sustains us?
description: Some Kentuckians become so rooted in this place that it is difficult to think of one without the other. Wendell Berry was such a Kentuckian. He died Monday at age 92 at his beloved Lane’s Landing Farm in Port Royal, Ky.  Poet, novelist, essayist, teacher, farmer, conservationist, and dissenter, he spent a lifetime asking: What […]
text:
Wendell Berry and the now King Charles met at the  Cathedral of the Assumption on the day of Prince Charles' visit in 2015. (Photo by John Nation)Some Kentuckians become so rooted in this place that it is difficult to think of one without the other. Wendell Berry was such a Kentuckian. He died Monday at age 92 at his beloved Lane’s Landing Farm in Port Royal, Ky. 
Poet, novelist, essayist, teacher, farmer, conservationist, and dissenter, he spent a lifetime asking: What do we owe to the place that sustains us?
It is an old question in Kentucky, a state blessed — and sometimes burdened — by the abundance of its earth. Limestone and timber, coal and tobacco, fertile fields and flowing rivers have brought prosperity. Yet too often we mistake possession for stewardship, taking what the land yields without asking what must be returned or preserved for those who follow.
Berry answered from Henry County, along the Kentucky River, where generations of his family had lived. He came home, farmed with horses, walked the fields, knew his neighbors, watched the seasons turn and wrote from that attentive life.
He understood that anyone who speaks for the land ought first to know one place intimately — its creeks and hollows, good ground and poor, abundance and limits. From that small piece of Kentucky came a vision that reached far beyond it.
He opposed war, strip mining, industrial agriculture and heedless consumption, challenging the notion that whatever can be done profitably ought to be done. His criticism of Kentucky came from affection, not contempt. He loved the place too much to flatter it. When mountains were torn apart for coal and small farms disappeared, he warned that something more precious than efficiency was being lost. When modern life assured us that progress was inevitable, Berry asked: Progress toward what?
Such questions did not always make him popular. They made him necessary.
Wendell Berry said that to inherit land was not simply to own it; it was to accept its care.
He gave that idea human form in Port William, his fictional Kentucky community, where people are joined by memory, necessity, affection, obligation and forgiveness. They share work and sorrow, bury their dead and remember those who came before. Belonging there is more than geography; it is a covenant with the land, neighbors, the dead and those not yet born.
That idea traveled far. When Charles, then Prince of Wales, came to Louisville in 2015, Berry introduced him at the Cathedral of the Assumption. The prince called Berry “a very special son of Kentucky” and said he had “long been a hero of mine.” One man was born to inherit a kingdom; the other chose to tend a Kentucky hillside. Yet both understood that inheritance is not merely what we receive, but what is placed in our care.
That understanding ran through Wendell Berry’s life. In an age that celebrated mobility, he celebrated staying. Against enormous institutions, he defended the farm, town, household, and neighbor. And when information was mistaken for wisdom, he reminded us that wisdom begins with attention—to a field after rain, a river’s bend, a wounded mountainside, an old man’s memory, a country churchyard’s silence.
Someday today’s arguments will seem distant. Institutions will change, fortunes disappear, and much we mistake for permanence will be gone.
But the Kentucky River will still turn through Henry County. Rain will fall on the fields. Someone will plant in spring, hope for a harvest and walk toward evening beneath a tree planted long ago by hands he never knew.
Perhaps that person will understand that the ground beneath his feet was never entirely his. Others walked there before him; others will follow.
For a little while, it was entrusted to his care.
Wendell Berry understood that. He spent a lifetime teaching Kentucky the same.
That may be the finest definition of stewardship we have.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Data shows 94,000 Virginians have dropped their ACA insurance since last year
description: (Photo by Getty Images)
text:
The U.S. House will begin debate in committee this week on a bill that would cut Medicaid spending. (Photo by Getty Images)Of an estimated 100,000 people whom state health leaders predicted were vulnerable to losing their Affordable Care Act insurance in Virginia, 94,000 have dropped it so far this year, according to new numbers from the State Health Benefit Exchange. 
There were 389,000 enrollees in 2025 and 295,000 enrollees as of this week. 
The reduction is attributed in part to the expiration of subsidies that had helped expand the ACA marketplace to people whose incomes are further below the federal poverty level. Debate over the issue triggered a government shutdown last year and Congress ultimately elected to let the subsidies lapse.  
This spring, when the decline in Virginia ACA enrollees was at 33,000, State Health Benefit Exchange Director Keven Patchett called the reduction the “biggest drop-off in the first quarter that we’ve seen.” 
Virginia Association of Health Plans director Doug Gray said at the time if the state could keep the number of people forfeiting their insurance under 100,000, he’d “call that a victory.” 
People filter on and off the ACA as their income levels or employment-provided insurance status changes, but Del. Rodney Willet, D-Henrico, surmises the drop offs this year may largely be due to the expired subsidies. 
It’s why he and fellow state lawmakers earmarked $150 million in Virginia’s current budget to create a temporary version of the expired assistance to help Virginians between 138% and 250% of the federal poverty level. 
Eligible Virginians will be able to tap into that relief when marketplace enrollment opens in November. The state-level subsidies are meant to help offset costs for purchasing insurance in the state exchange and participants could save about 70% on their monthly premiums. 
Still, it’s a temporary fix to a long-term challenge, Willett acknowledged. Lawmakers devoted about a third of the state budget to healthcare this year.  
“We did the best we could with the budget,” Willett said. “But trying to sustain that for years and years would be tough.” 
The reconciliation bill Congress passed last summer includes forthcoming changes to Medicaid eligibility and hospital funding mechanisms. 
Of Virginia’s nearly 2 million Medicaid enrollees, more than 500,000 will be subject to new work requirements and additional verification paperwork each year, while about 5,800 lawful immigrants will lose coverage. 
Some of these people may be able to explore the state marketplace but others may lose health insurance altogether.
Gov. Abigail Spanberger recently issued an executive order to streamline the work of ensuring eligible Virginians don’t lose coverage 
Meanwhile, the pending hospital funding mechanisms may also contribute to potential closure or reduced services for 13 rural hospitals, a state report found. Hospitals predict a $31 billion reduction in the state’s Medicaid funding over the next decade. 
As part of negotiations during the reconciliation bill debate, federal lawmakers created the Rural Health Transformation Fund, a $50 billion investment for states over the next five years. Last week, officials announced the disbursement of $122 million of Virginia’s $189 million piece of that pie. 
The money can be used to boost initiatives in rural areas to compensate for both longstanding healthcare access issues and potential shortfalls stemming from the reconciliation bill. 
“(Those dollars) in no way replace what’s happening with the (Big Beautiful Bill),” Willett said. “They will help around the edges, but this is a multi-billion dollar impact with the Medicaid disruption.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: After FAA certification, Washington Manassas Airport to offer commercial flights
description: The Federal Aviation Administration announced on Monday that the Washington Manassas Airport can begin offering service to certain commercial passenger airlines, opening the door to more flight opportunities for the Washington region, including Northern Virginia.  Washington Manassas Airport, formerly  Manassas Regional, will become the fourth commercial air[...]
text:
A passenger's view from a plane's wing. (Photo by Julia Shumway/Oregon Capital Chronicle)The Federal Aviation Administration announced on Monday that the Washington Manassas Airport can begin offering service to certain commercial passenger airlines, opening the door to more flight opportunities for the Washington region, including Northern Virginia. 
Washington Manassas Airport, formerly  Manassas Regional, will become the fourth commercial airport in the Washington region, giving travelers another choice and possibly expanding economic activity, local leaders said.
The agency said the airport is the first to receive the operating certificate in 53 years, a milestone that will be followed by a build-out of modern infrastructure and technology to enable safe, sustained commercial passenger service.
“The certificate serves as FAA’s official seal of approval, confirming that this airfield’s safety protocols, emergency response capabilities, and operational infrastructure meet the rigorous federal standards required to support regional passenger airlines,” said FAA Associate Administrator for Airports Dan Edwards. “It’s a huge win for regional connectivity and for the local economy.”
Leaders from various levels of government joined Edwards for the announcement at the airport on Monday.
The FAA said the airport received its Part 139 Airport Operating Certificate after demonstrating compliance with multiple federal safety standards, including runway and taxiway pavement conditions, aircraft rescue and firefighting, emergency planning, wildlife hazard management and personnel training.
According to the agency, the airport has also received more than $46 million in federal funds over the past five years to support critical infrastructure improvements, including runway rehabilitation, a new passenger terminal opening in fall 2027, and construction of a new air traffic control tower, which is scheduled to be completed in 2029.
Airport director Juan Rivera said the facility’s new commercial certification capped an intentionally rigorous process designed to protect passengers.
“Getting a Part 139 operating certificate is not an easy process, and quite honestly, it should not be,” Rivera said. “The requirements are rigorous for a reason. At the end of the day, this is about safety and security of our flying public, and that’s something that we take seriously here at the airport every single day.”
Greg Campbell, director of the Virginia Department of Aviation, framed the airport’s switch from general aviation to commercial service as a rare, complex, and highly significant upgrade driven by local leadership that is expected to yield major economic and connectivity benefits.
“Moving an airport from a general aviation airport to an air carrier commercial service airport with the FAA is a big deal, and I’m so glad that we could be here today,” Campbell said.
He added that the milestone makes Manassas Airport Virginia’s 10th air carrier or commercial service airport.
Rivera said he hopes the airport will celebrate its first commercial flight in November 2027, offering about three or four round-trip flights a day to vacation destinations. He did not specify which air carrier is being considered, only that it would be low-cost for travelers.

name: Michigan Advance
title: As James pushes local control on data centers, past congressional votes sought to limit just that
description: U.S. Rep. John James of Shelby Township, the Republican nominee for governor, has staked his campaign’s data center platform on local control. But in Congress, he voted for legislation that would expressly prohibit state and local governments from regulating artificial intelligence systems — including data centers. “My priority is frankly local control, prot[...]
text:
U.S. Rep. John James speaks to reporters after submitting his nominating petitions to the Michigan Bureau of Elections in Lansing in his bid for Republican nominee for governor. April 20, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. U.S. Rep. John James of Shelby Township, the Republican nominee for governor, has staked his campaign’s data center platform on local control. But in Congress, he voted for legislation that would expressly prohibit state and local governments from regulating artificial intelligence systems — including data centers.
“My priority is frankly local control, protecting our water, protecting and preventing pollution, making sure that electricity bills do not go up, and also making sure that we prioritize blighted and brown fields over productive green farmland,” James said of data centers at a gubernatorial debate in early July. “That would be my moratorium, that would be our standard. We absolutely cannot have an additional data center until we protect the people and communities. That’s no NDAs, that’s making sure we don’t have the ground, air, and water, also the noise pollution, and making sure that, again, we protect local control.”
However, James voted in May 2025 for the U.S. House’s version of H.R. 1, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which included an explicit 10-year moratorium stating that “no State or political subdivision thereof may enforce any law or regulation regulating artificial intelligence models, artificial intelligence systems, or automated decision systems.”
GOP Gubernatorial candidates (L-R) Mike Cox, John James and Perry Johnson on stage at a debate hosted by Fox 2 Detroit. July 8, 2026. | Screenshot
That moratorium, part of a $500 million investment in an “artificial intelligence and information technology modernization initiative,” did not make it into the final version of H.R. 1 that became law. However, as a member of the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, James voted in favor of the specific moratorium three times: twice voting to advance it out of committee, and once voting against an amendment that would have removed it from the bill.
“John James voted for H.R. 1 to deliver historic tax relief to working families across the country. His approach to data centers has been clear: no new data centers until we protect our people,” Alyvia Bailey, a spokesperson for the James campaign, wrote in a statement to the Michigan Advance. “He will re-establish local control, ensure no utility rate increases for residents or secret deals, protect our water and air, prioritize brownfields, and preserve farmland.”
Bailey did not directly address questions about James’ votes for the moratorium within the House version of H.R. 1.
The National Conference of State Legislatures, a bipartisan organization representing the interests of state legislatures, cautioned against a vote in favor of that provision, writing that it would “circumvent their authority to regulate the permitting, construction and operation of data centers within their borders” for states. 
“This will severely limit the ability of states and localities to make decisions regarding the siting and operation of these large-scale projects, raising costs for ratepayers, jeopardizing zoning decisions that protect our mutual constituents and impacting existing infrastructure such as power grids and generating facilities,” Tim Storey, the group’s CEO, wrote in a letter. 
Meanwhile, James, who has aligned himself closely with President Donald Trump and received his endorsement in the primary election, must now navigate Trump’s enthusiastic support for data centers. 
In a post Monday on Truth Social, Trump said that the United States should “let Data Reign” and that if communities push back against data centers, they “want to end up being backwards and poor.” 
President Donald Trump speaks at a roundtable event at the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency on Thursday, July 23, 2026. The event promoted the administration’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge that seeks to cap utility prices in communities that have new data centers. (Screenshot from White House livestream)
But data centers remain unpopular in Michigan. A survey conducted Aug. 22 through Aug. 28 by EPIC-MRA found 73% of respondents were opposed to “current federal tax breaks and other federal policies that were put in place to encourage and speed up the development of data centers.” Meanwhile, a Detroit Regional Chamber poll conducted in May 2026 found that while an overwhelming majority opposed data centers in their regions, with regulations in place, “a plurality of Michigan voters would shift to consider a data center within 25 miles of their homes.”
James has continued emphasizing his messaging in favor of local control in the lead-up to the primary and in the weeks since, even as the head of his party has publicly disagreed.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“My position is we need to have a plan to protect our communities. Until we do, then we have to make sure that we have local control,” James said on CBS Face the Nation on Saturday. “Our electricity bills can’t go up. We must protect our water. We have to prevent pollution, that includes land, air, and noise pollution, and then we need to make sure that we prioritize blighted brownfields over productive green farmland.”
The push for local control in data center development crosses party lines — James’ Democratic opponent, Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, said at the Michigan Democratic Party nominating convention on Saturday that “there needs to be a moratorium on data centers unless we know that we have those guardrails in place.”
“If any corporation, be it a data center or anyone else, wants to come to Michigan, they have to play by our rules,” she said. “They cannot use or abuse our natural resources. They cannot drive up energy costs, and they have to have the will of the people and the welcoming of their community on their side if they want to set up shop in any community in the state.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: A hemp farmer has some questions for Rhode Island’s next attorney general
description: Last October, Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha joined 38 other state attorneys general in signing a letter urging Congress to change the federal definition of hemp. On Aug. 4, Neronha signed another multistate letter, this time urging Congress to reject any effort to “delay, repeal, suspend, or weaken” hemp restrictions enacted in November 2025. [[...]
text:
CBD products grown in compliance with Rhode Island state law in Hopkinton may naturally exceed  more than 0.4 milligrams of THC per package, which violates a new federal definition of hemp enacted late last year.
(Photo courtesy of Lovewell Farms)Last October, Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha joined 38 other state attorneys general in signing a letter urging Congress to change the federal definition of hemp. On Aug. 4, Neronha signed another multistate letter, this time urging Congress to reject any effort to “delay, repeal, suspend, or weaken” hemp restrictions enacted in November 2025.
I have now written twice in the last year about the problems with this federal policy and its consequences for Rhode Island farmers and small businesses. I write as the co-founder of Lovewell Farms, Rhode Island’s only USDA-certified organic hemp farm, founded in 2018. I write this with nearly 20 years experience in cannabis and drug policy. Lovewell Farms supports strong regulation of hemp products, including testing, reasonable potency limits, child-resistant packaging, accurate labeling and restrictions on sales to minors. 
What we do not support is describing Rhode Island’s regulated hemp industry as something that is harmful.
That was one of the central problems with the October 2025 attorneys general letter. It described a national hemp market in which products are sold “without consistent age restrictions, labeling standards, or safety requirements,” while discussing gummies and beverages marketed to children and synthetic cannabinoids produced through chemical conversion. Those concerns may be legitimate in states that have failed to regulate hemp products. They do not accurately describe Rhode Island. Neronha signing this letter made it appear he agreed with these claims, and that they were reflective of our state’s program.
But Rhode Island has a state-regulated hemp program. Businesses like mine operate under state licenses and are subject to the exact same requirements governing testing, potency, labeling, packaging and age restrictions as the state’s medicinal cannabis program. The state has also placed specific limits on THC in consumable hemp products. There is certainly room to debate whether those regulations should change, but it is simply inaccurate to describe Rhode Island’s hemp market as unregulated and unsafe. 
This distinction became particularly important after Congress enacted a new federal definition of hemp last November. Rhode Island Sens. Jack Reed and Sheldon Whitehouse both opposed an amendment that would have removed the hemp provision, and their offices subsequently told Rhode Island Current that they did so “at the urging of the vast majority of the state attorneys general.” Neronha’s participation in the October letter therefore had consequences beyond Rhode Island. It provided the justification for a congressional vote that now threatens farmers nationwide.



Quotation







What we do not support is describing Rhode Island’s regulated hemp industry as something that is harmful.


This August letter is more troubling after the U.S. House of Representatives on Tuesday passed legislation that would give farmers another month before the new definition takes effect. The provision is part of a short-term government funding bill to avoid a federal shutdown this fall. It keeps the federal government funded through Dec. 11 and was already approved by the Senate in early August. If signed into law by President Donald Trump, the effective date of the hemp product ban would also be moved to Dec. 11. Rather than support that effort, Neronha joined other attorneys general in asking Congress to reject any delay or modification. 
The problem remains that the federal definition is much broader than the synthetic and highly intoxicating products discussed throughout both letters. The August letter itself acknowledges that the new law excludes final hemp-derived cannabinoid products containing more than 0.4 milligrams of total THC per container. That threshold does not merely eliminate synthetic delta-8 products or high-potency THC gummies. It threatens ordinary, naturally extracted, full-spectrum CBD products containing trace amounts of THC like those manufactured on our farm.
This is important for farmers like me. CBD-rich hemp flower plants naturally produce small amounts of THC. Full-spectrum extracts preserve most of the natural cannabinoids in the plant. Our products can therefore be non-intoxicating, produced without chemical conversion, and compliant with state law, all while containing more than 0.4 milligrams of THC per package.
The August letter nevertheless states that the new definition will preserve “safe, nonintoxicating hemp products” and “will not inhibit the cultivation of hemp.” For cannabinoid hemp farmers, those assertions deserve considerably more scrutiny. Congress should be able to prohibit synthetic intoxicants or establish reasonable national standards without defining naturally occurring, non-intoxicating full-spectrum CBD products out of existence.
AG candidates: Please answer the following
This issue now has particular relevance in Rhode Island because Neronha is term-limited. The state will elect a new attorney general this year, and that person will inherit the authority to sign letters like these on Rhode Island’s behalf. The candidates for attorney general should therefore explain their positions on hemp before the primary election.

Do you support Rhode Island’s existing regulated hemp industry? 
Do you believe naturally occurring full-spectrum CBD products should remain legal? 
Do you support the federal 0.4-milligram-per-container standard, even when it prohibits non-intoxicating products that are legal under state law? 
Do you support distinguishing those products from chemically converted intoxicating cannabinoids? 
Will you consult Rhode Island regulators, farmers, and licensed businesses before signing national policy letters that make factual claims about our state?

When an attorney general signs such a letter, the signature carries the authority of the state. As the congressional response to the October letter demonstrated, those signatures can influence federal policy. The August letter suggests that there is still a substantial disconnect between the national hemp debate and the businesses operating under Rhode Island law.
The next attorney general has an opportunity to approach this differently. Rhode Island does not need someone who automatically agrees with the hemp industry, nor should the industry be exempt from scrutiny. We need an attorney general who understands the laws already in place and distinguishes between regulated and unregulated markets, intoxicating and non-intoxicating products, and synthetic cannabinoids and the naturally occurring compounds found in a legal agricultural crop.
Rhode Island has already chosen to regulate hemp rather than prohibit it. Our next attorney general should explain whether they intend to defend that decision, or abandon it.
