name: North Carolina Newsline
title: US House censures NC Rep. Chuck Edwards for inappropriate conduct, harassment
description: The U.S. House of Representatives voted Tuesday 413-2 to censure Rep. Chuck Edwards, a Republican representing western North Carolina, for his inappropriate conduct towards two female staffers working in his office. Edwards stood in the well of the House to hear the reading of censure after the vote. A lengthy House Ethics Committee investigation released […[...]
text:
Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-NC) talks to reporters as he arrives for a House Republican conference in the basement of the U.S. Capitol on September 01, 2026 in Washington, DC.  (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)The U.S. House of Representatives voted Tuesday 413-2 to censure Rep. Chuck Edwards, a Republican representing western North Carolina, for his inappropriate conduct towards two female staffers working in his office.
Edwards stood in the well of the House to hear the reading of censure after the vote.
A lengthy House Ethics Committee investigation released this summer found “substantial evidence” that Edwards created a “hostile work environment.”
In its report, the House Ethics Committee found Edwards gave the two young female staffers gifts including jewelry worth over $1,000, a Las Vegas trip, and “designer purses, guns, shoes, flowers, a laptop and cell phone, KitchenAid mixer, robotic vacuum, vacations, tickets to performances, and one-on-one dinners.”
On another occasion, Edwards skipped a House vote to decorate a Christmas tree with a female staffer, according to the Ethics review.
Ethics Committee Chairman Rep. Michael Guest, R-Mississippi, said Tuesday while the committee found no evidence that Edwards engaged in sexual activity with the women, he violated rules prohibiting sexual harassment.
“The committee reviewed Rep. Edwards conduct and determined that he engaged in persistent, unprofessional, and inappropriate conduct,” said Guest. “While Rep. Edwards denies that his conduct was intended to be sexual or romantic, his pattern of behavior would lead a reasonable person to interpret it as such.”
“The committee found that Rep. Edwards was at a minimum blind to the reality, and at worst, dismissive of the impact his conduct had on the careers and well-being of the women on his staff,” Guest said.
Edwards denied the findings of the ethics committee report, insisting that his behavior, while perhaps ill-advised, didn’t rise to the level of sexual harassment. He used some of his time on the floor to apologize to the two staffers, both of whom subsequently left their jobs.
“I’m sorry that my actions, my judgment, or the way that I express the friendship ever puteither of you in an uncomfortable position,” said Edwards. “My intentions were only grounded in what I understood our friendship to be and in genuine admiration and respect I had for each of you, not only as professionals, but as people.”
Edwards then apologized to his wife.
“Teresa, you stood beside me through a lifetime of challenges, sacrifices, successes, and disappointments,” Edwards said. “I’m deeply sorry that my judgment and my actions put you in a position where you had to endure embarrassment, hurt, public scrutiny, and questions that no wife should ever have to face.”
Edwards stressed that his acknowledgement of regret and poor judgment was not an admission of sexual harassment. “Generosity is not sexual harassment,” he said. “Caring deeply about the people with whom you’ve worked for years is not sexual harassment.”
He asked his colleagues to spare him from a label that would mar his name and record in Congress.
“A censure by this House carries the weight of history,” said Edwards.
Rep. Mark DeSaulnier (D-CA), ranking member on House Ethics, dismissed Edwards’ arguments.
“Rep. Edwards may not have made physical advances or explicit propositions, but sexual harassment does not require either,” DeSaulnier responded. “His conduct was inappropriate, unwelcome, and most importantly, created a hostile work environment.”
NC Rep. Edwards drops reelection campaign following ethics probe, urging of Republican colleagues

Rep. Teresa Leger Fernandez, D-New Mexico, called Edwards’ behavior “disgusting and horrible.”
Fernandez chastised Edwards for threatening the careers and safety of his staff with his behavior, and breaking a pledge to his constituents to act with dignity and integrity.
“These women lost their jobs because of Mr. Edward’s behavior. He should lose his,” said Fernandez. “It’s time we reform the rules in Congress, so abusers like Edwards are at least stripped of committee assignments or expelled if the offense calls for it after an investigation and after a vote of the full floor.”
After the vote, Edwards released a statement saying while he respects the U.S. House, he does not accept their conclusion.
“I will not confess to conduct I did not commit simply to make this moment easier,” wrote Edwards on social media. “The House has spoken. So have I. I will leave this chapter with my head held high and finish the job Western North Carolina sent me here to do.”
Edwards, who has represented North Carolina’s 11th congressional district since 2023, dropped his bid for reelection August 5th.
The North Carolina Republican Party selected state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom of Henderson County to fill Edwards’ spot on the ballot against Democrat Jamie Ager.
This story has been updated to correct the House of Representatives vote count to censure.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: CHI St. Vincent no longer part of Blue Cross Blue Shield of Arkansas network
description: CHI St. Vincent will not be part of the Blue Cross Blue Shield of Arkansas network after the Little Rock-based hospital system and the insurer failed to reach an agreement on renewing their contract, both sides announced Tuesday. The two failed to reach an agreement during negotiations over the past several months about how much […]
text:
(Getty Images)CHI St. Vincent will not be part of the Blue Cross Blue Shield of Arkansas network after the Little Rock-based hospital system and the insurer failed to reach an agreement on renewing their contract, both sides announced Tuesday.
The two failed to reach an agreement during negotiations over the past several months about how much the insurer reimburses CHI St. Vincent. 
“This was not the outcome we have been working toward, and please know that we have not and will not walk away,” CHI St. Vincent said in a statement on its website. “We remain fully committed to reaching a new agreement as quickly as possible, but the agreement must equitably address the need for fair reimbursement for the care we provide.”
Blue Cross Blue Shield of Arkansas said it was disappointed but appreciated the care the hospital system had provided to its members. 
“We are committed to exploring approaches that ensure our members receive high-quality care that is also cost-efficient, and we have communicated to CHI St. Vincent and CommonSpirit Health that if their focus or circumstances should change in the future, they have an open invitation to rejoin us in this work,” Alicia Berkemeyer, executive vice president and chief health management officer for Arkansas Blue Cross, said in a news release.
CHI St. Vincent, a part of Chicago-based CommonSpirit Health System, operates hospitals in Little Rock, Hot Springs, Morrilton and Sherwood. 
The stalemate means that claims with dates of service of Monday or earlier will continue to be reimbursed at in-network rates, Blue Cross Blue Shield said. 
Blue Cross members may be eligible to receive services with in-network coverage for the lesser of 90 days from the date they receive an out-of-network notice or until the condition for which they are being treated is resolved, if transition to another provider would be inappropriate or unsafe, the insurer said. More information about that coverage can be found online. 
The stalemate occurred as hospitals around Arkansas have had to scale back services because of the rising cost of services and the relatively low reimbursement rates they receive for providing care.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico lawmaker resigns from job with DA, accuses AG of ‘attempt to disrupt’ Epstein commission
description: The New Mexico state representative who leads the House’s investigation into the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein on Tuesday announced she had resigned from her job with a local district attorney amid mounting criticism.
text:
New Mexico Rep. Andrea Romero (D-Santa Fe), pictured on Aug. 5, 2026, said a recent letter from state Attorney General Raúl Torrez advising district attorneys not to hire sitting state lawmakers was an “attempt to disrupt” her work leading the state House investigatory subcommittee on Jeffrey Epstein. (Danielle Prokop for Source NM)The New Mexico state representative who leads the House’s investigation into the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein on Tuesday announced she had resigned from her job with a local district attorney amid mounting criticism.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
State Rep. Andrea Romero (D-Santa Fe) on Tuesday also said Attorney General Raúl Torrez’s recent advice that district attorneys across the state should not hire sitting state lawmakers was an “attempt to disrupt” her work leading the state House’s investigatory subcommittee on Epstein.
Romero’s employment with the First Judicial District Attorney’s Office came under scrutiny in recent weeks as Republican lawmakers called for an ethics investigation. House Minority Whip Alan Martinez (R-Rio Rancho) recently requested a legislative ethics investigation and said her work with the local DA’s office violated state laws that prohibit sitting lawmakers from simultaneously working as state employees.
Romero had previously defended her employment by citing a 2024 opinion from Torrez’s office, which cleared fellow Epstein commission member Rep. Andrea Reeb (R-Clovis) to serve as a special prosecutor in the prosecution of Alec Baldwin. Baldwin’s lawyers, citing the same law as Republican lawmakers, said Reeb’s work on the case was unconstitutional. She ultimately resigned from the case.
In a Monday letter to district attorneys statewide, Torrez wrote that his 2024 opinion “has been read more broadly than intended.” He instructed any DA’s office employing a lawmaker to rectify the situation immediately and noted that he would not pursue legal action against any office that had previously hired a lawmaker “based on an honest misunderstanding of our 2024 opinion.”
In a news release responding to Torrez’s letter, First Judicial District Attorney Mary Carmack-Altwies’ office said the agency was “disappointed” by Torrez’s directive but would comply with it.
“Andrea Romero sought appropriate guidance from the Attorney General’s Office before accepting a part-time position with the FJDA, and our Office relied on that guidance,” the statement said. “Romero is a licensed attorney whose professional experience made her well suited for a part-time role in our office. At a time when New Mexico continues to face challenges recruiting and retaining attorneys in public service, we believe qualified professionals should have opportunities to serve their communities in different ways.”
In a Tuesday statement issued through a New York-based public relations firm that represents Monica Lewinsky, Romero said that she had resigned from her job at the First Judicial District Attorney’s Office and said that she had previously “sought and had received explicit authorization to be allowed to hold both positions, a fact the AG’s office was well-aware of.”
She said she was “deeply disappointed” by Torrez’s Monday letter and saw it as “an attempt to disrupt the work of our Survivor Truth Commission that seeks justice for the many young people who were harmed by Jeffrey Epstein and his co-collaborators in our state.”
Torrez early this year reopened a criminal investigation into Epstein and sued the federal government for allegedly blocking the release of files related to the late sex offender. In August, Torrez joined U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.) to announce new federal legislation that he said would make it easier for law enforcement agencies across the nation to file legal challenges against the U.S. Department of Justice when it refuses to release Epstein-related documents.
Although Romero did not cite specific examples, she said that Torrez’s letter would impact other state lawmakers and force them to resign from their jobs.
New Mexico is the only state in the nation to not pay its lawmakers. Voters will have the choice in the Nov. 3 general election to change that.
“Serving as a legislator remains the greatest honor of my life, and no attempt to distract from our work will succeed,” Romero said.
The New Mexico Department of Justice did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Judge halts data center construction on public land
description: A federal administrative court has temporarily revoked authorization to build a massive data center near Boulder City, concluding the federal government likely erred when it approved the project construction on public land without a proper environmental analysis.  The Interior Board of Appeals ruled Tuesday that the Bureau of Land Management’s decision to ap[...]
text:
The Bureau of Land Management “acted arbitrarily or capriciously when it determined that the data center project is 'substantially the same' as the solar plant project for purposes of its NEPA analysis,” the judge wrote. (Photo: Bureau of Land Management)A federal administrative court has temporarily revoked authorization to build a massive data center near Boulder City, concluding the federal government likely erred when it approved the project construction on public land without a proper environmental analysis. 
The Interior Board of Appeals ruled Tuesday that the Bureau of Land Management’s decision to approve the construction of the Townsite Data Center on public land using a prior unrelated environmental analysis likely violated the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA).
Townsite Solar 2 LLC  — the project developer — originally received federal approval in 2023 to build a solar power generation and battery storage facility on the 88.5-acre parcel, but requested an amended right-of-way grant in 2025 to build a data center instead. 
Federal land managers did not study the effects of the data center project in a new environmental analysis, and instead approved the change in July after determining the data center project “is essentially like” the solar plant project and that it would have “similar anticipated impacts.”
The order comes after the Center for Biological Diversity and Boulder City filed an appeal in July against the Townsite data center, which became the first data center approved on BLM land in the United States.
An administrative judge determined there was persuasive evidence that BLM “acted arbitrarily or capriciously when it determined that the data center project is ‘substantially the same’ as the solar plant project for purposes of its NEPA analysis.”
The order prevents the data center project from moving forward while the Interior Board of Appeals considers legal challenges against the proposal. 
“We’re thrilled that this data center has been stopped dead in its tracks,” said Patrick Donnelly, Great Basin director at the Center for Biological Diversity in a statement. “The Trump administration is pulling out all the stops to let tech companies build massive data centers on our public lands. This tremendous victory proves communities have the power to fight back and win.”
The federal administrative court found that the appeal was likely to succeed on their claims that the BLM’s analysis of the solar plant project’s environmental effects was insufficient because the projects are not  “substantially the same”.
The temporary pause was granted after the Center for Biological Diversity “demonstrated that permanent and irreparable harm is likely to occur” if construction of the data center continued before the appeal is settled, and that those “harms outweigh the temporary financial harm to Townsite from the delay.”
Boulder City also filed an appeal and petitioned for a temporary pause on the project while their appeal makes its way through the federal process. However, the city’s petition was declared moot given the panel granted the Center for Biological Diversity petition seeking a pause. 
In the order, the Interior Board of Appeals consolidated both appeals filed by Boulder City and the Center for Biological Diversity and expedited the appeals. The panel ordered BLM to respond by Sept. 21.
Construction of the Townsite Data Center could have major implications for public lands throughout the West, and especially in Nevada where about 80% of the land is managed by the federal government.
In July, the Boulder City Council unanimously voted to appeal the BLM approval for a data center on an 80-acre BLM-owned parcel about three miles west of the city’s borders.  
Nevada Rep. Dina Titus, who represents the district where the data center would be located, sent a letter to federal land managers demanding answers about how the agency is reviewing proposals for data centers on public land following the approval of the BLM’s amended plan.
Titus Tuesday applauded the Interior Board of Land Appeals’ decision to halt the development of the Townsite Data Center. 
“The judge ruled for transparency and public accountability in granting a stay based on the BLM’s misuse of an environmental impact statement for a solar farm as justification for a data center. The two are vastly different.” Titus said in a statement. “I’ve said since day one that this was not only improper but illegal.”
Gov. Joe Lombardo, to whom Titus had also written seeking clarification about data centers on Nevada public land, and Townsite Solar 2 LLC did not immediately respond to requests of comment about the order. A spokesperson for the Interior said the department does not comment on litigation matters.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa nurses cited for patient-care issues or working without a valid license
description: State regulators have sanctioned Iowa two nurses for working more than a year without valid licenses and two nurses for patient-care issues. The Iowa Board of Nursing alleges that Baxter McNeal, 56, of Anita, while employed as a registered nurse at the Caring Acres Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in Anita, failed to provide proper assessments […]
text:
Caring Acres Nursing and Rehabilitation in Anita. (Photo via Google Earth)State regulators have sanctioned Iowa two nurses for working more than a year without valid licenses and two nurses for patient-care issues.
The Iowa Board of Nursing alleges that Baxter McNeal, 56, of Anita, while employed as a registered nurse at the Caring Acres Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in Anita, failed to provide proper assessments and interventions with regard to two residents of the home after they experienced a change in condition.
The board has disclosed no information as to when the alleged conduct occurred or the impact on the patients.
After charging McNeal with one count of failing to assess, accurately document, evaluate, or report the status of a patient, the board agreed to resolve the case with a settlement that calls for McNeal’s license to be placed on probationary status for one year. As part of the settlement, McNeal has agreed to complete 30 hours of educational training on ethics and standards of care.
Board records indicate that McNeal was convicted of drunken driving in 2003 and 2006, which led to him receiving a probationary nursing license from Nebraska regulators. In 2007, the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services initiated steps to revoke McNeal’s nursing license due to allegations that he had tested positive for alcohol. The board and McNeal later settled the matter by censuring McNeal and imposing a $500 civil penalty.
According to board records, McNeal was again convicted of drunken driving in 2010, which resulted in his Nebraska nursing license being placed on probation for five years.
In June 2012, McNeal received an Iowa nursing license and, according to the board, in 2014 he was convicted of felony operating a vehicle while his driver’s license was revoked. That conviction resulted in his Nebraska nursing license being suspended for six months. In September 2014, McNeal relinquished his right to practice in Iowa.
In January 2018, the Iowa Board of Nursing reinstated McNeal’s license to practice.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach McNeal for comment.
Other Iowa nurses recently sanctioned by the board include:
Sabryna Simon of Fort Dodge — The board alleges video evidence shows that on Sept. 11, 2025, Simon directed profane language at an infant client, and then “removed the client from the client’s highchair and placed the client on the floor.” The board, which has not disclosed where the incident took place, charged Simon with committing an act or omission that might adversely affect a patient’s welfare; failing to assess, accurately document, evaluate, or report the status of a patient; and engaging in behavior that is contradictory to professional decorum.
To settle the matter, Simon recently agreed to have her license placed on probation for two years. As part of the written settlement, Simon agreed to a provision that states she “shall not engage in the practice of No Home Health Care” — that terminology is left unexplained in the agreement — during her probation. Simon also agreed to complete 60 hours of educational training on ethics and documentation.
Suzanne Mentzer of West Des Moines – The board alleges Mentzer practiced as a registered nurse at The Iowa Clinic for more than a year, from April 23, 2024, through Aug. 7, 2025, without a valid nursing license. She and the board recently agreed to a settlement that calls for Mentzer to pay a $1,000 civil penalty.
Delilah Heuton of Atlantic — The board alleges that in April 2025, while Heuton worked at Heritage House Senior Living Community in Atlantic, it was discovered that she had been working without a valid nursing license for more than a year, since December 2023 when her Iowa license had expired.  She and the board recently agreed to a settlement that calls for Heuton to pay a $550 civil penalty.

title: Haitian college student who lost temporary protected status dies after walking into traffic
description: This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is contemplating suicide, please call or text the National Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988. A 20-year-old Haitian college student died in an apparent suicide Monday, which his father said came after the student was forced to wear an ankle monitor by U.S. Immigration and […]
text:
Signs from a recent rally against immigration enforcement actions targeting Haitian immigrants in Springfield, Ohio. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal)This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is contemplating suicide, please call or text the National Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988.
A 20-year-old Haitian college student died in an apparent suicide Monday, which his father said came after the student was forced to wear an ankle monitor by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Pierre Damas Bel, a Wright State University student, reportedly walked in front of a semi-truck on Interstate 70 on Monday after being bullied by his classmates for wearing an ankle monitor, according to his family.  
“He called me at 8:03 on a video call, (and said) ‘I’m not feeling okay mentally because of the bullying,’ and I told him to come home so we can talk,” Damas Bel’s father Pierre Ronal Bel, said in a statement.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Around 11 the police showed at my door to report that my son threw himself under a truck.”
The Ohio State Highway Patrol did not respond to a request for the incident report. 
Haitians living in Springfield are required to report to the ICE offices in Blue Ash or Westerville to accept ankle monitors. 
This started after the U.S. Supreme Court allowed President Donald Trump to end temporary protected status for the 330,000 Haitians who’ve fled violence in their home country. Legal protected status for Haitians officially ended on July 27. 
“This is one of the most tragic outcomes of the Trump administration’s cruel and inhumane attacks on the Haitian community,” Guerline Jozef of the Haitian Bridge Alliance said in a statement. 
Jozef said he believes the Trump administration is “fully responsible” in the death of Damas Bel, based on the statements the student made to his father, “that he could no longer bear the stigma that comes with having this ankle monitor device on his foot.” 
Damas Bel was a first-year student studying neuroscience and had hopes of going to medical school, according to his Instagram. He came to the United States in 2023. 
“I came to this country to pursue my education. I didn’t come here to commit a crime or hurt anyone,” he wrote in a July post. “Yet now I’m walking through the streets of the United States with a GPS monitor on my leg, carrying a feeling of shame and humiliation that I never imagined I would experience.”
“I came here to study, to build my future, and to live a better life not to be treated like a criminal. So now, how am I supposed to play college sports with a GPS monitor on my leg?”
Damas Bel graduated from Springfield High School in May. 
“We are heartbroken by this devastating loss,” Wright State President Sue Edwards said in a statement. 
“Pierre was an active honors student who was passionate about soccer and was already actively engaged in his classes and the campus community,” Edwards said in a statement. “The University mourns the death of Pierre and extends our deepest condolences to his family, friends and loved ones during this unimaginably difficult time.” 
Damas Bel’s father said his son “felt like he was treated like an animal” because of the ankle monitor. He also said his son was not given his Reserve Officers’ Training Corps uniform at Wright State because of the ankle monitor.
Wright State had “no confirmed information regarding complaints or investigations into bullying,” university spokesperson Deena John said in an email.
“This is a horrible, horrible tragedy,” Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine told reporters Tuesday. 
About 15,000 Haitians live in Springfield, with a mixture of temporary protected status, citizenship and other legal status.
Haitian Support Center Executive Director Viles Dorsainvil has been with the family since Monday.
“I was just speechless,” he said. “Why was I speechless? It was because I have been experiencing on a daily basis what some of our Haitian brothers and sisters have been through with this program of shackling.”
Damas Bel had two younger siblings, ages 15 and 3. 
Carl Ruby, pastor of Springfield’s Central Christian Church, said the 15-year-old is “extremely scared” of being sent back to Haiti, and though the family wishes they could send Damas Bel’s body back to Haiti, “that is not an option.”
“They just want to get through the next day,” Ruby said.
Yola Lamarre, an advocate with the Haitian Community Network, said Pierre shared a lot of his depressive thoughts with her after the ankle monitoring began. 
“Pierre was not a criminal; he was treated as one,” she said. “… we’re going to miss you.”
Hundreds of Haitians are currently wearing ankle monitors, advocates said. 
More than 40 Haitians in Springfield have been detained by ICE — including two Haitian pastors. 
ICE agents are detaining people in Springfield in shopping plazas, gas stations and apartment complexes. 
The U.S. Department of State currently has a Level 4 “Do Not Travel” advisory for Haiti “due to the risk of crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest, and limited healthcare,” according to the agency.
A top security official and chief of staff to the nation’s defense minister was kidnapped in June. 
Follow Ohio Capital Journal Reporter Megan Henry on X or on Bluesky.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Rhode Island’s Vietnam veterans have waited decades for a memorial. Now they know where it will be.
description: In 1967, Ernie Boisvert returned from Vietnam, having served about a year before he was injured in a rocket launcher attack that killed his platoon’s lieutenant. He came back to a country that was different from when he left it after being drafted at age 20. “I didn’t want to be seen with my uniform […]
text:
Veterans stand with American flags during an event announcing the future site of a statewide Vietnam veterans memorial along the Providence River in downtown Providence on Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)In 1967, Ernie Boisvert returned from Vietnam, having served about a year before he was injured in a rocket launcher attack that killed his platoon’s lieutenant. He came back to a country that was different from when he left it after being drafted at age 20. 
“I didn’t want to be seen with my uniform in the city or in the town, because we were not appreciated for what we did,” Boisvert told a crowd of over two dozen veterans and state officials who gathered Tuesday on a grassy parcel downtown beside the Providence River.
“We didn’t go there because we volunteered. Some of them did. I was drafted,” said Boisvert, now 80, of Woonsocket. He serves as president of the Rhode Island state council of the Vietnam Veterans of America.
Boisvert told the crowd assembled that a Vietnam veterans monument could soon occupy the state-owned land on which he stood — a tribute four decades in the making he hopes will materialize sooner rather than later. September marks the 60th anniversary of his departure for the Southeast Asian war zone.
“I’m asking all of you to help us now to make sure that we get this monument done as soon as possible,” Boisvert said. “As I say, I’m 80.”
The monument would honor the approximately 21,000 Rhode Islanders who served during the Vietnam War. The U.S. National Archives lists 209 fatal casualties of the war whose home state of record was Rhode Island. The site chosen for it is on the same walking path that connects the Rhode Island IX Memorial — which honors the nine Rhode Island Marines who were among the 241 U.S. service members killed in the October 1983 terrorist bombing of their barracks in Beirut, Lebanon — with the Remembrance Garden of Great Providence and the Rhode Island Irish Famine Memorial.
Joining Boisvert at Tuesday’s speaking program were Gov. Dan McKee, Rhode Island Director of Veterans Services Kasim J. Yarn, and state Rep. Sam Azzinaro. Also in attendance were Secretary of State Gregg Amore, General Treasurer James Diossa, and state Reps. Carol Hagan McEntee, Deb Fellela, and Arthur Corvese.
Azzinaro, a Westerly Democrat who chairs the House Committee on Veterans’ Affairs and who served in both the National Guard and the Army Reserve, thanked the crowd for coming to attend the event despite the not-so-uplifting weather. A rainy spell had been cast over the city all morning, and the crowd gathered underneath tents which had been set up for the event on the land adjacent to 146 Dyer St. in downtown Providence. 
“Thank you all for being here on this bright sunny day in Providence,” Azzinaro joked.
Still, Azzinaro said, it was “a terrific day in the city of Providence.”
That’s because it’s taken years — decades, in fact — to confirm a site for a statewide Vietnam memorial.
The newly selected parcel was first announced on Aug. 19, with Azzinaro noting in a press release the rationale for the choice: The state owns the land. There’s parking and street access nearby. The parcel’s close proximity to the 195 District Park and much-loved Pedestrian Bridge situates it in a highly walkable and visible part of the capital city’s downtown area. And the parcel of land is in an attractive waterfront spot, with the planned memorial overlooking the Providence River — a generous view even on a rainy, gray Tuesday afternoon. 
Azzinaro previously met with the governor’s team to confirm the state land’s availability. He also conferenced with the Rhode Island Department of Transportation, the I-195 Redevelopment District Commission and Rhode Island Energy to ensure the site’s suitability.
Secretary of State Gregg Amore, left, speaks with Vietnam veteran Ernie Boisvert during an event announcing the future site of a statewide Vietnam veterans memorial in Providence on Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. State Rep. Sam Azzinaro, a Westerly Democrat, stands at center. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
Four decades on

The state has been searching for such a suitable location for practically half of Azzinaro’s life. The 82-year-old state rep described for the crowd the carousel of options that state government has ridden over the years, with the only success being a Vietnam memorial installed at the Rhode Island Veterans Memorial Cemetery in Exeter in 1985. 
All other efforts failed, Azzinaro noted, starting with an attempt to build a memorial on the State House grounds in 1983.
“As we know, it did not happen,” Azzinaro said.
Similar attempts in 1986 and 1988 also died, though the latter — which would have appropriated $5,000 for a Vietnam memorial at the then-coming-attraction Waterplace Park, with a POW flag flown overhead — was resurrected in 2016, Azzinaro said. 
“Nothing happened,” he reminded the audience.
The current effort started to take shape in 2021, when Azzinaro introduced a resolution to create a commission to study and provide recommendations for a plan to fund, design, and erect a Vietnam memorial in the city of Providence. 
The legislature approved Azzinaro’s resolution in 2022, with a final report due by Jan. 31, 2023. That deadline was eventually extended to Jan. 31, 2025, and the same year the House OK’d another extension for the Vietnam Memorial Commission, authorizing its work through April 2028.
Now, Azzinaro, who chairs the commission he helped create, said of the long-anticipated memorial, “This is going to happen right here.” 
Still, there’s plenty of work to be done, McKee said, adding he plans to include funding for the memorial’s design in his next state budget proposal. Organizers will also seek private donations to help pay for the project’s realization.
McKee, who graduated from college the same year the draft ended, described the Vietnam War as his generation’s defining conflict.



Quotation







I’m asking all of you to help us now to make sure that we get this monument done as soon as possible. As I say, I’m 80. 


– Ernie Boisvert, president of the Vietnam Veterans of America State Council of Rhode Island 


“I had friends that served,” McKee said. “And friends that didn’t come back. So this is a moment for me, too.”
The governor addressed the veterans in the crowd: “This memorial is one way of saying that we see you, we honor you, and we will never forget you. Serving your country takes courage. We can never fully repay that sacrifice, but we can make sure it’s remembered.” 
The Vietnam Veterans of America State Council of Rhode Island has already opened a charitable account for private donations.
 State Veterans Services Director Yarn said Tuesday that Vietnam veterans remain Rhode Island’s largest veteran population.
“We should never ever, as a nation, turn our back on the people that volunteered or [were] volun-told to serve their nation,” Yarn said.
For Boisvert, that initial reluctance to don his uniform has long since ceded to the power of his bonds with his fellow servicemembers.
“I was drafted with about 30 guys from here, from Rhode Island,” Boisvert said. “From the day we got drafted to the day we came home, we were together…It’s a brotherhood that you cannot forget. I still get together with these guys once a year.”



Quotation







Serving your country takes courage. We can never fully repay that sacrifice, but we can make sure it’s remembered. 


– Gov. Dan McKee


Boisvert said his service forged unbreakable bonds with his fellow servicemembers — an ethic of brotherhood which continues to substantiate the Vietnam Veterans of America’s efforts.
The national group’s guiding principle, Boisvert said, is simple: “Never again will one generation of veterans abandon another like they did to us.” 
Boisvert’s group has already “lost a few” men over the years, he said, and he’s well aware of the passage of time.
“We need this memorial,” Boisvert said. “We need to thank those who served, and we need it today.”
Veterans and state officials gather on the future site of a statewide Vietnam veterans memorial along the Providence River in downtown Providence on Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. The state-owned parcel sits adjacent to 146 Dyer St. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)

name: VTDigger
title: ‘We’re not going to have a business’: Vermont companies say Trump’s renewed trade war with Canada has them scrambling, again
description:
“It becomes almost impossible to manage a budget within the context of this environment,” said the co-founder of cheesemaker Jasper Hill Farm.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ‘We’re not going to have a business’: Vermont companies say Trump’s renewed trade war with Canada has them scrambling, again.
text:
Mateo Kehler, co-founder of Jasper Hill Farm, criticizes President Donald Trump’s latest round of tariffs on Canadian goods at a panel at Jay Peak Resort hosted by U.S. Sen. Peter Welch, D-Vt., on Tuesday. Photo by Shaun Robinson/VTDigger
JAY — Mike Desmarais, who sells snow grooming equipment at a dealer in Newport, is planning to deliver three new vehicles to Canadian customers this month. The machines currently cost about $500,000 Canadian dollars each, he said — but soon, they could cost far more.
Two of the machines were made in the U.S. If the tariffs Canada plans to impose next week take effect, in response to the latest tariffs enacted by President Donald Trump, they will be subject to new duties of 50%, he said. That CA$250,000 per vehicle is an amount so large it’s hard to know what his small business should do in response. 
“How do you address that?” Desmarais asked a room of business leaders from around the state Tuesday, speaking at a panel hosted by U.S. Sen. Peter Welch, D-Vt.
Throughout the panel, hosted about 5 miles south of the U.S.-Canada border at Jay Peak Resort, Desmarais and others shared a similar sentiment. They thought business was on the upswing after a slump caused by Canadians who have spurned Vermont since Trump took office a second time. But the president’s newest tariffs, which took effect last month, washed away that glimmer of hope.
In recent weeks, “the workbooks have just slammed shut,” Desmarais said.
Last year, when Trump first imposed tariffs on Canada — which have since been ruled illegal — “Canadians were disappointed. They were disillusioned. They were sad. They were surprised,” said Steve Wright, the president of Jay Peak Resort. The resort, which typically draws half its visitors from Canada, has said it saw a 35% drop in cross-border visitors over the 2025-26 ski season.
“This year around trade policies, they’re angry,” he said. “And you can’t talk to anger.”
Jasper Hill Farm, the renowned cheesemaker in Greensboro, had its worst business year ever in 2025, co-founder Mateo Kehler said. The company had been rapidly growing its business in Canada, he said, until relations between the two countries plummeted last year and that growth “went absolutely cold.” 
The company was excited recently when a Canadian importer put in an order for the upcoming holiday season, he said. He saw it as a sign of things turning a corner. But then, the importer canceled after Trump announced the latest round of tariffs. 
“So it looked like half a step forward, and about three steps back,” Kehler said.
Jasper Hill has been in the process of modernizing its manufacturing facility at the Vermont Food Venture Center in nearby Hardwick. The company has had to pay tariffs as high as 50% on new cheesemaking equipment it’s bought from Canada for the project, he said, costs that have been “devastating” to its bottom line.
Before the latest tariffs were announced, it ordered another machine to automate a particularly tedious part of the cheesemaking process. But the company has not taken delivery of it yet and left it on the other side of the border, because no one is sure exactly how much it’s going to cost, he said. 
“It becomes almost impossible to manage a budget within the context of this environment,” he said. “It’s horrendous.”
Welch, at the event, touted a bill he introduced last week with U.S. Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-NY, that would repeal the 1930 federal law Trump used to enact the latest tariffs and that would order refunds to everyone who has paid the new duties so far. 
The senator acknowledged that there is little hope of the bill becoming law with Republicans controlling both houses of Congress. While a growing number of GOP senators have voiced opposition to at least parts of Trump’s trade plans, the president’s policies enjoy far broader support among Republicans in the U.S. House. 

Mike Desmarais, owner and CEO of the snow grooming equipment dealer Track Inc., says President Donald Trump’s latest tariffs could force his business to close its doors at a panel hosted by U.S. Sen. Peter Welch, D-Vt., at Jay Peak Resort on Tuesday. Photo by Shaun Robinson/VTDigger

“If you’re a member of Congress, and you’ve been elected to represent the people you represent, you’ve got to put them first,” Welch said.
Desmarais, the snow equipment dealer, said he appreciated the bill but thinks that the only solution is more members of Congress getting elected this fall who will repudiate the president’s efforts. He said he’s unsure how his company can continue operating in Vermont, or out of its offices in Wisconsin and Quebec, without a shift in political power.
“If these tariffs stay active, we’re not going to have a business,” he said. “We’re going to close.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Hezekiah Watkins gets birthday wishes at Mississippi Civil Rights Museum
description: Civil rights icon Hezekiah Watkins shares with visitors what it was like to be the youngest Freedom Rider at 13 years old in 1961, at the Two Mississippi Museums, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026, in Jackson.
text:
At age 79, civil rights veteran Hezekiah Watkins would do it all over again.
As a teenager, Watkins became the youngest of the Freedom Riders, an interracial group of activists who challenged racial segregation on interstate buses and bus facilities in the South. 
He celebrated his birthday at the Mississippi Civil Rights Museum on Tuesday. A crowd of visitors and staff from the Mississippi Department of Archives and History gathered in the center gallery. Under the glow of the museum’s light sculpture, he recounted how his journey as an activist began with a case of mistaken identity.
Watkins was born in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, but raised in Jackson. At age 13, he became obsessed with the Freedom Riders.
In 1961, despite warnings from a pastor and his mother, Watkins and a friend went to the Greyhound bus station in Jackson to watch the Freedom Riders demonstrate. 
The boys began playing, and Watkins’ friend shoved him inside the bus station. Two police officers grabbed him. When asked, he said his birthplace was Milwaukee. The police took this to mean he was an activist from out-of-state, and they arrested him.
“I was not a Freedom Rider,” he said. “I was just a nosy little Black boy trying to navigate his way through this racist town.”
Watkins and other Freedom Riders were put on death row, where normally inmates sentenced to death were housed at the notorious Mississippi State Penitentiary at Parchman. There, he endured days of horrible abuse. 
“It was unbelievable to me, because I’m 13. I don’t know anything about the prison system. I don’t know anything about Parchman prison. I don’t know nothing,” he said.
Chris Watkins, left, surprises her husband Hezekiah Watkins with birthday balloons at the Two Mississippi Museums, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026, in Jackson.Civil rights icon Hezekiah Watkins with his book “Pushing Forward,” at the Two Mississippi Museums, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026, in Jackson. Watkins was the youngest Freedom Rider at 13 years old in 1961.Souvenir buttons available at the Two Mississippi Museums showing a 1961 mugshot of a 13-year-old Hezekiah Watkins, the youngest Freedom Rider, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026, in Jackson.Civil rights icon Hezekiah Watkins at the Two Mississippi Museums, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026, in Jackson. Watkins was the youngest Freedom Rider in 1961 at just 13 years of age.Judy and Rims Barber, right, stop by the Two Mississippi Museums to wish fellow civil rights icon Hezekiah Watkins, left, a happy 69th birthday, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026, in Jackson. Watkins was the youngest Freedom Rider in 1961 at just 13 years of age.Apparel available at the Two Mississippi Museums bearing the 1961 mugshot of a 13-year-old Hezekiah Watkins, the youngest Freedom Rider, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026, in Jackson.Civil rights icon Hezekiah Watkins at the Two Mississippi Museums, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026, in Jackson. Watkins was the youngest Freedom Rider in 1961 at just 13 years of age.Souvenir magnets available at the Two Mississippi Museums bearing the 1961 mugshot of a 13-year-old Hezekiah Watkins, the youngest Freedom Rider, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026, in Jackson.
Watkins said he later learned that then-U.S. Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy sent attorneys to check on the condition of the Freedom Riders. Those attorneys visited Parchman, where they discovered a 13-year-old was being held on death row.
President John F. Kennedy called Gov. Ross Barnett to ask if a child was being held at Parchman, which the governor denied. The next day, one of the governor’s aides told him there was, and that he had lied to the president. Gov. Barnett ordered for Watkins to be released to Jackson police.
At this point, Watkins’ mother and community had been searching for him. His mother thought she’d be picking up his remains. When they reunited, she cried out to God in thanks, and they tearfully embraced. His mother had to sign several documents designed to limit his activities. They went home, where Watkins said his mother “beat the hallelujah out of me.”
That fall, activist Pastor James Bevel tried to recruit Watkins into the movement. Watkins initially wanted nothing more to do with it, but Bevel won him and his mother over. 
Bevel took Watkins to downtown Jackson, which opened the teen’s eyes to the realities of racial hatred in Mississippi. 
“I knew there was a difference in communities – churches, schools, and you know all of those things. I was aware of that, but I was not aware of how much we was hated by being Black,” he said.
“By being exposed, my mind was made up that I got to do something.”
Watkins went on to become the youngest Freedom Rider, participating in the Mississippi Freedom Summer Project in 1964 and getting arrested over 100 times.
Decades later, he’s still dealing with the trauma from his experiences, but he doesn’t let it get him down. He said he’s thankful to be alive, and to be “in my right mind.”
“There were so many Freedom Riders who are not with us today. There are so many Freedom Riders who are with us today, but that trauma has torn apart” these individuals, he said.
Watkins works at the Two Mississippi Museums, where he shares his story with people of all generations. He worked with writer Andrea Ledwell to create his autobiography, which was published in 2019. In 2023, he returned to Parchman for the unveiling of a historic marker.
Watkins received an official apology from the city of Jackson in January 2026 on Martin Luther King Jr. Day. In March, a street in Jackson was named after him.
He implored the audience at Tuesday’s gallery talk to get out and vote.
When asked what he wanted people to take away from his story, he said, “that you’re never too young or too old to get involved in any situation. Whether it’s being a Freedom Rider or just a concerned citizen, if you see something, say something.”
After Watkins finished his talk and answered questions, the audience sang him “Happy Birthday.”

title: 9 justices on the Supreme Court or 13? Numbers battle revived in Congress
text: WASHINGTON — As public opinion of the U.S. Supreme Court flags amid decisions that have roiled the nation, Democrats renewed calls ahead of the midterms to expand the high court, while House Republicans are considering a constitutional amendment this week that proposes to cap the number at nine.Just Monday, the court gave the green light to President Donald Trump’s ballroom expansion and is expected to issue a major ruling soon on Trump’s vote-by-mail order that could throw the midterm elections into chaos. Over the weekend, Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., said, “I think that we are in a position now that calls from some significant actions taken by the Congress.“And we ought to expand — and 13 is a pretty good number. A baker’s dozen would be a good number to have on the court,” the 17-term House Democrat said on NBC News’ “Meet the Press with Kristen Welker.”Clyburn said conservatives on the court, specifically naming Justice Clarence Thomas, have decided to “take the country back” in time.In late April, the Supreme Court’s conservative super majority struck down a protection in the Voting Rights Act that assured the vote of majority Black congressional districts could not be diluted.In June, the court upheld the Constitution’s 14th Amendment guaranteeing birthright citizenship, but the decision was not unanimous. Four justices dissented, arguing that there are some exceptions for certain babies born to immigrants on U.S. soil, depending on their parents’ immigration status.Clyburn is not the only Democrat to call for court expansion. Former Vice President Kamala Harris, a likely 2028 presidential hopeful, also advocated for a 13-justice high court during July 31 comments at the National Urban League meeting in Nashville, Tennessee.Other high-profile Democrats have said in recent weeks and months they want to see change at the Supreme Court, including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., Sen. Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro.As for public opinion, Pew Research found that just over half of Americans have an unfavorable view of the Supreme Court, according to survey results published July 30, a near historic low.A Gallup poll published July 28 found confidence in the Supreme Court at a record low of 33%.Constitutional amendmentWhile many Democrats’ answer to the dissatisfaction is to add more justices, the House is poised to vote as soon as this week on a Republican resolution to propose a constitutional amendment that would codify the number of justices at nine.House Republican leadership is expected to bring the resolution to the floor under a suspension of rules, meaning that a two-thirds majority would be required to pass it.The resolution would also have to pass the Senate to begin the seven-year clock for three-fifths of states, or 38, to ratify it.Johnson fears 'political palooza'House Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters on Capitol Hill Tuesday that he expects the resolution to hit the floor Wednesday.Johnson accused the Democratic Socialists of America, whom he referred to as the “communist socialists in the Democrat party who are taking the party over,” of wanting “to pack the U.S. Supreme Court.”“We’re gonna make sure that doesn’t happen,” the Louisiana Republican said.“There’s a couple of Democrats here in the House who have suggested that they’re not on board with the Democratic Socialists of America, just a few. They’re gonna get a chance to show us tomorrow. … Nine justices has worked well.”Johnson added expanding the court risks turning into “a political palooza.”His office did not respond to a States Newsroom request for comment on whether he believes the resolution would succeed or if leadership has put the bill on the floor calendar to send a message ahead of the November midterm elections in which control of the House is at stake.Rep. Andy Biggs, R-Ariz., introduced the resolution in January 2025. The resolution was referred to the House calendar on July 6 of this year. Biggs won the GOP primary for Arizona governor in July.Biggs argued in early June that his resolution would protect the court from people “threatening to pack this iconic American institution to ensure favorable outcomes for their causes.”“This action will protect the Court’s legitimacy, preserve the checks and balances that safeguard our cherished freedoms, and ensure every American's rights remain secure – no matter who holds political power,” he said in a statement after the House Committee on the Judiciary advanced the legislation. Rep. Derrick Schmidt, R-Kansas, signed on as a cosponsor in early June, and Rep. Rick Allen, R-Ga., on July 16. Both men are in solidly Republican districts, according to the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter.‘Magical thinking’Not all think that expanding the Supreme Court or restricting its size to nine justices will fix what many see as serious flaws.Gabe Roth, executive director of the nonprofit Fix the Court, said both ideas are “pretty cynical positions.”“I think it just is part of this magical thinking that all of a sudden we're going to have 13 justices and everything is going to be okay in the federal judiciary. That voting rights will come back, abortion rights will come back, and that's not how cases reach the court,” said Roth, whose organization advocates for “non-ideological fixes.”On the “keep nine” side, Roth said there’s a belief that the court now has a “perfect construct.”“It’s not,” he said, adding “I don't see why keep nine is a good idea other than to try to rile up the base.”Instead Roth wants to see term limits gradually phased in over time.“Every democracy that's younger than ours has term limits or age limits for their apex court justices. Forty-nine out of 50 states have term limits, age limits, or retention elections for their apex courts,” he told States Newsroom in an interview Tuesday.The Supreme Court lacks term limits “because King George was firing colonial judges, and so some monarch’s mental decrepitude shouldn't be a reason for maintaining something 250 years later,” Roth said, referring to Great Britain’s King George III at-will firing of judges in the colonies.Founders of the United States wrote into the Constitution several guardrails against influencing the court, including giving judges lifetime appointments, according to the American Bar Association.Roth supports legislation introduced last year by Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., that would limit a justice’s Supreme Court service to 18 years, and would give each president a chance to nominate one justice during their first and third years in office.That means the number of justices could fluctuate at times, depending on retirements or deaths.“It's basically like you add a new justice every two years, and you know, if there are 10 or 11 justices for 10 or 15 years, so be it,” he said.Democrats “came to the number four because that would give Democrats a 7-6 majority. It's not like they're pulling four out of thin air,” he said, referring to advocates who want 13 justices.The system would be “fair” and “regularized,” Roth added.“​​So we don't have a system where Trump gets three (nominations) in one term, and then Jimmy Carter got zero in his one term.”Eight cosponsors, all Democrats, joined Khanna’s legislation. They include Reps. Don Beyer, D-Va., Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich, Sean Casten, D-Ill., Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., Daniel Goldman, D-N.Y., Juan Vargas, D-Calif., Summer Lee, D-Pa., and Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz.Both Rep. Hank Johnson, D-Ga., and Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., have sponsored other legislation to create term limits for Supreme Court justices.Johnson’s bill, first introduced in 2023, has 86 Democratic cosponsors. Sens. Cory Booker, D-N.J., Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and Alex Padilla, D-Calif., joined Whitehouse to reintroduce their term limits bill in July. Jennifer Shutt contributed to this report.

text:
An entry sign for the Pennsylvania Turnpike near Everett, Bedford County on October 14, 2025. (Photo by Jessica Kourkounis for the Pennsylvania Capital-Star)OKLAHOMA CITY – Oklahoma drivers can now use their electronic toll deduction device in five more states, the Oklahoma Turnpike Authority said Tuesday.
Late last month, OTA added six new tolling entities to those that can autobill PikePass holders, said Joe Echelle, OTA executive director.
PikePasses will now be honored by the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission, Illinois State Highway Authority, Skyway Concession Company in Chicago, Massachusetts Department of Transportation, Indiana Toll Road Concession Company and the North Carolina Turnpike Authority.
OTA will also recognize toll passes held by motorists in those jurisdictions. 
“This is a major deal for us,” Echelle said. “We see lots of out-of-state traffic.”
Oklahoma already has PikePass interoperability agreements with other tolling entities in Kansas and on certain toll roads in Texas, Colorado and Florida. 
Motorists driving on turnpikes in those jurisdictions, who have recognized transponders, will have their tolls automatically deducted from their prepaid accounts.
Oklahoma has used the PikePass system since 1991. 
The new agreements may not cover every toll road in those states. A listing of covered out-of-state toll roads can be found at Pikepass.com.
“This provides seamless travel for our PikePass customers,” said Amanda Boulden, OTA director of IT and tolling operations.
Boulden said OTA plans to add additional states and tolling entities.
“As additional tolling entities are added, customers will have access to an increasingly connected tolling network,” she said.
Tolls paid through PikePass are up to 50% lower than those paid with PlatePay.
Under PlatePay, a picture of the license plate is taken as a vehicle travels to certain points on the toll roads. The vehicle’s registered owner is sent an invoice for the tolls.
“This will make billing, tolling much easier for us,” Echelle said. “Less collections have to go out. Less PlatePay. So, it’s a major cost savings to our operations.”
Oklahoma has 1.3 million PikePass accounts, said Lisa Shearer-Salim, OTA spokesperson.

title: Tina Peters has not accepted California county elections job
description: Former Mesa County Clerk Tina Peters did not accept a position with a California county’s elections office, she said in a statement Tuesday.  Peters, a prominent election denier who was convicted for her role in a breach of her office’s election system, was rumored to be up for a job with the Shasta County Elections […]
text:
Former Mesa County Clerk Tina Peters, center, leaves the courtroom after her trial in Grand Junction on Aug. 12, 2024. A jury found her guilty on 7 of 10 criminal charges. (Sharon Sullivan for Colorado Newsline)Former Mesa County Clerk Tina Peters did not accept a position with a California county’s elections office, she said in a statement Tuesday. 
Peters, a prominent election denier who was convicted for her role in a breach of her office’s election system, was rumored to be up for a job with the Shasta County Elections Office in Northern California. Shasta County Clerk Clint Curtis told a conservative radio host that he intended to hire her as the new assistant registrar of voters, The New York Times reported. 
Any reports that say she accepted a position with Shasta County are not accurate, and she has not accepted any position with the county, Peters said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“There have been discussions about ways I might assist with election integrity and ballot-authenticity efforts, but no formal role has been accepted,” Peters said in a statement. “This has never been about just one county. My concern is for all 3,144 counties in America and whether every citizen can trust that our elections are free, fair, and transparent.”
A Mesa County jury convicted Peters on multiple felony counts, including three counts of attempting to influence a public servant. During her 2024 trial, Peters, a Republican and staunch supporter of President Donald Trump, spread conspiracy theories about voting machines, as she had previously done after the 2020 presidential election.
Colorado Gov. Jared Polis commuted Peters’ prison sentence, and the Colorado Department of Corrections released her on June 1. Nothing in her parole plan prevents her from accepting a job in elections, according to The Colorado Sun. 
Since her release from prison, Peters has doubled down on her so-called election integrity advocacy work and unsubstantiated claims that compromised voting machines allow fraud in elections. 
“My advocacy is focused on ending reliance on electronic election processes and voting-machine systems that cannot be fully trusted, verified, or secured from foreign components, outside access, or outside influence,” Peters said. “America must end the use of unverified mail-in ballots and return to election practices that are transparent, auditable, and worthy of public confidence.”
Voting systems are forbidden from being connected to the internet in Colorado. Background-checked secretary of state staff are responsible for installing voting software onto voting system computers throughout the state. Other safeguards, such as risk-limiting audits, ensure the accuracy of election results and voting machines in Colorado.
Trump has repeatedly claimed that mail-in voting is susceptible to widespread fraud. There is no evidence for that, and mail ballot fraud is extremely rare. Colorado’s post-election audits regularly confirm that ballots are counted accurately.
Claims of widespread fraud in the 2020 election have been debunked by elections officials, experts, media investigations, law enforcement, the courts and Trump’s own campaign and administration officials.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, decried the possibility of Peters working in elections in California and said he would direct the state corrections department to block any transfer of her parole to the state. He then celebrated reports that she declined a job offer. California’s two U.S. senators wrote to California’s secretary of state raising concerns about reports that Shasta County sought to hire Peters. 
Peter Ticktin, Peters’ attorney, said in a statement that Newsom’s comments go against the privileges and immunities clause of the 14th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution.   
Shasta County officials voted to censure Curtis for remarks made to employees and for working on his campaign while on the job at the county. The county also asked the state to investigate Curtis after he certified the primary election and then made unverified claims about the election and his staff.

title: Joint Finance Committee votes to release PFAS settlement funding
description: The Wisconsin Joint Finance Committee approved the release of nearly $10 million in PFAS settlement funds to the Department of Natural Resources Tuesday, concluding a years-long process to offer help to residents of Marinette County whose drinking water was contaminated with PFAS chemicals In June 2026, the Marinette County Circuit Court approved a settlemen[...]
text:
A sign warning people not to drink water contaminated with PFAS chemicals in Marinette. (2019 photo by Erik Gunn/Wisconsin Examiner)The Wisconsin Joint Finance Committee approved the release of nearly $10 million in PFAS settlement funds to the Department of Natural Resources Tuesday, concluding a years-long process to offer help to residents of Marinette County whose drinking water was contaminated with PFAS chemicals
In June 2026, the Marinette County Circuit Court approved a settlement in the State of Wisconsin v. Tyco Fire Products LP. The agreement marked one of the first efforts to hold polluters accountable for PFAS “forever chemical” contamination in Marinette. 
Under the settlement, Tyco agreed to provide safe drinking water to households including by installing new deep wells, maintaining associated treatment of new and existing wells and providing bottled water or treatment to households without a deep well. 
Tyco also agreed to provide more than $9.9 million to the state’s PFAS fund, which was established in the state’s 2023-25 budget and holds funding for the mitigation of PFAS contamination. The settlement did not specify how the funds should be used, but a legislative committee had to sign off before the DNR could use them. 
The DNR held two listening sessions in Marinette to get input on how to use the settlement money and used the feedback to come up with a plan, which includes using the funds for activities that provide safe drinking water and health information to impacted residents.
Settlement money in the state of Wisconsin has to be approved for use by the Joint Finance Committee under state law. Gov. Tony Evers had urged the budget committee last month to release the funds so they could be put to use as soon as possible. 
“I’m glad that these critical investments will be getting out the door to get PFAS out of our water for good and ensure every Wisconsinite has access to clean, safe drinking water,” Evers said in a statement after the committee voted. “This is a big step in the right direction, and the DNR will continue to collaborate with local leaders and communities to ensure we get these funds out the door and to the impacted communities to address their most urgent needs in a timely fashion.”
The committee unanimously approved the release of the funds to the DNR’s general program operations appropriation in 2026-27 to provide PFAS-free drinking water and health information to residents of the City of Marinette and the Town of Peshtigo affected by PFAS contamination. 
The transfer of the funds to the general operations will allow for “expeditious allocation of the settlement funds to the impacted community in accordance with preferences expressed by local residents,” according to papers prepared by the Legislative Fiscal Bureau. 
Between $6 million and $9.2 million, or about 90% of the funds, will be used to provide safe drinking water to owners of private wells contaminated by PFAS. Up to $1 million will be used for private well testing, up to $7 million will be used for deep well installation and up to $1.2 million will be used for in-home PFAS treatment installation. Some of the funds will also be used for long-term operations and maintenance, though that cost is to be determined. 
Between $20,000 and $50,000 will be used to offer blood serum testing for PFAS to residents of the city of Marinette. 
Between $500,000 and $750,000 will be used to support a community liaison consultant to help residents access settlement funds. Sen. Eric Wimberger (R-Gillett), who voted for the release of the funds, expressed concerns about the use of funds for that purpose. 
“We’re talking about 500 people, and we’re going to be paying upwards of that amount to essentially fill out your forms,” Wimberger said. “The bulk of what you’re doing is great. You got to deal with these immediate problems with the wells which it focuses on, but there are also long-term problems up there, which is keeping biosolids out of the environment to begin with.” 
Biosolids are the byproducts of municipal wastewater treatment utilities that are sold or given away to farms to be used as fertilizer. The DNR grants permits that allow for the spreading of them, but biosolids from places with PFAS contamination in the water are contaminated and could pollute the water near the field where they’re spread. 
As Evers and lawmakers, including Wimberger, have worked on PFAS issues, Wimberger expressed concerns about farmers being held responsible for spreading PFAS through contaminated biosolids. The issue created gridlock that held up funding to address PFAS contamination for years. 
“I hope that in the future, you at least focus a little bit on maybe some treatment plants located at the landfill site, so it doesn’t get into the municipal treatment facilities and onto our farms,” Wimberger added.

title: FSU shooting victim alleges school was negligent in keeping campus safe
description: Nearly a year and half after the mass shootings on Florida State University’s campus, a victim has filed a negligence lawsuit against the university. In the suit, filed in Circuit Court in Leon County Monday, graduate student Madison Askins alleges the Student Union at FSU lacked proper security to prevent the shootings. Two people dead, […]
text:
Florida State University Police Chief Jason Trumbower provides details on the shooting at FSU on April 17, 2025. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Nearly a year and half after the mass shootings on Florida State University’s campus, a victim has filed a negligence lawsuit against the university.
In the suit, filed in Circuit Court in Leon County Monday, graduate student Madison Askins alleges the Student Union at FSU lacked proper security to prevent the shootings.
Two people dead, six injured, suspect in custody after FSU shooting

“On the date of the incident, Defendant owed Plaintiff, as a student, a duty to exercise reasonable care for the safety of the plaintiff,” the six-page complaint argues. 
Represented by Morgan & Morgan, Askins seeks damages worth more than $50,000.
FSU breached its duty by “negligently failing to inspect or adequately inspect the area in and around the student union of the Premises where students are instructed to go under the supervision and/or instructions of Defendant’s agents, representatives and/or employees for entry/exit of its Premises, to determine whether the dangerous condition existed at the time Plaintiff was in the area,” the suit claims.
The FSU Board of Trustees is the sole defendant. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Defendant is responsible for the negligent acts and omissions of its agents, servants and/or employees, or any other company, entity or agency responsible for maintaining the Premises in a safe condition under the doctrine of respondeat superior.”
The complaint cites the doctrine of respondeat superior, which, according to Daniel J.H. Greenwood, a Hofstra University law professor, “is the doctrine that states that an employer is responsible for an employee.”
The alleged shooter, Phoenix Ikner, remains in jail awaiting trial, which has been postponed until the summer of 2027.
Following the 2025 shooting, Askins spoke with ABC News from her hospital room, saying she played dead after being shot. According to that report, she was wounded in her lower back.
Alleged FSU shooter consulted ChatGPT on when to attack, sexual scenarios with a minor

Families of the two people who died in the shooting filed lawsuits against ChatGPT.  The first suit, filed in May, claims the alleged shooter was “co-conspiring” with its AI chatbot. A similar suit was filed last week. 
The state filed suit against ChatGPT earlier this year, alleging the company should have known the damage its chatbot would cause.
FSU did not respond to a Tuesday afternoon request for comment.
The shooting prompted passage of a package of provisions related to campus safety during the 2026 legislative session, including allowing authorized faculty members to carry guns.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Grand Forks Dems blast special session priorities, call for focus on families
description: Grand Forks Democrats who are running for office criticized North Dakota’s Republican-led Legislature as reactionary and called on lawmakers gathered for a special session to instead focus on helping families. The full Legislature will meet starting Wednesday for a special session called by Republican Gov. Kelly Armstrong to consider regulating kratom and re[...]
text:
Nicole Derenne, a Democratic-NPL candidate for District 42 House, speaks Sept. 1, 2026, during a news conference in Grand Forks. (Photo courtesy of Northern Valley Democratic-NPL)Grand Forks Democrats who are running for office criticized North Dakota’s Republican-led Legislature as reactionary and called on lawmakers gathered for a special session to instead focus on helping families.
The full Legislature will meet starting Wednesday for a special session called by Republican Gov. Kelly Armstrong to consider regulating kratom and related substances. 
State lawmakers last year considered two bills related to kratom and ultimately approved a bill that called for a study. But a committee of legislative leaders chose not to pursue the study.
Armstrong in August declared a public health emergency, citing in part recent deaths linked to kratom and similar substances.
North Dakota Legislature prepares for second special session this year

Democrats during a news conference Tuesday said state leaders waited for kratom to become a crisis before acting.
“Now our legislators are scrambling to write legislation and policy on a drug that they could have spent the last year-plus researching, but they chose not to,” said Katie Benton, who’s running for District 17 Senate.
Republican lawmakers said during recent discussions of a Kratom Working Group that a lot of new information has come to light about kratom and similar substances since the last session.
Benton also blasted Republican legislative leaders for proposing a $35 million line of credit for the stalled Military Gallery construction project without first investigating why construction on the building started without the necessary private funding.
“This supermajority doesn’t govern by planning. It governs by crisis, and it’s costing North Dakotans in money, in stress, and in feeling ignored,” she said.
District 42 House candidate Nicole Derenne said lawmakers should have advanced a bill related to childcare funding for the special session. A bill sponsored by Senate Minority Leader Kathy Hogan, D-Fargo, proposed $9 million in state funding to get some of the neediest families off of a growing waitlist for childcare assistance. A legislative committee in a split vote did not advance the proposal to the special session.
“We are calling on the Legislature to take up this bipartisan bill and provide emergency funding for the childcare assistance program to move families off the wait list,” Derenne said.
No pause on data centers but North Dakota special session to debate nondisclosure deals

Tyler York, a candidate for District 43 House, questioned why lawmakers aren’t doing more to address a housing shortage.
“This week’s special session proves the state government can move quickly when leaders decide something is urgent,” York said. “So why is housing not treated as urgent?”
York also called for a pause of data center development to give the state time to develop base guidelines while preserving counties’ ability to adapt stronger rules. 
A legislative committee is studying data centers and artificial intelligence ahead of the January regular session, but legislative leaders rejected a proposal for the special session to consider a data center moratorium. Lawmakers will debate this week a temporary pause on nondisclosure agreements for data centers and other industrial development.
Republicans hold all but 11 seats in the North Dakota House and five seats in the Senate. All statewide offices are held by Republicans.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC families face higher back-to-school costs as school year begins
description: North Carolina families and educators warned Monday that rising back-to-school costs are putting additional pressure on households and public schools as students return to classrooms.  The comments were made during a virtual press conference hosted by the left-leaning advocacy group Progress NC. School supply costs are 7.7% higher this year than last year, o[...]
text:
Signs in a school tout a school supply drive in 2018 (Photo: Office of the NC Governor) North Carolina families and educators warned Monday that rising back-to-school costs are putting additional pressure on households and public schools as students return to classrooms. 
The comments were made during a virtual press conference hosted by the left-leaning advocacy group Progress NC.
School supply costs are 7.7% higher this year than last year, outpacing inflation, according to an analysis by the Groundwork Collaborative and The Century Foundation. The groups also found that school lunch costs have risen 10.7% over the past year.
Wake County parent and former public school educator Brittany Gregory said families are being asked to cover classroom costs. Gregory said her daughter began kindergarten this week, and her school supply list included Clorox wipes.
“I explained that Clorox wipes were not just for our daughter or just for the kids in the class, but they were the supplies for her classroom because our schools and teachers do not always have everything that they need,” Gregory recalled telling her husband, who had asked why the Clorox wipes were on the list.
“Families are not only buying pencils, notebooks, and crayons for their own children. We are also being asked to fill the gaps in classrooms,” Gregory said.
The concerns come amid low teacher morale across the state. North Carolina scored +8 on Education Week’s 2026 Teacher Morale Index, compared with +13 nationally. The state ranked 42nd among states, according to the EdWeek Research Center.
North Carolina’s score was lower than those of Georgia (+13), South Carolina (+16), Tennessee (+10) and Virginia (+12). The index measures teachers’ past, present and anticipated perceptions of their working conditions on a scale of -100 to +100.
In Western North Carolina, local school districts face added financial pressure, nearly two years after Hurricane Helene damaged mountain communities and school infrastructure.
Adam Hege, a member of the Watauga County Board of Education, said rising costs are hitting local schools on multiple fronts. “As we headed back into school this year, our people are facing even more challenges with tariffs and skyrocketing gas prices negatively impacting the cost of living. 
Hege pointed to those factors as the main drivers pushing up expenses for baseline necessities, including school supplies, bus maintenance, facility upkeep, and cafeteria meals.
As back-to-school prices rise, donations fill the gap for North Carolina teachers, families

At the same time, Hege criticized state leaders for expanding the private school voucher program, arguing the legislature is funneling public money to private schools while continuing to underfund traditional public districts.
State Rep. Zack Hawkins, D-Durham, echoed similar sentiments, calling the situation an “education priority crisis.” He targeted the state’s Opportunity Scholarship Program, which uses public funds for private school tuition, noting its budget has ballooned from $25 million in 2022 to nearly $600 million this year.
Although the state budget enacted this year gave raises to teachers and other school employees, Hawkins said it leaves behind veteran teachers, who mostly received only one-time bonuses. 
“The goal should be ensuring that every North Carolina child, regardless of where they live, or where their parents are from, or how much they earn, they should have an excellent education, too, and that starts with making sure that we solve this affordability crisis,” Hawkins said.
