title: USPS whistleblower predicts ‘catastrophic’ effect on elections under Trump vote-by-mail order
text: The U.S. Postal Service rushed the development of electronic tools to comply with a Trump administration policy placing new restrictions on mail-in voting, and defied a court order to stop work on the system, according to an explosive whistleblower complaint published Tuesday by Democratic U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal.The unnamed whistleblower predicted the result could be “foreseeable catastrophic disruption to our coming nationwide elections based on the reckless pursuit of readying a new, insufficiently tested, poorly planned mail-in ballot screening system.”The system contains several massive flaws and, with virtually no time to spare before the November elections, USPS officials kept on developing an online verification system in violation of a Massachusetts judge’s injunction, the whistleblower said. The system’s verification standard is “a zero percent failure rate,” meaning that any batch of ballots that contain any single ballot with an error would result in an entire batch being rejected, the whistleblower said. The verification system itself is suspect due to a hurried and untested development of an online portal that states were to use to upload voter and ballot information for verification by federal officials, the whistleblower said. Up against a tight timeline ahead of the midterm elections, the agency also continued to develop an online tool related to the regulation, despite the federal court order to pause the work, according to the whistleblower.No specific USPS officials were named as responsible for directing the work to continue in defiance of the courts. USPS did not immediately return a request for comment from States Newsroom.States were expected to begin using the system as soon as Tuesday, according to the whistleblower.Potential for millions of missing ballotsThe allegations from the whistleblower, a federal official whose exact role is not specified, were detailed in a report by Whistleblower Aid, a nonprofit legal group that is representing the whistleblower. Blumenthal, of Connecticut, attached the report to a letter to U.S. Postmaster General David Steiner.“The apparently sloppy and rushed manner in which the Federal Ballot Mail Portal and supporting IT systems are being built poses significant risk,” the report said. “Potentially millions of American voters may not receive their mail-in ballot this election cycle in a timely manner, or at all.”The new policy, which President Donald Trump initiated in a March executive order, has been the subject of intense legal fighting over the past few weeks that continues with an appeal now sitting at the 1st Circuit Court of Appeals. Democratic state officials and voting rights groups have said the regulation would likely disenfranchise voters.Blumenthal said the USPS should reject the policy entirely.“We urge you to abandon this ill-conceived, unconscionable plan and ensure that all Americans can exercise their constitutional right to vote, including by mail, without interference by USPS,” he wrote.‘Problems at every stage’In a final rule published Aug. 21, the Postal Service said states would use a to-be-developed online portal to upload information about the envelopes being used for mail ballots and the voters who received them. USPS would also use the portal to verify that all ballots and voters complied with the requirements set out in the new rule.But the project was beset with several challenges, in part spurred by the unrealistic timeline for development, the whistleblower said.The whistleblower’s disclosure “identifies problems at every stage of USPS’s development of the Portal, demonstrating deeply flawed plans for implementation,” Blumenthal wrote.A project of the portal’s size and importance would normally “take nine months to a year or more” to finish, according to the whistleblower’s disclosure. Smaller current Postal Service IT projects have been given eight-month timelines, according to the whistleblower. USPS began developing the mail ballot portal in June, just three months before it was to be introduced and less than five months before Election Day, according to the disclosure.Individual elements of the tool have not been sufficiently tested, “rendering meaningful testing of the project impossible,” the whistleblower said.“The Whistleblower believes that there has been insufficient internal testing of the system,” the disclosure said. “Such testing is critical to determine whether it will work on September 1, when states could be expected to start using it.”Software developers on the project have “considerable concern” that the project skipped “standard principles of testing and debugging new software before launch,” the whistleblower said.One faulty barcodeThe IT problems heighten the danger of another major issue: a policy of rejecting entire batches of ballots based on a faulty barcode on a single ballot.According to the whistleblower, “the administration has hidden the high likelihood” that standard raises for major disruptions in ballot delivery. “As presently designed, if even one bar code on one single ballot in a bulk-mailing of 10,000 ballots fails to properly scan during the verification process, the entire batch is rejected and sent back to the state - effectively stopping the ballots from being mailed to voters,” the report said.A misread barcode could result from something as simple as a voter’s changed name after marriage or a move of address, Blumenthal said.Court orderThe whistleblower said the USPS paused work for about a month after Judge Indira Talwani in the U.S. District Court of Massachusetts issued an injunction against Trump’s executive order, finding, in part, that it likely violated the U.S. Constitution’s provision granting states the power to administer elections.But USPS officials then ordered work to resume on the project, in defiance of the judicial order that remained in effect, the whistleblower said.The whistleblower added that the agency ignored another temporary restraining order Talwani, who was appointed by former President Barack Obama, issued last week and upheld Monday, and continued to work on the project.In his letter to Steiner, Blumenthal asked if that was true and posed several other questions stemming from the whistleblower's report, and asked for a response by Friday.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Rep. Diamond proposes gaming reform to save skill games and boost tax relief
description: Rep. Russ Diamond (R-Lebanon) said in a news release Tuesday that taxing slot-machine-like skill games could also provide nearly $1 billion in additional property tax relief for homeowners.
text:
A Pennsylvania Skill game in a Delaware County convenience store. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)With the future of skill games in Pennsylvania on the line, a Lebanon County state lawmaker is proposing an update to the commonwealth’s Gaming Act to legalize the gambling machines before they’re forced to go dark.
Rep. Russ Diamond (R-Lebanon) said in a news release Tuesday that taxing slot-machine-like skill games could also provide nearly $1 billion in additional property tax relief for homeowners.
“Pennsylvania’s gaming law was originally written for a much different era,” Diamond said, noting the legislation would bring skill games under regulation as the industry faces a legal deadline.
Skill games are video-based gambling devices that allow players to place a bet on the outcome of a game of chance to win a jackpot. They differ from casino games in that they offer players a chance to win back their money by completing a skill element, though few take the opportunity, opting instead to bet again for a shot at a big win.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Critics say they’re predatory, appealing to those who can least afford to lose money gambling; risk exposing children to gambling; and contribute to crime in neighborhoods where they’re common.
The state Supreme Court in June invalidated what it called “deeply flawed” lower court decisions that it said improperly excluded the machines from regulation under the Gaming Act and the Crimes Code.
State courts had ruled skill games are not covered by the Gaming Act or the state’s general ban on unregulated gambling. As a result, skill games have existed and proliferated for more than a decade in a legal gray area, becoming common fixtures in neighborhood stores, restaurants, gas stations, private clubs and even dedicated skill game parlors. 
Recognizing that thousands of small businesses and private organizations such as fire companies and American Legion posts depend on revenue from the machines, the court stayed the effect of its decision for four months. That means Skill Games will be illegal starting Oct. 13, unless the General Assembly passes legislation to legalize them.
Gov. Josh Shapiro has proposed legalizing and taxing skill games as a new revenue stream in his last two budget addresses, but the legislature has been unable to agree on the details.  
Efforts to pass skill games bills ended with an impasse last year in the Senate over the tax rate and other details. The commonwealth’s casino industry, which has lobbied heavily against them, is taxed at a hefty 55% and pushed for a comparable rate.
Skill games in a Virginia corner store. (Ned Oliver/Virginia Mercury)
Senate leaders endorsed a plan to tax skill games at 35%. Sen. Gene Yaw (R-Lycoming), whose district includes skill game maker Miele Manufacturing, sponsored competing legislation to tax the machines at 16%. Yaw and Sen. Anthony Williams (D-Philadelphia) also introduced a bill to impose a monthly fee of $500 per machine, a proposal favored by the industry.
Diamond’s proposal would regulate and tax skill games at 20% with a limit of five machines permitted only in clubs, restaurants and bars with liquor licenses and qualified truck stops. It would also reduce the tax rate for casino slot machines and online casino games to 49.9%.
The legislative package would establish a defined formula to maximize property tax relief, provide reliable annual funding for the Race Horse Development Trust Fund, nearly double money available for gambling addiction treatment and provide revenue for the state’s General Fund, Diamond said.
Noting that property tax relief is now “hidden away” on school property tax bills, Diamond’s proposal would make the refunds more tangible by issuing the money as a “gaming dividend” payment to each of the commonwealth’s 2.87 million qualified homeowners. 
“Every time I talk about property taxes, people complain about not seeing the relief from casinos promised by politicians more than 20 years ago,” Diamond said. “This set of bills will increase property tax relief for 96% of Pennsylvania’s homeowners and deliver it directly into their hands. The amount of relief they receive will grow in direct proportion to the annual growth of all forms of legal gaming in the Commonwealth.”
Even without growth in legal gaming in the next fiscal year or additional revenue from legal skill games, every qualified homeowner would receive a dividend payment of at least $702 annually, the news release said. In Diamond’s Lebanon County district, that would equate to an annual increase in tax abatement of $459 to $602, depending on which school district they live in.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Reynolds calls for a ‘total ban’ on kratom and synthetic variants in Iowa
description: Gov. Kim Reynolds joined state law enforcement and public health officials Tuesday in warning Iowans of the risks associated with kratom and its newer, synthetic variants. Kratom is typically marketed as a natural or herbal supplement for pain and anxiety, and is commonly sold in liquid, capsule and powdered form at gas stations and convenience […]
text:
Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds, center, speaks at a Sept. 1, 2026, press conference about the risks associated with kratom. (Photo by Clark Kauffman/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Gov. Kim Reynolds joined state law enforcement and public health officials Tuesday in warning Iowans of the risks associated with kratom and its newer, synthetic variants.
Kratom is typically marketed as a natural or herbal supplement for pain and anxiety, and is commonly sold in liquid, capsule and powdered form at gas stations and convenience stories.
At Tuesday’s press conference, Reynolds and others stressed that the product’s availability does not equate to safety.
“Kratom is not a supplement, it is not a medicine, and it is not safe,” Reynolds said. “These products are widely accessible, often sitting on shelves in gas stations and convenience stores, and many Iowans may not realize the serious risks they pose.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Kratom contains psychoactive compounds, including 7‑hydroxymitragynine, or 7‑OH, that act on opioid receptors in the brain. Dr. Robert Kruse, the state medical director at Iowa’s Department of Health and Human Services, cited growing concerns about concentrated and synthetic 7‑OH products that are now flooding the market.
“Concentrated and synthetic 7-OH products can have powerful opioid-like effects and pose serious health risks,” Kruse said. “The fact that these products are sold over the counter does not mean they are safe. They can lead to dependence, severe illness, overdose and death.”
Reynolds and Kruse said there have been 45 kratom‑associated deaths in Iowa that have been confirmed since 2024. Sixteen of those deaths occurred in the first seven months of 2026, they said, and Iowa Poison Control has received 68 calls so far this year related to kratom exposure.
On Aug. 26, 2026, the federal Drug Enforcement Administration classified three synthetic kratom‑derived compounds — mitragynine pseudoindoxyl, MGM‑15 and MGM‑16 — as Schedule I controlled substances. In addition, 7‑OH is currently under review for emergency classification as a Schedule I controlled substance.
DPS Commissioner Stephan Bayens urged Iowa retailers to closely review the specific products on their shelves, as any reliance on packaging claims could lead to the illegal sale of controlled substances.
Kruse and Reynolds indicated Iowa DHHS intends to expand its statewide public awareness  campaign to include new messaging about the dangers of kratom and synthetic 7‑OH. In addition, they said, the Iowa Board of Pharmacy is currently considering emergency rules to address the issue.
Reynolds: ‘I do want to see a total ban.’ 
Earlier this year, the Iowa House passed, in 69-26 vote, House File 2133, a bill that would have designated kratom products — including both substances made from the Mitragyna speciosa plant and its synthetic equivalents — as Schedule I hallucinogenic substances.
Under that legislation, people found possessing kratom would have faced a serious misdemeanor charge for their first offense, an aggravated misdemeanor for their second and a Class D felony charge for subsequent offenses.
However, the Senate version of the bill, Senate File 2192, never made it to the floor for a vote, so the products — excluding those recently classified by the DEA as Schedule I substances — remain legal for both sale and possession.
At Tuesday’s press event, Reynolds was asked why she didn’t push for passage of the Senate bill before the Iowa Legislature adjourned.
“You’re assuming we didn’t,” she said. “We did. I think this was something I supported, I was in favor of.”
She later said she had voiced her support for the measure in discussions with senators but wasn’t certain as to why they didn’t bring the legislation to the floor for a vote. “I did support it, and I don’t think that would be surprising considering my track record on illegal substances,” she said.
During the 2026 session, Rep. Ray Sorensen, R-Creston, introduced an amendment to the House bill that would have limited dosage amounts and implemented age restrictions, labeling and testing requirements for kratom products. He said such changes, by regulating rather than banning kratom, would “do more to protect Iowans than placing kratom into Schedule I (status) and pushing the entire market underground.”
“Prohibition removes safety controls,” Sorensen said at the time. “Right now kratom remains legal — products can be tested, labels can be required, age restrictions can be enforced. (If) it becomes Schedule I, the legal market disappears. Products move to black markets, there’s zero testing, there’s no consumer protection. For concerns of safety, banning the product entirely may actually make it less safe.”
Sorensen’s amendment failed in a 44-51 vote.
Reynolds said Tuesday she continues to support a total ban on not only the natural kratom products but also their synthetic spin-offs. “I do want to see a total ban,” she said, “otherwise it’s just too easy to skirt around it and we’re dealing with the same thing… I would advocate for a total ban.”
Kruse encouraged Iowans to familiarize themselves with the signs of an opioid-type of overdose and to call 911 and, when necessary, use naloxone to rapidly reverse the effects of such an overdose. For non‑emergency concerns about adverse reactions, he said, Iowans can call Iowa Poison Control at 1‑800‑222‑1222.
The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration warns kratom consumption can lead to addiction, and that “several cases of psychosis resulting from use of kratom have been reported.” Additionally, medical institutions like the Mayo Clinic state kratom use has resulted in side effects such as liver damage, high blood pressure and weight loss.

name: Daily Montanan
title: In effort to move hay, governor temporarily relaxes some road rules
description: Montana has temporarily relaxed some rules for the amount of time truck drivers can be on the road in an effort to help ranchers feed their cattle.  In a Monday executive order, Gov. Greg Gianforte waived several motor carrier regulations including “hours of service” limits that dictate how much a driver can work and load […]
text:
Montana Gov. Greg Gianforte delivers the State of the State address before a joint session of the Montana Legislature on Jan. 13, 2025. (Micah Drew/ Daily Montanan)Montana has temporarily relaxed some rules for the amount of time truck drivers can be on the road in an effort to help ranchers feed their cattle. 
In a Monday executive order, Gov. Greg Gianforte waived several motor carrier regulations including “hours of service” limits that dictate how much a driver can work and load size restrictions.
Montana has been battling dry and severely dry conditions for six years, said the executive order, under a separate 2021 drought declaration. The order is set to expire on Sept. 13, 2026.
Montana Department of Agriculture Director Jillien Streit said it was an effort to cut red tape.
“When our producers are facing tight supplies and economic pressures, they do not need to also battle regulatory provisions that can slow down the essential movement of feed,” Streit said in a press release. “I appreciate Governor Gianforte lifting service requirements around hay delivery ensuring that our farmers and ranchers can do more with their precious time as it can be a bottleneck in volatile times like these.”
Hay is generally cut through the summer and into fall in Montana. Drought can adversely impact the amount of forage available to cattle throughout the summer and fall, leading ranchers to rely more heavily on bought feed, such as hay.
The press release from the Governor’s Office said the rules were relaxed for “certain carriers.” It’s not the first time Gianforte has suspended motor carrier regulations  — Governor’s Office spokesperson Charlie Roth said he did so in 2021, 2024 and 2025 for various reasons, including fire response, another hay hauling and to support fuel delivery for heating.
“With the persistent drought, it was essential that we eliminate any roadblocks that threaten the viability of our producers and their operations,” Gianforte said in a press release. “Through this executive order, we will ease motor vehicle restrictions to help producers get hay where they need it to go.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas attorney general’s race nears toss-up designation in ‘Democratic-leaning midterm’
description: OLATHE — The Kansas attorney general’s race is the latest to gain recognition from national political observers, who began cautiously adding to Democrats’ November chances following the August primaries. In a rematch from four years ago, Attorney General Kris Kobach, the Republican, is still favored to beat attorney and former law enforcement officer Chris M[...]
text:
Kris Kobach seeks a second term as Kansas Attorney General. He appears at a Kansas Chamber candidate forum on Aug. 27, 2026, in Olathe. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)OLATHE — The Kansas attorney general’s race is the latest to gain recognition from national political observers, who began cautiously adding to Democrats’ November chances following the August primaries.
In a rematch from four years ago, Attorney General Kris Kobach, the Republican, is still favored to beat attorney and former law enforcement officer Chris Mann, but Sabato’s Crystal Ball, an election forecasting arm of the Center for Politics at the University of Virginia, readjusted its rating of the race from “likely Republican” to “leans Republican,” which is closer to a toss-up than a safe Republican seat. 
“Kobach’s hardline approach to such issues as immigration were once out of the Republican mainstream, but his style and substance is more at home in the MAGA-focused second Trump term. The question is how well that will play in a more Democratic-leaning midterm,” wrote Louis Jacobson, senior columnist for the politics center.
Republicans are still predicted to clinch key statewide and federal offices, including the Attorney General’s Office, the U.S. Senate and the governor’s seat, which has been held by Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly for the past eight years. 
“Democrats getting a credible contender for U.S. Senate, as well as governor, probably helps Mann’s odds,” Jacobson said.
On Aug. 4, Sabato’s Crystal Ball adjusted the U.S. Senate rating from “safe Republican” to “likely Republican” after the Rev. Adam Hamilton won a crowded Democratic primary. He faces Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall.
Mann and Kobach faced off in 2022, when Mann lost by fewer than two percentage points.
Both the Democratic Attorney General’s Association and the Republican Attorney General’s Association have waded into Kansas, backing their respective party candidates with campaigning and advertising support.
The Republican group announced on Aug. 25 a $7 million, 13-state ad blitz that included a mix of digital and TV ads in Kansas. It described its effort as an “aggressive early offensive barrage.”
“RAGA will spend more this year politically than in any year in its 27-year history, and the stakes have never been higher,” said Adam Piper, the group’s executive director, in a news release. 
The Democratic group on Thursday criticized Kobach’s involvement with the nonprofit We Build the Wall. During his 2020 U.S. Senate campaign, Kobach violated federal election and campaign finance laws when he purchased and used the nonprofit’s 295,000-person donor list for under market value.
Kobach acknowledged to reporters Thursday that “there’s going to be a lot of outside spending” on the Kansas attorney general’s race leading up to November.
“But as a candidate, it doesn’t really change my strategy,” Kobach said. “I’m still running on the same record. I’ve still got the money that I’ve raised, and I’m going to spend it the way I’m going to spend it in terms of the advertising and things we do.”
Mann said his campaign has raised four times as much as Kobach’s in 2026. He raised about $787,000 from Jan. 1 to July 23 while Kobach raised roughly $196,000, according to state campaign finance records. Kobach had $607,000 on hand going into the Aug. 4 primary, and Mann had about $643,000.
“Those are all from the small-dollar donors,” Mann said. “I think our average donation is around $150. Eighty-three percent are from Kansas, and we’re proud of that number. If other organizations want to spend in this race on my behalf, then that’s up to them, and, frankly, we have to be able to combat the dark money that’s coming at us. So we’ll make sure that we have the resources we need to do that.”

name: Delaware
title: Del-One uses AI to nearly double lending capacity without adding staff
description: Delaware’s largest credit union says its digital assistant reviews auto-loan documents in minutes, offering other businesses a model for adopting AI within their existing systems DOVER, Del. — Del-One Federal Credit Union is using artificial intelligence to expand its auto-lending capacity without increasing its staff, offering a Delaware example of how busi[...]
text:
Pictured L-R – From Del-One, CIO Marc Kidwell, CBO John Chartrand, CXO Horacio Garcia-Korosec, President & CEO Dan McCarthy, and Joseariel Gomez-Ortigoza, Founder and CEO of Shastic.
Delaware’s largest credit union says its digital assistant reviews auto-loan documents in minutes, offering other businesses a model for adopting AI within their existing systems
DOVER, Del. — Del-One Federal Credit Union is using artificial intelligence to expand its auto-lending capacity without increasing its staff, offering a Delaware example of how businesses can incorporate AI into everyday operations.
The credit union has deployed an autonomous digital assistant named Valeria to review documents submitted by automobile dealerships through Del-One’s indirect lending program. The technology, developed by Shastic, works within Del-One’s existing MeridianLink lending platform.
Del-One said the system could help its two-person funding team increase indirect loan production from approximately $8 million to $15 million per month without hiring additional employees.
“With Valeria, we believe we can nearly double our indirect production, from $8 million a month to $15 million, without adding a single person,” said John Chartrand, chief operating officer of Del-One. “We want our people to think, not enter data.”
AI handles paperwork, employees make decisions
When an auto-loan packet arrives, Valeria reads the documents, creates a funding checklist and flags missing, incomplete or inconsistent information before a Del-One employee begins the final review.
The process takes less than 15 minutes per packet, according to the credit union. Del-One said Valeria has completed more than 500 reviews without clearing a defective packet.
The AI system does not determine whether an applicant qualifies for credit or whether a loan should be approved. Those decisions remain with Del-One employees. The technology completes repetitive document-review work and provides an auditable record of its findings.
The distinction is important as financial institutions and other businesses explore ways to use AI while maintaining human oversight of decisions affecting customers.
“The model here is that our best people manage exceptions, verification and strategy; the digital workforce handles the box-checking, staring and comparing,” said Dan McCarthy, president and CEO of Del-One.
Working within existing systems
Del-One’s approach illustrates how an organization can adopt AI without replacing its primary software systems. Instead of purchasing an entirely new lending platform, the credit union added the digital assistant to a system its employees already use.
The strategy also represents a shift from treating AI as a general-purpose tool to assigning it a specific, measurable business responsibility. In Del-One’s case, that responsibility is checking dealer loan packets for missing or conflicting information.
Del-One said it has deployed two digital assistants and identified other potential applications in lending, account opening and collections. Each would perform a defined back-office function while employees retain responsibility for decisions, unusual cases and member interactions.
A potential AI road map for other businesses
The experience provides a potential road map for other businesses considering AI. Companies can begin with a focused project inside their existing systems, while regional technology and business consultants such as Trellist Marketing and Technology can help identify appropriate processes, develop an implementation plan and manage the organizational transition.
“What Del-One is doing reflects a pattern we see across every industry right now,” said Maria Gunther, CEO of Trellist Marketing and Technology. “Businesses do not need to replace their core systems to get real value from AI. They need to give it a specific, well-defined job inside the systems they already run.
“The first step for most companies is not a big platform decision. It is identifying one repetitive, high-volume process where a person is currently doing work a machine can do faster, then keeping human judgment in charge of the exceptions and the relationships. That is how AI transformation actually takes hold in an organization — one clearly scoped responsibility at a time.”
Building a digital workforce one role at a time
Shastic describes that approach as building a “digital workforce,” with AI agents added one role at a time to perform defined back-office responsibilities.
“Every credit union is trying to figure out how to get real value from AI,” said Joseariel Gomez-Ortigoza, founder and CEO of Shastic. “Del-One has shown what it looks like in production: not one tool, but a digital workforce added one role at a time, on a platform they already own.”
The initiative could allow Del-One to process a larger volume of loans without increasing administrative costs at the same rate. It also could shorten the time between a dealer submitting a complete loan packet and receiving funding.
Del-One, founded in 1960, describes itself as Delaware’s largest credit union. Its mission is to create an easy and enjoyable banking experience in which convenience is combined with personal service.
Shastic develops autonomous digital assistants that perform lending-related administrative work within credit unions’ existing technology systems.

Human oversight: The technology does not make credit or loan-approval decisions

name: Mississippi Today
title: Trial dates set for those accused of making threats in Nolan Wells’ case
description: Christine Wonsley, mother of Nolan Xavier Wells, center, is comforted by her husband, Elmore Wonsley, from left, attorney Ben Crump and the Rev. Al Sharpton during Wells' funeral at Center Pointe Church in Ocean Springs on Monday, July 20, 2026.
text:
Two people from out of state accused of threatening to kill or hurt witnesses in the Nolan Wells death investigation appeared in federal court in Mississippi this week.
California resident Joseph Alfredo Vasquez Dumarce and Illinois resident Edward James Porter were indicted Monday and are scheduled to stand trial this fall in Gulfport. Both are charged with a felony that has a maximum sentence of five years in prison and up to a $250,000 fine. 
Both pleaded not guilty. Federal prosecutors have argued for Dumarce and Porter to remain in detention. 
Porter’s trial is scheduled for Oct. 5 with U.S. District Judge Taylor McNeel. Dumarce’s trial is set for Nov. 2 before U.S. District Judge Sul Ozerden.
Jackson County Chancery Judge Ashlee Cole, one of the targets of Dumarce’s alleged threats, attended the hearing. Dumarce, 27, allegedly threatened to bomb her office, writing in social media messages and comments that the judge should “ask god for forgiveness,” according to court records.
Dumarce, who is from Sacramento, also is accused of threatening Cole’s children, including her stepson Warren Hudson. 
Hudson traveled to Horn Island by boat with Wells and other friends on July 4 and returned to Ocean Springs without Wells. Friends have told investigators that Wells chose to stay behind and said he would get a ride back to the mainland. Wells was found dead July 6 off the barrier island. 
Accompanying Cole at the hearing was attorney Tyler Cox, who is representing Hudson and two of Wells’ other friends and said he plans to file a defamation lawsuit against the Rev. Al Sharpton. The men’s legal team argues that Sharpton falsely accused them of playing a role in Wells’ death. Sharpton denies defaming the men, whose names he did not know, when he asked them to come forward during a virtual prayer vigil. 
Porter, who is from Berwyn, Illinois, outside Chicago, allegedly threatened to kill the father of 
Bart Edmiston Jr., another friend of Wells, the Sun Herald reported. 
The 32-year-old sent text messages saying he knew where they lived and included their address, according to court records. Porter also allegedly threatened to cut Edmiston’s father up and put him into a suitcase. 
Edmiston, a former high school football teammate of Wells, was at Horn Island the day he went missing. He towed the boat of Wells’ friends back to the mainland after it took on water. In a previous statement, Edmiston denied he had anything to do with Wells’ death and said he plans to sue those spreading misinformation about him. 
Two other out-of-state people have also been charged with making death threats in the Wells case. 
Jacksonville, Florida, resident Brandon Ephraim Washington allegedly sent threatening calls and messages to two witnesses, according to court records. The attorney representing the Edmiston family told the Sun Herald that Bart and his father were the targets of the threats. 
Washington is expected to face prosecution in Wyoming federal court, where the alleged crime happened. Edmiston is attending college in that state.
Michelle Edwards of Cincinnati is accused of calling in bomb threats to the George County Chancery Clerk’s Office and the Jackson County Sheriff’s Department on July 23. The sheriff’s office is leading Wells’ death investigation, and George and Jackson counties are both in Chancery Judge Cole’s district.
Edwards used a blocked phone number when she called the clerk’s office 21 times, according to the criminal complaint. During the calls, she allegedly said, “Do not go outside,” “the clock is ticking,” and “die.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico’s top court denies Project Jupiter request to partially resume air quality case
description: The New Mexico Supreme Court on Tuesday unanimously denied a request from Project Jupiter’s developers to partially resume proceedings on the New Mexico Environment Department’s air quality permit application hearing for the massive data center under construction in Doña Ana County.
text:
The New Mexico Supreme Court denied a request to partially resume proceedings on the air quality permit hearing for the Project Jupiter data center, pictured from the air on June 26, 2026. (Courtesy of Alexa Reynaud, Food & Water Watch, with aerial support provided by LightHawk)The New Mexico Supreme Court on Tuesday unanimously denied a request from Project Jupiter’s developers to partially resume proceedings on the New Mexico Environment Department’s air quality permit application hearing for the massive data center under construction in Doña Ana County.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Supreme Court in August paused the air quality permit hearing, which was scheduled to begin Sept. 14, after the Santa Fe-based clean energy organization New Energy Economy filed a petition arguing that the hearing was premature since a natural gas pipeline needed to fuel the project has yet to clear its own regulatory hurdles.
Yucca Growth Infrastructure, one of Project Jupiter’s developers, in its own Supreme Court filing argued that the justices should partially resume proceedings, particularly by allowing attorneys on both sides of the matter to submit their pre-hearing filings.
The New Mexico Environment Department has until Nov. 23 to make a final decision on Project Jupiter’s air quality permit, and keeping the hearing paused could run the risk of making that deadline “impossible to meet,” Yucca Growth Infrastructure’s attorneys wrote.
In a unanimous filing Tuesday afternoon, the state Supreme Court justices denied the developer’s request without further comment.
Contested New Mexico hearing officer for Project Jupiter air quality permit hearing recuses himself

“A developer cannot manufacture an emergency and then use that emergency to strip the public of meaningful participation,” Mariel Nanasi, New Energy Economy’s executive director, said in a statement. “Project Jupiter chose its technology, chose its schedule, and chose to pursue construction while critical governmental approvals remained unresolved.”
A spokesperson for Yucca Growth Infrastructure did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Other parties to the case, including the New Mexico Environment Department, have until Wednesday to file responses of their own. NMED did not immediately respond to a request for comment. 
Wednesday also marks the deadline for the Office of the State Engineer to file a response in a related Supreme Court case, in which the Center for Biological Diversity accused it of violating state law by approving the drilling of an emergency well for Project Jupiter without first holding a public hearing.

name: Washington State Standard
title: ICE released man formerly detained in Colorado without his ID in unfamiliar state
description: Rudy Villeda Mejía, who spent just over four months in immigration detention in Aurora, Colorado, is home with his family in northern Washington state. His journey home was drawn out, as his family and attorney struggled to locate him when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement released him in a state more than 2,000 miles from […]
text:
Rudy Villeda Mejía, pictured holding his granddaughter, fears deportation back to his native Honduras due to violence he faced in the country. He has lived in the U.S. since 2010. (Photo courtesy of Mabel Shaffer)Rudy Villeda Mejía, who spent just over four months in immigration detention in Aurora, Colorado, is home with his family in northern Washington state.
His journey home was drawn out, as his family and attorney struggled to locate him when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement released him in a state more than 2,000 miles from home after the agency nearly deported him.
A judge ordered on Aug. 3 that ICE release Villeda Mejía, 47, from detention because he has a pending application for a T visa, which is designated for victims of human trafficking. That makes him part of a protected class under a May court order from California that blocked ICE from detaining immigrants with pending T visa applications, along with other visas for crime victims.
Villeda Mejía is adjusting after his return home and is back to work at his roofing business, which suffered financial losses while Villeda Mejía was detained, struggling to repay debts for new equipment the company purchased.
“Now he’s just trying to catch up with work,” Genaro Shaffer, Villeda Mejía’s stepson, said. “We have all these roofs that we’re doing, and he’s just constantly working, working, working every day. It’s got to be exhausting after going straight from detention to work.”
Villeda Mejía, originally from Honduras, has lived in the U.S. since he entered without authorization in 2010, when he was kidnapped by a violent cartel in Mexico that brought him over the border, according to a notarized personal statement Villeda Mejía submitted with his visa application.
ICE arrested Villeda Mejía at Denver International Airport on March 30. He was detained at the ICE detention center in Aurora until early August, when ICE moved him across the country to a “staging facility” in Louisiana — the final stop before ICE deports someone, according to Henry Hollithron, Villeda Mejía’s Denver-based attorney.
Shortly after he arrived in Louisiana, Judge Regina Rodriguez of U.S. District Court in Colorado ordered his release. Her order prohibits ICE from re-detaining Villeda Mejía unless it demonstrates at a hearing that he is a flight risk or danger to the community.
 Stripped of passport

Villeda Mejía’s wife flew to Louisiana, where the couple rented a car to drive back to Washington, according to Shaffer. That was only after the family and Hollithron scrambled to narrow down exactly where ICE released Villeda Mejía.
ICE told one family member he was still in Aurora. Another person detained in Aurora told a different family member he was no longer in Aurora. Hollithron’s office heard he was in Oakdale, Louisiana. Then that changed to Alexandria, Louisiana, and again to Winnfield, Louisiana.
“We’re sure he’s in Louisiana somewhere. We just don’t know where in Louisiana he actually is, because the left hand doesn’t know what the right hand is doing,” Hollithron said. “This is the reality of families dealing with immigration detention. You can’t even find your relatives half the time.”
Shaffer said he ultimately learned that ICE flew Villeda Mejía to Arizona and then to Texas, and he was driven from Texas to Louisiana.
ICE has arrested and deported thousands of immigrants across the U.S. since President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025 as part of his mass deportation scheme, which ensnares immigrants who lack permanent legal status. While the Trump administration has said those efforts target criminals, many of those arrested do not have criminal records, only civil immigration violations.
The latest hurdle was getting back Villeda Mejía’s passport and work permit, which remained in Colorado after ICE transported him to Louisiana. Without an ID, Villeda Mejía couldn’t fly home from Louisiana, Hollithron said, and even if he had his ID, his family feared that ICE would attempt to detain him at the airport again.
ICE’s Denver Field Office declined to answer Newsline’s questions about Villeda Mejía’s transport out of Colorado, plans for his deportation or its retention of his personal documents.
Shaffer said Villeda Mejía has now received back his passport and work permit with support from U.S. Rep. Rick Larsen’s office. Larsen is a Democrat who represents the district in Washington where Villeda Mejía’s family lives.
“My office stands ready to help people detained by ICE access legal services and help loved ones locate their family members in ICE custody,” Larsen said in a statement, which included a link to his visas and immigration page. “After an individual or their family member fills out a privacy release form, my staff can advocate on their behalf to federal agencies like ICE and (U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services).”
 ‘Imagine the worst day of your life’

While the immediate legal hurdles have ceased, Shaffer said his stepfather is now regaining strength after months in detention led to new difficulties with back pain. Hollithron said some of Villeda Mejía’s Bell’s palsy symptoms also flared up after he didn’t receive medication while detained. Shaffer said Villeda Mejía’s hair has started to turn gray, too.
“The conditions that he lived in were like, imagine the worst day of your life, and then imagine living that … for 120 days straight,” Shaffer said. “Worst sleep, worst food, people threatening to beat you up, it’s horrible.”
He said what his family has gone through with ICE can happen to anyone.
“Rudy had perfect records, like, you couldn’t be more clean,” Shaffer said. Villeda Mejía attended every check-in scheduled at the Seattle Field Office until he was detained this spring.
Shaffer said hiring a good lawyer and asking members of Congress for help are the best ways to get movement from ICE.
“ICE will do everything against you possible unless they are personally liable for their actions,” Shaffer said. “The only thing that matters to them is a (judge’s) order.”
This article was originally published by Colorado Newsline, part of States Newsroom, a nonprofit news network supported by grants and a coalition of donors as a 501c(3) public charity. Colorado Newsline maintains editorial independence. Contact Editor Quentin Young for questions: info@coloradonewsline.com.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: A clean energy super PAC zeroes in on little Rhode Island. Its target: Dan McKee
description: Eight days out from the Sept. 9 primary, Gov. Dan McKee’s reelection campaign is attracting national attention — and not the positive kind. A clean energy super PAC funded by solar developers and Silicon Valley entrepreneurs is spending $500,000 on a pair of McKee attack ads, the group announced on Monday. The organization, Invest in […]
text:
The end of a 30-second video attacking Rhode Island's Democratic Gov. Dan McKee that dropped Monday, Aug. 31, 2026, lists the source of the ad as Invest in America's Future PAC. The primary is Sept. 9. (Screenshot)Eight days out from the Sept. 9 primary, Gov. Dan McKee’s reelection campaign is attracting national attention — and not the positive kind.
A clean energy super PAC funded by solar developers and Silicon Valley entrepreneurs is spending $500,000 on a pair of McKee attack ads, the group announced on Monday.
The organization, Invest in America’s Future PAC, received its funding from a super PAC, the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition PAC. Formed in May, the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition PAC has spent more than $3.6 million to attack candidates who do not support its clean energy goals. Until now, they have focused exclusively on incumbent Republican members of Congress, according to filings with the Federal Election Commission.
McKee is the first Democratic candidate, and the first running for a state office, targeted by the group. 
“Governor McKee is playing politics with Rhode Island’s affordability crisis, blaming it on the clean energy transition and running on delaying our climate goals,” Chis Coffey, a PAC spokesperson said in a statement. “That’s disqualifying — especially in a state that depends on thousands of renewable energy jobs.”
Trailing Foulkes by double digits in recent public polls, the embattled incumbent governor continues to tout an energy affordability plan built upon rollbacks to existing state renewable energy and energy efficiency programs. The contested plan was put forth in McKee’s fiscal 2027 budget proposal, but largely dismantled by lawmakers in the final spending plan that started July 1.
McKee’s campaign criticized the attempted influence of deep-pocketed “crypto billionaires. Chris Larsen, a tech billionaire and co-founder and executive chairman at Ripple Labs, a cryptocurrency firm, is the largest donor to the PAC, having contributed $6 million, according to federal campaign filings. None of the donors are based in Rhode Island.
“Governor McKee’s campaign is built on the people who show up to work every day – not on out-of-state money trying to buy an outcome Foulkes couldn’t earn herself,” Sophie Mestas, a spokesperson for McKee’s campaign, said in an emailed response Tuesday. “This state isn’t for sale, and neither is this election.” 
McKee’s Democratic primary challenger, Helena Buonanno Foulkes, did not respond to requests for comment.
The pair of 30-second attack ads, which will run on broadcast stations and online, echo many of the criticisms Foulkes has lobbed against her opponent, denouncing his ineffective approach and accusing him of cronyism.
“Dan McKee’s been asleep at the wheel, busy handing out favors to his donors” the male narrator of one spot declares, pulling headlines and text clips from the state’s investigation into McKee’s handling of the botched education contract to the ILO Group. The dual Rhode Island State Police and Attorney General probe concluded there was not enough evidence to press charges against McKee or his administration for awarding the school reopening contract to a firm with inside connections. But the investigation spawned plenty of criticism, an ethics complaint and a new law the following year prohibiting bid-rigging. 
“Dan McKee works for insiders, not for you,” the ad concludes, as black text flashes across the screen, reading “Vote No on Dan McKee.”
Requisite filings with the Federal Communications Commission detailing ad placement and run dates were unavailable as of Tuesday afternoon. The Rhode Island Board of Elections had not received the independent expenditure report detailing the PAC spending against McKee as of Tuesday morning, Ric Thornton, campaign finance director, confirmed.
The outsiders
What little outside spending has infiltrated the gubernatorial primary this year has mostly benefited McKee. The governor’s campaign received a $225,000 campaign boost in late August from a labor-backed political organization, Working Forward Rhode Island. The tax-exempt group formed in May lists Ernie Almonte, former state auditor general, as the group’s treasurer, as first reported by WPRI-TV 12. The funding spent on mailers and digital ads on McKee’s behalf includes $125,000 from the Democratic Governors Association, according to state campaign finance reports.
The Invest in America’s Future PAC said its anti-McKee spending aimed to “even the playing field,” noting that “nothing” has been spent on Foulkes in the race.
Foulkes is one of a handful of state and local candidates to receive financial support from Collective Action for Education, a local advocacy group whose own funds include $150,000 from a billionaire-led dark money group that supports pro-charter school campaigns, the Providence Journal reported. Collective Action for Education spent just over $7,000 on mailers for Foulkes from Aug. 6 to 10, according to state campaign finance reports.
UNITE HERE, A national labor group representing hospitality, hotel, airport and food service workers, including in Rhode Island, spent $100,000 in July to support Foulkes and Providence mayoral challenger David Morales. The campaign finance report does not specify how much the group spent on each candidate. 
Foulkes and McKee’s campaigns each announced their final pre-primary TV spots on Monday and Tuesday, respectively. McKee’s 30-second spot opens with a still from his beloved 2022 ad featuring his late mother, Willa McKee, before touting his union support. 
“This is a choice between a governor who fights for you and Helena Foulkes, a corporate CEO who donated to Mitch McConnell and put profit over working people,” McKee says, seated at the same kitchen table where he and his mother played cards in his 2022 commercial.
Foulkes’ final TV ad does not mention her opponent at all, instead reiterating her message of change as images of her family and supporters flash across the screen. 
“Together, we can change Rhode Island, and create a future all our children and grandchildren deserve,” Foulkes says.
Foulkes’ campaign spent nearly $237,000 to air the spot 1,727 times across the three major local networks — WPRI-TV, WJAR-TV and Coastal ABC — as well as Fox affiliate WNAC and the CW, between Tuesday and Sept. 9.
McKee’s filings were not immediately available. Federal law requires broadcast television stations publish political ad purchases within one day of receiving them. 
Foulkes had already spent more than $2.3 million on various commercials across local broadcast and cable stations since May, according to filings with federal regulators. McKee spent just over $620,000 in the same time frame. No order forms from McKee’s campaign have been filed with any Rhode Island broadcast or cable networks since early August.
Reporter Christopher Shea contributed to this story.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Former Michigan Strategic Fund board member blasts decision to fund UP’s Copperwood Mine
description: Last week, the Michigan Strategic Fund Board voted to allocate $50 million in state funds to support site preparation efforts for a mining project in the western Upper Peninsula. However, one former board member is questioning the decision after state lawmakers repeatedly failed to appropriate the cash the board approved for the project in 2024. […]
text:
Public commenters lined up out the door to speak against a $50 million grant supporting the Copperwood Mine project in the Western Upper Peninsula under consideration by the Michigan Strategic Fund Board on Aug. 25 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)Last week, the Michigan Strategic Fund Board voted to allocate $50 million in state funds to support site preparation efforts for a mining project in the western Upper Peninsula.
However, one former board member is questioning the decision after state lawmakers repeatedly failed to appropriate the cash the board approved for the project in 2024.
After the board’s meeting on Aug. 25, Cindy Warner, who served on the Michigan Strategic Fund Board from 2019 to 2025, sent a letter to Quentin Messer, CEO of the Michigan Economic Development Corporation and the president and chair of the Strategic Fund.
In the letter, which was circulated by the Economic Development Responsibility Alliance of Michigan, Warner raised concerns that the board had used funds from a project she’d voted on while serving as a member, stating “At no time was ANY approval that I provided, for any project, transferrable, to ANY other project, ever.”
During a media briefing before the Aug. 25 vote, Michelle Grinnell, chief communications and attraction officer for the Michigan Economic Development Corporation, told reporters that the funding used to support the mining project was appropriated to the Michigan Strategic Fund through a budget supplemental in Fiscal Year 2022 that included $50 million for site readiness. 
Because the funding had already been transferred to the Michigan Strategic Fund, Grinnell said the board did not need to seek legislative approval for the funding like it did with the $50 million it approved for the project in 2024.
Grinnell said the money was initially set aside for other projects which never came to fruition, freeing up the funds to support the new site readiness grant for the Copperwood Mine. 
Michelle Grinnell, chief communications and attraction officer for the Michigan Economic Development Corporation discusses a $50 million site readiness grant for benefitting the Copperwood Mine under consideration at the Michigan Strategic Fund Board during its meeting on Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
When asked for more details on the source of the $50 million, Danielle Emerson, the public relations manager for the Michigan Economic Development Corporation, told Michigan Advance that the majority of the funding was never brought before the board.
“While the MEDC accounted for it internally, with the expectation of using it for projects in our pipeline, those projects did not ultimately move forward,” Emerson explained.
However, among that $50 million was $3.86 million which the board had previously approved for a project in Bath Township that was never disbursed, Emerson said. 
Warner told Michigan Advance on Friday that she’d received a nearly identical response to her letter.
Emerson said the board’s authority is not constrained by positions taken by former members, and that “there is no law, policy or precedent that provides individuals who no longer serve on the Board with the authority to determine, or override, the decision of current members of the MSF Board.” 
In her own response to Messer, Warner maintained that she would not allow the board to leverage her approval from any previous projects.
In addition to her concerns about the strategic fund board leveraging funding previously approved for other projects, Warner criticized the board for sidestepping the Legislature when Copperwood Resources Inc. still had not met the requirements put in place when they approved the project in 2024.
As a condition of the previous grant, Copperwood Resources Inc. was required to secure $150 million in financing for the project before the end of 2025 – with the option of a 12-month extension – before it could begin receiving funding.
Environmental advocates blast House budget for providing $50 million in support of Copperwood Mine

Under the newly approved grant, the company must meet the same terms. However, it has until March 31, 2028 to do so.
Highland Copper – Copperwood Resources’ parent company – has received a letter of interest for $250 million in debt financing from the Export–Import Bank of the United States. 
“Highland will seek to convert that into a binding loan in 2027, which will satisfy the State of Michigan’s requirements,” the company said in a statement.
Emerson said the project is subject to the same terms and protections as it was in 2024 through the new grant agreement. She noted that because the Legislature never transferred the requested grant funds to the project, the company never held an executed agreement with the Michigan Strategic Fund.
But Warner questioned why the project was still under consideration when Copperwood Resources Inc. hadn’t secured funding two years after the board initially approved funding.
“The reality is, for a strategic site readiness grant, the basic threshold is that a company has financial viability,” Warner told Michigan Advance. “This company does not have financial viability to do a $425 million project. They didn’t when it was brought to us in 2024. We gave them two years, and they still don’t have proof of financial viability.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: WA officials decry Trump administration’s reported ramp-up in voter fraud investigations
description: The Trump administration is reportedly redoubling efforts to root out voter fraud in a number of states this week, including Washington. Washington officials are troubled at the news as President Donald Trump and his Department of Homeland Security continue to look for widespread election fraud for which there is no evidence. CNN on Monday reported […]
text:
An election worker in Thurston County processes ballots on Thursday, Oct. 30, 2025, in Tumwater, Washington. (Photo by Jake Goldstein-Street/Washington State Standard)The Trump administration is reportedly redoubling efforts to root out voter fraud in a number of states this week, including Washington.
Washington officials are troubled at the news as President Donald Trump and his Department of Homeland Security continue to look for widespread election fraud for which there is no evidence.
CNN on Monday reported the anticipated ramp-up in Department of Homeland Security voter fraud investigations, citing internal agency guidance.
A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson declined to comment on the Washington operation, saying the agency can’t comment on “any active investigations” but is “actively rooting out and investigating election fraud wherever it can be found.”
It’s the latest electoral pressure point between the state and the federal government just weeks before ballots go out for the November midterm elections.
The Trump administration has also pushed for Washington’s voter rolls. And it has threatened to withhold federal funding for states that don’t adopt its desired changes meant to ensure that noncitizens are purged from the rolls.
Secretary of State Steve Hobbs called reports of the surge in voter fraud investigations “another attempt by the federal government to cause chaos and confusion ahead of the midterms.” 
Hobbs, a Democrat, noted Washington had just five documented cases of voter fraud out of 90 million ballots cast between 2008 and 2025. 
Attorney General Nick Brown, also a Democrat, said he has “no reason to believe this is a legitimate inquiry by DHS.”
“Washington state’s elections are secure thanks to the work of state and local leaders across the ideological spectrum,” he said in a statement. “No matter where the threat to our elections comes from, Washington will hold firm on the rule of law at this critical moment for democracy.”
Neither Hobbs nor Brown had additional information about the investigations beyond media reports. 
The Department of Homeland Security has turned to an arm of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to lead the probes, looking for noncitizen voters. 
Starting Tuesday, the guidance CNN reported says, Homeland Security Investigations is embarking on a “coordinated criminal voter fraud surge initiative to pursue investigative leads, conduct field interviews, and support timely prosecutorial review.”
Washington is among nine states where these actions are expected. The others reportedly are California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin.
“We have repeatedly demonstrated that illegal aliens can and do vote in our elections,” the unnamed Homeland Security spokesperson said in an email. “Under President Trump, HSI is committed to restoring integrity to our election systems and ensuring that American citizens and only American citizens are electing American leaders.”
The agency cited four cases in 2024 and 2025 of arrests connected to noncitizen voter fraud. 
Trump has pushed hard for Congress to pass the SAVE America Act, which would require proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote and to show photo identification before casting a ballot. Democrats oppose the proposal.
His administration has also used the Department of Homeland Security to search for noncitizen voters. Federal officials have claimed they found tens of thousands of wrongfully registered voters. 
“Our message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences — including criminal charges and deportation,” the agency spokesperson said.
Hobbs countered that the department is “wasting taxpayer dollars investigating a phenomenon we know to be false.”
He added: “I know that my office and county election officials across Washington state remain focused on administering a secure and fair election for Washington voters this November.”

name: Delaware
title: La Red gala celebrates 25 years of care and a vital role at Milford Wellness Village
description: Community health center is a key partner in the Village’s effort to give Milford-area families coordinated access to medical, behavioral and dental services MILFORD, Del. — La Red Health Center will celebrate 25 years of expanding health care in Southern Delaware during an anniversary gala Sept. 24, while highlighting a mission that has become an importa[...]
text:
La Red Health Center will celebrate 25 years of expanding health care in Southern Delaware during an anniversary gala Sept. 24, while highlighting a mission that has become an important part of the Milford Wellness Village.
 
 
Community health center is a key partner in the Village’s effort to give Milford-area families coordinated access to medical, behavioral and dental services
MILFORD, Del. — La Red Health Center will celebrate 25 years of expanding health care in Southern Delaware during an anniversary gala Sept. 24, while highlighting a mission that has become an important part of the Milford Wellness Village.
The 25th Anniversary and Community Awards Celebration will run from 6 to 10 p.m. at the Hyatt Place Dewey Beach. The event will recognize the community partners, business leaders and supporters who helped La Red grow from a bilingual telephone referral line into a comprehensive health center serving more than 15,000 patients annually.
“This event is very special for La Red, we aren’t only celebrating the milestone of turning 25,” said Rachel Hersh, La Red’s President and CEO, “we are honoring our founders’ vision and the commitment of everyone involved that has led to La Red become a flourishing healthcare center that 15,000 people rely upon every day for their healthcare needs. It really is a testament to what communities can do when they work together.”
For residents of Milford and northern Sussex County, La Red’s work is visible at 21 W. Clarke Ave., where the organization operates as a key service partner within the Milford Wellness Village.
The Village brings more than 30 health, education and community-service organizations together on the former Milford Memorial Hospital campus. Its goal is to make care more accessible and coordinated by allowing residents to find multiple services in one location.
La Red plays a vital role in that model by providing a direct entry point into primary and preventive health care for children, adults, seniors and families — including people who may have difficulty obtaining care because of cost, insurance status, language or transportation.
A health care anchor within the Village
La Red moved its Milford Family Practice into the Milford Wellness Village as the former hospital campus was being redeveloped into a collaborative health and wellness center.
The move gave La Red room to expand pediatric and adolescent care, adult and senior services, women’s health, behavioral health and oral health services in northern Sussex County.
That combination makes La Red more than another tenant at the Village. It is one of the organizations helping the campus fulfill its central purpose: connecting residents with care in a convenient setting where medical providers, rehabilitation programs, laboratories, child care organizations and social-service agencies can work near one another.
“La Red was the first tenant to join the Milford Wellness Village and significantly enhanced its facility when it moved here, including the addition of a brand-new, six-chair dental center,” said Meir Gelley, founder and owner of Milford Wellness Village. “As a medical home serving uninsured and underinsured residents, La Red is a key component of primary care at the Village and plays a vital role in making quality health care accessible to the Milford community.”
The Village’s model is intended to reduce the stress of traveling to separate locations for medical appointments, testing, rehabilitation and support services. For patients with multiple health needs — particularly older adults, families with children and people
managing chronic conditions — having services concentrated on one campus can make it easier to remain engaged in care.
La Red contributes broad family health services to that network. Its Milford center provides adult and senior care, pediatric and adolescent care, women’s health and prenatal services, health screenings, treatment for acute illness and chronic disease management.
Services also include behavioral health care, dental care, substance-use disorder treatment, laboratory services, cancer screening referrals, HIV screening, diabetic retinopathy screenings and help obtaining affordable medications.
La Red’s presence ensures that the Milford Wellness Village includes a community health provider whose mission is specifically focused on reaching people who might otherwise fall through gaps in the traditional health system.
From hotline to health network
La Red’s story began before its formal incorporation in 2001, when it operated as a 24-hour telephone hotline. The service helped people with limited English proficiency connect with bilingual physicians who offered discounted medical care.
In 2001, a group of Sussex County physicians joined with a hospital, community center, faith-based organization and local government to establish La Red Health Center.
“La Red” means “the network” in Spanish, a name that reflects both its origins and its continuing reliance on partnerships.
The organization became an independent ambulatory care center in 2003 and later received full status as a Federally Qualified Health Center. That federal designation helps nonprofit, community-based providers deliver care in areas where residents may face financial barriers or shortages of medical services.
Today, La Red operates health centers in Georgetown, Seaford, Milford and a mobile health unit. It welcomes patients regardless of insurance status, income, language or background.
Care beyond an appointment
La Red’s role extends beyond examinations and treatment.
Bilingual community health workers, known as promotoras, help patients understand medical information and navigate the health system. Transportation assistance helps residents reach appointments, while the organization’s mobile health unit carries primary care, vaccinations and pharmacy assistance into Sussex County communities.
La Red also helps patients enroll in insurance programs, obtain medications and coordinate care among providers.
Its outreach includes support for people experiencing homelessness, individuals returning to the community after incarceration and businesses seeking employee wellness programs.
The Produce RX program works with local farms to provide fresh fruits and vegetables to patients in need. On-site services through the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants and Children, commonly known as WIC, offer nutrition education and assistance to families at La Red’s Georgetown location.
Those programs support the same principle behind the Milford Wellness Village: Health is affected not only by what happens during a medical appointment, but also by whether a patient has food, transportation, information and access to continuing support.
Partnerships drive the mission
La Red works with hospitals, schools, nonprofits, businesses and government agencies across Sussex County. Its regional partners include Bayhealth, Beebe Healthcare, TidalHealth Nanticoke, the Delaware Division of Public Health and the Sussex County Health Coalition.
At the Milford Wellness Village, that collaborative approach is built into the campus itself. La Red operates alongside organizations providing rehabilitation, skilled nursing, child care, laboratory testing, mental health support and other services.
The arrangement allows La Red to serve as both a health care provider and a connection to a larger network of help.
The anniversary gala will recognize the people and organizations that have sustained that network during La Red’s first 25 years. It will also raise support for the health center’s future work, including its efforts to improve access and health outcomes for families in Milford and across Sussex County.
Individual gala tickets are $175. Sponsorship opportunities are available at several levels.
